#### The Political Example — Majority Rule in Aristocracies and Democracies

A **Political example** we shall touch in passing. Let the question be: *In an Aristocratic or Democratic legal state, does the ***major part*** have the right of the whole, if the major and minor parts dissent from each other?* Or (what comes to the same): *in the Aristocracies and Democracies which are given, is there some right in the society of the major part, and do the votes of the major part prevail?*

I proceed thus:

> *Either there is some reason for expediting affairs in it, or there is not. Not the latter — for it must altogether be believed to have been the will of those entering into society that there be some reason for expediting affairs, since otherwise the society would have been entered into in vain. Not the former alternative without consequences either — for if there is a reason for expediting affairs, either there will be ***no empire of associates upon one another*** in those matters where there is place for dissensions and contradictions, or there will be some ***right of a part over a part***. The ***prior*** repugns the nature of society — for nothing is more pernicious to human society than ***anarchy***, which cannot long consist anywhere, where each one undertakes to perpetrate everything according to his own arbitrium; and contradictories cannot simultaneously be done. Therefore, the ***posterior*** standing: either there will be a right of the minor part over the major, or of the major over the minor. Not of the minor over the major, for it is manifestly iniquitous that the major part follow the minor: from this it would be collected that ***inferiors can naturally command superiors*** — which is utterly absurd. ***That also is ratified and prevails more, which the greater number seem to approve*** (witness Aristotle, Politics VI c. 2). Therefore ***naturally, with pacts and laws (which impose a form on the handling of affairs) set aside, the major part has the right of the whole***.*

The great men: **Hugo Grotius**, *De Jure Belli & Pacis* II c. 5 § 17; and **Hermann Conring** in his most accurate *Dissertation political on Subjection and Empire*.

#### The Theological Example — The Perspicuity of Scripture in Things Necessary for Salvation

We wish ***Theological examples*** also to be at hand. There is a controversy between our Theologians and the Papists concerning the ***perspicuity of Sacred Scripture*** in those things which are necessary for knowledge for eternal salvation; and indeed a ***double question*** comes into controversy: one ***de iure*** (whether Sacred Scripture, in those things which are necessary for knowledge for eternal salvation, ***ought to be*** perspicuous); the other ***de facto*** (whether Sacred Scripture, in those things which are necessary for knowledge for eternal salvation, is ***in act*** perspicuous).

**The affirmative of the prior question**, orthodox Theologians prove, among other reasons, thus:

> *Either Sacred Scripture ought to be infallible, or it ought not. If not, it is not Sacred Scripture — because Sacred Scripture is the Word of God, and the Word of God ought to be infallible: for if it ought not be infallible, it could be fallacious; and so either God could have been deceived (which fights with God's infinite knowledge), or He could deceive (which repugns God's infinite goodness). If it ought [to be infallible], ***it ought also to be perspicuous***, since by obscure Scripture we could easily have been led into error.*

**The affirmative of the posterior question** (the question of fact, whose weightier reason our Theologians judge should be had) they prove against the Papists by this reasoning, among several other arguments:

> *Either God through Sacred Scripture willed to teach us perspicuously what is necessary to be believed for eternal salvation, or He did not will. If He did not will, then Sacred Scripture deceives — for the words of Sacred Scripture have it thus:*
>
> ***"These things have been written that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in His name"*** *(John 20:31). Likewise:* ***"Search the Scriptures, for in them you think to yourselves to have eternal life; and these are they which testify of me"*** *(John 5:39).*
>
> *(To pass over other Scripture-dicta which most luculently testify that God seriously desires the salvation of men, and wills to teach us perspicuously the way of arriving at eternal salvation.) What Sacred Scripture expressly testifies cannot not be of infallible truth. If the former — i.e. if God willed through Sacred Scripture perspicuously to teach what is necessary to be believed for eternal salvation — then either God ***could*** perspicuously hand down in Sacred Scripture the things necessary to be believed for eternal salvation, or He could not. If He could not, He is not the true God — which is impious. Whence rightly ***Hilary***, De Trinitate VIII:* ***"Was He, who is virtue, in such weakness that He could not speak forth what He wished to be understood?"*** *To which a similar passage in* ***Lactantius***, lib. VI c. 12. *If He could — and simultaneously, as has been shown, He willed to teach us perspicuously by His Word the way of arriving at eternal salvation — surely Sacred Scripture altogether, in those things which are necessary for knowledge for eternal salvation, will be perspicuous. For He who wills to teach us perspicuously the way of arriving at eternal salvation, and is also such a perfect master of speaking that He can teach perspicuously, has taught us that way perspicuously.*

Others also proceed thus:

> *Either the Papists affirm that there can be shown a dogma necessary for knowledge for salvation which can be confirmed by no perspicuous testimony of Sacred Scripture, or they deny it. If they deny, then it is left that Sacred Scripture in those things which are necessary for knowledge for eternal salvation is perspicuous. If they affirm, the burden of proof lies on the Papists; but by experience they will learn (nay, they long ago have learned) how difficult (that is, utterly impossible) it is to show a dogma necessary for eternal salvation which can be confirmed by no perspicuous Scripture testimony. And indeed our Theologians stand ready to confirm each single dogma — both of things to be believed and of things to be done — by perspicuous testimonies of Sacred Scripture. Nor however do they wish ***consequences*** to be entirely removed and excluded: for what is deduced by necessary and evident consequence from a proposition revealed in perspicuous words is equally perspicuous with it, equally certain with it.*

#### The Juridical Examples — Three Cases from the Digest

Nor are ***Juridical examples*** at all lacking.

Perhaps a perspicuous and easy example is furnished by ***L. Si inter me & te*** 15, D. *de exceptione rei iudicatae*. The words of the law run thus:

> *"If there was a controversy between me and you concerning an inheritance, and you possess certain things from the same, I others, nothing prevents me from suing you and you me in turn concerning the inheritance. If after this it begins to be judged, it matters whether it has been pronounced that the inheritance is mine, or the contrary. If it be pronounced to be mine, the exception of res iudicata will harm you — EX IPSO, QUO MEAM ESSE PRONUNTIATUM EST, EX DIVERSO TUAM NON ESSE PRONUNTIATUM VIDETUR. If, however, mine not to be, in like manner is understood to have been judged: QUIA DUM AJUNT MEAM NON ESSE, HOC IPSUM AJUNT TUAM ESSE."*

Add ***L. Pomponius*** 40, D. *de Procuratoribus*, where among other things is noted: *"When it is judged that a thing is mine, it is simultaneously judged that it is not another's."* The Jurists of most eminent name demonstrate the mind of the law and simultaneously the use of our proposed axiom in this way:

> *Either the thing is mine (which, after res iudicata, you began to sue from me), or it is not mine. If it is not mine, why by sentence has it been pronounced that the thing is mine? If it is mine, either simultaneously it is yours, or it is not yours. If it is yours, how could it be mine? — since two cannot be lords of the same thing in solidum, nor can two possess the same thing in solidum (**L. si certo loco** 5, **L. si duobus** 25, D. Commodati; and **L. possideri** 3, **L. ex contrario** 5, D. de acquirenda possessione). If it is not yours, by no right can you sue it.*

Another ***everyday example*** Cicero and Boëthius furnish in the *Topics*. A husband bequeathed to his wife the ***usufruct of his goods***; he had wine, oil, and other things which are consumed by use. The question is asked: ***are these owed to the wife?*** And thus they decide:

> *Either usufruct properly consists in wine, oil, and those other things which are consumed by use, or it does not consist. If it does consist, usufruct will not be ***usufruct***, but rather ***abusus***. If it does not consist, therefore these are not owed to the wife in the present case.*

Add ***L. constituitur*** 2, Institutes *de usufructu*.

Again, if a frequent occasion is otherwise given to Doctors and Interpreters of Civil Law to prove and commend the use of this axiom, a beautiful one — unless all things deceive me — is furnished by these words of ***L. aut aut, aut ille*** 124, D. *de verborum significatione*:

> *"These words — ILLE AUT ILLE — are not only ***disjunctive***, but also ***subdisjunctive*** speech. Disjunctive, as when we say* ***AUT DIES AUT NOX EST*** *— where, with one posited, it is necessary that the other be removed; likewise, with one removed, the other to be posited. In the same manner, a verb can be subdisjunctive. There are two kinds of subdisjunctives:*
>
> *One, when of the proposed ends ***both cannot be, yet both can be absent***, as when we say* ***AUT SEDET AUT AMBULAT*** *— for just as no one can do both simultaneously, so someone can do neither, as he who reclines at table.*
>
> *The other kind is when of the proposed ends ***thus neither can not be, that both can be***, as when we say* ***OMNE ANIMAL AUT FACIT AUT PATITUR*** *— for there is nothing which neither acts nor suffers; but one can simultaneously act and suffer."*

— ❦ —

(b) The **Theological example** — perspicuity of Scripture in things necessary for salvation, the double question *de iure* / *de facto*: (de iure) Scripture-is-Word-of-God → must be infallible → must be perspicuous (else God could be deceived or deceive, repugning His infinite knowledge/goodness); (de facto) John 20:31 and John 5:39 + Hilary *De Trinitate* VIII and Lactantius VI.12's *si potuit* dilemma; the Papist burden-shift: either admit no dogma lacks perspicuous Scripture-confirmation, or bear the proof — and necessary-and-evident consequence from a perspicuously-revealed proposition is equally perspicuous and equally certain. (c) The **three Juridical examples**: (1) *L. Si inter me & te* 15 D. *de except. rei iudicatae* + *L. Pomponius* 40 D. *de Procuratoribus* — the res-iudicata either/or (if mine → not yours; if not mine → yours; cross-references to D. commodati and D. de acquirenda possessione); (2) The Cicero/Boëthius *Topics* usufruct case — wife bequeathed usufruct of consumable goods (wine/oil): either usufruct consists in them (then it's *abusus* not *ususfructus*) or not (then not owed); cross to *Institutes* de usufructu; (3) *L. aut aut, aut ille* 124 D. *de verborum significatione* — the Roman grammatical distinction between *disjunctive* (AUT DIES AUT NOX — both possible negated) and two kinds of *subdisjunctive* (AUT SEDET AUT AMBULAT = both-not-simultaneously but both-can-be-absent; OMNE ANIMAL AUT FACIT AUT PATITUR = none-neither but both-can-be). T18 opens the **Abusus Practicus of Axioma II** — three abuses in particular: (1) treating as *immediate oppositions* what are *mediate* (the first and most to-be-detested; the Moral example of *omnis ignorantia invincibilis actionem reddit involuntariam* — the ajens vs. negans with the common initial-trap syllogism); (2) and (3) to follow.]*

#### Practical Abuse

A ***threefold abuse*** of this axiom in particular is given.

#### The First Abuse — Treating Mediate Oppositions as Immediate

The ***first abuse***, worthy of animadversion before the rest, is when very many hold for ***immediate opposites*** those things which are ***not immediate opposites***. For it cannot otherwise come about than that these stick in errors, as long as they cannot or will not change the sentence of their mind — and so much the more do they prostitute themselves, the more acerbly or impudently they urge the ***immediate opposition*** where they rashly believe it to be, when yet it is not.

Let us see one or two examples of the matter.

#### The Hunter's Invincible Ignorance — Voluntary / Involuntary / Non-Voluntary

In Morals it is asked: ***Does every invincible ignorance render an action involuntary?*** So it may seem to beginners, who commonly defend the ***affirmative*** of the question and impose it upon themselves by this reasoning:

> *Every action which proceeds from an agent labouring under invincible ignorance is either voluntary to such an agent, or involuntary. A third cannot be given. But it is not voluntary to him. For whatever action is voluntary to an agent proceeds from the agent's free arbitrium or will. But that which was not, nor ought to have been, known to the agent — or what comes to the same, that of which the agent laboured under invincible ignorance — could not come to be by the agent's will, since the will is never borne to the unknown, by that saying* ***"Ignoti nulla cupido."***

These things may be said to beginners and those like them. The contrary can easily be evinced by one single case:

> *A hunter, going out at first dawn into the forest, kills by chance a man whom he neither knew, nor ought to have known, nay nor could have known, to be lurking there — so that it is certain the slayer laboured under invincible ignorance. The disquisition comes: ought this slaying be called ***involuntary*** to the slayer?*

We say: nothing can be answered to this question by the one asking, because he silently passes over a circumstance which contributes most greatly to the decision of this question, and without knowledge of which the decision is awaited in vain. Namely, it is necessary first to know: ***Would the hunter, absent invincible ignorance, have been going to do the same, or not?*** Or, to use terms received in the Moral forum: ***Was that invincible ignorance antecedent, or concomitant?*** Or (as pertains to the present case): was that invincible ignorance ***ἀκούσιον*** (*unwilling*) or ***οὐχ ἑκούσιον*** (*not-willing*)? — which is the Greeks' distinction.

With deliberate study we have been silent about this circumstance, which we now determine: namely, that invincible ignorance in the given example was ***concomitant*** and ***ἀκούσιον***. For the hunter would have been going to do the same, had he known his enemy to be lurking there — the enemy to whom he had long since threatened ultimate harm, and whose slaying, when he sees it has befallen, he congratulates himself on the event — not responding to a recent attempt, yet exactly responding to a long-standing wish.

With this circumstance duly perceived, he must be rude in every practical doctrine who cannot acknowledge that this slaying was not involuntary to the hunter here and now. Let us repeat the same example (which at first sight these or those may have treated as diverse from the prior), yet so repeat it that the circumstance which earlier in the state of the question was suppressed is now had in express words added:

> *Either that hunter in the given case acted ***according to*** his will, or ***against*** his will. A third is not given. But he did not act against his will (as is plain from what has just been deduced). Therefore he acted according to his will. Therefore invincible ignorance will be given which leaves the action voluntary.*

This decision forensic practice seems to confirm, since a slayer of this kind, caught and convicted, is punished. ***But truly, there was leapt from one extreme to the other*** — as if a third could not be given between what is done by a rational agent *according to his will* and *against his will*. That the hunter in such a case by no means acted against his will, is most true, and the reason given no longer allows us to doubt: nay, as *"of the unknown no desire,"* so of the same there is no aversion — for the same reason that obtains on both sides. But that reason also was solid, by which in the immediately preceding ratiocination it was evinced that the action was not voluntary to the hunter in question — that is, by which locution the same is signified: ***the hunter did not act according to his will***. Therefore the hunter in the adduced case neither acted *according to his will*, nor acted *against his will*, but (which is the ***middle***) ***apart from his will*** (*praeter voluntatem*). Nor is it any obstacle that that hunter caught and convicted is punished. For he is not punished as the ***voluntary cause*** of the slaying — because the slaying was by no means voluntary to him — but ***on account of the ex-post-facto (as they speak) willed slaying***, or more accurately speaking, on account of the ***voluntary approbation*** of the non-voluntary slaying, is he affected with penalty.

Therefore ***non-voluntary*** lies open more widely than ***involuntary***: between *voluntary* and *involuntary* a middle is given, as the present case teaches; but between *voluntary* and *non-voluntary* no middle is given. The present case argues an example of a fact neither *voluntary* nor *involuntary*, yet ***non-voluntary***.

#### The Second Moral Example — The Opponent's *Produced-from-Itself vs. Produced-by-God* Dilemma

Another Moral example it pleases to adduce, and that in fewest words. Since in the explication of the preceding axiom (where we indicated the practical abuse by a Moral example) it was shown with what acerbity the sentence is contradicted whereby ***Morality*** can be considered to have itself antecedently to the will of God as binding His subject — let us see whether the adversary's reason by which he impugns that sentence does not itself offer the example of a notable ***abuse of the present axiom***. His reason is this:

> *Morality considered as having itself antecedently to the will of God binding its subjects, is either produced from itself, or is not produced from itself. A third is not given. If it is produced from itself, therefore it will be the cause of itself; therefore a being-from-itself or independent besides God is given. If it is not produced from itself, either it will be produced by God, or it will not be produced by God. If it is produced by God, therefore it cannot have itself antecedently to the will of God, because nothing is produced by God unless He has decreed to produce it. If it is not produced by God, therefore another is given who besides God has produced it. Who then besides God formed the natures of things?*

It is answered **first**: ***a third is given here***. For when morality is considered as having itself antecedently to the will of God binding His subjects, we treat of morality ***as a possibility*** — that is, of the necessary habitude (agreement or disagreement) of voluntary acts with rational nature *qua* such (as it is abstracted from uncreated and created). Nor is it considered as ***produced or to be produced***, but precisely as ***possible***, and thus and not otherwise possible. The matter stands here just as if the man who used so jejune a reasoning had wished to argue thus:

> *If animal can be considered as having itself antecedently to man and brute, as having itself antecedently to every generation, then either animal having itself antecedently to man and brute will be produced from itself, or it will not be produced from itself, but by another.*

Ridiculous and plainly inept would have been this collection. For when animal is considered in the common and ***qua*** such, in vain is it asked concerning its production — because there is no question of ***existence*** (which is of a singular thing: for whatever exists, by that very fact that it exists, is singular; but the term of production is ***existence***, not ***possibility*** — of which there was treated at length in the preceding axiom). ***Possibility*** neither God nor another formed, nor did it fashion itself.

**Secondly**, the morality of acts of God — that is, the real agreement of God's acts with rational nature qua such, which, because it is of moral consideration, can indeed be denominated *morality*, inasmuch as it is given in act — does not depend upon the will of God binding Himself as a subject.

**Thirdly**, the morality of acts of rational creature, inasmuch as it is given in act, if it be precisely considered as it agrees in the being of morality with the morality of acts of God, altogether has itself antecedently to the will of a superior.

**Fourthly**, a wonder if the contradictor should not in the end set up ***every baseness as produced by God***. More things on this matter may be seen from the preceding axiom.

#### The Theological Example — The Arian & Photinian Attack on the Trinity

By a ***Theological example*** we shall demonstrate the abuse of this axiom. The ***Arians and Photinians*** strive to impugn the eternal production of the second and third persons of the Divinity — and so the divinity of the Son and Holy Spirit — among others by the following argument:

> *If the Son and Holy Spirit were produced from eternity, either they were produced ***from some subject*** or ***in dependence on a subject***, or ***from nothing***. A third is not given. If the former, they are not true God, because true God is immaterial: but to be produced from a subject is to be produced from matter — whence whoever is produced from a subject must be material. If the latter, then they will be a creature, because to be produced from nothing is to be ***created***.*

So the Antitrinitarians abuse our axiom. And indeed thus it is, if anyone could suffer himself to be persuaded that between ***production from a subject (or dependent on a subject)*** and ***production from nothing*** no third production is given — he could easily slide into the most pestilential error of the Antitrinitarians. For this is more certain than certain: whatever is produced in either of these two ways (i.e. either from some subject, or from nothing) is not true and eternal God, but creature.

But Students of Theology, instructed in better and salutary things, know a ***third mode of production***: namely, ***that the one produced be of the same numerical substance as the one producing***. For orthodox Theologians by unanimous consent teach, and from Sacred Scripture demonstrate by arguments beyond every exception, that:

> *God the Father produced the Son from His substance from eternity; the Father and the Son produced the Holy Spirit from Their substance from eternity — so that both are produced ***of the substance of the one producing***: the Son, namely, of the substance of the Father; the Holy Spirit of the substance of the Father and the Son.*

Not that the ***substance or divine essence*** be a material principle, from which the Son and Holy Spirit have been produced — but because the Father by generation communicated His substance or essence to the Son, and the Father and Son by spiration communicated Theirs to the Holy Spirit — such that that very essence which is in the Father (as in the person producing the Son) is wholly in the Son; and that which is in the Father and the Son (as in the persons producing the Holy Spirit) is wholly in the Holy Spirit. And on this account the Son is said to be produced ***of the substance of the Father***, the Holy Spirit ***of the substance of the Father and the Son***. Hence our Theologians show that in this mode the Son and Holy Spirit have been produced:

> *Whatever persons are produced, are produced either from some subject, or from nothing, or ***of the substance of the one producing***. But the Son and Holy Spirit are produced neither from any subject nor from nothing — for otherwise they would not be true and eternal God, but creature, since whatever is produced in either of those two modes is creature. Therefore it is left that each is produced of the substance of the one producing: namely, the Son of the substance of the Father, and the Holy Spirit of the substance of the Father and the Son.*

And because the substance or essence of divinity is one, most simple, and plainly indivisible, it necessarily follows that the Son is produced ***of the substance of the Father***, and the Holy Spirit ***of the substance of the Father and the Son***, in such wise that the one receives that very essence which is in the Father, and the other that very essence which is in the Father and the Son — and that essence whole and undivided. If anyone further press here, ***how*** the Father could have communicated His whole essence to the Son, and yet the whole essence of the Father have remained, and simultaneously also be the essence of the Son — this indeed our Theologians judge that they can neither attain by thought, nor sufficiently explicate.

Three worked examples: (a) **Moral — Hunter's Invincible Ignorance**: *Does every invincible ignorance render an action involuntary?* — the beginner-trap *either-voluntary-or-involuntary* dichotomy exposed. The suppressed-circumstance method: was the ignorance ***antecedent*** or ***concomitant***, ***ἀκούσιον*** or ***οὐχ ἑκούσιον*** (Greek distinction)? In the long-standing-enemy case the ignorance is concomitant and ἀκούσιον; the hunter neither acted *according to his will* nor *against his will* but ***apart from his will*** (praeter voluntatem). Not that the divine essence be a *material principle*, but that by generation the Father communicated His whole essence to the Son, and by spiration the Father and Son theirs to the Holy Spirit — the same essence wholly in each. #### Ethico-Politico-Juridical Examples of the First Abuse

We add ***Ethico-Politico-Juridical examples***. Let us repeat the case proposed above p. 185, but under other circumstances:

> *Between Accius and Maevius there is a controversy concerning an inheritance; Accius possesses certain things from the same, Maevius others; Accius sues Maevius, and Maevius sues Accius for the inheritance. It is pronounced that the inheritance ***is not*** Accius's. Thence Maevius, after res iudicata, begins to sue Accius for the inheritance, resting on this reason:* ***"It has been judged that the thing is not Accius's; therefore it is mine, because if it had been judged that the thing was Accius's, then it would not have been mine."***

But Maevius ***abuses our axiom***, and holds for immediate opposites what admit a middle. For if it has been pronounced that the thing is not Accius's, nothing is understood to have been judged concerning Maevius's right, because ***a third is given between*** *mine* ***and*** *yours*: the inheritance can be neither mine nor yours, but ***a third party's***. Why, if it had been judged that the thing was Accius's, the collection would rightly be: *Therefore it is not Maevius's* — the reason is: because ***immediate opposites cannot simultaneously be affirmed of the same***. But that this does not hold — *the thing is not yours, therefore it is mine* — is plain from the fact that it can be a third's, nor does it repugn that ***mediate opposites*** be simultaneously denied of the same. See **L. Si inter me & te** 15 D. *de exceptione rei iudicatae*.

#### The Judge's Abuse of VOLUIT / NOLUIT — The *Non Voluit* Middle

Let there be another question. Some judge, in arguing, proceeds thus:

> *Either Titius ***willed*** to inflict the damage which he brought upon Sempronius, or he ***was-unwilling***. A third is not given.*

The question is asked: is this collection by the judge rightly made? ***It is denied***: for a third is given between ***VOLUIT*** and ***NOLUIT***, namely ***NON VOLUIT***. This middle (or third) we shall illustrate by two examples.

Let us assume, in place of the first example, the case proposed above § 15 concerning the hunter — of whom, when he had killed his enemy, it cannot be said that he ***was-unwilling*** (*noluerit*) to kill him, since he would altogether have been going to kill him had he known him lurking there; nor can it be defended that he ***willed*** (*voluerit*) to kill him, because of that of which someone labours under invincible ignorance (so long as it is thus unknown — namely unknown both in itself and in its cause, as the Ethicists speak), ***no volition is given***. Therefore it must be said that this hunter ***NON VOLUERIT*** (*did-not-will*).

**You say:** *"If he did not will-against, therefore he willed."* It is answered: ***no consequence***. For both are true: ***NON NOLUIT*** (he did-not-will-against), ***NON VOLUIT*** (he did-not-will). For if this is false — *Hunter* ***NOLUIT*** — that is true: *Hunter* ***NON NOLUIT***. And if that is false — *Hunter* ***VOLUIT*** — this is true: *Hunter* ***NON VOLUIT***. Therefore between ***VOLUIT*** and ***NOLUIT*** the third is ***NON VOLUIT***; and thus from ***NOLLE*** to ***NON VELLE*** the consequence holds, but not from ***NON VELLE*** to ***NOLLE***.

#### Ulpian's *De Tributoria Actione* — The Dominus's Patience as Middle

The ***other example*** is furnished by **L. Huius quoque edicti** 1 pr. and § ***scientiam*** 3, D. *de Tributaria Actione*. For thus Ulpian:

> *"***Of this edict too the utility is not least***, so that a master — who otherwise has the privilege in a slave's contracts (since he is held liable only ***de peculio***: the estimation of which peculium is made, after what is owed to the master is deducted) — nevertheless, if he ***has known*** (SCIERIT) his slave to transact business with a peculiar merchandise, is called into tribute by this edict as it were an extraneous creditor."*

And § 3 of the same law then follows:

> *"We take ***SCIENTIA*** here to be that which has also ***will*** — but (as I think) not ***will***, but ***patience***. For the master ought ***not to will*** (***non debet velle***), but ***not to will-against*** (***non nolle***). If therefore he knows and does not protest nor contradict, he will be held in the tributary action."*

What example could be clearer? Hence the Jurists derive the foundation of the distinction which they teach to intercede between the ***actio tributoria*** and the ***actio exercitoria***, when they teach that in the ***exercitoria*** the slave must contract ***by the master's will***, but here (in the ***tributaria***) only by his ***patience***. See **L. utilitatem** 1 § ***licet*** 20, and **L. si servus** 6, D. *de exercitoria actione*.

#### The Second Abuse — Overgeneralizing: Contradictory Rationes Lack a Middle

We shall note the ***second abuse*** of this axiom. This occurs when the Doctor or Auditor of some discipline or faculty (whichever it be) trusts more than is right in the ***axiom***:

> ***"Whatsoever things import contradictory rationes, between them no middle is given."***

So far is this proposition from being able to be called of perpetual truth that it in fact deceives often, even if it be limited in this way:

> ***"Whatsoever things with respect to the same import contradictory rationes, between them no middle is given."***

**For example**, ***ens reale*** and ***ens rationis*** import contradictory rationes: because *ens reale* exists apart from the operation of the mind — apart from being-objectively-in-the-intellect; *ens rationis* does not exist apart from the operation of the mind — not apart from being-objectively-in-the-intellect. ***To exist apart from the operation of the mind*** and ***not to exist apart from the operation of the mind*** are contradictories. But there is no doubt that ***a middle is given between ens reale and ens rationis***, as above (from Scaliger and others) we showed to the same § by several examples.

So too ***univoca*** and ***aequivoca*** import contradictory rationes with respect to the same (namely with respect to that in which they agree): for they agree in this, that they have the same name in common according to all grammatical accidents. But according to that same name, ***univoca*** have the same definition; ***aequivoca***, according to that same name, do not have the same definition. Certainly, to have the same definition according to the same name, and not to have it, are contradictory rationes with respect to the same. Yet no one skilled in more accurate (and so Greek) Philosophy will be ignorant that ***middles are given between univoca and aequivoca***.

#### Three Further Examples of the Second Abuse

Let us take a ***Physico-Theological example***. There have been those who have denied that heaven and earth were created by God, and that the first humans were created by God, using this ratiocination:

> *Whatever is produced is either produced ***from nothing*** (and so is ***created***), or ***from something*** (and so is ***generated***). But heaven and earth were produced by God from matter and form, Adam from a clod of earth, Eve from Adam's rib. Therefore their production will not be called creation, but ***generation***.*

Let there be an ***Ethico-Political example***. There are those who struggle tooth-and-nail to maintain that only ***two species*** of change of law are given — or only two precise modes by which law is changed: ***abrogation*** and ***dispensation***. This collection has perhaps misled them:

> *When the obligation of law is removed, either it is removed from every subject (that is, from everyone who was before obliged), or indeed the obligation of law is removed from a subject of the law — but not from all; some remain who are still obliged just as others were before, before they were made free from the obligation. If the former, it is ***abrogation***; if the latter, ***dispensation***. Therefore no middle genus of change will be given — because in order to the change of law, and so with respect to it, abrogation and dispensation import contradictory rationes.*

For these are contradictory rationes: ***so to remove the obligation that no one remains obliged***, and ***to remove the obligation yet not so that no one remains obliged***.

Let there be a ***Political-Juridical example***. It is asked: ***Besides the Natural Law — by which all men, and so all Nations (since they are men) are obliged — is there given a special positive and voluntary Law of Nations?*** Many strive to prove the negative thus:

> *Either the Law of Nations receives the power of obliging from the free will of a Superior willing thus to oblige his subjects, or it does not receive the power of obliging from such a will. A third is not given. If it does, either that Superior will be God — and so it will be ***voluntary divine law***, such as what was given to the whole human race (which, however much given, would still not be the ***Law of Nations***, concerning which the present question is moved); or that Superior will be the King, or he who in a commonwealth holds a right equal to Kings' (as Aristocrats in Aristocracy, the people in Politeia). But Nations taken together have no Superior on earth. If the latter — and yet the Law of Nations is a true law — therefore it will be, as to the thing itself, ***Natural Law***, which is called Law of Nations by accident, after it has come about that other men have come together into this nation, others into another.*

But these and innumerable other arguments will not easily find faith, provided those who trust in them have made perspicuous to themselves ***how far it can be firmly collected from contradictory rationes that the things which import them cannot admit a middle***.

#### The Governing Distinction — Immediate vs. Mediate Contradictory Rationes

That this be rightly perceived, it must be ***prenoted*** that in ***two modes*** can it happen that two things import contradictory rationes:

**(1) Immediately.** For example: ***man*** and ***brute*** with respect to ***animal*** import contradictory rationes, because man is a ***rational animal***, brute is a ***non-rational animal***. So ***ens reale*** and ***non ens*** simpliciter import contradictory rationes, because ens reale is that which really exists, non-ens is that which really does not exist.

**(2) Mediately.** For example: ***man*** and ***dog*** with respect to ***animal*** import contradictory rationes, because man is a ***rational animal***, dog is a ***non-rational animal***. So ***ens reale*** and ***ens rationis*** simpliciter import contradictory rationes, because ens reale is said to be what really exists; ens rationis in truth does not really exist.

With this prenoted, we lay down ***two observations***:

**I.** When two things import contradictory rationes ***immediately***, it must be seen whether they do so ***simpliciter*** or ***with respect to the same third***. If the former, they plainly do not admit a middle: e.g. ***ens*** and ***non ens*** plainly admit no middle. If the latter, with respect to that *in respect of which* they import contradictory rationes they admit no middle, yet taken simpliciter they always admit a middle: e.g. ***man*** and ***brute*** admit a middle (as a stone, a plant), yet admit no middle with respect to ***animal***, because no animal is given or can be given which is not either man or brute.

**II.** When two things import contradictory rationes ***mediately***, then they altogether admit a middle. E.g. ***ens reale*** and ***ens rationis*** import contradictory rationes ***mediately***, because *ens rationis*, through the mediation of *non-ens*, is that which really does not exist. For *non-ens* lies wider than *ens rationis*; hence *non-ens* ***immediately*** signifies what does not exist, ***mediately*** signifies *ens rationis*; whence a middle is given between *ens reale* and *ens rationis* — e.g. *ens potentia*, *privatio*. So ***man*** and ***dog*** with respect to ***animal*** import contradictory rationes ***mediately***, because dog is a non-rational animal through the mediation of ***brute***; and brute lies wider than dog. Hence ***brute*** immediately signifies non-rational animal, ***mediately*** signifies dog; whence a middle is given between man and dog — e.g. ***lion, ox, horse***.

If these things be attended to, one will proceed more safely, nor (as we said) have arguments like the one adduced and the like for things that are beyond every exception, solely on this title that they pedlar as their foundation the truth of the saying ***"Whatsoever things import contradictory rationes, between them no middle is given."***

So ***univoca*** and ***aequivoca*** import contradictory rationes, yet not ***immediately***, but ***mediately***. For things having the same definition according to the same name lie wider than univoca; things having the same name yet not the same definition according to the same name lie wider than aequivoca — of which treatment will be had in the following chapter five.

So although with respect to a creature, ***to be produced from no matter*** and ***to be produced from some matter*** import contradictory rationes, nevertheless that which is produced from matter is not immediately said to be ***generated***. For either that matter is ***suitable*** to receive a form, or ***unsuitable*** (one which has no potency to receive a form except a very remote one). If the former, then it is called ***generation***. If the latter, and the form cannot be introduced into it except by the omnipotence of God, then it is called ***creation*** — not indeed ***simpliciter***, but ***secundum quid***; likewise ***mediate creation***. If however something is immediately produced from nothing, then it is said simpliciter to be ***created***.

In like manner, although when the obligation of law is removed either it is removed from every subject or not from every subject, nevertheless ***abrogation*** and ***dispensation*** do not immediately import these contradictory rationes. For the ***removal of obligation from every subject*** lies wider than ***abrogation*** — since ***abrogation*** and ***derogation*** agree in this, that each is a removal of obligation from every subject: all obligation of law is removed from every subject both when the law is abrogated and when it is derogated — there, when the obligation is removed as a whole; here, when it is removed in part.

So these are contradictory rationes: ***to receive the power of obliging from the free will of a Superior willing to bind his subject***, and ***not to receive the power of obliging from such a will***. Meanwhile, it is still disputed whether a law not receiving the power of obliging from the free will of a Superior willing to oblige his subject may still be judged to lie wider than the ***Law of Nature*** — such that a law not receiving the power of obliging from the free will of a Superior may again either (a) arise from the ***nature of the thing***, and so be ***Natural Law***, which can also be called the ***primary Law of Nations***; or (b) not arise from the nature of the thing, and yet (resting on the will of nations grounded in inevitable necessity or ineffable utility) be denominated ***Law of Nations absolutely***, that is, ***secondary Law of Nations***. See, if it please, the **Introduction to Hugo Grotius's work *De Jure Belli & Pacis*** l. 1 c. 1 question 6, from p. 311 to p. 333 — where this matter I have attempted to ventilate more prolixly than it has now pleased me to adduce in passing as an example.

Sedulously therefore, I believe, must care be taken that we do not pedlar whatsoever contradictory rationes as ***definitions***. For whoever has for accurate definitions whatsoever contradictory rationes (which are often nothing less than definitions) will easily be deceived into holding ***mediate*** for ***immediate***. Thus deceive themselves and deceive others those who hold the following for true definitions, or even for suitable descriptions:

> ***Ens rationis*** *is that which does not exist apart from the operation of the mind.*
> ***Aequivoca*** *are those which have the same name, and according to that name do not have the same definition.*
> ***Generation*** *is production from something.*
> ***Abrogation of law*** *is removal of obligation from every subject.*
> *The question is still ***sub judice***: whether ***Positive Law*** be rightly described by* ***the decree by which a Superior from merely free will binds his subject to compose his actions after that superior's prescript***.

— ❦ —

#### The Third Abuse — Immediate Oppositions Treated as Mediate

The ***third abuse*** we shall indicate most briefly: namely, as many abuse this axiom while they hold ***mediate*** for ***immediate***, so not a few impose on themselves and others while they hold ***immediate*** for ***mediate***. The narrowness of paper does not suffer this to be taught by many examples. One or two we shall touch only in passing.

#### The *Deus est Homo / Homo est Deus* Case — Personal Predications or Essential?

There are learned men who, when it is asked ***what sort of mode of predication*** the following are: ***"God is man," "man is God"*** — namely, whether they be ***essential*** or ***accidental*** — reply nothing other, and pronounce that nothing other can or ought be answered, than that they are ***personal predications***.

Yet other learned men (no less learned) think that if the question is thus formed and so answered, not only is nothing answered, but a ***suit of contradiction*** is written against the perpetual and immutable truth of our axiom *Quodlibet est vel non est*. Their reason is this: they say that the question now is not — ***are these predications "God is man," "man is God" personal predications*** (as the Theologians call them), since this itself is not called into any doubt, and is sufficiently manifest to all? — but uniquely the question is this: ***in each of these true and proper predications, does the predicate pertain to the essence of the subject, or not?*** For they will this to be the sense, and no other, of this question — and they otherwise rightly observe that essential and accidental predications are commonly so defined that such formulas do not fit except in received predications (nay, not even all of these), which however is said to come about by the vice of those who treat the Logical and Metaphysical doctrines negligently or snoringly.

They urge further: he who denies this proposition — ***in every true and proper predication (an affirmative finite proposition), either the predicate pertains to the essence of the subject, or does not pertain*** — simultaneously denies this proposition: ***Quodlibet est vel non est***. For with respect to the subject in a true and proper predication, ***to pertain to the essence of the subject*** and ***not to pertain to the essence of the subject*** are immediately contradictory rationes. Hence just as, if it be asked whether these predications — *"God is man," "man is God"* — be *true* or *false*, *proper* or *improper*, it does not suffice to have answered "they are personal," so neither (they think) does it suffice to the question *are they essential or accidental?* to answer *they are personal*. But let these things be left to their own place, and we shall say no more of them.

#### Further Examples — Bodin's Harmonic Proportion; Middle Modes of Acquisition

Many other examples lie ready, where men wishing to go most safely by a middle course reject extreme sentences, held as ***immediately contradictory***. To this point belong those who, with ***Bodin***, in the exercise of particular justice find a third genus of proportion between the geometric and the arithmetic — namely the ***harmonic***. To this point too belong those who think that between ***occupation*** (besides which no other natural originary acquisition is believed to be given) and ***derivative acquisition***, middle genera of acquisition intercede — ***division, concession of servitude, constitution of pledge, specification***.

But it often happens that middle sentences are sought where they cannot be found. Therefore, for discerning the abuse from the use of our axiom, it brings the greatest moment, in Morals and Politics, in whatever department of Law, and in Theology, ***to know the difference between formally contradictories and virtually, or immediately, contradictories***. Thus for example we infer most rightly:

> *Titius is ***sui iuris***. Therefore he is not subject to another's right.*
> *Titius is bound. Therefore he is not freed.*
> *Titius is a slave. Therefore he is not free. He is a slave. Therefore he is not a child-of-the-household.*

So the Apostle at ***Romans 6:18, 20, 22***: *"But being freed from sin, you have been made the servants of justice"* — for *"you were the servants of sin, free from justice."* These we have noted in this place, and the use and abuse of this most beautiful axiom we have noted. He will scarcely be able to use it rightly, who does not sufficiently have perceived the use and abuse of so many ***dilemmas***.

### Axioma III

> ***Non entis nulla sunt praedicata.***
>
> **Of what is not, there are no predicates.**

#### Sense of the Axiom

Of that which does not actually exist, but can nevertheless exist, ***no accidents of the fifth predicable*** — that is, no contingent predicates of present time — can be, with truth saved, affirmed as denominating ***intrinsically and positively***. For example: ***the rose in winter is a non-ens***. For we posit that it does not exist in the nature of things at that time, but can exist. Since therefore the rose in winter does not exist, for that reason it also has no accidental predicates, so-called in opposition to the fifth-predicable accident. For example: it cannot, with truth saved, be affirmed of the non-existent rose that it is ***red*** or ***white***.

He therefore does not happily enough understand the truth of this saying who does not know how to distinguish:

**(1)** between ***non-ens possibile*** and ***non-ens impossibile***;
**(2)** between ***necessary predicates*** (among whose number are also the fifth-predicable accidents — for essential predicates are of a fourfold genus, since there are ***four necessary predicables***) and ***contingent predicates*** — which are commonly called ***accidental predicates absolutely***, like the fifth-predicable accident, because it is a ***contingent predicable***, and ***κατ' ἐξοχήν*** (par excellence) is wont to be called the ***accidental predicable***;
**(3)** between ***negative*** and ***positive*** predicates;
**(4)** between ***contingent predicates extrinsically denominating*** and ***contingent predicates intrinsically denominating***;
**(5)** between ***predicates of present, past, and future time***.

#### Confirmation

Certainly it is clear from the terms that ***affirmative contingent predicates, intrinsically and positively denominating, of present time*** cannot, with truth saved, be given to a non-ens — because the truth of such predicates ***prerequires the existence of that of which they are truly enunciated***. For this reason they are called predicates ***of present time***.

#### Demonstration per Absurdum et Impossibile

For if of that which does not exist there were given predicates which ***prerequire its existence***, then that whose predicates they are would simultaneously exist and not exist — which is most absurd and impossible.

#### Practical Use

By one or two examples we shall illustrate the use of this axiom.

#### The *Alterius Poenam Luere* Question — Can One by Nature's Law Pay Another's Penalty?

Thus there often arises a question, not only in Moral and Civil Philosophy, but also in Theology and Jurisprudence, that is signal and sufficiently notable: ***Can anyone, with nature's law saved, pay another's penalty?***

Those who defend the ***affirmative*** chiefly use these reasons: **(1)** that on account of the ***crime of lèse-majesté*** posterity are punished; **(2)** that by ***suretyship*** one can be killed; **(3)** that Christ Himself sustained another's capital punishment.

But if we use our axiom, the ***negative*** will be demonstrated most easily. For penalty is of a crime, because it is an evil of passion, which is inflicted on account of an evil of action. Whence, because the penalty must altogether be rendered to the crime — and thus every obligation to penalty arises from merit; but merit is personal (as having its origin from the will, than which nothing is more properly ours, whence it is called ***αὐτεξούσιον***) — rightly ***he cannot be punished who has merited no evil***, as ***Seneca*** at *De Ira* II c. 4 writes: ***"Nothing will be more iniquitous than that someone be made heir of his father's hatred."*** For which reason also ***Hierocles*** defines penalty as ***medicatrix malitiae***. And ***Hieraticus*** calls justice, from this side (as its noblest), ***εἴς τινας προκαθαρτικήν τε ὄντα, καὶ εἰς ἐπανορθωτικήν*** — ***the exacting of penalty from those who first injured***.

With them agree also the ***Christian Emperors Arcadius and Honorius***, **L. Sancimus** 12, C. *de poenis*, saying: ***"We sanction that there be penalty where there is harm."*** And after a few lines: ***"Let sins therefore hold their own authors; nor let fear progress further than the crime shall be found. Let this be intimated to each individual judge."*** To this point too pertain the words of ***Callistratus the Jurist***, **L. crimen** 26, D. *de poenis*, so pronouncing: ***"Crime or paternal penalty can inflict no stain on the son. For each one is subjected to his own lot by his own commission, nor is he constituted a successor of another's crime. And this the Divine Brothers*** (Antoninus Philosophus and Verus) ***rescribed to the Hierapolitans."*** And that commonplace: ***"Noxa caput sequitur"*** (the penalty follows the person). The same ***Augustine*** hints at *Epist. 105*: ***"God Himself were unjust, if He condemned any as innocent."*** And what could be clearer than the testimony of Sacred Scripture, which stands at ***Ezekiel 18***, verse 4: ***"Lo, all souls are mine; both the soul of the father, and likewise the soul of the son, are mine; the soul that sinneth, it shall die."*** Verses 5 and following: ***"For when any man shall be just,"*** etc. — ***"this just man shall altogether live."*** And verse 20: ***"The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor shall the father bear the iniquity of the son; the justice of the just shall be upon himself, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon himself,"*** etc. But all and each of these sayings rest on the truth of our axiom.

What pertains to the contrary reasons:

**(1)** That the goods of a parent are confiscated by reason of the crime of lèse-majesté, by which some discomfort and calamity may fall also upon the children — properly that is not a penalty. For ***of a non-ens there are no predicates***; whence what one does not have, cannot be snatched from him. But the goods of the parent, so long as he lives, are not the children's, nor are these goods preserved for them from the parent to the last breath. Which Alpheno the Jurist too has noted — **L. qui civitatem** 1 § *si quis*, D. *de interdictis & relegatis* — when he asserts that the father's penalty takes nothing of right from the children except what from him was going to come to them; those things, however, which are owed not from the father but from the nature of things, remain intact to them.

**(2)** By suretyship a mere man cannot be killed — since man is not his own, but God's, who gave him the body, the members of his body, and life, not that he destroy them, but that he preserve them. Whence, because no one has a right over life such that he can himself take it from himself, therefore neither can anyone bind another to take it from him. For ***what one does not himself have, he cannot give to another, since of a non-ens there are no predicates***.

**(3)** What was adduced concerning Christ does nothing to the present point, where the question was about ***mere man***, who is not lord of his own life. Christ in truth was Lord and Prince of all human life, who, as true God, had given human life to Himself; whence He could bind it to be taken away. ***For things that are, have predicates.***

#### The Grotius Example — The Unborn and Tacit Relinquishment of Right

Another ***Politico-Juridical example*** we shall note, in which indeed Grotius expressly and abundantly demonstrates the use of this axiom. Thus he at ***De Jure Belli & Pacis*** II c. 4 § 10:

> ***"A most difficult question arises: whether a right of the yet-unborn can be lost by such a tacit dereliction?"*** *If we say they cannot, nothing is contrary to the tranquillity of empires and dominions. For in the definition just given — when, namely, Grotius in the preceding §§ had asserted that by the right of taking-possession the controversies about kingdoms and the boundaries of kingdoms, and about "mine" and "yours", are extinguished — ***since most want things to redound to their posterity, this he confirms***, ***it will seem wondrous how silence can harm those who could not speak — namely, since they did not even exist — or how the deed of others can be to the damage of others.***

Grotius, going on to demonstrate his sentence solidly, most happily calls our axiom into aid:

> ***"To this knot," he says, "the solution is according to that of ULPIAN: 'Of one who is not yet born, there is NO RIGHT, because NO ACCIDENTS ARE OF ONE NOT YET EXISTING.' Wherefore, if the people, by whose will the right of ruling proceeds, changes his will, to those who are not yet born — as to those for whom nothing has yet been acquired — he does no injury. That the people, however, has expressly changed his will — as a finite one — is believed tacitly to have changed. For of ***tacit*** and ***express*** there is the same rule, and the same force. With the will of the people therefore changed, with no right of those who were able to expect still existing, but the parents (from whom they were going to be born, and who had a right to be used in its own time) having forsaken that right — nothing stands in the way, but that it may be occupied by another as forsaken."***

Thus Grotius; from whom luculently it is plain how great a moment the genuine use of our Axiom brings to deciding controversies of both Natural and Civil Law.

Grotius adds in the cited place:

> *"We are treating of Natural Law. For by Civil Law other fictions can be introduced, so that the law meanwhile may sustain the person of those who are not yet, and so hinder that nothing be occupied against them. Which however it is not rashly to be judged that the laws will — because this private utility greatly repugns the public."*

#### Practical Abuse

#### The Socinian Denial of Original Sin — The Ethico-Theological Example

An ***Ethico-Theological example*** of practical abuse is furnished by the doctrine of **Socinus and his disciples**, by which they audaciously deny that ***original sin*** is given — because *to guilt is required proper will*, and *penalty is consequent to guilt*; but in man, while he is being born, no proper will is given, nor could it have been earlier. Who indeed does not see that the whole opinion of Socinus and the Socinians rests on our axiom ***Non entis nulla sunt praedicata***?

On the contrary, as by the common consent of our Theologians it can most firmly be proved from ***Romans 5:12*** that original sin is given, so these themselves go off into various ways, and some here, others there, mode of explication pleases.

**There are those** who thought: by reason of the moral union of the will of Adam and his posterity — by that very fact that Adam transgressed the law given to him by God in paradise, of not eating of the fruit of the tree, simultaneously ***all his posterity in him transgressed the same law***: Adam, indeed, ***physically*** (that is, by real action); his posterity, however, ***morally*** — namely by interpretative consent.

**Others** thought it not absurd that the ***will-to-sin of posterity, foreseen by God*** (whereby, if they had existed, and the same matter of sinning had been objected, they would equally have been going to sin), should be imputed to posterity for guilt no less than Adam's ***actual will*** was imputed to Adam.

**Still others** judged that it is more simply said that ***the sin of the first parents is imputed to us and is ours***, because its ***effect redounds to us***, or because it is ***the cause why its effect is in us*** — since original justice is a moral perfection due to man ***qua such***, that is, agreeing with and owed to his rational nature, whose ***defect*** on this account is also a moral evil, that is, ***sin***.

For the rest, whatever be the case concerning the various explications of this kind — the examination of which does not pertain to our Schools, and much less is of this place — orthodox Theologians commonly inform us that, although by adversaries sin in general is defined through the ***voluntary*** or ***προαιρετική*** (deliberately-chosen) ***transgression of law***, yet we ought piously and simply to acquiesce in the definition handed down by the Holy Spirit Himself, when sin is defined at ***1 John 3:4*** through τὴν ἀνομίαν (anomia / lawlessness): ***ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶ ἡ ἀνομία*** — ***sin is the lack of conformity with law***. By which definition piously and rightly observed, ***everything which is not conform to the law will be sin***, whether that sin be ***voluntary*** or ***innate***.

From these things said hitherto, it is easily collected that ***all force and all vigor is lacking*** to Socinus and the Socinians' argument.

#### The Transit Question — The Politico-Juridical Example

In place of a ***Politico-Juridical example***, it will be lawful to touch this Politico-Juridical question: ***Whether lands and rivers, and any part of the sea in the proprietorship of some people, ought to lie open to those who seek transit for just causes*** — e.g. because they are seeking by just war what is their own, or because they desire commerce with a distant nation?

Those who defend the ***negative*** sentence believe that a transit demanded, and from the ***not-at-all-vain fear of grave peril*** denied, is denied by a naturally just cause. For it is unworthy of any free man, and least of all to be borne, that he be necessarily imperiled by another and laid bare to injuries.

But the patrons of the ***affirmative*** sentence — and especially among them ***Hugo Grotius***, *De Jure Belli & Pacis* II c. 13 — urge that ***"my right is not taken away by your fear"***. Meanwhile, we would wish the matter to be of ***higher judgment***: ***does not Grotius and those who feel with him by this very fact set up predicates of a non-ens?***

> ***"What right have you to pass through another's with his Prince unwilling? — which you would not have to pass through the field of a certain private Titius (L. 3 § ult. D. de injur.) unless servitude be acquired. But let no one think that the liberty of territory, which is the universality of fields, is not diminished without consulting the owner and by one's own authority, when passing through — since by permitting a journey through one single tract the liberty of each one is diminished. Nay, if by servitude of way, drive, path, duly constituted by law, the liberty of an estate is diminished, why should it not be diminished by the fact of the passerby, usurpingly? But grant, I say, that the right is yours — I will concede altogether that it must be insisted on, if from thence I am to fear for my security. For security is among the external goods of the Republic, which must be attempted by none unwilling, usurpingly — since this repugns the condition of a free man, and it is servile to be forced by inevitable necessity to fear from another."***
>
> — **Herr Strauch**, Jurist, *Dissertation on the Imperium of the Sea*, c. 8 § 2.

— ❦ —

*[T22 closes: the **Abusus Practicus of Axioma III** complete, and with it Axioma III closes. (a) **Ethico-Theological — Socinus's denial of original sin**: Socinian argument — to guilt is required proper will, penalty consequent to guilt, newborn has no proper will nor could have — rests entirely on *non entis nulla praedicata*. **Lutheran response**: Rom. 5:12 proves original sin by common consent. Three orthodox-explication families surveyed: (1) moral-union explanation (Adam physically transgressed, posterity morally by interpretative consent); (2) foreseen-sin-will explanation (God foreseeing their equal sin had they existed, imputed to them); (3) simplest explanation (Adam's sin imputed because its effect redounds to us; original justice is a moral perfection due to man *qua such*, hence its defect is sin). (b) **The decisive move**: Scripture's own definition of sin — ***1 John 3:4*** *ἡ ἁμαρτία ἐστὶ ἡ ἀνομία* = *carentia conformitatis cum lege* — captures voluntary ***and*** innate sins. (c) **Politico-Juridical — Transit through foreign territory for just causes**: Grotius *DJBP* II.13 maintains *ius meum metu tuo non tollitur* (my right isn't removed by your fear) — but Strauch (*De Imperio Maris* c.8 §2) counters that Grotius sets up predicates of a non-ens: what right have you to pass through another's land with the Prince unwilling? Servitude-of-way argument (L. 3 § ult. D. de iniur.); security as external good of the Republic; it is ***servile*** to be forced by inevitable necessity to fear from another. T23 opens **Axioma IV** — Veltheim's own axiom substituted here: ***A reali ad ens reale non valet consequentia*** (from "real" to "ens reale" the consequence does not hold); Sensus (the world was possible-of-production before being produced — this is *reale* but not *ens reale*); Confirmatio (objective potency = non-repugnance, not an existent thing); Demonstratio per Absurdum (else multa simul essent et non essent).]*

### Axioma IV

In the place of this [axiom] we put the following saying:

> ***A reali ad ens reale non valet consequentia.***
>
> **From "real" to "real being" the consequence does not hold.**

#### Sense of the Axiom

Its sense is: ***something can be called "real"*** which nevertheless is not ***an ens reale***. For example: ***that the world could-have-been-produced before it was already produced is a real thing***, but is not ***an ens reale***. Cf. of this first chapter § 14 with the notes p. 66.

#### Confirmation

Besides what we have adduced in the just-cited pp. 66 ff., it pleases to confirm the matter by this example: that ***potency*** which they commonly call ***objective potency***, in which the world is said to have been before it was produced by God, and which signifies the same as ***non-repugnance*** (according to which something is apt to be the object of divine active potency, so that through this it may come to be) — this is ***not something real existing in things***. Which is easily perceived from this: that it is set up to be in things ***not yet existing, before they exist***. "For what is in a thing not existing cannot be something existing," are the words of ***the Blessed Stahl***, *Institutiones Metaphysicae* c. 5 §10 p.m. 51.

It is, however, something ***real***, because it does not depend on the operation of the intellect. For from *being in act* to *being able to be*, the consequence holds. Therefore from ***being in act independently of the intellect*** to ***being able to be, or having been able to be, independently of the intellect***, the consequence also holds. But that ***being able to be or having been able to be independently of the intellect*** is a ***real potency***. Therefore the consequence holds from ***ens reale*** to ***reale***, but not from ***reale*** to ***ens reale***.

#### Demonstration per Absurdum et Impossibile

Because ***reale*** formally says only that which does not depend on the operation of the intellect — but ***reale ens*** besides independence from the operation of the intellect also argues ***true and real existence*** — surely, if from ***reale*** to ***ens reale*** the consequence held, many things would simultaneously be and not be, which is most absurd and impossible. For example: that the world could-have-been-produced before it was already produced, we have shown to be ***something real***. Now if ***reale*** is the same as ***ens reale***, then the world, before it was already produced, would not-have-existed and would-have-existed: not-have-existed, because it was not yet produced; yet would-have-existed, if from ***reale*** the consequence held to ***ens reale***.

#### Practical Use

#### The Moral Example — Is Moral Turpitude an *Ens Reale*?

It pleases to adduce a ***Moral example***. It is often asked: ***Is moral turpitude itself*** (which the Moralists rightly deny to be sin, and by a barbarous name call ***peccaminositas***) ***— considered precisely, as it says ἀνομία — an ens reale?***

Some prove the ***affirmative*** by the following argument:

> *Whatever qua such says a real relation, that qua such is a ***real being***. But moral turpitude considered precisely, as it says ἀνομία, says a real relation. Therefore moral turpitude, considered precisely as it says ἀνομία, is a real being.*

The Major they think from this to be sufficiently manifest: that every real relation is a real being. The Minor they assert abundantly to stand from this: that ἀνομία, as moral turpitude formally argues, is a real relation to law — and indeed a real ***dis-agreement*** with law.

How others may respond to this argument, in the most right fashion they note beforehand: it is now no longer the question of ***sin*** — much less of actual or original sin — but uniquely now the question is of ***moral turpitude itself***, considered precisely as it says ἀνομία. For as much as ***man-blind*** and ***blindness***, so much do ***the deed ἄνομον*** and ***ἀνομία*** differ. Now they deny the Major of the adduced argument. The reason for the denial they seek in this saying: ***from "real" to "ens reale" the consequence does not hold***. Therefore they think ***something can be a real relation, yet not be an ens reale***. A manifest example of a real relation which is not an ens reale we adduced above at p. 67.

#### The Theological Example — Divine Relations *ad intra*

Let there be ***Theological examples***. Every Student of Theology must know that in divinis ***real relations*** are given — which the Theologians call ***relations of God ad intra*** — namely ***paternity***, ***filiation***, and ***the procession of the Holy Spirit*** — and the Theologians teach that these are founded in ***real actions of God ad intra***: paternity and filiation (of which the former is the property of the first person, the latter of the second) being founded in ***generation*** (since to this — that one person be *generating*, the other *generated* — follows that the one is Father, the other Son); and the procession of the Holy Spirit being founded in the act of ***spiration***, whose term is the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father and Son by eternal spiration (since He is equally called the Spirit of the Son, as the Spirit of the Father is said, Galatians IV. 6).

Hence the Theologians show such a ***real order*** and ***real distinction*** between the divine persons: ***The Father*** is not from another being, nor from another person of divinity, and is that person of divinity from whom the others are — namely the Son by generation, the Holy Spirit by spiration. ***The Son of God*** is not from another being, but is He who is from another person of divinity — namely from God the Father alone by generation — and is He from whom another person is: namely the Holy Spirit by spiration. ***The Holy Spirit*** is not from another being, but is He who is from other persons of divinity — namely from the Father and the Son by spiration.

That ***generation*** and ***spiration*** (which are and alone are called by Theologians ***personal acts***, because they are proper to some one or some persons of the divine persons; and are also called ***notional acts***, because by them the divine persons become notable) are real actions of God ad intra, the Theologians prove, because the term of each is real and really produced. The term of the former is the Son really generated from eternity, who is the ***image of the Father*** (Col. I. 15; Hebr. I. 3). The term of the latter is the Holy Spirit, who is neither called the Son, nor the image of the Father or of the Son, nor is said to be generated — but ***proceeds from the Father and the Son***.

From this Theologians' doctrine (which, with their best peace, we recount and venerate), it is of its own accord clear that from the real actions of God ad intra are given ***real and really-distinct relations of God ad intra***, founded in those real actions. Every suitable cultivator of orthodox Theology therefore sees ***the use of our axiom***: for although those relations are real and really distinct, nevertheless they are not ***real and really-distinct beings***, but remain ***one and the same numerical being and as to the thing itself God Himself***, equally as the three persons of divinity are and remain ***one numerical being, one God in essence***. Therefore it is not permitted to argue from ***real*** to ***ens reale***, from a ***multiplication of reals*** to a ***multiplication of real beings***.

— ❦ —
