#### The Politico-Juridical Example — Real Denomination without Real Inherence

We append ***Political and Juridical examples***. There is no doubt that stable and certain subjects are given which can be truly and really denominated by ***relations and qualities*** which occur in Moral and Civil Philosophy and in all Jurisprudence — subjects to which such relations and qualities can be really and distinctly attributed. Meanwhile, no necessity compels us to call those very relations and qualities, as formally considered — politically or juridically — ***real beings*** (*entia realia*). For by the consent of all Philosophers and of the most learned men, the notion of ***being*** is Metaphysical, and nothing is counted ***being*** except what is either ***substance*** or ***accident***. But now no one of sounder judgment would say that those very relations and qualities which, and in so far as, they are of Moral, Political, or Juridical consideration are ***accidents*** inhering in others as in subjects as true and real beings — much less would anyone hold them for ***substances***.

Therefore the most erudite men — not only Philosophers, but also Theologians and Jurists — distinguish between ***the subject of a true and real denomination*** and ***the subject of true and real inherence***. The latter does not prerequire all real relations and real qualities (since not every real relation is a real being); the former, however, altogether does. Let us take an example:

Thus the ***two accomplices of one and the same crime*** are said to have a real relation to each other — a relation which lacks any subject in which it really inheres, if the foundation is sought from the moral ἄνοια or ἀνομία itself. Thus ***Majesty in the abstract and formally considered*** is the ***supreme power of ruling a commonwealth***; and he is said really to have it who in the Republic has the capacity to commit and omit such acts to which the committing or omitting he could be obliged by none of mortals, nor was he obliged by any either natural or positive right. Whence they are subject to another's right in nothing, so that by another's human arbitrium they cannot be made void.

Thus ***servitudes*** have as subject either an estate or a person. For the Jurist notes **servitude** as ***a right in another's thing constituted*** (**L. si fundus servitus** 2 D. *de servitutibus praediorum rusticorum*). ***Right*** here signifies ***a moral quality*** or ***condition of a thing***. And this is a moral faculty, active and passive — e.g. a ***way of passage*** is an active moral potency of going in the dominant estate, and a passive one in the serving estate. Therefore servitude can be ascribed to the thing — when, e.g. the subject of the active servitude is called the dominant estate, the subject of the passive servitude is the serving estate; it can also in another sense be called the subject of servitude ***the person*** to whom active servitude is attained (as he who has a right of passage); likewise the subject of passive servitude is the person who is compelled to suffer something in his own thing or not to do. In like manner, as thing serves thing or person, by this reason too can thing or person be denominated subject of ***real or personal*** servitude. But from all these it is by no means evinced that such relations ***cannot be given*** unless they inhere in a certain subject.

Here an elegant occasion would offer itself for discussing the ***common foundation of the Fictions (as they call them) of Law***, both ***positive*** and ***natural***. But on this matter we have treated *ex instituto* in our ***Jurisprudentia Moralis***, and below in the ***Apparatus Metaphysicus*** it will perhaps be said.

#### Practical Abuse

#### The Modi-Nomenclature of Moral Entities — Veltheim's Polemic

In these times are found those who publicly deplore ***the carelessness of Philosophers***, which they pronounce to be at fault that ***MORAL ENTITIES*** (which indeed existed as long as the human race existed) have not yet been digested into order, nor have their indoles been more carefully handed down — things so eminent that the world would still have been ignorant of them unless they had arisen for us. We would even be of the greatest thanks to them, if they had conferred to public utility ***that which was passed over by all those held and still held, by the unanimous consent of the most cordate men, as suitable Doctors or Writers of Moral Things***; or if they had corrected what all had slipped on.

Now such is the ***new, so to speak, Philosophy of Moral Entities***, that if you subtract the new locutions, not much of it will be left. For:

**First**: who, mediocrely versed in the writings of ***Aristotle's Analytics***, of the ***Greek Commentators*** and ***of other Masters famous in our age*** (from whom — to name a few in last place from the many — enough is now to have praised, from the Spanish ***Joannes Nunnesius***, ***Melchior Racotius***; from the Germans ***Philippus Scherbius***, ***Michael Piccartus***, ***Johann Felwinger***, Herr ***Hermann Conring***, Herr ***Melchior Zeidler***; from the Italians ***Caesar Cremoninus***, ***Jacobus Mazonius***, and ***Felix Accoridontis***) will not know that these all asserted every ***discipline*** to be ***real***, and to treat ***its own things***: ***Physics the Physical***, ***Ethics the Ethical***, ***Politics the Political***, etc.? These ex professo treated the question how much diligence and prudence the inquiry of any ***genus of things*** requires, and with how much caution it must be observed ***that moral things not be treated physically or mathematically***, but as moral things ethically, as political things politically, as juridical things juridically.

**Secondly**: everywhere in Aristotle's Moral and Civil Philosophy stand the finest and most learned warnings, by which he explicitly professes that ***MORAL and CIVIL THINGS*** are to be accepted by ***true knowledge and certain demonstration***, nor truly to be understood by ***mere opinion***, and hence it behooves a man to be well instructed by both general (that is, Analytical) and special pedia, so that he understand the ***indoles and nature of MORAL and CIVIL THINGS***, and so far seek that which is exquisite in the ***GENUS of MORAL and CIVIL THINGS*** as the ***NATURE OF THOSE THINGS permits***, and know rightly how each thing is to be received. ***Especially must it not be obscure to him, IN WHAT THINGS the subjects differ by species***, and of these one is first, another subsequent; or that of such things nothing at all is common according to the reason by which they are such, or very tenuously and narrowly: that one who philosophizes about any Moral or Civil doctrine, and does not look only to acting, ought to be nothing short of seeing everything, nor let anything slip, but ***treat the whole indoles of a MORAL or CIVIL THING*** with care, and ***open the truth of the whole NATURE of the THING***. See *Nicomachean Ethics* I c. 1, II c. 2, *Eudemian* c. 6, in *Politics* II c. 2 and following. Much more is had, by which Aristotle blames the ἀπαιδευσία of those who want to seem great Doctors of moral and civil things yet have not yet learned ***TO ESTIMATE THE FORCE AND NATURE OF MORAL THINGS AT ITS PROPER PRICE***; but our plan does not suffer these to be transferred hither.

**Thirdly**: with the same purpose Grotius in his work ***De Jure Belli & Pacis*** everywhere made mention of ***MORAL THINGS***, as when in the Prolegomena n. 40 in Moral matters he bids attention to what the ***NATURE of the act and of each THING*** bears; in n. 32 he names ***MORAL THING***. In the work itself an outstanding passage stands at l. 1 c. 1 § 4; again another is found in the same lib. 2 c. 3 § 11, where he excellently and learnedly discusses the ***NATURE of MORAL THINGS***: whence they come to be worthily known. ***"The nature of Moral Things,"*** he says, ***"is known not from duration (since of quantity there is no efficacy) but from operations: wherefore faculties producing the same effects are to be called by the same name. For duration does not change the nature of a moral thing."*** Omitting other many passages here.

**Fourthly**: how splendidly the great ***Felwinger*** has deduced the nature and indoles of moral and civil things (and these ex professo) from Aristotle and so from ancient Philosophy, is to be seen in his signal work ***De Civili Prudentia***, especially from chapters 7, 8, 9, 10, 11.

**Fifthly**: the same mode of philosophizing pleased the ***Jurists***, as could easily be demonstrated if the thing were not in the open. Therefore it will be equally to us whether in future ***MORAL THINGS*** be judged by this name (received everywhere and by all the learned) or should be called ***MORAL ENTITIES***. By us it is permitted — whether this latter at least be sanctioned by praetorian edict, or whether even by the thunderbolt of anathema be struck those who will not call them ***moral entities***. Meanwhile anyone sees that ***Philosophers and Jurists do not so easily use the appellation of beings***, because this notion is judged proper to Theoretical Philosophy.

Nor will we envy their authors if they call ***moral entities*** ***modes*** — or, if they prefer, ***accidents*** (which indeed prerequire some subject) — and set up ***four classes*** of them: ***moral state or order***, ***moral person***, ***quantity***, ***quality***. So that, for example, when a Doctor is created, a mass of moral entities of these classes is said to be imposed and superadded to a man physically already perfect: by that very fact that he is now in a ***new MORAL STATE*** or order in which he was not before; a ***new MORAL PERSON*** is judged imposed on him, since he is a Doctor who was not before; from the class of ***MORAL QUANTITIES*** a new estimation is superadded to him; from the class of ***MORAL QUALITIES*** a new title (as that he be called ***Doctor***, and know that a certain power, immunities, and privileges have been conferred on him).

But let us grant all these most willingly (which we altogether grant — for we prefer to sin on this side, to proclaim even those less meritorious under this title, than to vituperate the meritorious). Shall we for that very fact have believed that new things have been found? Have not Moral Philosophers at every time distinguished between the ***physical and moral state***, between the ***person of a physical and moral agent***, between ***physical and moral estimation***, between ***δύναμις and ἐξουσία***, ***physical potency*** and ***moral potency***? Could the doctrine of ***the moral estimation of circumstances***, both simple and compared, not be known and ought it not to be known to any beginners and much more to Masters of Moral things — where chiefly the moral estimation of ***person***, of its ***condition and state***, likewise of its ***quantity and quality*** is dealt with, while the circumstances ***WHO, WHAT, HOW*** are estimated? Are circumstances not called in all Ethicists' books the ***accidents of an action physically considered*** which are outside the substance of an act physically considered, and yet touch the act in some way, and which, if morally estimated, are rightly distinguished into ***essential*** and ***accidental***?

For the rest, I confess ingenuously what I feel: namely, that I cannot yet be led to believe that anyone can profit at all in solid practical doctrine, or with difficulty, unless he knows how to distinguish his ***moral entities*** not only into ***positive and suppositive***, but also into ***modes*** (which to the Authors of this Nomenclature are formally moral entities) — into ***affective and estimative***, into ***affective into formal and operative***, into ***operative into primary and arisen***, etc. — and simultaneously accurately know how to estimate his moralities as ***longitudinarias, latitudinarias, crassitudinarias, affectivas, aestimativas, operativas***, and his ***imputativitates, determinativitates, radicalitates, terminalitates, intrinsitates, extrinsitates, situalitates***, ***quantitates situalitatum***, ***talitates, ubicativitates, quandicativitates***, likewise his states ***tantitativos, talitativos, quandicativos, ubicativos*** — let these suffice as a taste of the doctrine of moral entities through so many ages hitherto neglected, in which times ***ἀπαιδευσία*** reigns.

I would more quickly believe that by such things moral doctrines are more intricated than extricated. Add Hornejus *Phil. Moral.* lib. 3 c. 12 h. 3. Meanwhile, so far is it from being the case that I should envy the Authors of their choragic praise which by this ingenious rather than profitable plan they are believed to have merited among those juniors who otherwise are easily caught like mice by any novelty's decoy — that in my best peace anyone, who merely wills, may believe this Philosophy of ***new moral entities*** (which indeed always existed, but now with the greatest emolument of literary matter have been digested into this remarkable order) composed of mere unions and moral gems — or rather, of some fifth essence — provided only they not so abjectly judge of all hitherto received Philosophy, and cease to pursue with most bitter hatred those to whom this ***market of moral terms***, in so far as it tends to the unjust contempt of ancient Philosophy, does not smile. But on this matter *ex professo* it is treated in the ***Jurisprudentia Moralis***.

#### The Manichaean Example — The Two-First-Principles Heresy

Another example, and that an ***unspeakable one*** of the abuse of this axiom, we most briefly append. The ***Manichaeans***, moved among other things by this reasoning — that since (even with no one thinking) the malice or turpitude of certain acts and habits is given, it cannot not follow that that malice or turpitude is something really existing in acts and habits, that is, ***a real being*** — fell into this most pestilential heresy, to set up ***two altogether first principles***, primal, co-potent, and co-eternal, but among themselves diverse: ***One good***, from which were all real good beings; ***another evil***, from which were all real evil beings. Likewise, that whatever is still transcendentally good in man and remains over is from the first good principle, that is, from the good God; but what is not transcendentally good, but totally evil in itself, and yet still a real and positive being, is from the other first evil principle, that is, from an evil God. See **Theodoret** *De fabulis haereticorum* c. ult., **Augustine** in his book *De haeresibus* 46, **Epiphanius** haer. 66.

Commonly this heresy is attributed to ***Manes*** (who even styled himself in his letters ***Manichaeus***, of which this is the inscription: ***"Manichaeus, Apostle of Jesus Christ"*** — from whom also those addicted to his heresy received the name ***Manichaeans***), as to its first author, and this perhaps because it prevailed more under him, so that he deceived more. For otherwise its origin is much more ancient: ***Cerdo*** indeed (as Augustine testifies in the book *De haeresibus* c. 21) nursed the same opinion. Before Cerdo this error was also taught by those heretics who were called ***Gnostics***, witness Augustine haer. 6. Of the same dogma the most ancient author to have been ***Zoroaster***, Plutarch hands down in his book *De Iside & Osiride*.

But what, pray, is the sequel? ***With no one thinking, the turpitude or malice of acts is given. Therefore it really exists in the acts, that is, is a real being.*** For ***from "real" to "real being" the consequence does not hold***. Surely also with no one thinking, blindness is given in the eye; nor however from this does it follow that it is a real being — because blindness is not given as something existing; but with no one thinking, by this incile it is said of the eye, when its opposite — namely sight — is not in it.

## Caput Secundum

### Of Existence and Absence

#### § 1

> ***The abstract of Being is Essentia; here it is taken as it signifies the same as real existence.***

#### Notes

**I.** *Essentia* has itself to *ens* as *albedo* has itself to *the-white*: for *ens* has essence, and the white has whiteness. And just as I cannot say *albedo est album* ("whiteness is white"), neither can I assert *essentia est ens* ("essence is being").

**II.** Yet from this it must stand that not every abstract really differs from its concrete. So neither in the present does *essentia* and *ens reale* differ in reality. Thus for example ***Deitas*** is abstract, ***Deus*** is concrete; yet God and Deity do not really differ. So too *essentia* and *ens* do not really differ, for otherwise Deity and God too would differ really. For what else is Deity than the divine essence, and what else is God than one having the divine essence? But all that is in God, is God Himself, since in God no real composition falls — as implying imperfection, of which in several places in its own place.

**III.** Commonly ***existence*** is described as ***that by which something is outside its causes***: e.g. the rose in spring, when it actually exists, is altogether outside those causes whence it had come forth. But many things can be desired in this formula of description: for what is chief, not everything that exists exists outside its causes — since also ***God*** exists, who could have no causes of Himself, since He is the first being from Himself. Add that, accurately philosophizing, through existence the thing is not outside its causes, but through ***production*** the thing becomes a thing, and while it is produced, it begins to be outside its cause.

**IV.** Nor does that description deserve a milder censure: ***existence is that by which something ceases to be outside its causes***.

**V.** There are others who say that ***essence is that by which, or whereby, being is being***; but something is being because it really is, and really-to-be notes nothing other than truly-to-exist.

**VI.** This doctrine has a signal ***use in Theology***, especially in the chief loci where the ***highest mysteries*** are treated — namely, concerning the ***mystery of the Most Holy Trinity*** and of the ***mystery of the incarnation of the Son of God***. For in the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity, one essence is given — that is, one essence, namely the divine essence — and so also one existence is given, namely the divine existence. On the contrary, in the mystery of the incarnation ***two really distinct essences*** are given, and so also ***two really distinct existences***: the divine essence and the human essence; or, as the more accurate Theologians express: ***the existence proper to the divine nature*** and ***the existence proper to the human nature***.

Meanwhile the most sacred caution must be kept, lest *essence* and *existence* be confused with ***subsistence*** — of which elsewhere, in its own just place and order, will be dealt. For now, with the leave of the venerable Theologians, let it suffice to be noted: that in the mystery of the Trinity ***three are given, not three***  — namely three really distinct ***persons***, three really distinct ***subsistences***; but one numerical essence or existence, one numerical being, namely God, in three really distinct subsistences among themselves. Contrary in the mystery of the incarnation: there are given ***two existences*** or essences really distinct, so that yet there is one numerical subsistence, namely the subsistence of the ***λόγος***, by which the two natures in Christ — each of which has its proper existence — are united and subsist, so that they constitute one suppositum, one person ***θεανθρώπινον***.

**VII.** The ***Scholastics*** called existence by a barbarous name ***actus entitativus***. The occasion of this appellation was the controversy between ***Thomas*** and ***Scotus***. For Scotus (born later than Thomas) asserted against Thomas that ***prime matter has its own existence***, though Thomas had always taught the contrary — namely that prime matter lacks its own existence, and exists by the existence of the form — making this argument:

> *Whatever is pure potency, says not act; and so does not have its own existence, since to exist is to be in act. But prime matter, as Aristotle testifies, is pure potency. Therefore it does not have its own existence.*

***Scotus*** responded by distinguishing between ***act*** as it is the same as ***form***, and ***act*** as it is the same as ***existence***. Act considered in the prior way he called ***actus formalis***, since by form matter is in act a composite; act considered in the posterior way he called ***actus entitativus***, since by existence that which has existence is said to be in act.

#### § 2

> ***The opposite of existence by one name is called ABSENCE, by which nothing other is signified than the negation of actual real existence.***

#### § 3

> ***Absence can be considered in two ways: (1) FORMALLY, as it expressly argues the negation of actual existence. The Scholastics call this negation formal negation, likewise incomplex negation — such as, for example, the absence of sight from a stone, the absence of sight from an animal, the absence of original justice from man. (2) As it in the terms is laid down and quasi tacitly lurks, or is contained implicitly: e.g. when I say "God wooden" — here I tacitly signify the absence of God, and in the notion of "wooden God" lurks the negation of the true divine existence. For "to be wooden" says to-be-material, to-be-composite, and so quasi denies God, who cannot be material, cannot be composite. This negation of the posterior kind is likewise called VIRTUAL negation, likewise VIRTUALLY COMPLEX negation, likewise CONTRADICTION IN TERMS.***

#### § 4

> ***To negation taken in the prior mode is wont to be referred the distinction between PURE NEGATION and PRIVATION: pure negation is nothing other than the absence of true and real existence from an INCAPABLE subject — e.g. pure absence or pure negation is the absence of sight from a stone, the absence of accident from God, the absence of matter from a Spirit. PRIVATION is the absence of true and real existence from a CAPABLE subject — as the absence of sight from the eye, which by one name is called "blindness"; the absence of light from the air, which we call by the name of "darkness"; the absence of original justice from man, who would have enjoyed it had he not through the Fall lost it.***

#### Notes

**I.** Beware of confusing ***privatio*** with ***privativum***: for privativum differs **(1)** from privation ***as concrete from abstract*** — e.g. blindness and the-blind differ most greatly: blindness is the privation; the-blind is the privative itself.

**II.** Privation differs from privativum **(2)** as ***included from including***: for privativum includes two things: that to which privation adheres, and the privation itself. For example, the-blind includes: the being from which sight is absent, which however would have been capable of sight unless its nature had been impeded; and (3) the very absence of sight.

**III.** Privation and privativum differ **(3)** in this: that privation is not and cannot be a true being, whereas privativum can be called a true being. E.g. blindness says no true existence, nor really exists; but the-blind is a true being, although that it be a true being it has not from blindness.

**IV.** On this account the ***Moralists***, wishing to express this difference in the doctrine on sin, distinguished between ***peccaminositas*** and ***peccatum***: ***Peccaminositas*** is really abstracted from pure negation and privation, for negation considered in itself says the absence of real existence in such a way that no subject is attended to, and much less looked at whether, if the subject be given, it is capable of that of which it is said to be absent, or is incapable. Then only can we properly declare whether that negation is to be called pure, or privation — if respect be had to a certain subject. Thus for example of ***God*** division is denied; of ***Peter*** division is also denied; but on the part of God it is pure negation, since God is not capable of division (because all things that are in God are God Himself); on the part of man it is not pure negation, but privation, because as man is really composite, so division does not repugn to him. It is said that the negation of division made of man is a privation — though the discourse is not of ***divisibility***.

#### § 5

> ***Pure negation and privation do not differ on the part of that which they signify in the directly act, but only on the part of their connotations, or those which they signify obliquely: namely, (1) pure negation connotes an INCAPABLE subject; (2) privation connotes a CAPABLE subject.***

#### § 6 — Doctrine's Place

> ***It must be noted that not only are existence and being really the same, but also existence and essence: existence and being, because being's existence is said, since existence is nothing but that by which being exists; whence if existence really differed from being, being would have received existence — which is absurd. For it would have received it before it existed, since through existence that exists which exists, and without existence nothing exists.***
>
> ***Existence and essence, because nothing is in act being unless it exists, since to exist is nothing other than to be in act being; but what is in act not being, that is in act non-being, and so truly is not being.***

#### Notes

**I.** This can also be urged for the latter assertion by the following reason: Because those who defend the contrary sentence expressly teach that existence is ***posterior*** to essence, and ***supervenes*** essence itself. Surely if existence really differed from essence, it would have to be in it really received, which is absurd. For how could something really be received into that which, as existing before it received the other, could not exist? How could that heat, which does not yet exist, how can he who does not exist?

**II.** To some this mode of philosophizing also pleases: ***Existence really distinct from being cannot be attributed to God, nor can essence really distinct from existence be with truth saved attributed to God. Therefore neither to being qua being can they be attributed. For whatever is attributed to being qua being, that also agrees with God, since God is being.***

**III.** The contrary sentence — that existence and essence do not really differ — is defended by all those who assert that ***being-in-potency is a true and real being***. For these admitting that being-in-potency does not have true existence, since nothing exists unless it be in act, want it to have a true essence, not indeed actual, yet possible — since something can be possible with no one thinking, yet not be actual; and so true possible essence can be without true existence, and so this differs from that really.

But by what right the Patrons of this sentence, or by what pretext of truth, do they distinguish between ***possible essence*** and ***actual essence***? By the same right it will be permitted to those who stand on the other part to distinguish between ***possible existence*** and ***actual existence***. Whence just as these themselves contradicting most willingly acknowledge and confess that ***possible existence qua such is not true existence***, so, with better judgment safe, it seems — as if (whether willing or unwilling) they must confess — that essence, as it notes the abstract of a true and real being, is not a true essence unless it be ***actual essence***; and that ***possible essence qua such cannot be referred to a true and real being as abstract to its concrete***. What was said — ***that something can be possible yet not actual*** — from this it does not yet follow that possible essence qua such is a true essence; nor further is it collected that true essence is possible essence. Thus ***animal*** can be without ***man***, and animal qua such is not man; yet because man is animal, man and animal do not really differ.

**IV.** Nor is there occasion to say that John's existence yesterday is not today's — because otherwise, he who existed yesterday would necessarily also exist today; yet one and the same yesterday and today was and is John's essence, since essence is immutable and placed in the indivisible. For as it is said: ***John yesterday was seeing, today is not seeing***; and so from being-seeing, seeing is said of John, from not-being-seeing he is denominated by seeing from himself — nor must we therefore collect diverse existences, nor essences, from diverse extrinsic denominations. But existence is an ***extrinsic denomination*** from time, whence the diversity of time does not argue diversity of intrinsic existence. In the way that to-be yesterday is not to-be today, by the same way yesterday's essence is not today's essence, in which existence yesterday was denied to be today's existence.

**V.** Much less do we believe this to be against the truer sentence — that by consent of all Philosophers the essences of things are called ***eternal***, when yet (if God be excepted) the existence of nothing can be called eternal, since God by His free will made all things in time to be existent. For thus essence is taken plainly otherwise, of which notion a whole chapter will be given below. Noting in passing: if in this sense the essences of all things be called eternal — as if they were always in act, without principle and without end — then the patrons of the contrary sentence would have what they wished; but this has not been asserted by them, nor can it be asserted without the most manifest falsity.

**VI.** There are those who think the real difference of existence and essence can be sufficiently proved from this: that they cannot be separated from each other, not even by divine potency. For actual existence cannot be given without actual essence, nor the latter without the former. The same they judge most rightly of possible existence and possible essence. For what is said — that possible essence is often given without existence — does not at all prejudice the reason adduced, because in the same way possible existence can be given without existence, and possible essence without essence. But we have not willed to use this ratiocination, because from the negation of real separation (likewise real separability, as they call it) the consequence does not immediately hold to the negation of real distinction. For things can be really distinct which are not really separable.

**VII.** It is wont to be inquired: ***Is existence a true and real being?*** For the negative this ratiocination could be made: *Whatever is a true and real being has a true and real existence. But existence is a true and real being. Therefore existence has a true and real existence.* The conclusion is absurd — therefore either Major or Minor. Not Major. Therefore Minor. On the contrary, for the affirmative is held to make this reason: because existence does not really differ from a true and real being; but unless it were a true and real being, altogether it would have to differ really from true and real being — which is absurd. The Scholastics thought to satisfy this difficulty by distinguishing: ***absolutely***, existence is being; ***by indirect speech***, existence is not being, as when it is asked: *is creation created, or not?* — where they distinguish between ***creation*** as it is the same as ***creation*** (the act of creating), and ***creation*** as (as creation itself is a creature) that is, the very created-ness. Just as therefore ***creation does not come about through creation***, so neither does existence have existence.

But there was no need for these subtleties, if it be simply answered: ***existence formally is not being, if being is taken for that which has existence; it is yet being, if being is taken for all that which is not nothing.*** For if the former mode be received, then surely as ***album*** notes the same as ***habens albedinem***, and whiteness itself is not white, since it has not whiteness, but is whiteness itself — so being is the same as ***habens existentiam***, whence existence is not being, that is, it has not existence, since it is existence itself. If the latter mode be considered, it easily is plain that existence is not nothing, because it does not really differ from being. Whence in the ***real or identical sense*** (as it is called in the Schools) this proposition is true: ***Existence is being***, since to the truth of a proposition in the identical sense it suffices that subject and predicate be, on the part of the thing, the same. In the ***formal sense***, as they call it, this proposition — ***Existence is being*** — is false, because the mode of knowing the abstract is one, the mode of knowing the concrete is another. For abstract and concrete signify one and the same thing, yet not in the same way. ***You say***: therefore in the identical sense this proposition will be true: ***Albedo est alba***. It is answered: no consequence. For between whiteness and the-white a real distinction intercedes; no real distinction is given between existence and being.

**VIII.** Between ***being*** and ***nothing***, therefore, no middle is given on the part of the thing; yet a middle is given in our mode of knowing — because existence is formally not being, nor nothing.

#### The Senses of *Nihil* (continuation of Note VIII of § 6)

There are also various significations of ***τὸ nihil***. And indeed in Sacred Scripture and Theology the more frequent significations are when ***nihil*** is said:

**(1) Of effect**, as: ***"Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing"*** (1 Cor. VII. 19) — that is, effects nothing nor avails to Christianity and true piety.

**(2) Of the absence of great value or price from a thing in which it ought to inhere**, as: ***"If I should have all faith, so as even to transfer mountains, but have not charity, I am nothing"*** (1 Cor. XIII. 2) — that is, of no price or value in the sight of God and in the edification of the Church.

**(3) Of a thing exceedingly small**, as it may be nearly the same as nothing, as: ***"To him that hath shall be given; from him that hath not, even that which he hath shall be taken away"*** (Matt. XIII. 12). Namely, of him having little; for otherwise it could not or could be taken from him who has nothing.

**(4) It is put for *of nothing*** — as **Matt. 23:14**, where it is placed for ***unjustly, in the way that it was placed to those who introduce innocent persons into the lower regions, as if nothing were being inflicted on them***. But these and other significations ***Flacius*** more accurately treated in his *Clavis* p. 735. It pleases to note the chief significations no less frequent in Philosophy than in Theology, and belonging to this place and consideration:

**(5)** First, ***nihil*** signifies the same as ***no being***, as: ***nihil est causa sui ipsius***. Whence Philosophers and Theologians rightly note that ***God is from Himself in a negative sense*** — that is, not from any other being — but not in an affirmative sense, since nothing is a principle producing itself.

**(6)** Secondly, it notes the same as ***no created being***, as when the Poet sings: ***"Nothing is in every part happy."*** Likewise, when it is said: ***"Without Him (the Λόγος) was made nothing that was made"*** (John 1:3).

**(7)** Thirdly, ***nihil simpliciter*** is of the same value as ***non-ens***: as ***τραγέλαφος (goat-stag) is nothing***, that is, non-ens. ***Purgatory is nothing***, ***Limbus Patrum is nothing***, ***Limbus Infantum is nothing***. ***These classes of the lower regions, which the Papists dream, are nothing*** — that is, no place is given in which, as in a prison after this life, souls are purged which in this life were not fully purged (that is, freed from sins) — however much the Papists set up this dogma for believing as so necessary that whoever denies it, him in gehenna they say must be tortured with everlasting burning. **Bellarmine** *De Purgatorio* I. 15. Nor is a place given into which they trivially introduce the souls of the Patriarchs and of all the Saints of the Old Testament before Christ's descent into the lower regions from the dead, which souls they assert to have borne in that place a temporal penalty of damnation, until, with the debt of original sin dissolved by Christ's death, they were freed from it and introduced to the fruition of celestial beatitude when Christ had descended into the lower regions. Nor is a middle place given between heaven and hell, in which neither well nor badly it goes with infants before baptism's use, whether in the maternal womb or dying immediately after birth. For our Theologians by many most solid arguments prove that such habitations are not at all given, but are pure fictions, partly Ethnic, partly Papist — so that the Papists, plainly unmindful of the base abuse of this axiom (***Non entis nulla sunt accidentia***), live when, e.g. they measure the times of penalties in purgatory as by a water-clock, and treat the various ***qualities*** and ***affections*** of them, which are altogether nothing.

**(8)** Fourthly, ***nihil*** argues the same as ***such-and-such non-ens***, e.g. ***"man, while he dies, goes into nothing,"*** yet he returns to dust. So it is said: ***"We know that an idol is nothing in the world"*** (1 Cor. VIII. 4) — as is plain from the context, when there is added: ***"and that there is no other God but one."***

**(9)** Fifthly, ***nihil*** is the same as ***no matter or no subject***, e.g. the more accurate Philosophers and Theologians say: ***prime matter, angel, and rational soul*** — and besides these, ***nothing***, that is, no other being — can be made ***from nothing***, that is, independently of every subject.

**(10)** Sixthly, ***nihil*** is the same as ***no preexisting matter***: thus Theologians, who believe heaven and earth were produced on the first day by God, explicate this proposition — ***"From nothing God made heaven and earth"*** — thus: God produced heaven and earth, when no being pre-existed (no matter, no subject) from which they could have been produced by God, that is, in whatever moment God made matter to exist, in the same moment He made it to exist under the form of heaven and earth. Others, who think light was produced first of all, say that God made light ***from nothing***, that is, independently of a pre-existing subject.

**(11)** Seventhly, ***nihil*** is the same as ***no suitable matter, no habile and disposed subject to a form***, that is, one in which the potency through which it concurs to the production of a form as subject or matter is not, except a very remote one — which is not simply to be called potency. For Theologians note in the locus ***De Creatione*** the production of a thing from a subject is twofold. First is the production of a thing from a ***suitable subject***, so that by the intervention of natural agents the potency of that matter can be led into act — and this production is ***generation*** rigorously and absolutely so-called, and this potency simply is called potency. Then another production is when something is produced from an ***unsuitable subject***, in which there is no potency except a remote one to the form. For ***remote potency*** is that which is not led into act except by the intervention of many acts and various mutations and alterations. And this production is called by the Theologians not generation but ***creation***, and that subject, because it is not suitable nor disposed to the form, is to them as it were ***non-ens*** and ***nothing***; and so the production of a thing from an unsuitable subject is to them as it were the production of a thing from nothing.

#### Note IX — Nihil Negativum vs. Nihil Privativum, and the Resurrection

**IX.** Perhaps there is no need to explicate at length the received distinction between ***nihil negativum*** and ***nihil privativum***. Thus by natural death man goes into ***nihil privativum***, not merely negative: for from man a cadaver comes to be. On the contrary, if God by His absolute potency should bring it about that some angel which already exists should cease to exist, that angel would go into ***nihil negativum***. Thus the Scholastics think a substance which goes into ***nihil privativum*** can be reproduced; a substance which goes into ***nihil negativum***, by no means. For when the Adversaries urge above others this argument:

> *Whatever is not reproduced by the same numerical action, that is not the same numerically. But a human body putrefied, or by whatever mode reduced to ashes, is not reproduced by the same numerical action. Therefore...*

And they prove the Major thus: action is for the sake of the effect, or for the sake of the thing produced (which they commonly call the ***term***); it is an influx by which being is communicated to the effect. If therefore it is not the same numerical action, the same numerical being cannot be communicated by it to the effect, and consequently it will not be the same numerical effect which is reproduced by it. The Minor they believe placed in confession: certainly, by a numerically different action is man generated and by a numerically different action is the dead one brought back to life — for that very action by which the body of man in the womb was formed, or by which man was first brought forth into the light, cannot by that potency be restored. This is what Nicodemus objected to Christ when He was inculcating ***regeneration***, **John 3:4**: ***"Can he enter again into his mother's womb and be born?"*** They confirm the matter thus: because action is not a thing, but the mode of a thing. But if the mode of a thing dies away, by no — not even by divine — potency can the same numerical be reproduced.

In order to respond to this argument the more accurate Theologians judge that it must be distinguished between the ***reproduction of that which is reduced to nihil negativum*** and ***of that which is reduced to nihil privativum*** — that is, into principles and elements, or into the matter from which it was composed. If the Major be understood of the reduction of something which is placed to have been reduced to nihil negativum, then they do not indeed concede it, but neither do they rashly deny it. For it does not appear to them how that which is reduced into nihil negativum can be produced the same numerically — since nothing of it survives, and by a numerically different action is the operation needed by which it may be reproduced. For if God's potency should destroy and annihilate an angel, and again produce one, since not by the same numerical action by which the angel was first established, so neither would he be reproduced numerically the same. But they dismiss this sense. For here the question for them is of the reproduction of the dead human body. But the human body in death is not annihilated, but only by putrefaction is resolved into principles and elements from which it was composed. Therefore the Major too is precisely to be understood of the reproduction of that which is resolved into matter and elements from which it had been composed. And in this manner the Major will be false. For whatever is resolved and has been resolved into its matter and elements, although it be reproduced by a numerically different action, nevertheless to that extent returns the same numerically, in so far as it is educed from the potency of the same numerical matter.

To the proof too they respond by distinguishing: either the action of the efficient cause by which that which has been extinct is reproduced depends on no matter, or it comes about with dependence on matter. If it depends on no matter, as creation or the production of something from nothing, by a numerically different action a numerically different effect to be produced they do not deny — since indeed every being which is now by action communicated to the effect must be numerically different. But if the action of the efficient cause comes about with dependence on matter, they ask again: whether it depend on the same numerical matter into which the body by putrefaction was resolved, or on a different numerical matter? If on a different, that by a numerically different action a numerically different effect be produced does not seem rashly to be denied. For example, if not from the same numerical ashes into which Paul's body was converted, but from any other matter whatsoever, a human body were produced — even if in figure, magnitude, temperament, countenance, color, and all lineaments it were similar to Paul's body — nevertheless it could not be judged the same numerical body which Paul had when he lived, because the being which through the action with dependence on different matter is poured into the effect is now different not only on the part of the action, but on the part of the numerically different matter. But if the action of the efficient cause takes place with dependence on the ***same numerical matter*** — as the resurrection of the dead — then by a numerically different action it does not repugn that the same numerical effect be reproduced. For the effect is wholly from the efficient cause; it is also wholly from the matter. Therefore also the same numerical being is communicated to the effect by each cause, albeit by one or another reason and causality of causing. Set down therefore: that the efficient cause acts through a numerically different action — if it nevertheless acts upon the same numerical matter, it will communicate to that extent the same numerical being, in so far as from the same numerical matter it has reproduced the lost form.

Philosophers say that material forms in corruption fall back into the potency of matter, and in generation are educed from the potency of matter. If therefore what has been destroyed and resolved into matter is reproduced from the same numerical matter with slight mutation, it will be the same numerically. For example: if a house be resolved into its material parts, and from these in turn be composed, no other numerical matter being assumed, then it will be the same numerical house. Likewise if water be converted into air, and the air again into water, the same numerical water will return. In both cases the action is numerically different by which both house and water are reproduced; yet on this account it is judged that the same numerical house and the same numerical water return, because from the potency of the same numerical matter the form of water and the figure of the house is again educed. And the reason is at hand why a numerically different action is no obstacle, so long as it come about with dependence on the same numerical matter: the efficient cause and its action do not enter into the essence of the effect. But if the effect is a composite something, so long as it exists, it consists of and depends upon matter. Whence, that the same numerical composite be reproduced, above all is required the ***same numerical matter*** — not withstanding that on the part of the efficient cause the action be numerically different, since with the composite produced the action ceases, but remains in the matter itself.

For which reason the ***foundation of the resurrection of the same numerical flesh***, orthodox Theologians sedulously inculcate, lies in this: that the bodies of the dead are reproduced by God's potency from the same numerical matter into which they have been resolved by putrefaction — which the ancient Fathers acknowledged. Whence, as often as it was to be disputed by them against the Ethnics, the same numerical matter, the same numerical ashes, they placed as the foundation. ***Tertullian*** De Resurrectione c. 63 writes: ***"Not only is the soul set aside; the flesh too has its bosom meanwhile — in waters, in fires, in birds, in beasts — when it seems to be dissolved into these, it is as if poured into vessels. If also those vessels have failed, when it has flowed out of them into their matrix the earth, as it were by circuits it is written back, that from it again it may be represented."*** And ***Augustine*** De Civitate Dei XXII c. 20 art. 1: ***"Far be it, however, that for the resuscitation of bodies and the restoring of life, the omnipotence of the Creator cannot recall all things which either beast, or fish, or fire has consumed, or whatever has collapsed into dust and ashes, or has been resolved into moisture, or has been exhaled into the breezes. Far be it that any bosom or secret of nature so receive anything subtracted from our senses, as to lie hid from the knowledge or escape the potency of the Creator of all."*** Cf. also his Commentary on Psalm 62.

## Caput Tertium

### Of Essence in the Formal Reason

#### § 1

> ***The notion of essence admits a twofold signification, both frequent in use and most necessary to be known. Of the prior — namely as it signifies the same as true and real existence — treatment has been given in the preceding chapter. Of the posterior — namely when it is received, as it is of the same value as "the first concept of a true being" — treatment will be given in this chapter.***

#### Notes

**I.** To scarcely anyone easily can this signification of essence be unknown, when ***essence is said to be the first concept of a true and real being***. This formula indeed owes its birth to the ***Scholastic Philosophy***, and rightly explicated can be admitted, chiefly because continuous use approves it.

**II.** As therefore two things are required for essence so taken — (α) that it be the concept of a true and real being, (β) that it be the ***first concept*** — so it altogether behooves us to leave a sufficiently suitable and distinct explication of each requirement briefly.

**III.** ***Scholastic authors*** have been the makers of the distinction between ***conceptus formalis*** and ***conceptus objectivus***. ***Conceptus formalis*** they call the ***cognition that comes about through the intellect***. For when through our intellect we know something, we are said to ***conceive*** it, and the intellect is said to conceive it; and so the very cognition of a thing is called ***the concept of the thing***. For example, when we know animal to be a natural mixed animated sentient body, the ***concept of animal*** is called that act by which the intellect knew of animal that it is a natural mixed animated sentient body. With deliberation we say: ***the formal concept in the Schools is called the cognition which comes about through the intellect***. For although elsewhere a twofold cognition is given — one whose principle is the intellect; the other whose principle is the sense — use has obtained that the former, not the latter, be judged under such a name.

**IV.** ***Conceptus objectivus*** the Scholastics call ***that which is known through the intellect, in so far as it is known through the intellect***. For example, of animal is known through the intellect that it is a natural mixed animated sentient body; whence the complex of these predicates, in so far as it is known of animal, is called by the Scholastics the ***objective concept of animal***.

**V.** More rightly might it be called ***the object of the concept*** — that is, the object of cognition that comes about through the intellect — than if it be called ***objective concept***. For when of animal it is known that it is a natural mixed animated sentient body, surely each one gathers that the object of cognition formed about animal is these very predicates taken simultaneously: natural mixed animated sentient body. Hence also the Scholastics call the ***formal concept*** the very cognition that comes about through the intellect, because when I conceive a thing through the intellect, the act by which I conceive the thing is, according to itself and the thing's truth, a conception — that is, a cognition that comes about through the intellect. But why they call the thing which is known through the intellect — in so far as it is known through the intellect — the ***objective concept***, each one easily attains, since (as we said) the thing is to that extent the object of cognition. But because terms and notions are not accepted as it pleases, but as use permits — and this distinction, received by use, has long been in the Schools of ***Philosophers and Theologians*** and frequently occurs in their writings and chairs — we deservedly retain it, and under this title we have judged it worthy of explication.

**VI.** Let the judgment be the same about ***notion***, likewise ***intention***, when in the Schools between ***formal notion*** and ***objective notion***, between ***formal intention*** and ***objective intention*** a distinction is made. For ***concept***, ***notion***, ***intention*** are here taken for the same thing: when the intellect knows something, it is said to tend into it, so that ***intention*** in the present signifies the act of the intellect, not of the will.

**VII.** From what has thus far been adduced, it flows of its own accord that by ***conceptus*** in the delineation of essence is to be understood not the ***formal concept***, but the ***objective concept***. Thus when it is commonly said that the first concept of animal is natural mixed animated sentient body, the sense cannot be that the ***cognition*** (by which it is known that animal is a natural mixed animated sentient body) is the essence of animal — since animal is a substance, but that cognition (which they call the formal concept of animal) is a true and real accident. Here therefore the sense is left: that the ***objective concept of animal*** — that is, the object of cognition of animal, namely natural mixed animated sentient body — is the essence of animal.

**VIII.** Further, essence was said to be the concept ***of a true and real being***. For not of each and every thing — whether it be a true and real being or not — is the first concept at once to be judged under the name of essence, as in the following will be said.

#### § 2

> ***The notion of "first concept" — namely whence the objective concept has this, that it is called "first" — deserves more accurate explication. Three things are required for an objective concept to be FIRST:***
>
> ***I. That it be the OBJECT OF TRUE COGNITION — namely, cognition to which there corresponds a true affirmative finite proposition. Thus for example a stone does not pertain to the first concept of animal, because when a stone is the object of a cognition formed concerning animal, cognition of this kind — such as that this cognition about animal is — is a FALSE COGNITION, and so a stone exists as the object of false cognition.***
>
> ***II. That it be the OBJECT OF NECESSARY COGNITION — that is, of a cognition necessarily true. Thus when I think of animal that it is DOCILE, the-docile cannot pertain to the first concept of animal, because, although it can be truly known of animal that it is docile, that cognition is not necessarily but contingently true — that is, so true that it can also be false.***
>
> ***III. That it be the OBJECT OF A COGNITION WHOSE REASON CANNOT BE GIVEN A PRIORI. Thus for example when I know animal to be MOBILE, CORRUPTIBLE, LIVING, APPETITIVE — and the like — these predicates cannot pertain to the first concept of animal. For an a priori reason can be given why animal necessarily is mobile, corruptible, living, appetitive — namely because it is a natural mixed animated sentient body. From which it is plain that nothing pertains to essence except what is apt to be predicated of a being truly, necessarily, and as its reason a priori.***

#### Note

Other significations of ***conceptus formalis*** occur in the Schools of Metaphysicians, concerning which in the following chapter it will be looked into.

#### § 3

> ***Essence, when it is called the first concept of a thing — namely of that thing which is a true and real being — is in turn taken in two modes: (1) for the WHOLE first concept of a real being; (2) for the first concept of a real being, not however the whole, but only the proprium. For example: the essence of animal is now said to be placed in that it is a natural mixed animated sentient body; now precisely in that it is SENTIENT. Each is most rightly asserted.***

#### Notes

**I.** The Scholastics distinguish between the ***total or adequate first concept*** and the ***partial or inadequate first concept***. The former is called the complex of all those true and necessary predicates of some thing of which an a priori reason cannot be given. The ***partial first concept*** the Scholastics call that which argues not all true and necessary predicates whose a priori reason cannot be given, but at least one or only some. For example, when I know animal to be a ***natural body***, "natural body" is a partial first concept of animal. So the partial first concept of animal is given when I know of animal that it is an animated body, or that precisely I know it is sentient.

**II.** Not every partial first concept is wont to be called essence, but ***the most proper partial first concept of the being whose first concept it is***. Thus they rightly judge who say the essence of animal is placed in this, that it is ***sentient*** — provided they understand by the essence of animal the first proper concept, plainly contradistinct from the first common concept. For the remaining predicates all, which equally pertain to the first concept of animal, are parts of the common concept. On the contrary, ***animated*** cannot be called the essence of animal, much less ***mixed*** or ***natural body***; indeed, not even ***natural mixed body*** can be judged under this name.

#### § 4

> ***These things are better perceived if the distinction of the partial or inadequate first concept into RECIPROCAL and NON-RECIPROCAL be adduced. For example: the reciprocal inadequate first concept of animal is SENTIENT; the non-reciprocal is NATURAL BODY. For not every natural body is animal; but every sentient thing is animal — that is, animal and sentient lie equally wide, but natural body and animal do not likewise.***

#### Notes

**I.** By the name ***essence*** comes therefore at least that partial first concept, or (which comes to the same) that part of the first concept which is reciprocal — such as is only the most proper and ultimate difference. For example: sentient with respect to animal.

**II.** Nor let anyone wonder why that part of the first concept, and not likewise the others, can undergo the denomination of ***essence***. For this part necessarily prerequires and presupposes all and single the remaining parts of the first concept — which cannot be said of any of the remaining parts, whether considered separately or conjunctly, because they always import a common concept in which the thing (of whose essence it is asked) agrees with others.

#### § 5

> ***Let the cultivators of more accurate Philosophy therefore beware lest they confuse among themselves: TO BE THE ESSENCE ITSELF, TO BE OF THE ESSENCE, TO PERTAIN TO THE ESSENCE.***
>
> ***To be the essence itself either notes the same as "to be the whole first concept of the thing," or signifies nothing else than "to be the partial first concept of the thing" — not however, except that one which is MOST PROPER to the thing whose first concept it is said to be.***
>
> ***To be OF THE ESSENCE imports the same as "to be a PART of the first concept of the thing." Thus for example: of the essence of animal is NATURAL BODY, of the essence of animal is MIXED, of the essence of animal is ANIMATED, of the essence of animal is SENTIENT — because all these when considered separately argue such things as deserve to be called parts of the first concept of animal.***
>
> ***To PERTAIN to the essence is called all that which notes the FIRST CONCEPT of a being, whether in whole or in part; or, what is the same, whatever is the object of true, necessary cognition of a true and real being, whose reason a priori cannot be given — whether something else likewise is the object of cognition of such kind, or not. Examples can be sought with easy business from what has been said.***

#### § 6

> ***RATIO FORMALIS and ESSENTIA differ: for ratio formalis lies more widely than essence, because every ESSENCE is a RATIO FORMALIS, but not every ratio formalis is an essence. For essence, speaking rigorously, notes the first concept of a BEING; ratio formalis says the first concept of a THING, whether it be a being or not. For example: the ratio formalis of BLINDNESS consists in this, that it is the absence of sight from an animal capable of sight by nature. So DARKNESS, DEATH, MORAL MALICE have their own rationes formales, but have no essences.***

#### Notes

**I.** This distinction between a ratio formalis which is simultaneously an essence, and a ratio formalis which is not an essence, has its own foundation. For the distinction between ***real*** and ***real being*** is not from nothing, as above p. 219 ff. was shown.

**II.** As therefore essence is one thing, what is of essence is another, what pertains to essence is another — so ***ratio formalis*** is one thing, what is of the ratio formalis is another, what pertains to the ratio formalis is another.

**III.** Sometimes ***essence*** and ***ratio formalis*** are taken for the same.

**IV.** The use of this chapter and the practical examples bearing on it will be shown in the following chapter.

## Caput Quartum

### Of the Notion "FORMALITER" in Received and Frequent Significations; Likewise of the Notions Opposed to This Notion

#### § 1

> ***It behooves the cultivator of more accurate Philosophy, and the genuine auditor and cultivator of any Faculty, to procure for himself knowledge of the various significations of the Metaphysical adverb FORMALITER — a notion whose use is various and frequent, and of which it cannot be denied that its signification, less rightly understood or infelicitly applied to a certain matter, has brought forth many difficulties, trifles, and absurdities.***

#### § 2

> ***(1) In the first place — I think, that we not expound all, but only the more frequent acceptations — FORMALITER often notes the same as "per rei existentiam aut veritatem" (through the existence or truth of a thing). For example: the Aristotelians treated whether the Sun is formally hot. The genus of the question is this: Does heat, with the truth of the matter saved, belong to the Sun — that is, does it really exist in the Sun?***
>
> ***The Scholastics here use this notion of the Metaphysical adverb just now explicated, and judge that from Aristotle's mind it must be said that the Sun is not formally hot — i.e. that heat does not really belong to the Sun — since heat is an elementary quality congregating homogeneous things and segregating heterogeneous; but Aristotle held heaven and heavenly bodies, and so also the Sun, to be simple bodies and of a quintessence (i.e. plainly distinct from the four elements), such that according to Aristotle's Philosophy they share nothing of the elements and elementary qualities.***

#### Note

Let there be another example. To the question: ***Are the physical perfections of creatures in God?*** — the Scholastics judge the response must be: ***the physical perfections of creatures*** (that is, that which is formally in creatures) ***are formally said not to be, nor to be able to be, in God*** — because, as they are physical perfections of creatures, they are ***created*** perfections; but God, as pure act (as the Schools speak) and so completely devoid of all passive potency, cannot receive anything created, nay cannot receive anything at all in Himself.

#### § 3

> ***To this notion of FORMALITER so explicated is opposed another Metaphysical adverb: EMINENTER. Something is said to be in another EMINENTLY, or to belong to someone eminently, when, according to the existence or truth of the thing, it is not in him nor belongs to him, nor perhaps can be in him or belong to him, yet in him there is something — or there belongs to him — something more noble or eminent, namely some noble or eminent force or virtue of producing that outside himself (which on that account is said to be in him EMINENTLY).***
>
> ***For example: the Scholastics, to the question whether the Sun is formally hot or not, respond that the Sun is not formally hot, but EMINENTER — that is, in the Sun there is no heat, but in the Sun there is a certain more eminent power by which the heat, which it does not have in itself, it can excite and produce in things of inferior nature, which they call sublunary.***

#### Notes

**I.** The adverbs ***EMINENTER*** and ***VIRTUALITER*** very often have plainly the same signification, so that *virtualiter* signifies the same as what we have just signified by the adverb *eminenter*.

**II.** By one or two practical examples we shall make the doctrine more illustrious. Thus, for example, a question is wont to be moved in Theology — which can be moved in other practical disciplines with suitable changes — namely: ***Is Theology a merely practical habitus, and the discipline that corresponds to it a merely practical discipline?*** There have been those who denied this, relying on this argument:

> *Many propositions are given in Theology which are plainly not practical. Therefore Theology is not merely practical.*

If to this argument we wish to respond, following the more accurate Doctors, we use the distinction adduced in the present §, and say that one proposition occurring in Theology (and the same judgment is to be had of Jurisprudence, Ethics, Politics) is ***formally practical***, another is ***eminenter or virtualiter practical***. And so no proposition pertains ***per se*** to the Theological Discipline unless it be practical, if not formally, at least virtually. Namely, just as the Sun was said not to be formally hot, yet to be able to effect heat, so many propositions in Theology are not formally practical, yet can effect practical propositions, if they be joined with other propositions formally practical and be made premises in Theological syllogisms. By a single example it pleases to illustrate this assertion. Thus for example this proposition: ***"Everyone truly believing in Christ is redeemed by the merit of Christ"*** is not formally practical. The reason is that this proposition dictates nothing to be committed or omitted. It remains meanwhile ***virtually practical***, which must be seen in this: if we join it to a formally-practical proposition, from it arises a third proposition or conclusion, and indeed a formally-practical conclusion. Let us make the trial:

> **Major:** *Whoever is redeemed by Christ's merit (from the power of sin, death, and the Devil) ought to love Christ above all things.*
> **Minor:** *Every believer in Christ is redeemed by Christ's merit (from the power of sin, death, and the Devil).*
> **Conclusion:** *Therefore every believer in Christ ought to love Christ above all things.*

Behold a formally-practical proposition drawn from a proposition which was not formally practical, yet joined to a formally-practical proposition — and it suffices for the Minor proposition that it be called virtually practical by the Theologians. Such ***virtually practical propositions*** certainly occur most frequently not only in Theology, but also in every practical discipline and in the doctrine of any department of law, and must be sought by all cultivators of such disciplines, if they will rightly consult their own studies.

— ❦ —
