#### Note III of § 3 — Bellarmine/Becanus Controversy on Individual Certainty of Salvation

Thus the Papists and our Theologians are in controversy among themselves: ***Can a true Christian and pious man be certain in the individual of his future eternal salvation*** — that is, can he be certain of the truth of this proposition which he forms about himself: ***"I shall be saved eternally"?*** Those [the Papists] maintain the ***negative***, that apart from a special revelation of God (on this the hinge of the controversy turns) ***no one can in the individual be certainly assured of his future eternal salvation***. We [the Lutherans] hold and defend the contrary and orthodox sentence.

Among other arguments ***Becanus*** in his *Manual* against our Theologians also urges this: ***Nothing is to be believed by true faith unless God has revealed it. But God has revealed neither to Luther nor to you that you shall be saved — for where does this revelation stand? Therefore...*** The Major he holds as manifest, because the ***adequate object of true and saving faith is divine revelation***.

To this argument, when our Theologians respond, again they egregiously commend the use of the rightly understood and from Metaphysics happily perceived distinction between that which is said to be ***virtualiter such*** and that which ***formaliter is such and ought to be called***. Namely: orthodox Theologians distinguish between ***formal revelation*** or ***formally revealed***, and ***virtual revelation*** or ***virtually revealed***.

If Becanus's argument be understood of ***formally revealed*** only, they ***concede the Minor***, but they ***deny and persistently deny the Major***. But if of ***formally and simultaneously virtually revealed*** — that is, if the Major and the whole of Becanus's argument be received of revelation of each mode — then our Theologians ***admit the Major***, but say ***the Minor to be most false***. These things we adduce not to send a sickle into another's harvest, but that we may teach the more happily we could reap the fruits of Theological wisdom if we had properly provided for ourselves in Metaphysics.

#### The Spiritus-Sanctus-Verus-Deus Syllogisms

An outstanding question is in fact to be sought: ***Whence can it be certainly established that some proposition is of saving faith?*** Certainly not only propositions which formally stand in Sacred Scripture and are revealed are of saving faith, but also those which are ***virtually*** revealed. Often a proposition is not extant in Sacred Scripture, but there are other propositions extant in Sacred Scripture which, premised, from them that proposition which is not extant is most rightly inferred. Often only one of the premises is extant in Sacred Scripture, not both — nor the conclusion. And although often only the Minor is extant, if nevertheless the Major, which is not found in the sacred code, be simply of absolute necessity and true in every genus, still (with truth saved and so-to-be-said) the conclusion ***virtually*** is had in Sacred Scripture.

Likewise it comes about not rarely that the Major proposition and that alone is ***formally*** in Sacred Scripture, so that nevertheless concerning the subsumption anyone can be most certain, although the subsumption formally does not stand in the Sacred books; so still the conclusion ***virtually*** is said to exist in Sacred Scripture. Nay it comes about also that neither of the premises is in Sacred Scripture, nor is the conclusion in it; yet still the conclusion is of Sacred Scripture together with the premises — because namely in Sacred Scripture there were propositions from which each of the premises (which do not expressly stand in the Sacred code) could or ought have been inferred.

Thus, for example, even if the proposition ***"The Holy Spirit is true GOD"*** did not formally and expressly stand in Sacred Scripture, it would be enough for this — that it be called a proposition of Sacred Scripture — that the premises from which this proposition is most rightly inferred and concluded be revealed in Sacred Scripture. Thus at **Acts V. 3 and 4**, joined, are both premises found. The ***Minor*** when Peter says that ***Ananias had lied to the Holy Spirit***. The ***Major*** when Peter asserts that ***Ananias had not lied to men, but to GOD***. The whole argument, which orthodox Theologians by unanimous consent so judge, most firmly concludes, if each of the premises is understood of Him to whom Ananias chiefly lied:

> *To whomever besides the Apostles Ananias lied, he is true GOD. But to the Holy Spirit besides the Apostles Ananias lied. Therefore the Holy Spirit is true GOD.*

The Major is plain from v. 4. The Minor from v. 3 of the same place.

So also from various places of Sacred Scripture the Venerable Theologians fetch the premises. For example, the Minor is had **Hebrews III. 7, 8, 9**; the Major **Psalm XCV. 10**; whence the argument comes to be, having this form:

> *Whomever the Israelites tempted in the desert, proved, saw His works, and with whom He was offended — he is true God. But the Holy Spirit the Israelites tempted in the desert, proved, etc. Therefore the Holy Spirit is true GOD.*

#### Three Chemnitz-Musaeus Trinitarian Syllogisms Against Vedelius

Further let us adduce examples of this kind where the Minor is of Sacred Scripture, but the Major is extrinsically assumed, and nevertheless the conclusion remains proper to Sacred Scripture. Let us hear especially the Most Venerable ***Herr D. Johann Musaeus*** in his treatise ***On the Use of Rational Principles by the Philosopher in Theological Controversies, Against Nicolaus Vedelius***, so disputing:

> ***"From the disputations which, as from times long ago, so no less in our age, the Doctors of the Church have published against the heterodox, it stands sufficiently clear that for the inference of a Theological conclusion they sometimes have taken ***one proposition from Scripture, and the other from reason***. For example: Sacred Scripture, when it teaches*** ***that God the Father from eternity begot the Son; that Christ is the true Son of God, God and man***, ***supplies three principles from which the Theologians build up three arguments, so that with each one they conjoin another drawn from reason, and nonetheless infer a THEOLOGICAL CONCLUSION***."***

**From the first — against the Sabellians** — thus they infer:

> *Those of which one is begetting and the other begotten, they differ really. But Father and Son in divinis are begetting and begotten. Therefore Father and Son in divinis differ really.*

**From the second — against the Arians** — thus:

> *A true son is of the same essence with his Father. Christ is the true Son of God. Therefore Christ is of the same essence with His Father.*

**From the third — against the Monophysites** — thus:

> *In which person there is one nature and in turn another distinct from the prior, in that person there are two natures. But in the Person who is Christ, there is one nature — namely divine (since He is true God) — and in turn another distinct from the prior, namely human (since He is likewise true man). Therefore in the Person who is Christ there are two natures.*

These are had **lib. II c. XI. 3 p. 419 and 420**, where several things may be consulted.

#### The *Virtualia Vi Formae Syllogisticae* Principle

Meanwhile it appears most luculently from what has just been adduced that a Theological conclusion is given, although the Major be extrinsically assumed — provided the Minor be Theological, and the Major (as above was said) be ***simply and most highly necessary***, so that not even by GOD's potency can it have itself otherwise. Of this kind of highly necessary and evident propositions were those just adduced: *Those of which one is begetting and the other begotten, differ really; A true son is of the same essence with his Father; In which person there is one nature and in turn another distinct from the prior, in that person there are two natures.* Nor shall we fetch from afar the reason, which the praised Man of the same chapter § 9 subjoins — and this most solidly:

> ***"The reason is because the union of the middle with one extreme, and the union of the extremes with each other, VIRTUALITER by the force of syllogistic form include the union of the middle with the other extreme. For example: if in the antecedent between the middle and one extreme (e.g. the minor extreme), as also in the consequent between each extreme, there is identity, it is necessary by the force of form that between the middle and the other extreme (e.g. the major) there be identity; or if in the antecedent between the middle and one (e.g. the minor) extreme there be identity, but in the consequent between each extreme there be division, it is necessary that also between the middle and the other extreme (e.g. the major) there be division," etc.***

#### The Photinian Error Against Finite Essences

On the contrary, when the Major proposition which is extrinsically assumed is not ***highly and absolutely necessary***, but only physically, or in a certain genus of things, or only probable — then what is inferred the orthodox Theologians deny to be of divine faith, since it is not collected by a ***necessary and evident consequence***. Thus badly the Photinians conclude:

> *Whoever has one essence, has also one subsistence. But God has one essence. Therefore God has one subsistence.*

For the Major proposition is necessary only in the genus of ***finite essences***. But what repugns a finite essence can well agree with the ***infinite*** essence of God. Just as what repugns a finite potency can agree with God's infinite potency.

#### The Minor-of-Scripture + Major-Extrinsic Case — The Vere-Credens-Peccata-Remissa Syllogism

So we have seen examples of conclusions of Scripture, likewise Theological, which required (that they be such) that the ***Minor propositions*** exist in the Sacred Code and be Theological. Further, not rarely the Major proposition at least is formally revealed in Sacred Scripture, with the Minor extrinsically assumed. For example: this ***Major*** is formally revealed in Sacred Scripture: ***"Whoever believes in Christ, his sins are forgiven him"*** (**Acts XIII. 38**, likewise **Acts X. 43**, likewise **Rom. III. 22**). Each true believer in Christ makes the subsumption or Minor proposition thus: ***"I believe in Christ."*** And because this subsumption is true and certain, the conclusion stands which the true believer in Christ thus forms: ***"Therefore my sins are forgiven me."*** The subsumption is not in Sacred Scripture ***formally*** revealed; there is nevertheless ***virtual revelation***. This the Venerable Theologians teach us from several places of Sacred Scripture. It will be lawful to adduce one by way of best example:

> *Whoever being endowed with the adoption-Spirit truly can call "Abba, Father," he too is certain to himself that sins are remitted to him on account of the same Spirit of adoption. But to each true believer in Christ the Holy Spirit testifies etc. Therefore...*

The ***Minor*** is of Sacred Scripture itself. The ***Major***, as orthodox Theologians teach us, is evident, because to be a son of God ***presupposes*** the remission of sins — since no one can be a son of God, nor with true faith call God his Father, unless sins have been forgiven him; and no one can believe that he is a son of God unless he also believes that his sins are forgiven him.

And this is what above was adduced from the Venerable Theologians' writings: that saving faith has for its object not only ***formal revelation*** and that which is formally revealed, but also ***virtual revelation*** and that which is virtually revealed — ***formally revealed*** for its immediate object, ***virtually revealed*** for its mediate object.

Scarcely need we adduce examples of Theological conclusions whose premises are not even formally extant in Sacred Scripture, yet other premises are contained in it, from which these premises as conclusions are inferred — since such examples it is of easiest labor to find, nor does the narrowness of a page dedicated to other matters contain them. We remit the eager and benevolent reader to the egregious and most useful ***Theological Dissertation*** on the question: ***Whether, apart from a special revelation of GOD, a Christian can from the word of God be certain of his eternal salvation?*** held in the prior year under the presidency of the most Venerable ***Herr D. Friedemann Bechmann***, from whose fifth section it will be easy to seek these matters, since the whole dissertation at once by a signal example declares the use of the present notion ***FORMALITER*** — as can be seen most luculently from § 1-10 of the first section.

#### The Civil-Law Parallel — Methodological Lesson

**V.** Another thing we must give warning of: whatever hitherto we have discussed somewhat prolixly concerning the use of the present notion and its opposite signification in the study of Theology and the erudite reading of Sacred Scripture, let not those neglect — that future cultivators of Civil Law may equally and perhaps more properly take hold of its use — to apply the ***file of judgment***. For as in Sacred Scripture, so also in the books of Roman Law — or in what is commonly called the ***Corpus Juris*** — altogether many things are extant that stand ***formally***, so that nevertheless ***virtually*** other things no less of this civil law are had in them; others, which contrarily nowhere in the Corpus Juris formally stand, however virtually are therein contained. The same judgment is to be had of the writings of ***Doctors*** who treat ex professo of some practical doctrine. For here commonly it is said: ***the mind of this or that Doctor is this; this or that he willed; these things he pedlared for truth, and so with truth saved it is pronounced***, although many times formally these things are not had in the Author himself nor were formally proposed by him. For solemn and perpetual it is to the Cultivators and Doctors of all faculties and disciplines, and ought to be, to ***distinguish between principles and conclusions***, nor does it appear how they can fulfill the office of a Doctor, or in a cathedra or on a pulpit rightly discharge it, unless they most carefully know how to distinguish between propositions ***formally*** extant in the text and in the writings of others, and those which ***virtually*** are contained in them, and join the latter to the former.

Meanwhile a great abuse is often noticed, when now ***virtually contained*** are said those which through no — not even probable — consequence are judged necessarily to follow (which could scarcely be inferred by a probable consequence); now altogether ***virtually contained*** are conclusions of this kind which others, against the testimony of their own conscience or even without judgment, had denied are therein contained. Each vice certainly is the more to be detested, the graver errors and more acerb controversies it can cause.

#### § 4

> ***FORMALITER (2) often signifies the WHOLE RATIO FORMALIS of a thing — that is, as the Scholastics speak, the FIRST and SIMULTANEOUSLY TOTAL or ADEQUATE concept of the thing. Therefore the genuine use of this notion, taken in this second mode, shows itself if to the question "What FORMALITER is this or that?" the response be made through the WHOLE RATIO FORMALIS. For example, when it is asked WHAT FORMALITER IS ANIMAL? the common response is: a natural mixed animated sentient body.***

#### Notes

**I.** It pleases to adduce one or another practical example easier of perception. Let us take a ***Theological example***. In Theology it is asked: ***What is predestination?*** Or (which comes to the same): ***What is the essential definition of predestination theologically received?***

Here the one willing to respond accurately and distinctly Theologically — but so as to respond Metaphysically (one thing being to respond out of Metaphysics, another to Metaphysically) — ought first to inquire into the ***genus*** of predestination. For that is first which is placed in the response to such a question: ***What then is predestination?*** No one even lightly versed in Theology would doubt that it is an ***action***. Now it is asked further: ***But of what is it the action?*** For every action respects an ***external cause***, which is thence denominated the agent cause. Of what therefore is this action, which is called predestination? Of an ***intelligent substance***. For of substances lacking intellect it is not to predestine anything. Further is asked: ***What sort of action is it?*** Is it ***external*** — i.e. outside the agent — or ***in the agent***? ***Internal***. For where would it be, if it were outside the agent? Further is asked: Since the action internal proper to an intelligent substance is at least twofold — ***intellection*** and ***voluntary internal action*** (for whatever has intellect, has also will) — is predestination intellection, or an action internal of the will? ***An action internal of the will***. There indeed concur in every predestination diverse internal acts, which partly pertain to the intellect, partly to the will. But the ultimate act, as we shall soon see, is of the will. Again it is asked: ***What sort of act?*** ***Volition*** or ***nolition***? Volition. ***What sort of volition***? Volition of effecting some thing. In what manner is such volition called, if we wish to express it by one name sufficiently fitting? ***Decree***. Therefore we now have the ***proximate genus*** of predestination — which, lest the discourse grow too much (which should indicate the whole ratio formalis of predestination), lest it be deprived of its ornament (which is brevity), is deservedly placed in it. That predestination is a ***decree*** is to be learned from the very voice and nominal definition of predestination. The voice itself scarcely occurs in secular authors, but is frequent in Ecclesiastical Writers, and denotes the same as the Greek word ***προορισμός***. Yet the verb ***destinare*** is frequently read in profane authors, and commonly to them notes the same as ***decernere animo***. Thus in Cicero it is said ***destinare diem necis***, that is, to decree a certain day on which someone is to be delivered to death. The particle ***prae*** denotes some priority — namely a priority of duration — which intercedes between the destination of the thing and the thing itself destined; so predestination by force of the word is the destination of a thing or person or ordination to a certain end before the thing or person itself was. But in Sacred Scripture the word is received of things and of persons.

Since therefore decree is truly and necessarily predicated of predestination, and in the genus of decree lies open wider than predestination, decree will be the ***genus*** of predestination. With the genus perceived, we must think about the ***differentiae*** to be found.

**Towards what** does predestination tend as it is precisely received at present? And of this first of all we must now look, partly for this cause: that in the ***essential definitions*** of practical disciplines which must be investigated, always the chief respect must be had to the ***end***, as in the preceding chapters we have taught; partly because predestination, by force of the word, is the destination or ordination of a thing or person to some certain end, as we have just said. ***Predestination is the destination of man to eternal life***. For by the Style of Sacred Scripture (as orthodox Theologians teach us), ***predestination***, taken for the destination of man absolutely and without any addition, never denotes the destination of man ***to eternal damnation***, but always imports either ***the preparation of grace*** or ***the ordination or destination of man to eternal life***. And this now, as it is received, is the final absolute end, i.e. the essential ultimate end: ***eternal life*** — as the places of Sacred Scripture openly indicate (from which indeed the venerable Theologians teach us the truth of this assertion): **Acts XIII. 48**: *"They believed, as many as were ordained to eternal life"*; and **1 Thess. V. 9**: *"God has appointed us, that we should obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ."*

Further: ***Of whom is predestination?*** (Or what comes to the same: ***What is the object of predestination?***) Predestination is a decree concerning eternal salvation to be conferred on men; and so it is of men — that is, the matter of predestination is men — as from the just cited places of Scripture, likewise **Romans VIII. 29**, manifestly stands. But is predestination of all men? Not of all, but of a few (**Matt. XX. 16**; likewise **XXII. 14**). For not all men become saved in time (**Matt. VII. 13-14**). Therefore neither were all from eternity predestined to eternal salvation. For the execution of a divine decree cannot not be conformed to the decree itself, so that in time no one is saved save him concerning whose eternal salvation to be conferred on himself God has from eternity decreed. But why from eternity is predestination not of all but of a few? The cause is not in the predestining God or in some absolute good-pleasure of His, but in the ***incredulity of men*** malignly resisting the voice of the Gospel calling them. For ***God so loved the world that He gave His Only-begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish, but have eternal life*** (**John III. 16**). Therefore none are predestined to eternal salvation except believers in Christ. But are all believers predestined? By no means, but only ***final*** believers (**Matt. X. 22**; **XXIV. 13**; **Mark XIII. 13**).

The ***object*** of predestination therefore is: sinful men. The ***reason under which*** (in the Schools called the ratio formalis objectiva) predestination is of sinful men — that is, under which sinful men are predestined — is: ***final faith foreseen by God from eternity***. And so the object of predestination is sinful men ***few*** with respect to the called, or also with respect to the wicked, and those who depart from this life without true faith in Christ (whose number is far greater), ***whom God foresaw to be final believers in Christ*** (**Rom. VIII. 29 ff.**).

But those who maliciously resist the divine will, who contemn the means of salvation, and persevere in their incredulity — these by their own fault perish, and their foreseen resistance and perseverance in incredulity is the cause why from eternity they were not predestined. And in this sense commonly the ***material object*** of predestination is called sinful men, and the ***formal object*** is final faith foreseen by God from eternity. For from this — that men are considered in God's eternal foreknowledge as miserable sinners — it is not permitted to infer that they were not considered as finally going to believe in Christ.

It is easy now to say ***by whom is predestination made?*** By God. God is the ***efficient cause*** of predestination made from eternity (**Eph. I. 4-5**; **Rom. VIII. 29**). The discourse is of the ***virtually such*** efficient cause. For predestination, since it is a decree of God, and so an internal action of the divine will, really does not differ from God, but is the very will of God, and so the very essence of God taken with the connoted object to which it is freely terminated, and in so far as by us it is conceived under the mode of a decree. By ***God*** is understood ***Father, Son, and Holy Spirit***. For as the three persons of the divinity by the same potency save men finally believing, so from eternity by the same will they decreed to save them. For predestination is an internal action of God; not an action ad intra.

Further, ***on account of what*** is God the author of predestination? In actions these two must be distinguished: ***on account of what?*** and ***for whose sake?*** The latter notes the ***final cause***, the former the ***impulsive cause***. When therefore it is asked, ***on account of what did God predestine us to salvation?*** — the sense is: What moved God to decree concerning our eternal salvation to be conferred on us in time? ***The merit of Christ apprehended by true final faith.*** For the merit of Christ apprehended by true final faith in time moves God, as the ***external impulsive cause***, that He may in act confer eternal salvation on men making the merit of Christ their own by true final faith. Therefore the same merit of Christ, through true final faith made the merit of those finally believing, moves God as the ***external impulsive cause*** that God from eternity should decree to confer in time eternal salvation on all those making the merit of Christ their own in time by true final faith, and foreseen by God from eternity. For the same was always the impulsive cause of a decree, which is the impulsive cause of the execution of a decree.

It is said: *the merit of Christ apprehended by final faith*. For although the passion and death of Christ be not only for our sins but for the sins of the whole world (**1 John II. 2**), yet to no one does it profit except to one believing, and to whom the merit of Christ is by faith imputed. He who does not believe is already condemned, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God (**John III. 18**).

***In whom*** was predestination made? ***In Christ.*** (**Eph. I. 4**.) Christ, and He alone, is the ***meritorious cause*** of predestination. For it does not repugn that one and the same person be simultaneously of one and the same act the ***physical efficient cause*** and the ***meritorious cause***. The physical efficient cause of predestination is Christ, as He is one with the Father and Holy Spirit, God; the meritorious cause of predestination, as by the force of His merit foreseen from eternity, moved God to predestination — i.e. the decree concerning eternal salvation to be conferred on those making the merit of Christ their own by final faith, i.e. believers in time.

Finally, ***what impelled God to this decree*** of eternal salvation to be conferred on men going to make the merit of Christ their own? ***The merely gratuitous favor of God***. ***God predestined us according to the good-pleasure of His will*** (**Eph. I. 5**).

Namely God from eternity had decreed to create man, and to equip them with such powers by which they could live rightly and obtain eternal beatitude. But at the same time from eternity He had foreseen that man would abuse his powers and sin, whence He willed from eternity to have mercy on the human race fallen through sin into utmost misery — insofar as it could come about with His justice saved — and willed that ***all should be saved*** (**Ezek. XXXIII. 11**). But because satisfaction had to be made to the divine justice, and no satisfaction at all could be furnished by men, God decreed to send His Son, who in assumed flesh should satisfy for the sins of all men (**Eph. II. 3, 4 and following**; **Col. I. 19**). And God from eternity willed that all should embrace the satisfaction to be furnished by His Son, and through it should be saved (**John III. 16**). And because faith is not of our own powers, God from eternity decreed through the Word and Sacraments to operate faith and kindle it in all those who should not contumaciously reject grace. Because God from eternity had foreseen that many were going to spurn the Spirit of grace and persevere in their incredulity, He therefore decreed to save those whom He foresaw from eternity to be believers in Christ and dying in this faith. And ***this ultimate act prerequiring all the rest*** — namely the decree by which God determined to save those whom He foreknew to be final believers in Christ — ***is formaliter predestination***, and is said to be predestination made ***according to the good-pleasure of the divine will***, that is, as it pleased God; so that God's good-pleasure according to the thing is the same as the grace of God or God's gratuitous favor, by which from eternity He embraced sinful men going to make the merit of Christ their own by final faith. Which is nothing other than if it be said: ***God from eternity by His glorious grace predestined us*** (**Eph. II. 6-7**).

From these things (which, by the best peace of the Venerable Theologians and our Preceptors, we have recounted from their writings, uniquely for the end that by an evident Theological example the mode of rightly responding to the question *What formaliter is this or that?* might be perceived), now easily can it be seen ***what formaliter predestination is***, as received among orthodox Theologians:

> **Predestination is the DECREE** (behold the ***GENUS PROXIMUM***!) **by which GOD** (behold the ***PHYSICAL EFFICIENT CAUSE and SUBJECT***!) **from eternity, out of merely gratuitous favor** (behold the ***INTERNAL IMPULSIVE CAUSE*** or ***προκαταρκτικήν***!) **in CHRIST** (behold the ***MERITORIOUS CAUSE***!) **constituted, unto the praise and illustration of the glory of His grace** (behold the ***FINAL CAUSE on God's part***!) **to confer eternal salvation in time** (behold the ***FINAL CAUSE on our part***!) **on sinful men** (behold the ***MATERIAL CAUSE or OBJECT***!) **whom from eternity He foresaw, by His grace, to be going to make the merit of Christ their own by final faith** (behold the ***EXTERNAL IMPULSIVE CAUSE*** or ***προηγουμένην***!).

And this is to have made perspicuous to oneself the ***FORM of predestination***. For when we know most rightly to respond to the questions: ***the decree which is called predestination, by whom was it made? by whose impulse? to whom? in whom? for whose sake? on account of what?*** — it stands sufficiently clear to us what is the ***form of predestination***, or (which comes to the same): ***how was predestination made?*** For in practical disciplines ***form*** is ***reason*** or ***mode***. For the rest, the genuine cultivator of a practical discipline must distinguish these three from one another well: *What are all and single the causes of some work or business? Whence can it stand sufficiently and over-sufficiently, and solidly be shown, that these are certain and necessary causes, and that this is the connexion of these very causes? And how from these causes rightly and sufficiently perceived in the analytic places can now solid and scientific conclusions be inferred?* Of the first at least we have treated, and in a certain way of the second. But to touch the third the plan of the present institute does not bear. Meanwhile the student of Theology who is a lover of truth believes the third brings the greatest moment to the study truly practical and to the use of its oratory.

#### Note II of § 4 — The Juridical Example: *Retrovenditio*

**II.** Let us use an example drawn from the midst of Civil Jurisprudence, whose genuine seat is ***L. si fundum*** 2 C. *de pactis inter emptorem et venditorem compositis*, and to which pertain ***L. si a te*** 7 C. eod., likewise ***L. si vir uxori suae*** 12 D. *de praescriptis verbis*, and ***L. si probare potes*** 1 C. *quando decreto opus non est*. But the question is this: ***What formaliter is retrovenditio?*** The Germans are wont to call it ***Ein Wieder-kauff***, and oppose it to ***Ein Erbkauff***. Yet less accurately is retrovenditio called that which is a ***pact of retrovenditio***. That it is a ***pact***, from the inspection alone of the Civil Law texts the cultivator of the LL. can abundantly stand clear. For thus the express words of this law — which is pronounced by the Jurists the genuine seat of this matter — run:

> *"If your parents sold a farm with the LAW that whether they themselves or their heirs offered the price to the buyer at whatever time, or within certain times, it should be restored — and you being prepared to satisfy the condition said, you prove that the heirs of the buyer do not care, so that the faith of the contract may be served, an action in prescribed words, or ex vendito, will be given to you, having regard for those things which, after the amount offered by PACT, have come to the adversary from that farm."*

But now it is looked at: ***Of what sort is this pact? That is, what is the efficient cause of this pact?*** This too stands most easily clear from the cited law as from a source: namely, the pact is ***adjoined to the sale-and-purchase***. Therefore the ***EFFICIENT CAUSE*** of this pact — if it has been express — is both ***the pactioners expressly***: namely, the ***SELLER*** asking that the thing sold be restored by this pact, and the ***BUYER*** promising what he has been asked. And in this manner anyone capable of sale-purchase can enter into a pact: thus either one, or two, or more sell with this pact; the minor of age, the pupil, the city, by the Magistrate's decree, can sell under this pact; to buy without. A vassal can sell with the lord's consent. There is, however, also a ***SUBJECT*** of this pact — the farm or merx. ***What is the MATTER around which this pact turns***? Answer: the merx and its price. The same matter is of this pact as of the contract itself. By the name ***merx*** is signified a thing not only immovable, but also movable and incorporeal — as regards express pact; differently for tacit, and for legal redemption of the Saxon law.

The thing is now entire, now with certain parts or rights reserved to the seller. Different things can be sold by the same contract, with only one or another reserved. The price consists in money, and must be just, lest the pact become suspect of usurary depravity; and that is held usurary which is about half the true value.

Further question: ***UNDER WHAT CONDITION is this pact made?*** — that is, ***what is the FORMAL CAUSE of retrovenditio?*** Answer: ***Under the condition of offering the price***. The buyer promises the return of the merx, if the seller offer the price. For thus the words of ***L. si fundum*** 2 C. de pact. inter emt. & vendit. sound: ***"That if WHENEVER or WITHIN CERTAIN TIMES he had offered the price to the buyer, it should be restored."***

Therefore the ***form*** — and so the ***primary internal end*** — of retrovenditio is: ***the convention and consent of commuting merx and price***, which (and this for the sake of the form's effect, likewise called the secondary end) is followed by civil obligation to transfer dominion and deliver the merx and to return the price. Therefore ***suitable external signs of mutual consent*** are required.

Further question: ***ON ACCOUNT OF WHAT is this pact entered? — i.e. what is the EXTERNAL IMPULSIVE CAUSE of retrovenditio?*** Here the rule is noted: *A sale-and-purchase with pact of retrovenditio, whose external impulsive cause (which the Greeks call* **προκαταρκτικήν**) *is a mutuum (as when the seller sought the buyer for money to be lent to him; or the creditor-buyer would not have given the mutuum unless the farm were sold under this pact) is not a true, valid sale, but the contract is judged pignoratitious and usurary, by which dominion could not be transferred.* The reason given: ***every thing which is given for the sake of a mutuum accedes to the lot, and so is a usura***; therefore the sale is only simulated, and in truth it is a mutuum — but illegitimate — and a contract fraudulent, to which the Law attributes no force or efficacy. But from this very rule a restriction is taken, if the mutuum is concealed and yet usurary depravity is detected. The exception: if no usurary depravity appears, then sale-and-purchase is held legitimate.

***CUJUS ERGO (In contracts and in pacts adjoined to a contract, OB QVOD and CUJUS ERGO are accurately to be distinguished) is retrovenditio? — i.e. what is the FINAL CAUSE of retrovenditio?*** Answer: that the seller recover the dominion of the thing sold, and the buyer recover the price. Each is an ***external end***. The seller intends indeed the recovery of the dominion, but it is not placed in the mere faculty of this: it is necessary that the deed of the buyer intervene; nay, this end can otherwise be hindered, as if the thing has in the meantime been sold at auction. Similarly, the buyer intends the recovery of the price, but it is simply placed in the arbitrium of the seller. Yet more and primarily recovery of the pristine dominion on the part of the seller deserves to be named the end rather than the recovery of the price on the part of the buyer. Which is more rightly understood if the question is decided: ***CUI*** (= what above all must be said to be the ***SUBJECT*** or ***SUBJECTIVE CAUSE*** of retrovenditio)? To the question ***CUI? — in whose favor is retrovenditio made?*** Answer: ***to the buyer, i.e. in favor of the buyer***. For in his favor the buyer obligates himself to restoration of dominion.

Although in those species of this pact which contain a determination of time, as to the adjection of time, in the favor of the buyer it is done; yet as to the necessity of restoring itself, and in all other respects — and in these too — the ***favor of the seller*** is involved. (For the rest, of the ***internal end*** above we treated, when mention was made of the form, and it was said: ***reciprocal obligation to restoration*** — namely, specifically on the part of the seller, the faculty of repeating the thing sold with the price offered, and also the right of acting or judicially repeating, in one word, the ***action*** given to this pact by law.) These things duly observed, it can solidly stand ***what retrovenditio formaliter is***:

> ***A PACT (Behold the GENUS PROXIMUM!) adjoined to sale-and-purchase (Behold the EFFICIENT CAUSE!), by which the buyer promises restoration (Behold the FORMAL CAUSE!) of the merx (Behold the MATERIAL CAUSE!), if the seller offer the price (Behold the OBJECT!), that the seller recover the dominion of the thing sold (Behold the FINAL CAUSE!), and the buyer recover the price (Behold the FINAL CAUSE EX PARTE EMPTORIS!).***

Those wishing to render themselves perspicuous of this matter beyond the strictly Metaphysical, consult ***Herr Johann Schilter***, *Praxis Juris Romani*, Part Three.

#### Note III of § 4 — The Ethico-Political Example: *Poena*

**III.** We shall assign an ***Ethico-Political example***. It is asked: ***What formaliter is a penalty (poena)?*** Here first we note: ***a penalty is a sad evil or an evil of passion*** — since every penalty is molestation and inflicted on the unwilling. Next asked: ***TO WHOM is a penalty inflicted?*** — i.e. what is the ***SUBJECT*** or ***MATERIAL SUBJECTIVE CAUSE*** of a penalty? A penalty is inflicted only on a ***delinquent***. For the essential and perpetual consequence of a crime is ***reatus*** (guilt). But where guilt, there also reatus. Therefore where the crime, there the guilty one.

Further: ***What is the OBJECT or MATERIAL OBJECTIVE CAUSE of a penalty?*** The ***delictum***, to which indeed the power of punishing is extrinsically terminated. Further: ***OF WHOM is it to inflict penalties, i.e. what is the EFFICIENT CAUSE of a penalty?*** It is not except of a ***rector qua talis*** primarily and per se — e.g. in a family of the father; in a republic of the king; in the universe of God. For the right to punish is the right to morally compel. But to compel in the genus of morals no one can another unless he preside, by ruling, over him whom he wishes morally to compel. It adds: he who is justly punished is obligated to the penalty; and to him to whom law cannot be brought, he is not obligated to the penalty — for ***obligation to penalty is (as the Schools speak) the formal effect of law***. Whence whoever does not have the right to bring laws, he has not the right to punish — or if he has, he has it dependently on another, who can exact a penalty of him as a Rector subordinated to himself.

Now the question is: ***BY WHAT AFFECT is a penalty inflicted?*** — i.e. what is the ***INTERNAL IMPULSIVE CAUSE*** (also ***προηγουμένην***) of a penalty? ***The desire of just vindication***, which some Moral Doctors call ***public grief***, likewise ***most just grief***. Further: ***ON ACCOUNT OF WHAT is a penalty inflicted*** — i.e. what is the ***EXTERNAL IMPULSIVE CAUSE*** (also ***προκαταρκτικήν***) of a penalty? ***The delictum***. ***IN WHAT MANNER*** — i.e. what is the ***FORMAL CAUSE*** of a penalty? ***That the equality of both evils (of passion and of action, of sad and of base, of evil of penalty and evil of guilt) be justly observed, rightly estimated***. Finally the question is: ***WHY, i.e. what is the FINAL CAUSE of a penalty?*** The penalty is inflicted ***for the moral emendation of life***. For although it emend not the delinquent whom it removes from the number of men living in society, it avails nevertheless to emend others, who are similar to the delinquent. For ***rector*** and ***subjects*** constitute the city as a certain ***mystical body***. Whence as the whole body is sick with sick hand or foot, so the whole society fares badly in this depraved member. Therefore ***an incurable wound must be cut off with the sword, lest the sincere part be drawn***.

From these to the question ***What formaliter is a penalty?*** will be answered:

> ***It is an evil of passion (Behold the GENUS!), in so far as to the delinquent qua such (Behold the SUBJECT or MATERIAL SUBJECTIVE CAUSE!) on account of an evil of action (Behold the OBJECT or MATERIAL OBJECTIVE CAUSE and EXTERNAL IMPULSIVE CAUSE!), by the Rector of society (Behold the EFFICIENT CAUSE!), with the equality of both evils rightly observed, which was rightly estimated beforehand (Behold the FORMAL CAUSE!), out of most just grief (Behold the INTERNAL IMPULSIVE CAUSE!) it is inflicted for the moral emendation of life (Behold the FINAL CAUSE!).***

Cf., if it please, the ***Introduction to Hugo Grotius's work De Jure Belli & Pacis*** chapter 20.

#### Note IV of § 4 — Full Definitions Not Always Required

**IV.** Not only are full definitions not always to be demanded, but sometimes they are not altogether to be exacted. For as ***demonstrations are not given of all things***, so neither ***definitions***. For nothing is so inimical to pedia as to have learned from ill-taught manuductors as if to the question — ***What formaliter is this or that?*** — in no case ever can it be answered except by a definition having all eight [Aristotelian causes]; of which in the following chapter more distinctly it will be treated. Meanwhile, how much moment to solid erudition is brought by having come to know this signification of ***formaliter*** and solidly to hold perspicuously the mode of rightly responding to the questions of all Faculties ***What formaliter is this or that?*** — all surely know who are not ignorant of the suitable and necessary means and auxiliaries with which must be equipped all those who in the Academy wish to seek the fruit of more solid erudition and more accurate studies. And this is the cause why the ***Doctors of all Faculties*** — to whom the studies of the Academic Youth and the increase of learned matters is a care at heart — so greatly commend to the Auditors the ***genuine understanding and solid knowledge of essential definitions, where they can be had***. It would be easiest to demonstrate, if it were done, that this has been the perpetual sentence both of the ancient and of today's Philosophers and the Doctors of the other faculties.

#### Note V of § 4 — Mathematics Is Not the Source of Non-Mathematical Definitions

**V.** Although we do not altogether deny that ***precognitio-mathemata*** bring a use and fruit not to be contemned to the further study of all Philosophy — nay, also in the studies of the higher Faculties (as they are commonly called) — nevertheless by the common consent of the most learned men it is false that the ***essential definitions*** of such disciplines or their demonstrations can be deduced from Mathematical sources and principles in even the smallest part — as if the Doctors of other disciplines ought to hand down their own things ***denominatively only***, but then it belonged to the Mathematician to ***estimate*** them, or to hand them down ***estimatively***. For all the learned agree that every single science and discipline has its ***own principles***, and every solid and accurate doctrine and demonstration must be sought from the nature of each ***subject matter***. For example: I should be inept if I wished to teach mathematics ethically; whence as mathematics cannot be taught ethically, so neither can moral matters be taught ***mathematically***. The teaching of those who attempt this reveals mere ***analogisms***, doing nothing or little to the matter itself, nay more ***intricating*** than ***extricating*** it, and more impeding the true and solid doctrine than aiding it.

#### Note VI of § 4 — Aristotle's Causal Definition and the Luna Eclipse

**VI.** On the contrary, the assertion of ***Aristotle and all Metaphysicians*** is that only through the ***causal definition*** (which includes in itself the cause of the attribute, why it belongs to the subject) can there be a solid and accurate response to the question ***What formaliter is this or that?*** — since only the ***causal definition is a truly real definition*** and most perfect of all. All ***Analytica*** also, together with the whole doctrine of teaching the truth accurately and solidly, deservedly with full voice re-echoes this assertion. For those who deny that essential definitions of things are real and more intimate (whether they will or no) by this assertion ***remove all real and more intimate cognition of a thing***, remove also every ***first mode of speaking per se***, and all accurate science and demonstration. For a thing is what it is through its ***essence*** and not through another cause; and of this essence an ***essential definition*** is given, to which in every single accurate and perfect demonstration one must at last recur.

**You say:** the ratio formalis of a thing can be demonstrated — e.g. the defect of light in the moon (which is the ratio formalis of a lunar eclipse) can be demonstrated from the interposition of the earth between Sun and Moon. It is answered: ***it is one thing to demonstrate that the Moon is deprived of light when it suffers an eclipse; it is another thing to demonstrate that the privation of light in the Moon is the ratio formalis of a lunar eclipse***. The former can be demonstrated; the latter cannot. For who would say that the diametrical interposition of the earth between Sun and Moon is the cause ***why*** the eclipse of the Moon is a privation of light in the Moon? This latter is the ratio formalis of the eclipse — nay, is rather the same thing as the eclipse itself. As therefore no cause can be given why the eclipse is the eclipse, so neither can the ratio formalis of the eclipse be demonstrated.

Therefore ***causal definitions are principles of demonstrations, not of essential definitions***; but ***essential definitions are not principles of demonstrations***, because as to the matter, essential definitions and the thing defined of that genus are the same throughout, and so to draw demonstrations therefrom would truly be nothing other than ***petere τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ***.

Meanwhile every cause (whence the definition is called causal) at last resolves into the ***ratio formalis of the subject***, not into some other external cause. Someone might say: hence it follows that for constituting the cause or middle of a demonstration the ratio formalis itself can be assumed. But the response is easy: although that which pertains to the essence of the subject be assumed, nevertheless it is not assigned as a proper and perfect definition of the subject, but inasmuch as it pertains to the causal definition itself of the predicate.

Let us examine the example adduced by the opponent part: to the question ***Why does the Moon suffer an eclipse?*** rightly indeed is it responded, ***on account of the diametrical interposition of the earth between Sun and Moon***. Yet every careful auditor will ask further: ***why is the globe of the earth diametrically interposed between Sun and Moon when this does not happen to other stars?*** The doctor responds: ***because the Moon is near the earth and of smaller quantity than the earth***. The auditor goes on: ***but if the fixed stars were nearer to the earth and of smaller quantity than the earth, they would not suffer an eclipse — how then does it happen that it befalls the Moon so affected?*** Here the doctor responds: ***those stars have their own light, the Moon does not; but all the light with which it shines to us constituted on earth it refers as received to the Sun***. From these it is plain that recourse must here be had to the ***essence of the Moon*** and so to its essential definition.

Nor is there what might be excepted — that the eclipse is only an external affection of the Moon, in that it befalls the Moon on account of some external cause. Grant it; still an essential definition of the Moon is needed. For if the careful auditor should ask (which, since he seeks solid erudition, he cannot not ask), ***what cause is there that on account of the earth's diametrical interposition between Sun and Moon the Moon is deprived of light, whereas if the earth could cast its shadow so far as to touch the fixed stars, these would not suffer an eclipse?*** The one rightly and duly discharging the office of teaching analytically neither wills nor can respond otherwise than: ***that this happens on account of the diverse essence of the Moon and of the fixed stars***. For the rest, it is most false that one who asks ***What formaliter is a lunar eclipse?*** wishes nothing other than ***what is the cause or middle*** — that is, by what reason the defined thing is said. For first, most distinct remain the questions: ***Why does a lunar eclipse happen?*** and ***What is the ratio formalis of a lunar eclipse?*** — as above was shown. Then, ***a causal definition is never sufficiently perfect***, but if the causal definition of a thing, where it can be had, be conjoined with the essential, then at last from it is born a ***most perfect and in every number absolute*** definition. Thirdly, what will be said about the subject's essential definition in this or that demonstration? Fourthly, let us cease to wonder why Auditors not yet distinguishing between most-ingenious ***φαινομένοις*** and erudite ***nugae*** suffer themselves to be so led as to believe that essential definitions are mere ***nomenclatures and grammatical involucra and hoods***. For example: let us suppose someone is dealing with a man unlearned and simple, yet simultaneously attributing to himself not a little. There is no need that you commit the definitions to memory: for if you learn, for example, the definition of animal — and this one, which they call real and essential, and through which is answered to the question ***What formaliter is animal?*** — ***Animal is a natural mixed animated sentient body*** — ***what, pray, have you learned?*** Mere five names: ***body, natural, mixed, animated, sentient*** — and nothing besides. Let us suppose this fable is acted: certainly unless he, filling the number of beginners, found such a doctor less accurate or less candid than he had hoped, he would so suffer himself to be imposed upon by him that he would cease to be in the number of beginners and shake off his ***ἐπαιδευσία***. We confess ourselves that an auditor at first dim can, when the given definition is pronounced a hundred times, hold it for merely nominal, nor can hold it otherwise — as if indeed this definition should cease to be a ***truly real definition***, which the rude auditor does not know how to hold for truly real. Many things truly ***are*** and remain, though to the rude they never seem so.

But what, pray, is the cause why these auditors or those are so easily deceived — e.g. why do they so easily believe the adduced definition of animal to be merely nominal? The cause is this: that the most real and truly essential definition of a thing (e.g. of animal) cannot be perfectly known unless one holds intimately perspicuous all the ***superior genera*** and all the ***more remote differences***. In like manner, one must have sufficiently and intimately known the ***forms***, because in these lie the essential definitions of composita; the genus itself also signifies some form in composite substances, although not so determinate a form as the difference expresses. For that cause ***Aristotle does not easily define composites, but forms alone***. Thus the Philosopher himself gives the essential definition not of the sentient, but of sense; not of the animated, but of soul; not of the mixed, but of mixture. Likewise he hands down no exact definition of natural body, but handles accurately the essential definition of nature.

But certainly there is no doubt that the auditor of right judgment, with the essential definitions of these forms rightly constituted and perceived (this truly is work, this is labor, which demands much judgment and effort, and which, when expended, allows one deservedly to congratulate himself on a great part of physical erudition) — in continuous fashion also understands the ***essence*** of the composites themselves. Therefore let it be said to a leaden auditor: the adduced definition of animal is not truly real, and that ***animal is a natural mixed animated sentient body*** is the same as ***animal is animal***.

#### Note VII of § 4 — Synonyms of *Ratio Formalis*

**VII.** Finally it must be known that whatever reason ***ratio formalis*** not rarely signifies the same as ***essentia***, by the same fortune they also walk pari passu: ***quidditas*** (as the Scholastics call it), ***natura, forma, definitio***. For they are synonyms of essence: ***quidditas*** and ***natura***, if ***natura*** be taken otherwise than in Physics, where it notes the principle of moving and resting in that in which it is primarily and per se. For many beings are given which are not such natures, nor have such natures — as is plain from the example of God and the Angels. Thus when we say ***one nature is in three persons of divinity***, ***in Christ there are two natures***, ***nature*** signifies the same as ***essence***. Sometimes, however, ***nature*** lies as wide as ***ratio formalis*** taken in its wider signification: e.g. when in Moral matters there is distinguished between ***from its own nature honest*** and ***from its own nature base***. In like manner ***form***, if not received for an incomplete being but in that signification which this saying intimates: ***Whatever is, is through its own form, i.e. its ratio formalis*** — deservedly will be called a synonym of ***essence***. There are those who, with the Scholastics, likewise distinguish between ***formal definition*** and ***objective definition***, and commonly it is wont to be distinguished between ***formal concept*** and ***objective concept***; and according to this sentence an essential objective definition will altogether be ***essentia***. Thus those who say the definition absolutely so called — that is, the essential definition — does not really differ from its defined, by ***definition*** do not understand the oration which declares the essence of the thing, but the ***essence declared by the oration***.

#### § 5

> ***To this second acceptation of the notion FORMALITER is opposed all that which either plainly does not pertain to the ratio formalis of the thing, or pertains indeed to the ratio formalis of the thing, yet is not the whole ratio formalis, but only of the ratio formalis — that is, a part of the ratio formalis.***
>
> ***For example: when animal is precisely considered as a NATURAL BODY — because thus it is considered at least according to that which is OF THE RATIO FORMALIS of animal. Again, if animal is considered as MOBILE, as CORRUPTIBLE, as LIVING, as APPETITIVE — animal is not considered FORMALITER, because these predicates do not pertain to the ratio formalis of animal, but flow from those which are OF the ratio formalis of animal.***

#### § 6

> ***FORMALITER (3) precisely argues the ESSENTIAL DIFFERENCE OF THAT (of which it is the essential difference) MOST PROPER. For example: it is rightly said that something is formaliter animal because it is SENTIENT.***

#### Notes

**I.** Let those things be repeated which in the preceding chapter three (§§ 3 and 4 pp. 265 ff.) were said of ***essence*** — that often it is taken precisely for the ***reciprocal partial first concept of a being***. In passing we add: that just as ***ratio formalis*** lies more widely than essence, so the ***reciprocal partial first concept*** lies more widely than the ***essential difference***. Hence it comes about that the more accurate Philosophers distinguish between ***essential difference*** and ***quasi-essential difference***.

**II.** A common, but most empty, persuasion has occupied the minds of many of the philosophizing vulgar — and there has driven very deep roots — as if the whole ***essential definition*** cannot be given unless it consists of ***two concepts***, which must be or at least can be expressed by two vocables — such that one be the ***first partial common or non-reciprocal*** concept, the other the ***first partial proper or reciprocal*** concept. How many errors this matter has given cause for and can again give cause for, no one well versed in Philosophy does not see.

Thus for example in vain anyone will desire the first proper or reciprocal concept of ***prudence***, which can be contained in a single word. However accurate this essential definition of prudence may be: ***it is a habit of the deliberative intellect practical with right reason*** — ***so that through this definition most accurately there be responded to the question "What formaliter is prudence?"*** — nevertheless there is no vocable in the given definition which separately taken expresses the notion which is most proper to the defined thing, so that of no other it can be essentially predicated. ***Habit*** is the genus of prudence; (habit) ***of the intellect*** is also science, intelligence, wisdom; (habit of the intellect) ***deliberative*** is also art; (habit) ***practical*** is also imprudence considered as a habit; (habit) ***with reason***, likewise (habit) ***with right reason***, is also art. Meanwhile if now it be asked: ***by what does some habit formaliter (taking the notion FORMALITER as explicated in the present §) become prudence?*** — accurately and most rightly it is responded through this: ***that it is (habit) PRACTICAL of the DELIBERATIVE INTELLECT WITH RIGHT REASON***. And thus in place of the response the ***essential difference most proper*** is signified.

Examples of this kind occur everywhere in the Metaphysical discipline. For example, when it is asked: ***What formaliter is a moral cause?*** — most rightly it is responded: ***it is an EFFICIENT CAUSE, FREE, MEDIATE***. Surely not every efficient cause is a moral cause, nor every free cause is a moral cause, nor every mediate cause is a moral cause, nor every efficient free cause is a moral cause, nor every efficient mediate cause is a moral cause, nor every free and mediate cause is a moral cause — and so the single essential predicates of a moral cause separately considered lie more widely than ***moral cause***. Meanwhile, if you form the question: ***by what does some cause formaliter (taking again the signification of ***formaliter*** as is of this §) become a moral cause?*** — accurately and most rightly it is responded through this: ***that it is EFFICIENT, FREE, MEDIATE***. Thus we have given the most proper essential difference of prudence and of a moral cause, by giving to each several differences — of which any one separately considered cannot be called ***most proper***, cannot be called ***ultimate***, but conjunctly taken constitute the ***most proper***, yet not the ultimate (because besides these conjunctly taken no other, of which with respect to it the ultimate could be said, is given).

Let therefore the cultivators of more accurate Philosophy and those loving solid erudition beware lest they ever dismiss this monitory from their eyes and minds, nor confuse the ***most proper difference*** with the ***ultimate difference***; and (which is chief) let them know and remember that single ultimate predicates often constitute, not the ratio formalis as its whole, but a part of the ratio formalis; and that solely through that itself whence the most proper part of the ratio formalis (whether it can be called ultimate or not) was to be sought.

Let us take a single — and a sufficiently known and useful — example from Moral Philosophy, which will be the subject of the next treatment.

#### Note III of § 6 — The Moral-Virtue Example Extended

**III.** It is commonly said that ***moral virtue formaliter consists in a mediocrity determined by the right reason of a prudent man*** — whence many sons of the Ethicists set up that mediocrity itself to be the essential difference of moral virtue, and for this cause urge the Aristotelian definition of virtue, which stands thus:

> ***ἐστιν ἡ ἀρετὴ ἕξις προαιρετικὴ, ἐν μεσότητι οὖσα, ὡρισμένῃ λόγῳ, καὶ ᾧ ἂν ὁ φρόνιμος ὁρίσειεν*** — ***a habit choice-making, consisting in a mediocrity with respect to us, as a prudent man would define it.***

But by the consent of more accurate Interpreters, Aristotle seems to indicate nothing else than ***that the essential difference most proper of moral virtue is not the mediocrity itself, but one must seek it from the mediocrity***, so that it is that very essential ***habitudo*** which moral virtue says to mediocrity — which habitudo the Philosopher could not have expressed, except by *ὡς* as an addendum (as the Schools speak), he had defined moral virtue, i.e. defined it with mention of mediocrity made.

**IV.** It will also help to have noted that as often as such definitions occur (which are certainly more frequent in practical disciplines), no one can perceive them sufficiently happily unless he first duly holds perspicuous those essential ***habitudines***. For example: the just-adduced definition from Aristotle's *Nicomachean Ethics* book two chapter six, the Moral Philosophy cultivator by no means sufficiently understands as long as it is not solidly and sufficiently attained in what that essential ***habitudo to mediocrity*** consists — on account of which habitudo mention was made of mediocrity in the definition of moral virtue. It pleases to touch the chief foundations from which that habitudo can be judged by the cultivator of Moral matters:

**First**, it must be known to him that there are given actions ***per se, intrinsically, and by their own nature honest*** to man; and that it is one thing for man to elicit and exercise those actions, and another for man ***promptly and expeditely*** to choose and ***by a singular facility of mind*** to exercise them. For it can happen that some man choose and exercise actions per-se, intrinsically, and by their nature honest and so of absolute necessity due, and yet not do it without molestation or difficulty. Therefore through this man avails ***promptly and expeditely*** to choose actions by their nature and per se honest, and to exercise them at the empire of the will by a singular facility of mind: because he is ***virtuous***, that is, endowed with the habit of virtue. For virtue, since it is a habit, does not give the first faculty of operating, but ***aids and facilitates*** it. From this is seen the essential ***habitudo*** which moral virtue says to mediocrity: for it is essential to moral virtue to aid the will, and make it easier for man to choose actions per se honest (and this because prescribed by the law of nature); it is also essential to moral virtue to assist the sensitive appetite that it may promptly obey the promptly commanding will.

**Second**, there are given actions ***per se, intrinsically, by their nature base***, which [the virtuous man] can and ought to shun and omit promptly and expeditely. For as it is virtuous to elicit and commit promptly and expeditely what per se and from its nature is honest, so also it is virtuous to shun and omit promptly and expeditely what per se and by its nature is base. Therefore something is a habit of moral virtue formaliter through this: that it is engaged about what is per se and intrinsically honest or base to man — in the way just indicated.

**Third**, there are given actions ***per se and by their nature neither honest nor base***, such that nevertheless the right reason of a prudent man judges their ***commissions*** better than their omissions, or ***omissions*** better than their commissions. (And truly it is an elegant doctrine-genus to know how to discern the ***precepts*** of right reason and nature from the ***counsels*** of right reason and nature — of which certainly there are very many.) Therefore moral virtue formaliter says also a ***habitudo to the prompt commission of such acts***, if the omission is better; or the ***easy omission***, if commission is better, although neither commission nor omission be per se due.

**Fourth**, there are given actions per se and from their nature neither honest to man, nor base, nor better than their opposites, nor worse — that is, actions plainly ***indifferent***, so that it matters nothing whether they be committed or omitted. In so far as such acts become the matter of ***voluntary law*** (whether divine, of which God alone, or human, of which man alone is author), to that extent moral virtue is a habit of reducing such acts to ***honestas***. For most distinct are: ***to reduce indifferent actions to mediocrity***, and ***to reduce them promptly to mediocrity***.

From these it perhaps more rightly stands clear through what some habit formaliter is ***moral virtue***, and in what sense moral virtue is said to be formaliter placed in mediocrity. For ***honestas*** (or what is the same, ***moral rectitude***) really differs in nothing from mediocrity — whence Aristotle, what he had judged under the name of ***μεσότητος*** (mediocrity), elsewhere calls ***ὀρθότητα*** (rectitude). For the same thing it is, whether you call moral virtue of man ***a habit of human appetite consisting in a mediocrity determined by the right reason of a prudent man***, or ***a moral habit of human appetite of living honestly***, or ***a moral habit of human appetite of rightly bearing oneself***. Now it was further incumbent on the Cultivator of Moral matters duly and happily to attain ***the whole doctrine on mediocrity of reason*** — both simple and compared — (which it is here neither of place nor leisure to hand down), and then at last could it more rightly stand clear concerning the genuine and most-proper essential difference of virtue.

For whether, following more recent writers, you set up that moral habits (which we commonly call ***honest***) are not honest if considered in themselves — because by no moral causality they touch the effect, as long as they remain habits and do not break forth into act (which sentence to weigh is not of this place) — or whether you pronounce that if considered in themselves they are truly honest: this nevertheless can be denied by no one — that the ***honest habit*** has this, that it is honest, from this: that man has compared it with honest actions. So it cannot formaliter be constituted in mediocrity unless above all a formal or essential respect be had to the mediocrity of the actions by which it was compared.

Extant on this matter is our dissertation under the title: ***Formale Virtutis ex Moralibus Aristotelis Principiis Offertum et a Nonnullorum Exceptionibus Vindicatum.***

#### Note IV of § 6 — Habitudes Essentiales

**IV.** This is further to be noted: ***as often as such definitions occur*** (which are certainly more frequent in practical disciplines), ***no one can perceive them sufficiently happily unless he first duly holds perspicuous those essential habitudines***.

[Explication of this requirement already included in Note III above, with the specific Moral-Virtue case worked through its four classes of actions.]

#### Note V of § 6 — Societas Formaliter in *Ordo Rectorius*

**V.** Thus those who desire to render perspicuous to themselves the ***doctrine on societies*** most rightly say that any society is formaliter placed in an ***order*** (of the person who rules, and who is ruled). For example:

> *the ***nuptial society*** in the order which husband and wife [observe between themselves];*
> *the ***paternal*** in the order which parents and children;*
> *the ***herile*** [master-servant] in the order which master and servant;*
> *the ***domestic*** in the order which paterfamilias and domestics;*
> *the ***pagan*** [village] in the order which the senior and junior patresfamilias;*
> *the ***maxime civil*** society (it is called ***maxime civilis*** since there is no external action of man which does not per se pertain to this society, or from circumstances can pertain to it) — that is, the ***civil*** in the order which those who have the faculty of ruling the city, and those to whom the glory of civil obedience has been left, among themselves observe, etc.*

But because any association, by which certain persons come together into one society for the sake of certain affairs to be expedited, is wont to be entered — yet affairs are expedited, or (if they can with difficulty and little happy or useful or certain success) they could not be [so expedited], except by an ***ordo rectorius*** and a sought-for ***ius imperii***. Surely if you say any species of society whatever is formaliter placed in the ***ordo rectorius*** (as it is called) which the associates observe among themselves, nevertheless unless they make known to themselves ***all the genuine and formal reasons*** of those affairs and all the rights (whether or quasi, active and passive) of the persons both who rule and who are ruled — these students who wish to learn ***Architectonic Politics*** with emolument and fruit can promise themselves little utility from such formulas as: ***Society is the state of persons observing a certain order among themselves; nuptial society is the society between husband and wife, etc.***

For that end extant is our whole dissertation (not so long ago re-struck in print), to which the title is: ***Jus Imperii Quaesitum.***
