#### Note VI of § 6 — Emtio-Venditio and the Chemnitz Sacrament-Number Controversy

**VI.** For the rest, it would be easiest by various practical examples to illustrate this third signification of ***formaliter***. Indeed, besides that these can be sought from the notes to the preceding § with the common concept omitted, they offer themselves spontaneously everywhere. For example: if you ask the ***Politicians and Jurists*** in what formaliter they believe sale-and-purchase to be placed, you will receive this response: ***when a price is given for a merx, and when a merx is given for a price***.

If you ask the ***orthodox Theologians***: ***whence formaliter does a sacred action have this, that it is a sacrament?*** The response will be: ***because it is divinely instituted, by which through an external and visible sign God not only seals the proper grace of the Gospel promise, but also truly exhibits the celestial goods promised in its institution and salvifically applies them to the believing.***

Let it be lawful here (by the good peace of the Venerable Theologians) to deduce something from their writings, uniquely (which is the scope always proposed by us) that of the use of Metaphysical notions it may happily stand clear: The ***Papists*** and ***our Theologians*** dispute among themselves about the ***number of sacraments***. They number seven sacraments, we two. The hinge of the controversy precisely turns on this: whence must it be judged — ***through what formaliter is an action a sacrament?***

**The Blessed Martin Chemnitz**, a Theologian most meritorious of the universal Church of Christ, in his ***Examen Concilii Tridentini*** carefully collected the ***conditions of sacraments*** — which he calls ***substantial*** (i.e. formal, essential) — of which none can be absent from a true sacrament. They are the following:

> **1.** that it have an external, material and visible element or sign;
> **2.** that that sign or external element have an express divine mandate;
> **3.** that it be instituted in the New Testament;
> **4.** that it not be instituted merely for a time, but ***unto the consummation of the age***;
> **5.** that there be present a divine promise of grace and effect or fruit of the sacrament;
> **6.** that that divine promise be annexed to the sign of the sacrament;
> **7.** that that promise be the promise of grace, that is, ***of gratuitous remission of sins and of reconciliation with God***;
> **8.** that that promise be not only signified or announced in sacraments in general, but by the virtue of God be offered, applied, and sealed to the single ones who use the sacraments with faith.

These are the requisites which the Blessed Chemnitz on Canon One of the Seventh Session collected from Sacred Scripture, and nearly all our Theologians today follow him; and on this foundation they dispute against the Papists that only ***two*** sacraments are given, inasmuch as to the other sacraments which the Papists superadd, not all these conditions agree.

Some of our Theologians meanwhile judge that it is not needful to contend so rigorously with the Papists about the number of sacraments, but that it suffices if only this be obtained against the Papists: ***that only two were instituted by Christ as a means of offering, exhibiting, and sealing grace*** (whatever be the case about the word ***sacrament***). And they urge this: ***the Apology of the Augsburg Confession***, when using the word *sacrament* more broadly, expressly reckons ***absolution*** among the sacraments; and lest someone say that there the word *sacrament* is received abusively, repeats the same in what follows and asserts in express words that ***the Sacrament of Penance can properly be called***, [that there is given] a ***sacrament properly so called taken in a looser sense***, defined there as ***a rite having God's mandate and to which the promise of grace is added***. But to a sacrament ***most properly*** (one thing is to receive proprie, another propriissime, since both — the proprie and the propriissime received — have their ratio formalis) and most strictly so called — as it is received by the Blessed Chemnitz and others — it is required also that there be some ***external sign*** or ***visible element***, through which as the medium grace is applied and sealed to man, according to the saying of Augustine *Tract. 80 in Johannem*:

> ***"The word comes to the element, and it becomes a sacrament, as a visible word itself."***

And on this account absolution is not a sacrament most properly so called, since there no corporeal element is applied to man when he is absolved from sins through the ministry.

For when the ***Papists*** contend that an external sign is found in absolution — namely the imposition of hands — our Theologians respond that this ceremony is not divinely instituted, since nowhere in Scripture is it read that the minister, when he absolves man from sins, ought to lay his hand on him; and besides, the imposition of hands is a ***transient action*** and no corporeal element. And so most rightly they collect that ***penance is not such a sacrament as Baptism and the Lord's Supper are***.

#### Note VII of § 6 — Cautio in Assigning Essential Differences

**VII.** One must proceed cautiously and safely in assigning the most proper essential differences of things, lest anyone take them from certain species subordinate to that whose most proper essential difference, or part of the most proper ratio formalis, is sought. For this mode of proceeding, so nakedly and crudely applied, surely cannot be approved; because not immediately does what agrees with one or two species also belong to the whole genus in its latitude. You would call those similar who hold this monitory in contempt — those who, from the fact that no species whatever of other animants is partaker of reason, would contend that it is necessarily required for the nature of animal in general that it be ***devoid of reason***, and so that ***man is not an animal*** — which latter however no one of sounder mind and body would deny. And indeed this caution is especially to be commended to the Cultivators of all Faculties.

#### Note VIII of § 6 — Against Partial-Ratio-Formalis Proofs

**VIII.** Too absurd are those who prove this or that formaliter to be such, yet are not first careful whether the ***whole ratio formalis*** belongs to it. We shall declare the matter by one or two examples, so that it may stand more clearly what end this very necessary caution had.

Thus Metaphysicians by unanimous consent and most rightly teach that the ***essential difference of impure act*** is that it be ***not immune from every imperfection***. Some assign this: that it has mixed into it a ***passive potency***. But both the former — and so far as the present goes, this latter also — may stand rightly in place of the most proper essential difference, and we may make the impure act formaliter consist in it. Meanwhile this exemplary Philosophy remains quite impure if you see it asserted that ***bodies are maximally impure acts***. For the reason adduced — namely, that natural bodies have mixed in a passive potency — is no reason: for natural bodies, although they have mixed in a passive potency (which no one denies), nevertheless neither are nor can be called ***impure acts***, because they are plainly not ***acts***. Of what therefore is plainly not an act, it is in vain asked whether it be ***pure act*** or ***impure act***. For of that from which is denied the ***first common concept of a thing***, from it are denied the species contained under that thing.

Let us take another example: on not a few of the sons of the Jurists and Moral Doctors has imposed this reason — to make them believe that ***God can dispense in the law of nature*** — because God is the author of natural law, and can interpret the natural laws, how they ought to be understood and whom they oblige and whom not. But of that from which is denied the first common concept of a thing, from it are also denied the species contained under that thing. But now the first common concept of ***dispensation*** is ***mutation*** (understand: of law). Therefore because the law of nature is utterly and simply ***immutable*** — that is, devoid of mutation — and so the first common concept of dispensation repugns the law of nature, most rightly it is asserted that the species contained under that common first concept, namely ***dispensatio***, repugns it.

Nor are those worthy of milder (if not graver) censure who, from this — that natural law is of absolute necessity and simply ***immutable*** by common consent of Philosophers, Theologians, and Jurists — strive to elicit this absurdity: that by this reasoning God alone can by no means be set up as immutable. For these themselves accuse either their own simplicity or their malice if either they cannot or will not grasp that never without the greatest absurdity can such an absurd be collected from the received sentence. For here the question is not of ***immutability in the sense in which it belongs to God alone***, but when it is asserted that the law of nature is ***simply and utterly immutable***, nothing else is signified than that so long as there exists one who is obliged by the law of nature, no derogation can be made from it, nor can anyone be dispensed in it, nor can it be abrogated. But if plainly there were no one whom the law of nature obliged, neither would the law of nature exist; and if this plainly did not exist, neither could it be abrogated, nor derogated, nor dispensed in — since abrogation, derogation, and dispensation are species of mutation which prerequires an existing law.

#### Note IX of § 6 — Essential Difference Can Lie Wider Than Its Subject

**IX.** This we also touch in passing: that ***the most proper essential difference sometimes lies more widely than that of which it is said to be the most proper essential difference***. For example: ***the most proper essential difference of impure act*** consists in that it is ***not immune from every imperfection***; yet not everything which is not immune from every imperfection is immediately an impure act. Thus ***rational*** commonly is set up as the essential difference most proper to man; yet ***rational*** lies more widely than ***man***: for the Angels too, and God Himself, are rational; our soul too is rational.

**You say:** how can an essential difference lying more widely be called ***most proper***? Response: it will be called most proper if it is considered precisely as it prerequires and tacitly supposes the first common concept with which it constitutes the species. For example: ***act not immune from every imperfection*** does not lie more widely than ***impure act***. ***Rational animal*** does not lie more widely than ***man***.

#### § 7

> ***FORMALITER (4) often indicates the essential difference of a thing (whose essential difference it is) NOT PROPER. When this signification obtains, and when not, must prudently be judged from the diversity of questions and from the scope of the questioner.***
>
> ***For example: if it be asked, through what does animal formaliter differ from mixtum (mixed body)? It is rightly answered through this: that it is ANIMATED. Through what does it formaliter differ from a stone? It is answered: that it is ANIMATED.***

#### Notes on § 7

**I.** With deliberation we have said that one must look to the ***scope of the questioner***. Thus if someone asked you ***in what formaliter does adultery consist?*** and you responded that formaliter it consists in that it is ***the pollution of another's wife***, you would rightly respond. But if he then said: ***"Therefore adultery is not per se base. For if an animal of external form resembling man, which however were not a rational and social animal, polluted another's wife, the pollution of another's wife by such an animal would not be base, yet it would be the pollution of another's wife"*** — here you would respond that you had no business with a trifler, since you had said adultery formaliter consists in the pollution of another's wife. For those who do not love trifles know well that the question concerning adultery was ***moral***. But everyone who begins to learn Ethics can and ought to know that nothing is a moral action unless it be ***free or voluntary***. This therefore was not expressly said by you, yet by you and all others endowed with sounder judgment it was supposed, that when adultery is said to consist formaliter in that it is the pollution of another's wife, always and necessarily must be understood ***voluntary pollution of another's wife***, that is, the act by which another's wife is polluted by one knowing and willing. Whence anyone sees that by an animal which is not rational, adultery cannot be properly and rightly so-called, since such an animal lacks reason and will.

**II.** Let us take a ***Theological example***. It is known to Students of Theology that ***conversio***, both in Sacred Scripture and in Theologians, is wont to be received in two ways: ***transitively*** and ***intransitively***.

If now it be asked: ***through what does conversion transitively taken formaliter differ from conversion intransitively taken?*** — from the writings of orthodox Theologians we learn the following:

> *Conversion transitive formaliter is the ACTION OF THE HOLY SPIRIT; conversion intransitive formaliter is the ACTION OF MAN.*

Here anyone easily sees that when conversion transitively taken formaliter is said to be of the Holy Spirit, conversion intransitively received formaliter is said to be of man — neither the ***essential difference most proper*** of conversion taken this way or that is signified, nor the ***whole ratio formalis***. Meanwhile, through what transitive conversion formaliter differs from intransitive is believed to be sufficiently and accurately signified by the response given. Here further it must be noted (by the best peace of the Venerable Doctors) that ***action*** is taken by them as it denominates one or another agent: and they call the ***action of the Holy Spirit*** that which formaliter denominates the Holy Spirit as agent; but ***the action of man*** that which formaliter denominates not the Holy Spirit but man as agent.

For example: the Holy Spirit through the Word illumines man's intellect, kindles faith in man's heart through the Word, etc. — therefore this illumination of man and production of faith in man formaliter is the ***action of the Holy Spirit***, since when the Holy Spirit illumines man's intellect and kindles faith in man's heart through the Word, He ***formaliter acts***, and from this action is ***formaliter denominated agent***. On the contrary, man acknowledges sins, grieves over them, fears the wrath of God, and believes in Christ the Redeemer — not the Holy Spirit. Therefore ***to acknowledge sins, to fear God's wrath, to grieve over admitted sins, to believe in Christ*** are formaliter actions of man, not of the Holy Spirit.

Further the use of the notion explicated in the present § stands useful if we further provoke to the information of the Venerable Theologians. Namely, they accurately teach that these two differ much from each other: ***for some action formaliter to be an action of man***, and ***some action to proceed from human powers*** — since some action can formaliter be of man, which nevertheless is not produced by man's natural powers. To this end they adduce the passage from Philippians II. 13, where the Apostle says: ***"It is God who works in you both to will and to effect, according to the good purpose of the mind."*** From these they assert it stands sufficiently and over-sufficiently that when man wills and effects anything good in Spiritual matters, that action formaliter is of man — by that very fact that he wills, that willing is man's willing; and by that very fact that man effects, that effecting is man's effecting. And nonetheless it is said that God acts in men that they may will and effect; and from this follows that man, what in Spiritual matters he effects, that he wills and effects not from his natural powers, but from the grace of the Holy Spirit — since God is said to act in us that we may will and effect.

Similarly in the present it must be said that conversion intransitively taken is indeed formaliter the ***action of man***, but not proceeding from man's natural powers. So that when man acknowledges his sins, detests them, converts to Christ, and believes in Him, he acts all these through the ***grace of the Holy Spirit***. Nay, the Holy Spirit Himself operates these in him through the Word, and man acts the same through the Holy Spirit.

Both significations of ***conversio*** the Theologians also prove from Sacred Scripture. The former (when it is received transitively), as it notes formaliter an action received in another, and signifies the same as ***to convert someone, or to lead someone back to a sounder mind***, from **Jeremiah XXXI. 18**: ***"Convert me, that I may be converted, since Thou art Jehovah my God"***; and **Luke I. 16**; **James V. 19-20**. The latter (when it is received intransitively), as it notes an immanent action and signifies the same as ***to convert oneself, i.e. to repent and return to a sounder mind***, from **Isaiah VI. 10**: ***"Lest the people convert itself"***; **Matt. XIII. 15**; **Mark IV. 12**; **Acts XXVIII. 27**.

For the rest, if we wish to learn from the Theologians ***what formaliter*** (taking the notion ***formaliter*** not as it is received in the present §, but for the ***ratio formalis***) is conversion transitively taken, what intransitively? The former formaliter is the ***action of the Holy Spirit***, by which first through the Word of the Law He leads man dead in sins into the true acknowledgment of his sins joined with serious contrition of heart; then through the Word of the Gospel He kindles in his intellect the light of faith, and in his will true trust in Christ, with the good purpose of amending his life in the future. The latter formaliter is the ***action of man***, by which, with sins acknowledged from the law, he fears God's wrath, grieves over admitted sins, raises himself again by faith in Christ with the purpose of amending his life through God's grace in the future.

Conversion taken in the prior signification is the same as the ***regeneration of the adult*** (for how infants are regenerated and are made partakers of Christ's merit, is explicated in its own place in treating of baptism) — if the word of regeneration be received strictly, as it is distinguished from justification and renewal. In the posterior accepted signification it is otherwise called ***poenitentia***.

#### Note III of § 7 — Juridical Examples: Retrovenditio Differentiated

**III.** Let us use ***Juridical examples***. Thus for example it is asked: ***through what does the pact of retrovenditio formaliter differ from the contract of pignus (pledge)?*** Answer: the pact of retrovenditio is ***adjoined to sale-and-purchase***; whereas ***pignus*** and ***sale-and-purchase*** are formaliter most distinct genera of contracts — the former is contracted ***re***, the latter ***solo consensu***. Some set up that the pact of retrovenditio can also be appended to a pignoratitious contract; but one thing is in today's law and Civil Roman law the ***pactum reluendi pignus***, another the ***retrovendendi rem emtam***. Plainly to a ***datio in solutum*** it can be adjoined, since this holds the place of sale-and-purchase (**L. si praedium** 4 C. *de evictionibus*).

It is asked again: ***through what does retrovenditio formaliter differ from the pactum protimiseos?*** Answer: because this does not determine the time of resale, but determines the buyer in the case of a future sale.

Again: ***through what does retrovenditio formaliter differ from the pactum de poenitendo***, which is also called ***pignus poenitentiae***? Answer: because here the time is not determined for the sale, but the whole sale is annulled, and the contrary is renounced — with a penalty however prestated.

Again: ***through what does retrovenditio formaliter differ from the Lex Commissoria, the addictio in diem, likewise the Pactum Displicentiae?*** Surely in this: with retrovenditio the Lex Commissoria, Addictio in diem, Pactum Displicentiae formaliter agree, that by them the seller can recover the dominion of the thing sold. Formaliter however they differ among themselves thus:

> The ***Lex Commissoria*** obliges the buyer to restitution of the thing under this ratio: ***unless within a certain time the price has been paid*** (**L. si ea lege** 1 C. *de pactis inter emtorem et venditorem compositis*; **L. qui ea lege** C. eod.) — or ***unless the remaining price has been restored within a certain time***;
> ***Addictio in diem*** obliges the buyer to restitution of the thing under this ratio: ***if a better condition is brought*** (**L. quoties fundus** 2 D. *de in diem addictione*);
> ***Pactum displicentiae*** obliges the buyer to restitution of the thing under this ratio: ***if it has displeased the buyer*** (**L. si res** 3 D. *de contrahendo, emtione*; **L. non est** 6 C. *de rescindenda venditione*).

But the ***pact of retrovendendo*** neither under that nor under this ratio obliges the buyer to restitution; it does oblige him, however, ***if to the buyer within a certain time the price is offered*** (**L. si fundum** 2 C. *de pactis inter emtorem et venditorem compositis*).

Therefore through this condition of offering the price the pact of retrovenditio formaliter differs from the Lex Commissoria, Addictio ad diem, and Pactum displicentiae. For by that condition existing — or implemented by the seller — the buyer is purely obliged to restitution. The condition adjoined to the promise of restitution also makes the pact ***conditional***, by which restitution is suspended; the contract itself however remains ***pure*** and is not made conditional, and purely is sold. Easily therefore it stands clear ***through what pact-of-retrovendendo formaliter is distinguished from absolute sale***. Consult the ***Magnificent Herr Schilter***, *Praxis Artis Analyticae* — already by us above p. 304 commended, and today the commendation we repeat.

#### § 8

> ***FORMALITER (5) not rarely denotes the ESSENTIAL PROPERTY of a thing. For example: formaliter through this is something called QUANTUM, because it is DIVISIBLE; formaliter through this is something called GOOD, because it is APPETIBLE; moral virtue formaliter consists in LAUDABILITY; formaliter something is animal, because it is APPETITIVE.***

#### Notes

**I.** From this it has come about that more accurate ***Metaphysicians*** called the ***proper essential*** ***formale consequens***, because it flows necessarily from the formal reason (as the Scholastics speak) — that is, because the predicate is ***necessary***, yet not ***essential***, since an a priori reason can be given why it necessarily belongs to the subject.

**II.** For the same cause Philosophers distinguished between ***ratio formalis a priori*** and ***ratio formalis a posteriori***; between ***definitio a priori*** (i.e. essential) and ***definitio a posteriori*** — the latter however opposed to mere ***description***; between ***essential*** and ***accidental*** predications; and these in turn they divided into ***extra-essential*** and ***accidental*** strictly so-called. For example: the formal reason of ***goodness*** consists in ***appetibility***, as they speak — if the ratio formalis is understood ***a posteriori***; but the ratio formalis ***a priori*** is ***convenience***. For something is ***appetible*** because it is ***convenient***. Something is ***divisible*** because it is ***extended***. Some habit is ***laudable*** because it consists in a ***mediocrity determined by the right reason of a prudent man***. Animal is ***endowed with sensitive appetite*** because it is ***endowed with sentient soul***.

**III.** Just as the notion ***formaliter*** when it says ***formale primum*** notes the essential difference, now most proper, now not proper (though the former signification is the more frequent) — so let the judgment be the same about the present notion. Namely, the ***essential property*** is one thing ***specific***, another ***generic***. For example: just as I rightly say that animal through this ***formaliter differs from a plant***, because it is ***appetitive***, so also I rightly assert that animal through this formaliter differs from a stone, because it is ***living***; from the heavens, because it is ***mixed***.

#### Note IV of § 8 — The Vita Aeterna Example

**IV.** The suitable application of this signification affords signal use in all disciplines and Faculties. Let us take a ***Theological example***. Among Christians it is so certain that there will one day be an ***eternal life***, that by the consent of all it is judged unworthy of the name of Christian who should dare ever to call into doubt what Sacred Scripture inculcates nowhere with insufficiently perspicuous words. It is asked therefore: ***what is ETERNAL LIFE formaliter?*** Or (which at last comes to the same): ***in what formaliter ought eternal life be placed?***

By the unanimous consent of our Theologians: ***the RATIO FORMALIS of eternal life is the beatific vision of God***, and eternal life ***formaliter consists in the beatific vision of God alone***. For just as elsewhere the ratio formalis of any formal end consists in the ***adeption or attainment*** of the objective end, so the ratio formalis of ***eternal beatitude*** (which in Sacred Letters is most usually called ***eternal life***) — as formal and ultimate end — cannot be placed in another than in that act by which we attain the ***ultimate objective end***, that is, ***God***, who is our ***objective beatitude***, and quasi possess Him as the ***Supreme Good***. We attain Him through an act by which He is objectively rendered present to us. But that act is the ***cognition of God*** — not ***abstractive***, as they call it (by which namely God is known not immediately in Himself but through creatures and their species or through revelation), but ***intuitive***, by which God is known immediately as He is in Himself.

For what could be objected — ***by what reason can it come about that by cognition we attain and acquire the thing which is the object of that cognition?*** — to this our Venerable Doctors most accurately respond that ***the reason of the cognition is different***, by which we know other things besides God, and of the ***intuitive cognition of God***. When we know other things, we know them only through ***species*** as images of things, and so we do not yet enjoy the things themselves. But when we know God ***intuitively***, God is intimately, immediately, and without an intelligible species united with the intellect, whence the intellect is so affected by the ***infinite perfection and goodness of God*** as the object known, that it cannot cease from cognition, and that the appetite is perfectly satisfied by that cognition of God. By this reason therefore the Theologians teach that ***to know God is altogether to enjoy God as the infinite and most perfect Good***.

With these premises premised, now comes into disquisition: ***Can eternal life also formaliter be placed in the love of God and in joy about God?*** Here already the use of the present signification of ***formaliter*** exerts itself: for the Theologians teach that with the intuitive cognition of God there coheres by an indissoluble nexus the ***most ardent love of God*** and ***ineffable joy about God***, so that through these acts man also enjoys God as the Supreme Good; and so not inconveniently these acts on the part of the will — namely that love and that joy — are referred to eternal beatitude as a ***formal end***.

That the most intense love toward God coheres with intuitive cognition of God is plain: for this is the force and nature of the good, that it draws the known will into love of itself; whence the more perfectly and clearly known is the good, the more ardently it is loved. Since therefore God is the ***supreme and infinite good***, in whom every reason of the good is given without defect, since He is also intuitively known so that all God's goodness is clear to blessed man, the will is necessarily drawn into the ***most ardent love toward God***. But if God is intuitively known and comprehended with most intense love, there cannot not be excited ***ineffable joy*** about the supreme and infinite good intuitively known and most intensely loved — so that through this joy also man enjoys God as the Supreme Good, inasmuch as by it he is most sweetly delighted and affected.

Let us see therefore the application of the present Metaphysical notion approved by the Theologians: ***the act by which God is objectively rendered present to us is not the love of God*** (as being formaliter — as such from itself — indifferent to present and absent object), ***nor delight*** (as being not except of a good already attained, and so following the attainment of the objective end). Therefore the ***most ardent love*** by which the blessed embraces God as the supreme and most excellent good, and the ***ineffable joy*** or delight in God perfectly known and loved, follow necessarily from the very ratio formalis of eternal beatitude, and so are regarded as ***essential properties*** of eternal life, but do not at all enter its very essence or ratio formalis. Just as no man in his perfect state is given who is not also ***risible and capable of discipline***, so these ***essential consequents*** of eternal beatitude make it to be in its perfect and whole state — in which if it be considered, it includes three principal acts: the ***intuitive cognition of God***, ***most ardent love of God***, and ***sempiternal joy in God known and loved*** — of which three acts one cannot be without the other.

Hence although in the blessed the act of love is by nature posterior to the act of the vision of God, nothing however prohibits that through love and delight as the ***ratio formalis a posteriori*** eternal life be described.

#### Note V of § 8 — Politico-Juridical: Pactum Retrovenditionis

**V.** Let us see ***Politico-Juridical examples***. In chapter 4 § 4 Note 2 p. 298 the essence of the ***pact of retrovendendo*** was indicated. Let us now perceive its ***essential consequents***. Of this pact — and of all other pacts — there is one single ***ESSENTIAL CONSEQUENT***: ***obligation***. We find Politicians and Jurists who think the essential consequent of pacts to be either ***obligation constituted*** or ***obligation to be dissolved***. Others, however, more accurately and more agreeably with Metaphysical principles, set up that there is given one ***essentiale consequens*** of pacts, namely ***obligation*** — as just said — of which also above p. 301 mention was made. For this happens to the essential consequent of a pact: that sometimes it is an ***obligation to dissolve a prior obligation***. Which also happens in the pact of retrovenditio: for although regularly the buyer by the action of sale perpetually has the seller obliged to permit the thing sold quietly to the buyer, the pact of retrovenditio effects that the buyer is obliged to the restitution of the thing, and so the obligation of the seller is removed.

That it may more stand clear concerning the suitable use of the present Metaphysical notion, let it be noted that of any sale — by whatever name finally it come — the ***ESSENTIAL CONSEQUENT*** is obligation to transfer dominion, and to pay the price, and finally the translation of the dominion itself. For no one can seem to have sold that thing of whose dominion it is sought that it not pass to the buyer. But that is either ***locatio*** or another genus of contract — so pronounces Labeo at **L. cum manubia** 80 § ***nemo potest*** 3 D. *de contrahenda emtione venditione*.

If therefore in every sale dominion is transferred, or at least there is obligation to transfer dominion through delivery, it is necessary that also in this [sale] to which the pact of retrovendendo is adjoined, dominion be transferred to the buyer — otherwise retrovenditio would be permitted in vain. Therefore from the essential consequent of sale-and-purchase (to which the pact of retrovenditio was adjoined), it is given accurately to perceive the essential consequent of the pact itself adjoined. Namely because sale-and-purchase is regularly ***perpetual***, unless expressly made ***in diem***, therefore also the translation of dominion is regularly ***in perpetuum***, both to heirs and single successors, unless by special pact it is made for a time and regularly constituted. Which is itself the ***essential consequent of this pact***, and indeed from the ***cause of offering the price***. Therefore the ***essential consequent*** is that dominion with the buyer sometime ceases to be, and is transferred retro to the seller returning the price to the buyer.

The ***essential consequent of the pact of retrovenditio*** the Jurists by a peculiar name and style call: ***the RIGHT to the thing sold to be restored sometime for the price***, or the ***RECIPROCAL OBLIGATION to the restitution of the thing and of the price***. Whence they distinguish the essential consequent of this pact into two equal parts: on the part of the seller from this pact arises the ***RIGHT and FACULTY*** of repeating the thing and the dominion of the thing by the offering of the price; on the part of the buyer the ***NECESSITY*** of restoring and transferring back the dominion — to which however concurs the obligation to return the price by the one about to revoke the dominion. To this it most of all makes to know ***when and how long that obligation is in pending efficacy***.

#### Note VI of § 8 — The Moral Example: Habitudo ad Legem

**VI.** Let us touch a single ***Moral example***. That the ***morality of those actions*** which are called ***in and per se, and by their nature, honest or base to man*** formaliter consists in a ***real habitudo to law***, so that ***honestas formaliter is agreement with law*** and ***turpitudo is disagreement with law*** — no one of the Moral Doctors has ever denied nor will deny. But this is what more accurate Moral Doctors deny: that the ***first formal*** and ***the very essence of that MORALITY*** can be constituted in habitudo to law; and they will that this habitudo is only the ***formal and essential consequent***, and that this is the ***definition of MORALITY in human actions a posteriori***, which expresses that which necessarily follows from the very ***essence of MORALITY of human actions*** called per se and by their nature honest or base to man. For:

**1.** One thing is morality ***as such***, another morality proper to human actions.

**2.** If the morality of human actions in the point of reason stands antecedently to the will of a superior, how can [we go] with the contradictor —

**3.** who had pronounced by praetorian edict that law in general must be defined through the decree of a superior — that the essence of morality can be placed in habitudo to law? Let those things be repeated which above c. 1 from p. 79 to p. 140 were disputed.

Certainly it is naturally prior that man have a rational nature from God, than that he be obliged by God by the law of nature. Therefore naturally prior is the necessary agreement or disagreement of these or those human actions with rational nature; naturally posterior remains the agreement or disagreement of those actions with law. For God cannot by law prescribe to man an act disagreeing with rational nature, or by law prohibit him from an act agreeing with the rational nature of man. Let therefore those loving accurate doctrine judge what is the ***ἀκρίβεια*** in this thesis: ***honestas and turpitudo are moral affections or qualities of human actions ARISING from agreement or disagreement with law***. But perhaps they will desire the reason brought by the contradictor, so that by it they may the more rightly judge between the most celebrated Man whom the adversary had refuted, and the adversary himself most celebrated.

The adversary's reason is this: ***"If anyone impugns this thesis*** (honestas and turpitudo are moral qualities of human actions arising from agreement or disagreement with law), ***the haruspices will announce a prodigy, that a bony-colored man has spoken."*** Have all things at last fallen to this, that not by reasons but by insults — the base offspring of impotent mind — received Philosophy be impugned by the celebrated Theologian?

#### Note VII of § 8 — Against the Dismissers of Syllogistic Demonstration

**VII.** If the plan of our institute bore it, we could easily demonstrate that those who reject this signification of the notion as plainly useless, or believe it to have very little use, can discharge the office of accurate Philosophers and Doctors with little happy success. For it matters much whether you have defined a thing ***a priori*** or ***a posteriori*** — that is, (to speak Metaphysically) whether you have rendered perspicuous those things which are essential to the thing, or only its essential consequents. By the consent of all men of exact judgment and solid erudition, those who define ***a posteriori*** — through essential consequents — define ***dialectically***; but those who define ***a priori*** and through things essential, define ***analytically***. Therefore those who hold such things over-and-above truly do not know what discrimination intercedes between accurate definition and definition opposed to it.

E.g. ***eternal life*** is most truly defined through ***sempiternal and ineffable joy***, all Theologians attesting to this; and Sacred Scripture itself asserts the same (both Old and New Testament): see **Isa. XXXV. 10**, **Matt. XXV. 21**, **John XVI. 23**. And this definition the rude vulgar perceives far more easily and with greater joy; but the most accurate Theologians deny that this is an ***analytic*** definition of eternal life, since it is only a ***definition a posteriori and dialectical***, for the reason brought above at p. 347.

So too ***justifying faith*** is truly defined through the act by which the justified man believes that his sins have been remitted to him through and on account of Christ's merit apprehended by faith. Yet this definition is not accurate — i.e. ***κυρίως***, not ***ἀναλυτικῶς*** is justifying faith qua such thus defined. For one thing is: no one has justifying faith, nor is a believer, unless he believes that his sins are remitted to him; another thing is: for the essence of justifying faith to consist in this act. For this is an ***essential consequent*** of justifying faith, not the essence of justifying faith placed in it. And so those who define justifying faith through this act do not define justifying faith ***a priori***; for if justifying faith a priori were so defined, man would be justified by faith through this: that he believes his sins to be remitted — and so would believe something false (since, when he thus believed, they would not be remitted, but by that act were to be remitted, since justifying faith qua such is the cause of justification, and so prior to justification). These things we have drawn from the writings of the Venerable Theologians, and certainly in orthodox Theology other such examples can occur everywhere.

The same thing the more accurate Doctors of Law inculcate, when e.g. they acknowledge no definition of any contract or pact as ***analytic and accurate*** where in place of the differentia the ***obligation*** arising from such contract or pact is determined and distinctly expressed. In Moral matters too and in Politics they often incur the same reprehension — for those to whom these Metaphysical doctrines reek because they savour of ancient Philosophy.

Why, e.g., among the recent Moral Doctors do not a few please themselves immensely with their ***moral imputativity***, defending with acerb contention that it is the ***formale of morality***, that in which morality formaliter is placed? Why do the recent Politicians peddle as the most accurate definitions of societies and associates such definitions which only indicate ***how many rights***? In few words: the more deeply the ***ἀπαιδευσία*** has driven roots into the minds of easily-credulous auditors, the less can the accurate Theologians, Jurists and Moral Doctors congratulate themselves on auditors suitable for perceiving solid doctrine and accurate definitions duly and rightly. Hence it also comes about that this or that cultivator of Theoretical Philosophy allows himself to be imposed on, and with that notable damage contemns the received rudiments and genuine foundations of ancient Philosophy — not only ***an osor***, but also a ***rodent*** of all Philosophy.

To pursue the matter in the present is not permitted. Still, I leave to the judgment of all who care for the studies and advantages of Academic Youth (chiefly those with whom the memory of the Jena Philosophers ***Stahl*** and ***Sennert*** — men most well-deserving of the studies of Theoretical Philosophy — thrives; nothing shall I now say of the most excellent merits of the living Doctors and Preceptors of Jena, whom may God preserve!): let them judge what Doctors mindful of their duty can promise themselves from such auditors who allow themselves to be persuaded that:

> ***"True demonstrations are not Syllogisms, nor can they come about by Syllogisation, since the Syllogism only collects diverse things of the same thing, by always subsuming the same under ONE PRO MULTIS TALIBUS said (whatever under the said of all) — and so it may easily be presumed that its force extends only to reasons of identity (between one and the same) in concrete speech, and by the quantity alone of wider or narrower repeated speech it defends the alterity of the conclusion from the premises. Therefore by this its chief function the mathesis with the learners is quite depraved around concepts, as Grammar around syllables and verses. For in truth syllogism in one always and the same, by one act of collection subsists, nor touches the diverse reasons of things or parts (of which however all finites consist) to be elicited. Nay, lest the Collector-of-identity should commit a μετάβασιν εἰς ἄλλο γένος — lest the identity which alone he cultivates be disturbed by any determination of diversity — he is seriously ordered, although mention of diversity (yet indeterminate, in so far as it is the opposite of identity, and so that the predicate from the subject be excluded as diverse) through NON, NON, NON is not prohibited to be made. Therefore the mode of demonstrating predicatively — that is, by syllogisation — in so far as he uses only syllogisation (i.e. only that from the said premises he collect the conclusion), so in turn repeats the premised conclusion as the said thing proposed (otherwise already known either per se or from elsewhere), by two sayings identically congruent with the proposed (commonly called parallel sayings) and conterminous — does nothing other than that he interprets it. And this has the species of demonstration in that case when the whole discourse of the syllogisation (the said parallel both sayings, no less than the thing to be explained) is of the highest truth (often also of the highest persuasion)."***

Thus for example (1) they take care to demonstrate that ***a BEING IS ONE*** from ***the reason of being*** — that is, that such is the reason, form, nature or essence of all beings — a labor from which Germans can be free, who without demonstration know through the phrase itself: ***"Ein Ding ist ein Ding, nehmlich daß ein Ding ein Ding sei: Denn wolte bey den Teutschen an der Wahrheit folches zu zweiffeln."*** The same Italians, French, and the other nations, learning in the vernacular tongue, understand. (2) ***That a being is EITHER THE SAME OR DIVERSE*** (which no one doubts) they think to be demonstrated from this: ***that a being is ONE***; and yet that ***RES, ENS, BONUM, ALIQUID, UNUM are synonyms (for memory called REBAV)*** they immediately at the beginning inculcate. (3) ***That every BODY is QUANTUM*** (i.e. extended) they demonstrate from this: ***that every BODY is EXTENDED***, whose face of demonstration is this:

> *Whatever is extended, THAT is extended.*
> *But every extended thing is extended.*
> *Therefore every extended thing is extended.*

That this is altogether of highest certainty — but a small measure of Wisdom this medium of demonstrating is for persuading the mind of more than the proposition itself can offer. Nor from such unison does any joy result (which is however the genuine character of true demonstration, with the accustomed ***Q.E.D.*** always to be subscribed). Of highest persuasion is the example (4) when they contend to demonstrate ***that MAN IS RISIBLE*** from this: ***that he is RATIONAL*** — although man laughs the less the more rightly he uses reason. And these are the ***DICTIONAL and PREDICATIVE demonstrations***, which they allow as the only ones to be fetched from Syllogisation.

#### Veltheim's Reply to the Three Specimen Attacks

**(1)** It is most true, even by the most accurate Metaphysicians, to demonstrate the unity of being — that a being is one — from this reason ***a priori***: because it has ***existence***. Nor does it appear what in this syllogism could be desired:

> *Whatever has existence is one. Every being has existence. Therefore every being is one.*

**You retort:** this is wanting — that it cannot be pedlared for a demonstration, since that syllogism only collects diverse words of the same thing. **Response:** of one who proves of the same thing the same really through really-the-same syllogistically, on that account at once this judgment cannot be made — as if he had only collected diverse words of the same thing. Such a judgment, if anyone brings without discrimination, will often be preposterous, jejune, and contrary to the judgments of all rightly sentient men. For one thing is to collect diverse words of the same thing ***known in one and the same mode***, another to collect by applied diverse words of the same thing ***known in most distinct modes***. If anyone will not admit this, in doctrines Theological, Juridical, Moral, Political and others he will so be engaged that he confuses everything, ***"Delphinum sylvis appingens, fluctibus aprum."***

For in Theology all things that are in God are God Himself, which no orthodox Theologian or sound-judgment Philosopher denies: now let someone judge whether, if one attribute of God is demonstrated of God from another, this is to play with mere words. Let there be compared what above c. preliminary § 15 p. 5 we said. Perhaps it will be excepted that the discourse is not of God, nor are demonstrations given in natural Theology. To both an easy response. To the former: meanwhile it still remains most false that every syllogistic proof is mere words of one and the same thing. To the latter: there are found those who deny demonstrations to be found not only in natural Theology and in all Physics and Metaphysics, but even in ***Mathematics*** — nor do the most accurate and cordate Doctors wonder at this much, when the same men so dispute as if demonstrations find a place almost nowhere, and in the meantime peddle inept paralogisms as demonstrations. But just as by the authority of these the most accurate Mathematicians are not terrified, so there is no reason why we should be terrified by their authority.

Nor is it as the opponent dreams: with the fire-signal cry ***Q.E.D.*** that even the most elementary and first-rudiments demonstrations, such as this (**that a being is one, because it has existence**), should be given — the most accurate Metaphysicians have never peddled this syllogism for an ***exquisite and most solid demonstration***, but as a ***first and elementary demonstration***, such as are also recited in Mathesis itself.

**(2)** Where do these [novatores] demonstrate that ***a being is one*** from ***that such is the reason, form, nature or essence of all beings***? For most accurate Metaphysicians far less hold for a demonstration ***a being is either same or diverse because it is one*** than ***a being is one because it has existence***. Was not God from eternity a being? But who, pray, would ask ***was God from eternity same or diverse something***? Besides God, no being was from eternity, with whom God might be ens-the-same-or-diverse; meanwhile, no one would ask so ineptly whether God were the same or diverse being with Himself from eternity.

That ***RES, ENS, BONUM, ALIQUID, UNUM are synonyms*** — this is most false. ***RES*** lies more widely than ***ENS***, as above we showed. ***BONUM*** flows from the first concept of being. The same must be said of ***UNUM***. ***ALIQUID*** cannot always be taken for being in its latitude, but is often narrower, and is the same as "some being" — yet one thing is being in general, another is some being. Nay, often ***ALIQUID*** lies wider than being. Thus when I conceive of blindness, of irrational man, if I think the body of man to be an animal connatural to the human mind, I can say I thought of something, although what I thought of is plainly non-ens. For the voice ***RES***, as we have just said, is more often employed also of those which are non-entia, as is plain from the example of significative voices.

**(3)** As for the ***corpus-is-quantum-from-corpus-is-extensum*** example — who, pray, of sound mind would ever demonstrate that ***every body is quantum*** (i.e. extended) from this: ***that every body is extended***? How much more it would have been profitable, while these things were being written and simultaneously both own and others' leisure was being lost, to learn the first rudiments of Physics!

#### Note VII of § 8 continued — Rebuttal of the Risibility Specimen; Massive Example-Expansion

**(4)** As for the fourth specimen — ***that man is risible is demonstrated from this: that he is rational, although man laughs the less the more rightly he uses reason*** — let it be named who are those who, as ***accurate Philosophers***, peddle this example as a most accurate and most evident ***demonstration κυρίως and par excellence***. That ***reason or intellect is the principle of the act of laughing*** (not ***effective***, since it is material, and so proceeds from a material faculty; but ***directive***) no one will deny; nor will anyone go into denial that ***man is risible*** is demonstrated from this: ***that man is rational***. In vain is urged against this demonstration that ***man laughs the less the more rightly he uses reason***. For:

**(a)** who does not advert that these two propositions are confused: ***man is risible*** and ***man laughs much***? The question was not why man laughs more or less, but why man is risible — as if indeed ***first act*** and ***second act*** (as it is distinguished in the Schools) — to be able to laugh in act and to laugh in act — were one and the same.

The matter stands as if someone denied that it can be demonstrated that the Moon can suffer an eclipse from this — that it is a body obscure in itself and enjoys borrowed light — and used this reasoning: because the Moon suffers an eclipse the less the more it enjoys borrowed light. Anyone would see these two questions ineptly confused: ***why can the Moon suffer an eclipse? why does the Moon in act suffer an eclipse?*** The latter happens on account of the diametrical interposition of the earth between the Sun and the Moon obscure in itself; the former, because the Moon is a body obscure in itself and receives light from the Sun.

**(b)** Perhaps the one who uses reason the more rightly can the less contain laughter — for although man laughs the less when he uses reason more rightly, still rationality remains the ***a priori reason*** by which it can be proved why risibility belongs to man; and so he washes a brick who calls this into doubt. If, as the opponents feel, with the sign ***Q.E.D.*** fulfilled with producing-labor must effect that ***the spirit of joy exults from the bosom of the thinking mind for wisdom thence obtained***, so that by the jubilation ***Q.E.D.*** all the cultivators of wisdom be called to the communion of joy — why could this not also have excited ***laughter***? — chiefly if the pourer of that nectar should offer himself glad to his associates.

Nor however do more accurate Physicists acknowledge this proof — by which risibility is demonstrated from rationality of man — as a solid demonstration, or one which primarily merits the name of scientific reason. Nay, let us finally suppose some Latins to have held the four adduced examples as most solid demonstrations (which however is not yet proved, nor before the Greek Kalends will be proved) — and to have placed the stern and prow of the art of demonstrating in these alone — was it the part of equity and prudence to abuse their trifles and simplicity to explode the solid method of teaching through reasons received by all, as if the syllogism (whether proposed by ***QUICQUID, ATQUI, Ergo*** or by ***CUM, Ergo***) ***collects ONLY WORDS diverse of the same things, by always subsuming THE SAME under ONE pro multis talibus said, and its force extends only to the reasons of identity between one and the same in concrete speech***?

Nay, even if finally it be said that by a single syllogisation a solid and real demonstration cannot be perfected — ***why not***, so long as what in antecedence were necessary knowns are rightly and well known? Is this therefore not a true and real demonstration — but mere dictional — in natural Theology: ***that there is a God, since He is Himself sufficient to Himself***, demonstrated from this: that He is the ***summum of all goods***, whose proper and essential consequent is ***αὐτάρκεια***? — for this demonstration too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration in Physics — but mere dictional: ***that the Moon diametrically opposed to the Sun suffers an eclipse***, demonstrated from this: ***the Earth intervening between both snatches away from the Moon obscure in itself the Sun's light***? — for this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration in Moral Philosophy — but mere dictional: ***that each one ought to conserve his own life as far as in him lies***, demonstrated from this: ***since we have it from God as if by right of a deposit and as possessors of good faith***? — for this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration in Moral Philosophy — but mere dictional: ***that for a penalty to be inflicted there is required a communicated guilt***, demonstrated from this: ***since the merit is αὐτεξούσιον, that is, having origin from the will, than which nothing is more properly ours***? — for this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration in Politics — but mere dictional: ***that for any society there is need of empire***, since ***otherwise the associates could not be contained in office*** — or what comes to the same, ***a reason for expediting the affairs for whose sake society was entered must exist***? — this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration in Politics — but mere dictional: ***that the association by which many patresfamilias come together into one people and city is the most perfect society***, demonstrated from this: ***that any external action of man either per se pertains to this society, or from circumstances can pertain***? — this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration — but mere dictional: ***the one believing in Christ has peace with God, tranquillity of conscience, hope of eternal life***, demonstrated from this: ***since he is justified before God*** (Rom. III. 22 ff.; IV. 5; V. 1-9)? — this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration — but mere dictional: ***Christ is to be loved above all things by us***, demonstrated from this: ***since by His merit we are redeemed from the power of law, sin, the devil, death, and hell***? — this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration — but mere dictional: ***all men, whether adult or infants, who desire to become partakers of Christ's kingdom need regeneration***, demonstrated from this: ***that through it they are rendered partakers of the grace of the Spirit lost through the Fall***? — this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration in Civil Jurisprudence — but mere dictional: ***that a pupil ought to die intestate***, demonstrated from this: ***that he is wholly in the power of his guardian, so-called from guardianship, which is a force and power in a free head to protect him who on account of age cannot defend himself, given and permitted by civil law — whence the guardian (tutor) is called as if ***tuitor and defender***, and the guardian is given to the person, not to the cause or thing*** (**L. certae autem rei** 4 Inst. *qui testamento tutores dari possunt*; whole title Inst. *de tutelis*)? — this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration — but mere dictional: ***that a filiusfamilias has not the right of making a testament (except however by the castrense or quasi-castrense peculium)***, demonstrated from this: ***that he is in the power of his parent, and apart from the castrense and quasi-castrense peculium (in which he is held as paterfamilias) he has nothing in goods as to free administration***?

Is this not a true and real demonstration — but mere dictional: ***that the heir must defend, approve, and defend the deed of the deceased***, demonstrated from this: ***that he succeeded to his universal right***? — this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration in the science of the Law of Nations and Civil Law — but mere dictional: ***the right of usucapio and prescription***, demonstrated from this: ***since otherwise controversies about kingdoms and the boundaries of kingdoms, and about "mine" and "yours", would never at any time be extinguished***? — this too was perfected by a single syllogisation.

Is this not a true and real demonstration in Mathesis — but mere dictional: when the ***equality of the sides of a triangle*** is demonstrated from the ***equality of the angles***? Innumerable examples of this kind from all disciplines and faculties it would be easy to seek, if the plan of the present institute demanded more. Meanwhile it must not be believed that every demonstration must always be absolved by a single syllogism, since the contrary very often obtains in every single discipline and faculty.

[Veltheim then offers two extended chain-demonstration examples: a Theological chain tracing why Christ redeemed us from death (1 Cor. XV. 55-57; 2 Tim. I. 10; Hebr. II. 14): He was conceived (Luke II. 21) that He might be born (Luke II. 11); born that He might suffer and die; suffered and died that He might render us redemption through His own death — which we could not have obtained unless He who had taken on Himself the vicissitudes of Redeemer had died in our place and so satisfied divine justice. And a Civil-Law chain on *to those [delicts] which have not the atrocity of a bad deed or crime*, slaves obeying their masters' commands are to be pardoned (L. ad ea 157 D. de regulis iuris; L. is qui in puteum 11, L. an ignoscitur 7 D. quod vi aut clam; L. sed si unius 12 § si iussu 1 D. de iniuriis): the chain being — no injury (L. illud relatum 3 D. de iniuriis et famosis libellis) → no will (velle non creditur 4 D. de diversis regulis iuris; L. ad ea 157 D. eod. tit.) → compelled by command (L. si quis maior 41 C. de transactionibus). Yet the enormous and grave delicts (parricide, treason, adultery) can be compelled by no human right — ***Deo magis quam hominibus obediendum*** (Acts 5:29) — Aristotle *Eth.* V c. 7; the Emperor's *sed naturalia* in *Instit. de iure naturali, gentium et civili*; Plato's parallel.]

For the rest, it still remains most true that even that conclusion which is demonstrated from such a reason — that this reason cannot be demonstrated from elsewhere — is truly and really demonstrated; so that if the reason which cannot be demonstrated from elsewhere should not suffice for a real and accurate demonstration, no other demonstration would be either (even if as a chain it were composed of a hundred enunciations as if linked in rings and connecting without interruption or hiatus).

#### Note VIII of § 8 — Immediate vs. Mediate Essential Consequent

**VIII.** Here therefore the use of the distinction between ***immediate essential consequent*** and ***mediate essential consequent***, likewise between ***more or less mediate essential consequent***, exerts itself. Thus for example the Doctors of Civil Law rightly teach that of any pact and contract the ***immediate essential consequent*** is ***OBLIGATION***; the ***mediate essential consequent*** they call ***the right of acting from the obligation (ius agendi ex obligatione)***. So, because ***where judgments cease, war begins***, what forbids that of pacts and contracts ***merely public*** (that is, which are between Majesty and Majesty, between Kings and Kings' equals) the ***immediate essential consequent*** be called ***OBLIGATIO***, the ***mediate*** ***IUS BELLIGERANDI (right to make war)***?

Let us take another example: Doctors of Theology and Moral Philosophy call ***CULPA*** the more immediate consequent, ***REATUS*** the more mediate essential consequent of sin — of which more will be treated in the doctrine on practical use and abuse of the axioms pertaining to the present chapter. This remains most certain: that these distinctions rightly explicated and applied make much for perceiving solid doctrines and demonstrations with fruit and judgment.

#### Note IX of § 8 — Priority in Conceiving

**IX.** By what reason it can come about that of those things which are really one and the same yet in our mode of conceiving (solidly founded in the truth of the same thing) are distinguished, one as naturally posterior from another as naturally prior may be demonstrated — on this an occasion of looking at will be given in the following chapters, which indicate the doctrine of causes. There too we shall more fully consider the ***essential consequent*** in so far as it can and ought be called ***FORMAL EFFECT***.

## Caput Quintum

### Of the Notion FORMALITER in Less Frequent, Yet Not Infrequent, Significations

#### § 1

> ***FORMALITER (6) often admits such a signification that by this voice is indicated the SIMPLEST concept of a thing — that is, the concept of the thing AS SUCH, as the Doctors of the Schools love to speak.***
>
> ***For example: if someone should argue thus — "Whoever is properly wise, into him accident falls, because wisdom is an accident. But into God accident does not fall. Therefore God is not properly wise" — then rightly it is responded by denying the Major proposition for this reason: that WISDOM AS SUCH or formally considered and WISDOM AS IT IS SUCH or materially considered are confused.***
>
> ***For to wisdom formally considered it is not required that it be an accident, but this only is required for wisdom AS IT IS SUCH, namely as it is CREATED. To wisdom AS SUCH it suffices if it be the SCIENCE OF THE MOST EXCELLENT THINGS. But if it be considered as it IS SUCH — namely CREATED — thus it is necessarily an accident; and if wisdom be considered as it is IN GOD, so it is necessarily SUBSTANCE, and as to the thing itself God Himself.***
>
> ***The CONCEPT OF A THING AS SUCH the Scholastics call the FORMAL CONCEPT, and oppose it to the concept of the thing AS IT IS SUCH, which they name the MATERIAL CONCEPT. Thus for example accident does not pertain to the formal concept of wisdom, but to the material concept — namely to the concept of wisdom as it is created, as it is in a creature. For this reason wisdom was called formally the SCIENCE OF THE MOST EXCELLENT THINGS.***

#### Notes

**I.** Above c. 3 § 2 pp. 262 ff. the ***formal concept*** was taken otherwise, and was contradistinguished from the ***objective concept***; now it is opposed to the ***material concept***. Therefore the notion ***FORMAL CONCEPT*** is not always received in the same manner.

**II.** There have been those who acknowledged the generation of the second person of the Divinity, but denied that the Son of God can properly be called ***begotten***, and called the generation of the Son of God ***metaphorical*** — which sentence orthodox and accurate Theologians have disapproved and still disapprove, as calling the present Metaphysical doctrine into aid, and accurately warning that those things which pertain to the ***formal concept*** of generation must by no means be confused with those which are ***material*** of generation — that is, which pertain not to generation as such but to it ***as it is such***, i.e. to the ***material concept*** of generation.

For those who with too incontinent tongue said the generation of the Son of God is metaphorical were suffered to be imposed upon by this: that in generation there must be present a ***suffering subject***, a ***passive potency*** is required; and because such things import ***imperfection***, therefore they feared to call the production of the Son of God properly ***generation***. But a ***suffering subject*** and ***passive potency*** are not required for generation ***as such***, much less for the generation of a ***living thing as such***, or for the generation of a ***person*** — but [they are required] for generation ***as it is such***, namely for the generation of some ***created being*** or ***creature***.

***Thomas*** in his *Summa Theologiae* says this to be the formal concept of generation — that is, he defines generation as such thus (speaking of the generation of a living thing): ***generation of a living thing AS SUCH or IN ITSELF considered is the origin of a living thing from a conjoined living thing, on account of similitude of nature***. Other Scholastics say the formal concept of generation is ***the communication of the same essence***. We shall now not dispute whether this can be defended — that this is the concept of generation considered in common, and indeed of univocal generation. Meanwhile this easily stands clear: ***that the formal concept of generation belongs to the generation of the Son of God, and it is properly so-called generation***. For it cannot be denied that through generation God communicated to the Son of God the ***same numerical essence***, that the generation of the Son of God is the ***origin of a living thing from a living thing***, so that nevertheless they are of the same essence (the Son of God and God the Father).

This is certainly most certain: that the eternal generation of the Son of God excludes every ***passive potency***; but for ***true and properly so-called generation***, if it be considered in its formal concept and as such, passive potency was by no means required, nor should this be included in the formal reason of properly so-called generation: that a suffering subject or passive potency be required.

Why the eternal production of the Holy Spirit ought not be called ***generation***, let us learn from the Theologians — who uniquely ***adore*** this tremendous mystery, that is, forbid [us] to scrutinize it, and bid [us] to acquiesce in the revelation of Sacred Scripture. The same ***Augustine*** hints, saying: ***"If anything intercedes between to-be-born and to-proceed, who, speaking of that most excellent nature, can explicate? For everything that is born indeed proceeds, but not everything that proceeds is born."*** Thus he. For the rest, we have willed to show nothing more than the use of the present notion: namely that ***passive potency*** is by no means required for the formal concept of generation or for generation as such.

#### Note III — The Deus-Non-Potest-Mentiri Controversy

**III.** We find today those who call ***dangerous doctrine*** a doctrine approved and received by all cordate Philosophers, likewise Jurists and Theologians: namely when it is taught that ***God, with His sanctity and justice saved, cannot act against His promises and oaths***, and that from this doctrine the ***greatest consolation*** must be sought by any truly believing Christians at every time of their life — chiefly in persecutions and calamities. But let us hear the reason by which the ***fabricators and nundinators of dangerous — nay, most dangerous — novelties*** strive to make a fucus to the simpler. Chiefly they urge this: that these modes of speaking — ***God with His sanctity and justice saved cannot lie, cannot stand against His revealed word, cannot act against what He promised and swore by His word*** — can easily be insinuated to the simpler as if in God there existed an ***obligation extrinsically accruing***, which would prohibit Him from undertaking certain actions from which otherwise His nature and will would not per se shrink; likewise, that the simpler can fall into these cogitations: as if there were another besides God who could coerce God, who could command God; likewise, that He is wont to be called ***servile*** who abstains from the grosser ... [truncated in OCR].

#### Note III continued — The Deus-non-potest-mentiri Doctrine Defended

[The novatores also urge that:] he is wont to be called ***servile*** who abstains from the grosser vices; likewise that ***justice*** is called ***a habit of appetite consisting in mediocrity of affections*** — which cannot fall into God, since it is perpetual and essential to affections that they be ***motions of the sensitive appetite***, arise on account of imagination of good or evil, happen with mutation of the body, etc.

But although the plan of the present institute by no means bears a prolix and altogether necessary examination of this new Philosophy, let us touch only what pertains to the use of the present notion. ***All these flow from the material concept***: for that ***obligation imports superiority*** must not be understood of ***obligation as such***, but of ***obligation as it is such*** — namely as it is ***voluntary***, so indeed that it draws its origin from the ***free will of a superior as such***. There is also given ***natural obligation***, i.e. that which has its origin from the ***nature of the thing***, founded in the nature of acts per se and by their nature due. Likewise ***that justice argues respect to a superior*** must be received of justice ***as it is such***, namely ***of inferior order*** — yet this respect is by no means included in the formal concept of justice.

Similarly, ***abstention from grosser vices*** does not at all pertain to the formal concept of ***sanctity***, but such [a sense] is wont to be referred to the sanctity of man ***after the Fall***, not to sanctity ***as such***, i.e. as it is abstracted from created and uncreated. By the same reasoning we must refer to the ***material concept of affections*** — namely as they are animal affections, i.e. common to man with the other animants — that they are ***motions of the sensitive appetite, arising on account of imagination of good or evil with mutation of the body***. For the ***formal concept of affection*** it suffices that it be the ***appetition or aversation of something known under the ratio of good or evil***. Let the same be judged about the ***formal concept of virtue***. Or if someone does not wish to philosophize thus about affections and virtues, it must be said: ***for the formal concept of justice it is not required that it be a moral virtue placed in the mediocrity of affections***.

It is to be grieved therefore that often men who prefer to be seen and called men of great judgment, rather than to be such, neglect the first suitable rudiments of Philosophy and necessary auxiliaries — or either refuse or cannot understand them; whereas anyone who has become accustomed to these fundamental doctrines (as they are called) can easily animadvert on their affected ignorance, or perpetual study of becoming famous through useless novelties, and insulting men to whom the studies and interests of Academic Youth are a care at heart. In vain surely will you point out to the ***osores*** and ***rosores*** of solid Philosophy the vanity of new doctrines altogether acknowledged by the more accurate.

#### § 2

> ***FORMALITER (7) denotes the same as ABSTRACTIVELY or IN THE ABSTRACT, so that to consider a thing FORMALITER is to consider it by reason of its abstract or in respect of the form denominating.***
>
> ***For example: formaliter — that is, abstractively — the blind man is considered if he is considered by reason of BLINDNESS. If the notion of this adverb FORMALITER is thus received, then to it is opposed the adverb MATERIALITER, so far as materialiter is the same as CONCRETIVELY.***

#### Notes

**I.** This acceptation is most frequent in the Schools of the more accurate Doctors.

**II.** One sufficiently versed in the terms will never confuse these two: ***to consider something formaliter***, and ***to consider it properly and accurately***. For example: ***sin*** can be considered in two ways: (α) formaliter, i.e. abstractively; (β) materialiter, i.e. concretively. Each consideration of sin is certainly proper and accurate. Whence when sin is considered concretively, it is considered properly and accurately, but not considered formaliter. Therefore one thing is ***to consider sin formaliter***, another ***to consider sin properly***.
