#### Note III of § 2 — Original Sin: The Abstractive/Concretive Distinction

**III.** We shall indicate the use of this notion in Theology — not in our words, but in the words of orthodox Theologians most meritorious of the whole Church of Christ. Thus the Blessed ***Johann Gerhard***, *Theological Loci* Tom. II § 88 p.m. 402, disputes:

> ***"When we say that depraved concupiscence is a positive quality, we do not understand this according to Metaphysical ἀκρίβεια. The Metaphysicians subtly distinguish between the thing itself and the evil adjacent to the thing, which they always call privative not positive something. When Scripture defines original sin not by mere privation but also by depraved concupiscence, it imitates the mode of speaking used by the Ethicists: for they acknowledge vicious habits and bad actions. More distinctly we propose the thing itself thus: The Papists dispute that original sin is only the privation of original justice, of that supernatural gift — meanwhile the very nature of man is still such as it was first established; we on the contrary pronounce that through original sin not only the concreated justice is lost, but also the very nature of man is corrupted in marvellous and miserable ways. That corruption of nature, which comprehends in all the powers of the soul a proneness and impulse toward evil, we call a positive quality — NOT AS IF ANY FORCE OF ACTING IN ITSELF AND PER SE WERE SIN, but because THAT FORCE OF ACTING IN MAN IS ONLY PRONE AND PROMPT TO SIN. Meanwhile we do not forbid that between the force of acting itself and the vice of that potency a SUBTLE distinction be made, just as between the action itself and the vice of the action a distinction is made."***

The same thing [Gerhard] expounds nearly in the same words in his *Confessio Catholica* lib. II specialis part III art. XXI c. 19 pp. 481-482, with the thesis: ***"Original sin is not a mere privation, but also a vicious quality."***

[Gerhard's three points unpacked]:

**1.** When we say depraved concupiscence is a positive quality, we do not understand it ***according to Metaphysical ἀκρίβεια***. ***METAPHYSICIANS SUBTLY DISTINGUISH*** between the thing itself and the evil adjacent to the thing (which they always call ***privative*** not ***positive*** something). Scripture when it defines original sin not merely by privation but through depraved concupiscence and so vicious quality imitates the Ethicists' mode of speaking (who acknowledge vicious habits and evil actions).

**2.** According to Metaphysical ἀκρίβεια, evil is considered in two ways: either ***ABSTRACTIVELY***, i.e. ***IN THE ABSTRACT***; or ***CONCRETIVELY***, i.e. ***IN THE CONCRETE***. ***CONCRETIVELY TAKEN***, evil comprehends also that which it deforms or vitiates — whether action, passion, habit, or substance — whence it is called ***evil action, evil passion, evil habit***. ***ABSTRACTIVELY TAKEN***, evil is nothing other than the ***very privation of some good or perfection***. In the ***prior*** sense sin is something positive ***NOT PER SE ET FORMALITER but PER ACCIDENS and MATERIALITER***, that is, by reason of the subject in which it inheres or which it concerns.

**3.** When we say original sin is a vicious quality, we oppose this to the Papists who set up that original sin is only the privation of some supernatural gift, and that meanwhile the very nature of man is still such as it was first established. We on the contrary pronounce that through original sin not only is the concreated justice lost, but the very nature of man is corrupted in marvellous and miserable ways — that corruption of nature which comprehends in all powers of the soul proneness and impulse toward evil, we call a ***positive quality*** — not as if some force of acting in itself and per se were sin, but because that force of acting in man is only prone and prompt to sin. Meanwhile we do not prohibit a subtle distinction between the force of acting itself and the vice of that potency.

These things are handed down at the cited place pp. 481-482, where more testimonies and suffrages of the Scholastics collected by the Blessed Gerhard may be seen. The same sentence he expounds again nearly in the same words at his *Isagoge* XXIV c. 1 th. 10.

#### Kromayer and Hopfner on the Same Distinction

The Blessed ***Hieronymus Kromayer*** in his *Theologia Positivo-Polemica* art. VIII thesi II provokes to these same ἀξιολόγητα words of the Theologian Johann Gerhard, and after he had added the sentence of the Blessed ***Gravver*** and the Blessed ***Himmelius*** who hold the same thing, by way of colophon he subjoins the ***Blessed D. Heinrich Hopfner's*** decision thus:

> ***"It would have been wished that the term 'positive' had not been introduced into Theological schools in this place. Our Academy of Leipzig and Herr Chemnitz says that sin considered in itself is a PRIVATION. Philip Melanchthon, who first infused this term 'positive', derived it from Thomas the Scholastic, and used it in a shorter sense. The Papists in this manner are not convinced, but also concede, yet they say that merely natural defect is given. Privation is twofold: either the absence of original justice, or such a quality which falls short from the law — whence a delictum is called as if a 'delinquium'. VICIOUS HABITS are considered CONCRETELY. The Ethicist considers good and evil not ABSTRACTLY but CONCRETELY by reason of its subject — that is, not only goodness and badness, but good and evil actions. What in Ethics are contraries, in METAPHYSICS are privatively opposed. Proneness to evil considered outside the acting subject (in the original sin) and outside the action (in the actuals) signifies most rightly PRIVATION, yet does not note any absence of good, but a defect from the norm — which here chiefly is to be looked at."***

The same praised Kromayer soon places this ***antithesis***: ***"Sin is something POSITIVE properly considered IN ITSELF and FORMALITER."*** See this ἀντίθεσις subdita pp. 479 ff.

#### Gravver's Decision on Original Sin

Let it also be lawful to transcribe here the words of the Blessed ***Albert GRAVVER*** from the *Praelections on the Augsburg Confession* art. II. For here to the question — ***Is original sin only privative, or also privative and positive?*** — after bringing arguments on each side, he subjoins this decision:

> ***"It remains that we now expound what must be set up concerning this question: whether indeed one or the other sentence should be rejected, or whether each can be defended in a sound sense. It must be known therefore that evil or sin can be considered in two ways, as the saner Scholastics observed, either ABSTRACTIVELY or IN THE ABSTRACT, or CONCRETIVELY or IN THE CONCRETE. CONCRETIVELY, when the received evil or sin concerns that which it deforms — whether action, passion, habit, or substance — whence is called 'evil action, evil passion, evil habit, evil substance'. ABSTRACTIVELY on the other hand, when evil or sin is taken, it is nothing other than the very privation of some perfection or good. In the prior sense we can concede that evil or sin is something positive — NOT PER SE and FORMALITER, but PER ACCIDENS***, as ***Thomas on Lombard's second book Dist. 34 question 2 from Avicenna hands down***, ***that is, materialiter or by reason of the subject in which it inheres or which it concerns. For evil or sin CONCRETIVELY taken is not one thing but two: a vicious subject + privation of order. The subject itself is 'FORMALITER' a POSITIVE thing; the evil adjacent to it is 'FORMALITER' not something positive but only PRIVATIVE. "A blind man in the concrete" signifies something POSITIVE not PER SE but PER ACCIDENS, that is, materialiter in respect of the eye, as subject of which blindness is, or in which blindness is. Hence it appears that each sentence rightly accepted can be admitted — THE POSTERIOR [the privative view] HOWEVER IS MORE CONSONANT WITH TRUTH, since it expresses WHAT SIN IS IN ITSELF, PER SE, AND FORMALITER considered. The prior opinion also says what sin is, (but) considered per accidens and materialiter."***

These things we have uniquely with this end recounted: that the use of this notion received by orthodox Theologians might sufficiently and over-sufficiently stand known.

#### Note IV of § 2 — The Majestas Formaliter Controversy

**IV.** To add a single example occurring in Politics and Jurisprudence: in my slender judgment many would have been going to philosophize more happily in the doctrine on the nature and indoles of the Republic — chiefly when the question is of a ***mixed Republic*** — had they known how to explicate more accurately ***what is majesty formally considered***. When they cannot do this, let no one wonder why they deny that a mixed Republic can be given, and (what is held of greater admiration by the less-skilled) why some of these deny that any true and formaliter so-called Republic besides a Monarchy can be given.

Namely: ***Majesty formaliter considered, in Metaphysical rigor, is not a real being*** — which must not be so received as if Majesty were a non-ens or pure fiction (since with no one thinking the ***true and real moral faculty or power*** — and that supreme — of ***governing the city*** remains). Cf. what we said above c. 1 pp. 224 ff.

**But let us see what is brought against this sentence:** ***"A hitherto unheard-of dogma was late enough promulgated by a disciple of Veltheim in public disputation, THAT MAJESTAS IS NON-ENS: namely because for Majesty it suffices to not have a superior, nor is the power of governing the city required; because immediately he shines with Veltheimian Majesty, who, ejected into a deserted region, has neither lord nor subject. These monsters of errors we commend to be exagitated by others."***

Were not the rage of calumniating excussed of all shame from the adversary, he would never have dared so improbably to feign monsters of errors. Is it of an ingenuous and good man to have nothing to say except with great liberty, without face, without mind, to detonate whatever his splendid bile has suggested? Thus is it consulted to the name of the celebrated Doctor of Natural Law? Shall we at once, as he or that one shouts ***"monsters of Velthemian errors commend to be exagitated by others"***, fall down and like boys about to be flogged acknowledge guilt — even if there be no guilt? He who warns is a man, if God be He who warns, it is equitable not to answer-back but simply to obey. But now he who warns is no less a man than he who is warned: it is equal, therefore, that he admonish more moderately and in turn hear, lest perhaps he be blind in judging.

To me is imputed by the adversary the ***grossest error*** — as if I had defended such a sentence from which necessarily follows that ***for Majesty it suffices not to have a superior, nor is the power of governing the city required***, and ***immediately he shines with Majesty who, ejected into a deserted region, has neither lord nor subject***. Nor however does the adversary collect from my writings what he so acerbly reprehends, but asserts that it ***was promulgated in public disputation at Jena by a certain Velthemian disciple*** — and so has wished to borrow matter for insult from this, together with whatever else was supplied him from his private commentaries. But this he does imprudently, dissimulating what I myself in this matter have set up — whence that one, whose disputation he calumniates, could have sought his own.

My sentence stands published in print in my ***Introduction to Grotius's books De Jure Belli & Pacis*** l. 1 c. 3 qu. X responsio ad secundum § p. 460 ff. up to p. 471 and qu. XI § 3 p. 486 ff. — where to this day it can be read by all. I am most certain that nothing has been said by me there which has not previously been said by most learned men and most celebrated Politicians. Where therefore have I taught such things from which a man sound of forehead, who does not maliciously rage, could infer — I shall not say by a prompt and easy consequence, but by any consequence whatever — standing my assertion, ***that for Majesty it suffices not to have a superior, nor is the power of governing the city required***?

I expressly defined Majesty through ***supreme civil power*** (cited loc. § 2 p. 379). I expressly defined ***civil power*** through ***moral faculty of governing the city*** (§ 1 of the same c. p. 378). After in the preceding chapter § 19 p. 23 ff. and § 15 p. 17 I had explicated what ***moral faculty*** is properly and accurately speaking. I expressly called ***supreme civil power*** that civil power or that moral faculty of governing the city ***whose acts are not subject to another's right***, so that they cannot be rendered void by the arbitrium of another human will — and I opposed to it ***subordinated civil power***, which I called that civil power whose acts are subject to another's right. I also simultaneously warned (which is otherwise most-known to all, and by no one of sound mind called into doubt): if someone has subordinated power of governing the city, that he has a Superior over himself; on the contrary, insofar as someone has supreme power of governing the city, that in these lands he has not a Superior over himself. I also distinctly recounted and expounded the parts of supreme power of governing the city at the subsequent §§ ibid.

Let the cordate Reader, lover of honestas, now judge what must be thought of such a man who, with every love of truth and honestas routed, exhibits so much hatred, so much malice, so much impudence that he has these words made to be set in print: ***"Namely from Veltheim's mind, for Majesty it suffices not to have a superior, nor is required by him for Majesty the power of governing the city; and immediately he shines with Majesty, in Veltheim's judgment, who, ejected into a deserted region, has neither lord nor subject."*** If some fury were to come from the lower regions to raise tumults, what could be more furious than this malicious fiction? But this is customary with the adversary — most manifestly false things he affixes to me, and yet from these words he excites most verbose tragedies. Why he has borne himself less verbosely here you may wonder — perhaps because the adversary saw that if he referred my sentence with due candor, anyone would see with the hands that an atrocious injury is being done to me.

For the rest, if I were now preparing to respond, all those things by which I explicated my mind would have to be repeated. Since however I do not see what good can arise from such rabid contentions, I judge it better to neglect [it] — meanwhile deprecating God that He may give to such an adversary a sound mind, worthy of the profession of Moral Doctor, in a sound body.

Let me offer the reader this taste, that he may estimate the truth of my sentence. I said ***Majesty, if considered ABSTRACTIVELY and FORMALITER in Metaphysical rigor, is not a real being***. I gave this to be proved thence: because one thing is ***potency*** (which in Metaphysical rigor says a true and real being), another is ***power or moral potency***. For ***power can be given without potency***: e.g. an unarmed traveller has the power of defending himself against an armed robber, but not the potency. A king exhausted of all things and destitute of forces has yet supreme power of waging war against the most opulent and most potent enemy, but has not the potency.

Whence I do not yet see what ***power***, likewise ***supreme power***, abstractively and formally considered, says other than ***licence***, likewise ***supreme licence***; nor does it appear what ***summitas*** (which is Grotius's diction) of licence, abstractively and formally considered, imports other than such a licence from which those acts have that they are called ***licit***, which are not subject to the right of any man as Superior, so that by the Superior's arbitrium they could be rendered void.

Meanwhile it remains most true that that ***moral potency*** which comes under the name of ***civil power*** is the moral potency of governing the city, and that moral potency which is wont to be called ***Majesty*** is the ***supreme moral potency of governing the city***. This the adversary himself cannot deny. Whence anyone sees how most-miserable is the consequence which the adversary knits when he so collects: ***"If Majesty formally and abstractively considered is not a real being in Metaphysical rigor, but a mere moral something — namely a moral potency — it follows that for Majesty it suffices to not have a Superior, nor is required the power of governing the city, and immediately he shines with Majesty who ejected into a deserted region has neither lord nor subject."*** Whence, pray, can this consequence in any manner be rendered probable?

The adversary himself, when asked whether Majesty formally and abstractly considered is a being, responds that it altogether ***is*** a being, and that this dogma is hitherto unheard-of if it is said that Majesty formally and abstractly considered is non-ens. He proves his sentence thus: because for Majesty it does not suffice to have neither superior nor subject, but is required that one be Superior and have the power of governing the city and subjects.

But let the prudent and equitable censor judge how the proposed question and the adversary's response agree between them. In the state of the question the subject of the controverted question was restricted to ***MAJESTAS FORMALITER AND ABSTRACTIVE CONSIDERED*** — that is, by reason of the ***SOLE FORMAL SIGNIFICATE*** (not simultaneously the MATERIAL or SUBJECT in which the FORMAL is), by which ***Majesty FORMALITER AND ABSTRACTIVELY considered*** is constituted in esse sub specifico — whether it be a being? Because by us the negative, by the adversary the affirmative is defended, therefore the subject of our question demands that we treat Majesty by reason of the SOLE FORMAL SIGNIFICATE abstracted from the MATERIAL, in which the FORMAL is, and that it be considered a true and real being. But the adversary says that Majesty formally and abstractly considered is a real being — and proves this because otherwise for Majesty it would suffice to have no superior, nor would the power of governing the city be required, and immediately he would shine with Majesty who, ejected into a deserted region, has neither lord nor subject.

Who does not see that the adversary, when he thus responds, contradicts himself? For it is the same as if he had said: ***Majesty FORMALITER and ABSTRACTIVE*** — that is, by reason of the SOLE FORMAL SIGNIFICATE considered — is a REAL BEING not ABSTRACTIVE and FORMALITER but ***CONCRETIVE*** taken. Which is a manifest contradiction. For if Majesty is considered as it says the person who has subjects, so it is not taken ABSTRACTIVELY but CONCRETIVELY.

Nay, if we further ask the adversary — ***Is Majesty FORMALITER and ABSTRACTIVE considered substance or accident?*** (since the immediate division of being is into substance and accident) — he responds that it is accident, and in species a ***quality***. It is further asked: ***If it is accident, and in species a quality, how can it come about that the same numerical Majesty migrates from subject to subject?*** (For example, someone abdicates Majesty from himself and transfers it to another: the same numerical Majesty which before was of the transferer, now by his translation ceases to be, and is of the one into whom it is transferred. Thus when it is asked why a Successor can change the will of his Royal Predecessor, it is wont to be responded, and most rightly, that by the same right which the predecessor used, and so having the same numerical Majesty, not another). Yet otherwise accident cannot be positively separated from subject, and so cannot the same numerical migrate from subject to subject.

Likewise it is asked: ***How can the same numerical Majesty be with numerically-many*** (as those Recentiores do not deny can happen, so long as they admit simple Polyarchy to be given, although they hold mixed as simply impossible)? Yet otherwise one numerical accident cannot be in two really and adequately distinct subjects.

Here the adversary responds that ***Majesty FORMALITER and ABSTRACTE considered is not a Metaphysical real being, but a Moral one***, not in that rigorous genus of Metaphysical beings but in the Moral. If now we further urge: ***Majesty ABSTRACTE and FORMALITER considered, since it is a real being, is it from itself or from another being?*** He responds that it is not from itself. Further: ***If Majesty ABSTRACTE and FORMALITER considered is from another being, is it created, generated, or produced in some other mode?*** He responds that it is generated. Again: ***If Majesty ABSTRACTE and FORMALITER considered is generated, therefore it is produced from matter — which is absurd.*** He responds by distinguishing between ***physical and moral generation***: Majesty is not produced from matter as it is wont to happen in physical generation. ***Whence then?*** He responds that ***pacts (through which the city coalesces) are the proximate cause from which Majesty as a MORAL QUALITY results***.

[Veltheim then quotes the adversary's extended description of how Majesty arises from pacts (Livy II.55: ***imperii vis omnis in consensu obedientium est***) and concludes:] Anyone meanwhile sees that here the discourse is not of supreme power ***ABSTRACTE AND FORMALITER CONSIDERED*** — that is, ***of the Metaphysical ABSTRACTION of its FORMAL FROM THE MATERIAL***. But we have spoken precisely of supreme power ***ABSTRACTE and FORMALITER considered***. Moreover the adversary himself confesses that the mode by which ***MORAL BEINGS*** (e.g. Majesty abstractive and formaliter considered) are produced is not ***creation***, and can scarcely better be expressed than by the word ***IMPOSITION*** — and that this mode has always indeed obtained, but has not been observed by anyone. This standing, it is not an ***unheard-of dogma*** that Majesty ABSTRACTIVE and FORMALITER considered is not a being, since whoever hitherto have spoken of some being have either understood ***God*** or ***a created being***, as the adversary himself confesses.

Nay, finally let us grant for the sake of argument that in this sense Majesty FORMALITER and ABSTRACTIVE considered is ***a BEING*** — namely not in a Metaphysical sense, but in a Moral — still, does not our sentence stand on firm foot, since we have spoken only of ***Being in the Metaphysical sense***?

**You retort:** this ***METAPHYSICAL ABSTRACTION OF THE FORMAL FROM THE MATERIAL*** is of no use, if namely one is warned that Majesty ABSTRACTIVELY and FORMALITER considered is not REAL BEING in Metaphysical sense. **Response:** altogether this assertion is of greatest use. For those who deny that a ***mixed Republic*** can be given, when they use these foundations — that (1) Majesty per se is some ***individuum***; (2) because otherwise the rights of Majesty could be separated from each other by real division; (3) someone could simultaneously have one and the same Majesty whole and not have it; (4) that the parts of Majesty — nay, even its smallest particles — are nothing else than whole Majesty; (5) that Majesty is an incorporeal thing, and so for the divided part it cannot be commonly possessed — in nothing (by the judgment of great and most celebrated Politicians) do they more suffer themselves to be imposed upon, than that they hold ***Majesty ABSTRACTIVE and FORMALITER considered*** as a true and real being in Metaphysical sense, and believe that what repugns physical beings also repugns Majesty ABSTRACTIVELY and FORMALITER considered — as from Aristotle, Grotius, Lampadius, Conringius, Piccartus, Giphanius, Boxhornus, and other most Political Men's writings I have attempted to deduce in response to these reasons at Introduction lib. 1 c. 3 q. 3 § 3. And when the adversary — immensely pleasing himself with the distinction between physical being and moral being, and between the mode by which physical beings and moral beings are produced (namely between creation and imposition) — does not also admit the distinction between ***physical division*** and ***moral division*** (though in our peace he could distinguish not only between physical and moral beings, but also between physical knives by which physical, and moral knives by which moral beings are divided), and preferred to call the Republic ***irregular*** and ***monstrous*** rather than what more accurate Politicians call ***mixed***, why does such Metaphysics please the adversary:

> ***"Majesty is not a whole composed of heterogeneous parts, such that they could exist separately, only on account of diversity of objects it is called ***potestas legislatoria, δικαστική, bellica***, etc. The error about the division of Majesty seems to have arisen chiefly from this — that it seemed that those parts could be considered without consideration of the whole; whence they concluded that Majesty too can exist separately, and so really be divided. But quantity can be considered without consideration of body, yet not exist separately. So, imagine the potential parts of a rational soul to be separately in diverse supposita — will not man cease to stand with himself?"***

Perhaps because every simile runs on four feet? But why does the adversary dislike that we — stare amphibolously — dispute in this manner: Imagine several most distinct bodies — one in this, another in that, a third in that part of the earth — and simultaneously imagine one and the same numerical head of all those bodies: what a horrendous, enormous, and inform monster not consisting with itself will you imagine? Therefore as in a natural body one head cannot be of many bodies, so also in a moral body? Therefore the same head cannot be of many peoples (which however severally constitute a perfect assembly)? Therefore the same person considered by diverse reason cannot be the head of many and distinct Moral bodies, so that with the ruling house extinguished the empire can revert to each people separately? Why, I ask, do these things so displease the adversary? Perhaps because every simile limps?

For the rest, that ***Majesty CONCRETIVE considered is a true and real being*** was never denied by me, and whoever says I defended this dogma affixes to me by most atrocious calumny. And why would Majesty not be a true and real being? — one which can not only affect calumniators with grave penalty but also amputate heads, which makes Kings and Princes most-like God and raises them to the summit above the summit on earth; which stands as an exemplar of divine providence, when to one man's nod so many legions, warming often under a different Sun, promptly rise. Of which ***Artabanus the Persian*** at Plutarch's *Themistocles*: ***"Among our many laws, this is the best: that the prince must be worshipped and adored, as the image of God who saves all things."*** And not undeservedly, as at Curtius: ***"The name of king, nations which live by laws worship as God."***

Those things may be seen, if it please, which I have treated in three prolix dissertations under whatever moderation of my own: one ***On the Right of Empire Sought***, one ***On the Sanctimony of the Bonds through which the Republic Coheres***, one entitled ***The Directive Scepter — Of the Existence of Majesty or Supreme Civil Power*** (from most humble reverence of mind toward the inviolable diadem, which to violate I have pronounced to be not only unjust but also impious), proposed at diverse times to public light and public examination before this suit was moved against me — to which I appeal uniquely for this end: that the adversary may see I do not at all care for calumnies refuted by the truth of the matter.

— ❦ —

#### § 3

> ***FORMALITER (8) sometimes signifies the same as "in the direct" (IN RECTO), and is opposed to that which is "in the oblique" (IN OBLIQUO). For example: above we said that pure negation and privation IN THE DIRECT or FORMALITER do not differ — for the absence of sight from a stone was called PURE NEGATION, on the contrary the absence of sight from the eye was called PRIVATION; each FORMALITER (i.e. IN THE DIRECT) notes the same, since it notes the same absence. IN THE OBLIQUE, however, they are altogether distinguished: because pure negation CONNOTES an INCAPABLE subject, privation CONNOTES a CAPABLE subject.***

#### Notes

**I.** This doctrine has its use chiefly in the matter of ***concretes***. For ***concrete adjectives*** in the direct always signify the SUBJECT, in the oblique the FORM. For example: ***justus FORMALITER***, i.e. in the direct, signifies the subject to whom justice is attributed; in the oblique, signifies justice itself.

**II.** They must not be confused — which however is not rarely done by some — the ***signification in the direct*** and the ***primary signification***. Of ***concrete adjectives*** this is perpetually true: that the signification in the direct is not the primary signification, but the secondary, and vice versa the signification in the oblique is not the secondary signification but the ***primary***. For example: ***justus*** signifies the same as ***habens iustitiam*** — whence in the oblique it signifies justice; yet the primary signification of ***justus*** is when it signifies justice: for all, when the voice ***justus*** is heard, first and distinctly conceive justice; the subject, however, to whom justice is attributed, we conceive only confusedly. Hence it can happen — nay, most often does happen — that several concretes signify the same subject, although their primary significations may be most distinct.

#### Note III — The Case of Concrete Substantives

**III.** The use of this doctrine in Theology it is lawful to indicate by a few examples. And it must be rightly discerned by a Theologian that the matter stands otherwise with ***concrete substantives*** than with ***adjectives***. Certainly among the Scholastics as among other Theologians — most of all in Scholastic Theology — it is acutely disputed: ***what do concrete substantives*** (which, namely, signify both nature and subsistence) ***FORMALITER, i.e. IN THE DIRECT, signify — nature itself or supposit?***

For example: the concrete substantive ***homo*** signifies both ***humanity*** and ***supposit having humanity***, that is, man or an existing individual; now it is disputed whether ***homo*** signify ***humanity*** or ***supposit having humanity*** in the direct. Why is this disputed? Because by the diverse signification of ***homo*** in the direct, the ***unity*** or ***multiplicity of signification*** can be inferred: namely, if ***homo*** in the direct signifies ***humanity***, then it most properly signifies that one humanity which is common to all men; if ***homo*** in the direct signifies ***supposit having humanity***, then it signifies that supposit as such — namely as having humanity.

In this matter Theologians make a signal use of this ***in recto / in obliquo*** distinction. For when it is said: ***HOMO IS A SPECIES***, this signification stands if ***homo*** in the direct signifies ***humanity*** or ***human nature*** — since human nature is a species. If ***homo*** in the direct signifies ***supposit having humanity***, then it is false to say ***HOMO IS A SPECIES***, since the supposit is a singular thing, not a species.

Likewise it is important to the understanding of the mystery of the Incarnation. For when it is said ***CHRISTUS EST HOMO***, this proposition stands if ***homo*** in the direct signifies ***human nature***: for Christ truly has human nature. If ***homo*** in the direct signifies ***supposit having humanity***, then the proposition becomes difficult: for in Christ the supposit is divine, not human — the supposit of Christ is the divine Λόγος. Hence the Theologians say that ***homo*** in Christ's case formaliter in the direct signifies human nature, and in the oblique the supposit — but in Christ the supposit having human nature is not a human person but the divine Λόγος. These matters belong to Scholastic Theology, where more fully it is treated.

The same is to be judged of other concrete substantives — e.g. ***filius***, ***servus***, ***dominus***, etc. All these have a double signification: nature in the direct, supposit in the oblique (or vice versa, according to diverse interpretation). The accurate Theologian must therefore distinguish carefully.

The use of this notion in Jurisprudence: ***heres*** in the direct signifies the person who succeeds; in the oblique the right of succession. ***Pater*** in the direct signifies the person who generates; in the oblique paternity. The understanding of many Civil Law questions depends on this distinction. See the examples adduced by the Jurists in treating of the terms of the various contracts and relations.

For the rest, we have adduced only these few things, that the use of this notion of ***formaliter*** as it signifies ***in the direct*** opposed to ***in the oblique*** may stand clear.

#### Note III of § 3 continued — The *Hic Homo* Predications of Christ

Thomas holds this sentence: that FORMALITER or IN RECTO they signify ***supposit or subsistence***, IN OBLIQUO ***nature*** — and this opinion prolixly he defends. Of its defence is also ***Gabriel Biel***. The contrary sentence ***Gabriel Vazquez*** maintains, setting up that concrete substantives of this kind in the direct or FORMALITER signify ***nature***, in the oblique ***supposit or subsistence***. But to neither part do the more accurate Philosophers and Theologians dare to simply addict themselves — nay, if the matter be Metaphysically estimated, they cannot. For certainly examples of such concrete substantives are given which now in the direct or FORMALITER signify that very thing which elsewhere they signify not in the direct or FORMALITER but in the oblique.

For example, let certain predications from the Locus On Christ be at hand. Thus if someone had seen Christ in the days of His flesh and shown Him with a finger saying: ***"This man" (namely Christ) "eats, drinks, wakes, sleeps," etc.*** — here surely it cannot be said that ***homo*** in the direct signifies ***ὑπόστασις***. For there is one single ὑπόστασις (as we must learn from Theology) of the two natures in Christ, and it is proper to the divine nature, and into it the Son of God assumed human nature. Whence when it is said: ***"This man" (namely Christ) "eats, drinks, wakes," etc.***, likewise, if someone had seen Christ suffering and dying and had said: ***"This man" (namely Christ) "suffers, dies"*** — who could without impious absurdity say that this is the sense: ***the ὑπόστασις of the divine (nature) eats, drinks, wakes, sleeps, suffers, dies, etc.***? Which sense would surely be most absurd. For as is learned from Theology, the ὑπόστασις by which the two natures in Christ are united and subsist is one and single and proper to the Λόγος. Hence if in the direct ***homo*** in the adduced propositions signified ***subsistence***, the sense would altogether be this: ***the divine ὑπόστασις united to human nature is dead; the same also drinks, wakes, sleeps, etc.*** — the absurdity of which sense even the blind sees. Therefore ***homo*** in these propositions FORMALITER or in the direct signifies ***human nature***, in the oblique ***ὑπόστασις*** — namely in this sense: ***human nature united to the ὑπόστασις of the Λόγος is dead***; ***human nature united to the ὑπόστασις of the Λόγος eats, drinks, etc.*** Which is certainly the same as if it were said: ***Christ according to human nature is dead***, and ***according to the same drinks, eats*** — which all orthodox Theologians assert can rightly be said.

On the contrary, if it be said: ***"HOMO IS GOD"*** — there surely ***homo*** signifies in the oblique what in the previously adduced examples it signified FORMALITER or in the direct. For I cannot explicate this proposition ***homo est Deus*** thus: ***human nature is divine nature***; nor can I with truth saved say ***Christ according to human nature is God***. And indeed one who by ***homo*** in the direct signifies human nature in this proposition — ***homo est Deus*** — would openly nurse the ***Eutychian heresy***, because no predication is true in any Discipline or Faculty unless those [things] which are signified in the direct by subject and predicate are on the part of the thing the same — which is of perpetual truth. For from what a thing is, the predication is called true. But what is predicated in the oblique, so that it still be truly and absolutely predicated, must altogether presuppose a true and real identity between those which are signified in the direct.

And although not a few of the Scholastics say that in this proposition human nature is signified in the direct, so that nevertheless there be simultaneously connoted the ***subsistence***, nevertheless they cannot be freed from the Eutychian heresy in every manner. For the sense would be this: ***human nature having ὑπόστασις is divine nature having the same ὑπόστασις*** — but this sense is most false, and nothing other than Eutychianism itself.

Therefore it stands most firmly: that in the direct by ***homo*** is signified ***ὑπόστασις***, in the oblique human nature — namely in this proposition ***homo est Deus*** — so that this is the sense: ***the one and same numerical ὑπόστασις in which the two natures of Christ (divine and human) are united and subsist, and by reason of which these two natures are predicated of each other with truth saved — not however in whatever manner, but by concrete terms, inasmuch as those [terms] primarily and in the direct signify the ὑπόστασις in which these two natures are united***.

For if we consult the venerable Theologians for information's sake, they cannot give us any other reason why ***God is predicated of man and man of God***, so that one nature by a concrete term is truly predicated of the other also signified by a concrete term, than ***the union of the two natures in the same ὑπόστασις***. It pleases to adduce the words of the Blessed ***Johann Gerhard*** declaring this matter most fully. Thus the most meritorious Theologian writes in the Exegesis of Locus 4 c. 9 Thesis 168:

> ***"The ὑπόστασις of the λόγος most tightly unites each nature, therefore also IN THE CONCRETE — that is, by reason and respect of that ὑπόστασις — they are predicated of each other. For the genuine sense of these propositions "God is man" and "man is God" is: of each nature, divine and human, in Christ there is one common ὑπόστασις by which they are most tightly and insolubly united."*** Thus he.

And thus he will [have it] by the voice ***homo*** and by the voice ***Deus*** in the adduced propositions to be signified in the direct ***ὑπόστασις***, in the oblique the natures — and he makes this sense: ***the ὑπόστασις of the divine nature is the ὑπόστασις of the human nature, and vice versa*** — that is, one is the ὑπόστασις by which the two natures of Christ subsist and constitute one θεανθρώπινον person. He who desires to know this matter more amply and from Metaphysical principles — that is, conformably to them — let him look at the Blessed ***Felwinger***'s *Dissertation on Predication*, which in his volume is the first, from § 31 to § 51.

#### § 4

> ***FORMALITER (9) indicates the same as "IN OUR MODE OF CONCEIVING." When the signification of FORMALITER is thus received, it is opposed to the voice received in the Metaphysical Schools: IDENTICE — which also is wont to be expressed thus: ***A PARTE REI***.***
>
> ***For example: I rightly say of milk — namely that it is simultaneously white and sweet — "WHITE IS SWEET"; but when I wish to philosophize more accurately, I say: "the white A PARTE REI is the same as the sweet," namely if one and the same thing is simultaneously white and sweet. Yet I deny that white IN OUR MODE OF CONCEIVING — that is, if it be considered as it is VISIBLE — is sweet, if namely sweet be considered as it is GUSTABLE or in the order of SAVOR; for one thing is color, another savor. If now by Metaphysical terms I must express this my speech, I speak thus: "WHITE IDENTICE IS SWEET; WHITE FORMALITER IS NOT SWEET."***

#### Notes

**I.** This doctrine is the foundation of a most useful distinction — necessary to the Doctors of all Faculties — between ***FORMAL SENSE*** and ***IDENTICAL SENSE***.

**II.** It is permitted by one or another example to illustrate this matter in favour of the most noble cultivators of Theology and Jurisprudence. Thus for example this proposition often examined by Philosophers and Theologians — ***the divine justice is the divine mercy*** — is a most true proposition ***IN THE IDENTICAL SENSE***, but remains most false ***IN THE FORMAL SENSE***. For the IDENTICAL SENSE of this proposition is: ***one and the same numerical thing is what is called divine justice and what is called divine mercy***; for divine mercy and divine justice are in God, and all things that are in God are God Himself, which are God Himself are one thing, since God is one thing, one numerical being. Therefore divine mercy and divine justice are one thing. On the contrary, the FORMAL SENSE of this proposition is: ***divine mercy considered as divine mercy is divine justice considered as divine justice***. Whoever has eyes of the mind sees that this proposition proposed in this formal sense is most false: for if it were true in the formal sense, then the mode of conceiving would be the same if I conceive God as merciful and if I conceive God as just. For the ***FORMAL SENSE*** besides the thing itself includes also ***our mode of conceiving***. Whence as most distinct are the modes by which we are bound to know divine mercy and divine justice when we wish accurately to know each, so it is most easy to grasp the reason why the proposed proposition — which in the identical sense was called true — in the formal sense must be judged false.

**III.** That there may be a single Political example too, let us take by way of example this question: ***Does the restitutio in integrum have place against the contracts of Princes?*** — e.g. ***should the exception of Princes against contracts which they made as minors be admitted?*** This question Politicians and Jurisconsults hold as one of the chief and much-vexed. But it is not of our institute to decide this question now; this however we intrepidly assert: that the noble use of the signification of FORMALITER and of the notion just explicated can be seen in this very arduous matter. For when ***Hugo Grotius*** at *De Jure Belli & Pacis* II c. 14 § 2, and other men of great name, distinguish between acts of a Prince or King which are of a Prince or King ***qua such***, that is, which are ***regal***, and his ***private acts*** — what can be easier than to explicate this Political doctrine (duly perceived first) by these Metaphysical notions? Or (which comes to the same) to apply the just proposed Metaphysical doctrine suitably to this matter? For often this proposition is true in the IDENTICAL SENSE: ***the Prince contracted***, likewise ***this act was of a Prince was a contract*** — so that nevertheless in the FORMAL SENSE it can still be false, if namely the Prince did not contract ***as Prince***, if the act of the Prince or King is to be considered not as regal, not as public, but as private or quasi-private.

#### § 5

> ***FORMALITER (10) is the same as "IN ACTU SIGNATO" (in signate act), so that to consider a thing FORMALITER is to consider the thing in signate act; to which is opposed: TO CONSIDER A THING IN ACTU EXERCITO (in exercised act).***
>
> ***Here it must be said what is called signate act, what exercised act. SIGNATE ACT is called the reason or notion of a thing common to a whole genus of diverse things, inasmuch as it is common to a whole genus of diverse things. For example: things diverse by a whole genus are PREDESTINATION (as it is considered in Theology), EXCHANGE, TEMPERAMENT, MORALITY: when therefore I well consider that to any of these things its causes can be assigned, the notion of CAUSE considered as it is common to things diverse by a whole genus is rightly called SIGNATE ACT. But if the cause of predestination be precisely considered, or the cause of exchange, so there is at hand EXERCISED ACT.***
>
> ***Whence for example: he who precisely knows WHAT A CAUSE IS considers the cause ***in signate act***. But when a student of Theology knows WHAT IS THE CAUSE OF PREDESTINATION, a student of Jurisprudence makes perspicuous to himself WHAT IS THE CAUSE OF EXCHANGE — so the students of Theology and Jurisprudence know the cause ***in exercised act***.***

#### Notes

**I.** Because the Scholastics say the ***ratio formalis*** or ***first concept*** of a thing is that through which something IN ACT is what it is, hence it has come about that they judged the ratio formalis of a thing common to things diverse by whole genus — likewise any notion common to things diverse by whole genus — under the name of ***ACT***.

**II.** They called ***SIGNATE ACT*** when they signified the ratio formalis of a thing or a notion common to things diverse by whole genus ***alone and considered in itself***, not as it belongs to this or that thing and simultaneously to others diverse by whole genus — e.g. when they considered what cause is, what foundation, etc.

**III.** But when such ratio formalis or notion is considered as it is applied to the matter or thing of a certain genus — so as it were this very notion is ***exercised***, when it is attributed to a thing of certain genus and suitably applied — thence they said ***EXERCISED ACT***. As when it is shown that the merit of Christ is the cause of predestination; likewise when it is deduced that ***intrinsic morality*** — by force of which acts are called per se honest or base, and so by their nature due or illicit — is the foundation of Jurisprudence and of all natural law, so that the fundamental law of nature is: ***by intrinsic reason, per se and by absolute necessity, the honest (base) is to be sought (fled)***.

**IV.** With study it was said that signate act is given when the ratio formalis of a thing or the notion common to things diverse by whole genus is signified — lest anyone call any thing or notion common to several things and considered in itself immediately ***signate act*** or likewise ***considered in signate act***. For example: whoever in common considers what a natural body is, what the law of nature is, not attending to inferiors — he for that reason is not said to have considered natural body or the law of nature ***in signate act***, since their inferiors are certainly of the same genus; nor are modes of speaking rashly to be introduced that depart from common and received usage.

**V.** Because the whole prior part of Metaphysics — that is, that which treats of things really abstracted from matter according to indifference — and the whole Analytic hand down ***SIGNATE ACTS***, that is, notions common by use to the genera of all and every discipline and faculty, therefore everyone free from preconceived opinions sees that Metaphysics furnishes to the Cultivators and Doctors of all Faculties and disciplines a ***greater use than it promises***.

#### § 6

> ***FORMALITER (11) argues the same as "IN SENSU COMPOSITO" (in composed sense), and is opposed to that of which this or that is said, and so is attributed to it ***in sensu diviso*** (in divided sense).***
>
> ***For example: if someone should argue thus:***
>
> > *A musician who builds a house is a true cause of the house, and so a true cause.*
> > *A musician who builds a house is a cause per accidens on the part of the cause.*
> > *Therefore a cause per accidens on the part of the cause is a true cause.*
>
> ***It is answered by denying the Major proposition, if it is considered IN SENSU COMPOSITO. Namely FORMALITER (that is, in composed sense), the musician when he builds is not a true cause — because although he truly builds and is a true cause, nevertheless he does not build as musician, and so as such — i.e. as musician — he is not a true cause of the house, but as architect, if namely the same is simultaneously musician and architect. On the contrary, if the Major proposition and conclusion in the adduced syllogism are taken ***in divided sense***, the whole argument is conceded. For it is conceded that a cause per accidens on the part of the cause (that is, that which in another sense is called a cause per accidens on the part of the cause) is a true cause; it is meanwhile denied that considered FORMALITER (i.e. if precisely considered as it is a cause per accidens) on the part of the cause is a true cause. For example: a musician who builds a house is a true cause, but FORMALITER is not a true cause, since he is not the cause of the house ***as musician***, although he be a most true cause of the house.***

#### Notes

**I.** It pleases to show the use of this signification by a Theological example. ***Becanus*** in his *Scholastic Theology* against our Theologians thus argues:

> *The act of justifying faith must precede justification.*
> *The act by which one believes his sins to be remitted does not precede justification.*
> *Therefore the act by which one believes his sins to be remitted is not an act of justifying faith.*

To this Jesuit's argument, when orthodox Theologians respond, they know how elegantly to use the proposed distinction. Namely they ***concede the whole argument*** if ***the act of justifying faith*** be taken FORMALITER — namely so that the act of justifying faith is the same as the act of faith through which formally faith is justifying. On the contrary, if ***in divided sense*** the act of justifying faith be said to be that act in which indeed the nature or formal reason of justifying faith does not consist, but which by an individual nexus and necessarily is conjoined with the act by which Christ's merit is apprehended, and proper to it — then surely the Major proposition is most false. For it is false (what Becanus had said) that the act of justifying faith must precede justification; since this holds only of the act of justifying faith if FORMALITER (i.e. in composed sense) it be considered — if namely that act be considered through which qua such faith is justifying.

Whence one thing is that some act is of faith and proper to the believer or truly believing; another thing is that in that act the nature of justifying faith in composed sense considered — that is, inasmuch as it is justifying — consists. For he who from the former to the latter argues, confuses divided sense with composed. And to this point tends the Metaphysical doctrine proposed; so the more accurate of our Theologians use the same, when against Becanus they defend that the believer does not exist who does not believe his sins to be remitted — so that therefore through this act, by which one believes his sins to be remitted, not a few of ours define faith, so that nevertheless they hold this for a definition ***a posteriori***. Cf. what was said above c. 4 § 8 Note 7 p. 353.

**II.** It is known to the cultivators of Themis the discrimen which stands in the books of Roman Law, when one thing is called ***the right common to man with brutes***, another the ***right proper to man*** — of which, whether it has use, not only the more accurate Moral Philosophers but also many most celebrated Jurisconsults greatly doubt. Meanwhile, those wishing to defend ***the right which nature has taught to all animals*** — if ever they proposed any argument which bears before itself a great appearance of truth — it is certainly this:

> *The judgment by which it is known that the fetus must be nourished is common to man with brutes.*
> *The judgment by which it is known that the fetus must be nourished is the law of nature.*
> *Therefore the law of nature is common to man with brutes.*

To this argument, if we respond, the Metaphysical doctrine just proposed easily comes to aid. For the Minor proposition, if the middle term be taken FORMALITER — i.e. in ***composed sense*** — is false; but if it be taken in ***divided sense***, it is true. More clearly: in ***composed sense*** this proposition remains most false: ***the judgment by which it is known that the fetus must be nourished is the law of nature***; in ***divided sense*** this proposition could be conceded. For it is the same as if you should argue thus:

> *The potency of knowing is common to man with brutes.*
> *The potency of knowing is the intellect.*
> *Therefore the intellect is common to man with brutes.*

This conclusion is certainly most false. When therefore from the ***undistributed*** to the ***distributed*** we proceed, a vice is committed in the form. But it is simultaneously also hinted that the judgment by which it is judged that the fetus must be nourished can be called natural law, yet this must not be understood FORMALITER — that is, in composed sense — but in ***divided sense***. For the rest, this proposition — ***the judgment of the human intellect by which it is judged that the fetus must be nourished is the law of nature*** — is FORMALITER (i.e. in composed sense) most true: for it stands that the law of nature is often taken for the ***dictate of right reason indicating the necessary agreement or disagreement of acts with rational nature***.

**III.** And let it suffice to have said this much about the various significations of FORMALITER. We have not however willed — which we ingenuously confess — to recount all, lest tedium be born to the reader. In the following when there is treatment ***in a peculiar chapter of MATERIAL and FORMAL***, more things pertaining to this will occur.

## Caput Sextum

### Of Commons to One — i.e. Analoga

Of those, if it be asked ***what FORMALITER they are?*** eruditely and sufficiently it can be responded, yet ***one and common FORMAL REASON*** either they altogether reject, or communicate unequally.

#### § 1

> ***What ***commons to one*** are, and how many classes of them are given, is perhaps most easily and by sufficiently convenient method shown if it be proceeded thus:***
>
> ***Two or several things signified by one and the same name, either according to the same name have the same FORMAL REASON, or do not have. If they do not have the same formal reason according to the same name — or have diverse formal reasons according to that name — so they are ÆQUIVOCA. Or they do not have diverse formal reasons according to that name, and so they are COMMONS TO ONE, which come closer to equivoca. If they have the same formal reason according to the same name, that formal reason belongs to them either equally — so they are UNIVOCA — or unequally, and so again they are COMMONS TO ONE.***

— ❦ —

#### Notes on § 1

**I.** There is no doubt that the doctrine ***de κοινοῖς πρὸς ἕν*** / ***commons to one*** pertains to Metaphysics in so far as to the question ***what formaliter they are?*** it can be responded. Nor can we not approve the judgment of a man of great name, ***Herr D. Dreierus***, which in his *Philosophia Prima* he brought forward: when at *disp.* III (which still treats of the nature and constitution of First Philosophy) § 15 p. 56 he writes: ***"The doctrine on commons to one has the greatest use in all Peripatetic Philosophy. The Scholastics, however, not observing the nature of this form, have perverted First Philosophy and nearly all solid reasoning of philosophizing."***

**II.** Meanwhile there is no reason to fear confusion of Metaphysical and Analytical doctrines. For just as one thing is to treat of ***ratio formalis***, another of ***essential definition*** (the former pertains to Metaphysics, the latter to Analytics), so when the Analytician ex professo teaches that ***commons to one cannot be accurately defined***, yet they can still be accurately taught and learned, he seeks the foundations from First Philosophy (which today they call Metaphysics), to which at last recourse must be had. For although no one think that through all the genera of disciplines they wander, and that in every genus of doctrine there occur innumerable examples of ***commons to one*** — they are nevertheless given in all disciplines and Faculties, and (with no one thinking) argue a true and real foundation by force of which, however much they are said multiply according to the same name, under one and the same name they can be reduced ***to one*** with no one thinking.

**III.** To most of today's cultivators of Philosophy this very doctrine on ***commons to one*** appears intricate, thorny, of little use, or utterly useless. But we the less wonder that such boredoms and hatreds against so necessary and most useful a doctrine are conceived, the more we weigh that few there are whom equitable Jupiter has so loved as to hold the Greek Philosophy in deserved price. Nay, if there are such today, by rare auxiliaries have they fortified themselves. Whoever despises them, Aristotle does them violence to the text; most often is more obscure than the text; and where he can still be understood by one skilled in the Greek diction and aid his reading, there by one ignorant of Greek speech he cannot be understood. And of commentaries, the clearer are to be chosen — of which the more ancient (who with Pallas more propitious sought out hidden senses) are to be preferred.

Who among today's students of Philosophy is easily [to be found] to whom even the names of the Greek Commentators are known — not to say who has read them, far less (what most needs to be added) who has read them ***with judgment***? On many lips floats this: ***"They are Greek, they ought not be read"***. What, few are found who even expend so little time on First Philosophy studies that they even with fugitive or scowling eye read those Latin writings in which the most excellent Men — from Aristotle and the best Ancients, especially the Greek Commentators — have by scientific method collected and composed the dogmas most necessary and most useful of knowing.

The most accurate ***Scherbius*** testifies somewhere that he often had need to engage with such patients where this almost pathognomonic sign of the disease had been seen: ***"A great fastidium, and a certain insolent contempt of all ancient Philosophy, conjoined with a perpetual itch of innovating."*** Let God avert that this symptom — as the most-praised Man most truly calls it, altogether similar to what sometimes is in pregnant women, who oppressed by great cachochymy neglect the best and most salutary foods, and in their place feed on charcoal and ashes — grow by days, and that of Horace obtain: ***"The greatest part of mortals is tossed by the same disease."***

**IV.** ***Scotus and all his followers denied, and persistently denied, that a middle is given between univoca and aequivoca***. Their reasons are the following:

**(1)** Because univoca and aequivoca import truly contradictory definitions, since univoca are those which according to the same common name have the ***same formal reason***; aequivoca are called those which according to the same common name have ***not the same formal reason*** but ***diverse***. But to have the same formal reason according to a common name and not to have the same formal reason according to a common name are truly contradictory definitions.

**(2)** Because neither in things nor in words can any middle be found between ***one*** and ***many***. Therefore neither between univocum and aequivocum, since univocum and aequivocum are opposed by ***signifying one and many***. This reason the most learned Scotist ***Johannes de Rada Aragonius, Episcopus Pacensis***, urges in his *Controversiae Theologicae inter Thomam et Scotum* lib. 1 sent. controv. 7.

**(3)** Because those which by other Scholastics are set up as middles between univoca and aequivoca — and called ***ANALOGA*** — either are:
- **analoga inaequalitatis** (which according to one common name have altogether the same formal reason, yet so that one having the same formal reason is more noble than the other, or if there be several, than the rest);
- **analoga proportionis** (which according to one common name have formal reasons diverse among themselves, yet in a certain proportion similar to one another);
- **analoga attributionis** (which according to one common name either have formal reasons neither the same nor diverse, or have the same formal reasons but not equally, but unequally communicated to them).

The first [analoga inaequalitatis] are univoca, because genus's being conjoined with a more noble difference in one than in another does not impede univocation. The second [analoga proportionis] are aequivoca, because they have according to one and the same name diverse formal reasons. The third [analoga attributionis] either are aequivoca (if they do not have the same formal reasons) or are univoca (if they have the same formal reasons in an unequal mode) — for that inequality is outside the common formal reason. For example: although accident is posterior to substance and depends on it, yet it is posterior and depends not ***in the formal reason of being*** or ***as it is being*** (since otherwise every being would be posterior and dependent), but ***in the reason of accident*** or as it is accident. In like manner, although substance is prior to accident and independent, yet it is prior and independent not ***in the formal reason of being*** but ***in the reason of substance***.

**V.** But to these arguments of Scotus and all with him today thinking the same, to respond is easy — difficult however it becomes to commend these responses to the Cultivator of Philosophy imbued with preconceived opinions, for whom it is always more difficult to unlearn than to learn.

**To 1.** It is responded by denying that ***univoca*** and ***aequivoca***, if each be strictly and in rigor received, import contradictory definitions. For neither are those perfectly called ***aequivoca*** which according to the same common name do not have the same formal reason; nor are those perfectly defined when they are defined as those which according to the same common name have the same formal reason. For each formula of definition is wider than its defined — because some things which are not univoca strictly and in rigor so-called have the same formal reason, and some things which cannot be called aequivoca strictly and in rigor such do not have the same formal reason, as from the following §§ will be plain. By what right therefore can those predications be called contradictory definitions of univoca and aequivoca which lie wider than the defined? It is the same as if someone wished to call these contradictory definitions of angel and animal: that angel is immaterial substance, animal is material substance — for substance immaterial lies wider than angel, and material substance wider than animal.

Here it could be excepted that it still remains most true that univoca and aequivoca with respect to the same import contradictory reasons, since it cannot be denied that univoca according to one and common name have the same formal reason, aequivoca according to one and common name do not have the same formal reason. It is responded that all these are most true, but from them it can by no means be evinced that a middle between univoca and aequivoca cannot be given. For not whatever imports contradictory reasons with respect to the same immediately for that reason spits out every middle — as above c. 1 Axiom II pp. 199 ff. up to p. 208 we taught. For they are not immediately contradictory reasons which univoca and aequivoca were said to import. For just as e.g. middle substances are given between angels and animals, so middles having one and the same common name are given between univoca and aequivoca.

**To 2.** We say that altogether a middle between one and several is given: a middle being, however, is none. Whence as to the present it must be given warning: it can happen that two or several things having one and common name, according to that name, neither have the same formal reason, nor have diverse formal reasons, as will soon be declared by several examples. For just as it does not follow that those who are not lords and possessors of one kingdom are therefore lords and possessors of several kingdoms, nor does it follow that those who have not one coat have several coats (since it can happen that one be lord of a kingdom, another not; one have a coat, another lack it) — so neither is it permitted to argue from those having one and common name yet not having one and the same formal reason according to that name, to those having diverse formal reasons according to that name.

**To 3.** It must be noted by way of response that by Thomas and those who stand on his side are called ***analoga attributionis*** those which by Aristotle are called ***commons to one***. The thing is the same, the mode of speaking new and certainly not very congruous. For ***analoga*** are so called from ἀναλογία, and analoga are nothing other than things having proportion. Therefore ***analoga proportionis*** will be things having proportion of proportion — a trifle. By the consent of all more accurate [persons] ἀναλογία (in Latin ***proportio***) consists in ***four terms***, of which as the first stands to the second, so the third to the fourth. In vain therefore is it distinguished between analoga proportionis, inaequalitatis, and attributionis — since analoga rightly and accurately so-called are not called except those which on account of ἀναλογίαν (that is, proportion) have the same name, not however the same formal reason signified by that name. For example: ***the foot of a man and the foot of a bed***; ***the head of a man and the head of the true Church***; the ἀναλογία between ***contractus voluntarius*** and ***contractus involuntarius***.

And although many things are simultaneously analoga and ***commons to one***, we nevertheless have no doubt but that analoga qua such — and so also those ***commons to one*** which are and inasmuch as they are ***analoga*** — can be referred, nay ought be referred, to ***aequivoca a consilio*** so-called. For those which on account of analogy are aequivoca, are aequivoca-by-counsel. ***Analoga inaequalitatis*** however — which certainly are nothing less than analoga — altogether remain ***univoca*** strictly and in rigor so called. For it is false that stag is less called animal, man more under the name of animal is judged. For however much man is more excellent than horse, nevertheless in man and horse — inasmuch as they are partakers of the genus (animal) — ***prior*** and ***posterior*** is not seen. For man is neither more nor prior to horse animal, but man and horse ***equally*** participate the formal reason of animal.

#### § 2

> ***Commons to one which come closer to univoca agree with univoca in this: that according to one and common name they have the same formal reason. They differ from univoca in this: that these [univoca] according to one and common name have the same formal reason belonging equally to each; those [commons to one] however participate the name and formal reason unequally.***
>
> ***For example: man and horse are univoca, and they have the name equally common, since they are equally called animals; and according to that name they have the same formal reason equally common to each. For man and horse are equally natural animated sentient substances; nor is prior or posterior seen in these species of animal, nor is it necessary that with one of these species removed, the other be removed.***
>
> ***On the contrary, substance and accident participate the name (ens) and the formal reason according to that name unequally — since substance is prior, accident posterior; and with substance removed, accident too is removed. Whence it follows that substance is more partaker of being — for this is the force of substance, that it makes accidents to be (as they lean on it); but that substance may be, it needs no help of accidents.***

#### Notes

**I.** These ***commons to one which come closer to univoca***, Thomas Aquinas called ***analoga attributionis intrinsecae***, which appellation many of today's Philosophers not only retain but also prefer to the mode of speaking of Aristotle and the Greeks. For the first, as far as I know, among Scholastics who wrote of analogues of various genera was Thomas, who expounded his mind frequently in his writings, chiefly in his *Commentaries on Aristotle's Metaphysical books*.

**II.** Why they call analoga ***commons to one***, no reason appears. For there analoga are given, where ἀναλογία has its place. But to all, as we have said before, it can stand clear that ἀναλογία — i.e. ***proportio*** — by unanimous consent of the learned consists in four terms. But no one in ***analoga attributionis intrinsecae*** (as they are called) will find these four terms. Whence we still desire the reason of the appellation — unless perhaps with a most ingenious Man it must be said that commons to one are called analoga (i.e. having proportion) because they never equally agree with one name but ***by proportion*** (i.e. unequally) are attributed — to which etymology scarcely anyone will give faith without laughter.

Therefore they said ***analoga attributionis*** lest anyone believe analoga simply so-called to be understood, which are called by them ***analoga proportionis*** — as if proportion of proportion were given. For the rest, why they call them ***analoga attributionis intrinsecae***, it is easy to attain: because they communicate one and the same formal reason (albeit not equally and with equal honor, as Suidas says). For example: ***soul*** in the order to nutrient (commonly called ***vegetative***), sentient, and intelligent is rightly said to be in the number of ***commons to one*** — but it cannot be denied that both nutrient soul, and sentient soul, and intelligent soul all by their nature and intrinsically — not only by extrinsic denomination — are ***soul***. Hence it also happened that Aristotle, going to explicate the nature or formal reason common to all souls, defined soul in common through ***ἐντελέχεια*** (which Latin Philosophers less happily rendered ***actus primus***) ***of an organic body having life in potency***. The whole Philosophy of the soul therefore is the ***science of commons to one***.

In like manner, if ***ens*** be considered as it says that which truly and really exists — or (as commonly the Schools speak) ***that which is outside nothing*** — it cannot be called into doubt that substance and accident by their nature and intrinsically, not merely by external denomination, are ***entia*** and rightly are reduced hither. Meanwhile (as in this very § we have warned), altogether a notable discrimen still intercedes between univoca strictly so-called and commons to one which come closer to the same. For those which are truly univoca are so called in the order to those which communicate one and the same nature ***equally and with equal honor*** (e.g. animal with respect to man and brute). On the contrary, those commons to one which come closer to univoca are so called in the order to those which participate one and the same nature ***unequally*** — e.g. nutrient, sentient, and intelligent soul unequally participate the nature of soul, which inequality consists in this: that in them there is ***order***, and one presupposes the other as prior and prerequires it. By the same reasoning inequality can be seen in substance and accident: remove by the impossible all substance, no accident will be given; remove accident, substance will still be given. Unless substance be given, no being will be given — whence that being may be, substance must be given, since being can still be given although no accident be given.

**III.** Aristotle and the Greek Interpreters, that this discrimen might be more accurately explicated, distinguished between what is common to many ***καθ' ἓν φύσιν*** (according to one nature) and what is common to many ***πρὸς μίαν φύσιν*** (to one nature): the former calling ***univocum***, the latter ***commune ad unum***, coming nearer — nay nearest — to univocum. And what we think worthy of noting: the Greek Interpreters, that they might discern these two by suitable reasons, said univocum strictly so-called argues ***nature placed above those with respect to which the universal is said***. For if for example someone wishes to know the nature of animal, he can equally well know it and sufficiently make it perspicuous to himself by knowing man as by knowing brute, and conversely. For it is certain that animal can be known per se with no respect had to inferiors, and can also be known through each inferior — that is, through man considered separately and through brute considered separately.

On the contrary, ***commons to one which come closer to univoca*** signify no common nature placed as it were above inferiors, because in one inferior such common nature can be more exactly known than in another; nor are such inferiors rightly and accurately called ***species***. For as before we showed, with some species removed — whatever it be, rightly and accurately so-called — the genus is not immediately removed: there remains equally that generic nature in the species remaining, whatever species finally you remove. Meanwhile, because inferiors considered in the order to a ***common to one*** coming closer to univocum are all and single formaliter such as they are called, altogether they approach most nearly to inferiors under univocum contained, and so in this sense are called quasi ***species*** of being — substance and accident; quasi ***species*** of soul — nutrient, sentient, and intelligent soul.
