#### § 3

> ***What signal use this doctrine on commons to one coming closer to univoca affords, is handed down most fully in the Analytics. Surely the whole doctrine on SOUL, on BEING, on SUBSTANCE, on ACCIDENT, on FIGURE, on NUMBER, on MOTION, on MORAL ACTIONS, their MORALITY, and the obliging RULE which we call LAW — in Theology on CREATION, PREDESTINATION, etc. — in Jurisprudence and Politics on DOMINION, on RIGHT (which the Jurists appropriately call by its own name), on CONTRACT and QUASI-CONTRACT, on WAR and its RIGHT, etc. — and six hundred other doctrines, nay innumerable, are far more happily and rightly learned, if the whole doctrine on these COMMONS TO ONE (those namely which come closer to univoca) has been strictly and rightly first perceived, whose first notion and foundation can and must be sought from First Philosophy itself.***
>
> ***This above all let it be noted: that what this very thing is to which the notion of our common to one can rightly and truly be attributed, can be learned and taught. For example: it can be learned and taught in common what SOUL is, before it comes to the nutrient, sentient, and intelligent soul; it can be learned and taught in common what BEING is, before descent is made to substance and accident; what moral action, what morality, what law, what figure, number, motion, etc.***
>
> ***Meanwhile let it be accurately held that an EXACT and in all numbers absolute definition of those things which belong to this class of COMMONS TO ONE (and so come closer to univoca strictly so-called) in vain is to be expected and urged.***

#### Notes

**I.** They labour ***ἀναισθησίᾳ*** (anesthesia) or at least are not yet sufficiently ***ἀκριβωμένοι*** (polished to precision) who do not know how to hold for most distinct: to ***hand down in common what this or that is***, and to ***hand down an exact and in all numbers absolute definition of a thing considered in common***. For from the former to the latter the consequence does not hold.

**II.** Thus for example I teach ***what in common BEING is***, when I teach that it is called ***ens*** which is ***outside nothing***, which truly and really exists, which apart from the operation of the mind is in act — that is, which is in act (although no one think it to be in act), which has true and real existence. By this formula certainly substance and accident are signified, as anyone easily sees. But no one would be so absurd as to assert the definition of being in all numbers absolute and perfect to be handed down in these formulas — for where then is the ***genus*** of being in common? Where is the ***specific difference***? Without genus and specific difference an accurate definition strictly so-called cannot be given, with all the saner spontaneously admitting this. In like manner, Aristotle before he had progressed in the books of the science of soul to treat of the particular genera of soul, antecedently defined indeed ***what soul is in common***, but soon added and warned: an ***imperfect and rude*** definition of soul in common was given, since the ***accurate and most rightly so-called*** can never be had — because soul is of the number of ***commons to one coming closer to univoca***.

#### Note III — The Massive Creation/Generation Example

**III.** By a luculent example, in favour of the Students of Theology, we shall illustrate the mode of knowing ***commons to one which come closer to univoca***.

To the question: ***What formaliter is GENERATION?*** — from Aristotle's natural Philosophy it is wont to be answered: ***it is a mutation from non-subject to subject, or from non-ens to ens.*** Wishing to express this response more clearly, they say generation is ***a mutation from the non-being of the substantial form to its being in matter***. (Whence also as they teach every mutation to be in some subject between two terms, so they adduce these three essential requisites of generation: ***subject*** [calling the matter], ***terminus a quo*** [the non-being of the form in matter], ***terminus ad quem*** [the being of the form in matter].)

Thence therefore occasion was born of inquiring: ***Since every substance (at least complete, for about incomplete there are still doubts) which is generated is produced from substrate matter — as they call it — or from some subject, is also every substance which is thus produced (so that it is produced from some subject or substrate matter) to be called ***generated***, if we wish to accept the term in rigor and to tread the footsteps of Venerable Antiquity (and chiefly Aristotle)?*** For thus Sacred Scripture supplies us with several examples of productions, as when in the creation of the whole world ***brute animals*** are said to be produced ***from earth***, ***fishes from water***, ***birds from air***, ***Adam from a clod of earth***, ***Eve from Adam's rib***. Likewise elsewhere ***a serpent from a staff***, ***wine from water*** are said to be produced; and innumerable other examples of such productions occur, about which the kind of production is controverted. What? — that it cannot be denied that heaven itself and earth itself were produced from matter: for they consist of matter, since they are natural bodies. Therefore it is necessary that they too were produced from matter — according to that: ***"As the thing has itself in becoming, so it also has itself in made-being."***

[Aristotelian apparatus established:] For out of nothing nothing comes (***ex nihilo nihil fit*** — the universally received Peripatetic axiom); not every mutation is a generation (only mutations between natural bodies with suitable disposed matter and prior alterations/dispositions); the ***materia prima*** doctrine with ***potentia proxima*** (not remote); ***alterations and dispositions*** are not themselves true causes of generation but the ***causa sine qua non***. Hence the Aristotelian argument:

> *Generation is mutation from non-ens to ens.*
> *But not every production from subject matter is mutation from non-ens to ens.*
> *Therefore not every production from subject matter is generation.*

The Minor stands because such productions as the Scripture examples listed (ex terra / ex aqua / ex gleba / ex costa) are from subjects which are not ***ens in potentia proxima*** (as the egg is potency of bird, seed of plant, water of vapour) but have only ***remote potency*** — not disposed to receive the substantial form.

[The two difficulties of the Aristotelian response:] **(1)** The division of production of complete substance into ***creation*** and ***generation*** seems immediate — all with Augustine *De Civ. Dei* XII and Damascenus *lib. 1 fid. orth.* c. 8 and *lib. 2 c. 1* define creation as ***production of a thing from nothing***. Whence firmly it seems to be deduced: generation is production of a thing from something as from matter subject to generation. **(2)** The concept of ***physical generation*** must not be confused with the ***general concept of generation***. For a thing to be and be called created, they rigorously require that ***according to itself as a whole*** (or, as the Thomists speak, ***inasmuch as it is a being***) it be produced from nothing — not as from matter or anything else pertaining to its constitution, but as from ***terminus a quo***, so that just as before according to itself as a whole it was nothing, so now according to itself as a whole it becomes something. Hence they distinguish:
- ***Physical generation*** = production from habile matter sufficiently convenient, by nature destined and adapted to such generation;
- ***Supernatural generation*** = production from naturally inhabile matter in which, with its own forces left to it, there is only remote potency to the being of the substantial form.

Both are true generation, agreeing in the common ratio of production from something as substrate matter.

#### Veltheim's Resolution — Creation and Generation Both as *Commons to One*

[Veltheim defers to Musaeus's *Theological disputations* from several years ago at **pars 1 disp. 5 § 1-4 pp. 122 ff.**]:

> ***"Creation is from the number of commons which to Aristotle are called ἀφ' ἑνὸς πρὸς ἕν (from one to one), and indeed of those which come closer to univoca. For πρώτως or primarily, creation is said of the production of a thing FROM NOTHING ἁπλῶς καὶ κυρίως, and secondarily also of the production of a thing from inhabile and indisposed matter — which, although absolutely speaking is production from some subject, yet secundum quid in comparison with generation can be called production from nothing."***

Thus Herr D. ***Johann Musaeus***, Preceptor of highest observance, who is to be consulted more fully there. Creation primarily is production of being from nothing; τὸ *ex nihilo* argues the negation of all substrate matter such production, whence existence of the thing as terminus of creation depends. Why creation secondarily is attributed to production of a thing not simply from nothing but from matter or subject (existing or pre-existing) which is of itself and by its nature inhabile and indisposed, is easy to say: because the subject, since it is not habile and disposed to the form, is as it were nothing — so that production of a thing from an inhabile subject is as it were production of a thing from nothing. Nor does this exclude ***creation from simpliciter nothing***: by analysis to the ultimate matter made from nothing, we at last arrive — as the Blessed ***Kromayer*** *Theologia Positivo-Polemica* art. 4 p. 268 teaches.

Hence the constant opinion of our Theologians: that ***bara*** (which the Latins render ***creavit***) more widely signifies production from mere nothing, but very frequently signifies action of this kind mentioned at present. From these it is now believed to shine forth why the venerable Theologians distinguish between ***creation simpliciter prima seu immediata*** and ***creation secunda seu mediata*** — a distinction so known and received in the Schools of Theologians that we deservedly groan with the words of the Blessed ***Gravver*** (Philosopher and Theologian in his own time), when at *Illustr. Quaest. Theol. cent. 1 disp. 5 q. 1 § 2 p.m. 186* after he had disputed thus: ***"There are some beyond the matter scrupulous who deny that the world is created from nothing — since certain things were made by God from pre-existing informe matter (yet created), which informe matter alone can be said to be created from nothing. For example: man is said to be created not from nothing but from the mud of the earth. But this coarse subtlety is not needed, since no one has ever been in the Church who taught that the world by reason of all and single its parts ῥητῶς is created from nothing"*** — he at last says: ***"Who sees not that in this a distinction between MEDIATE and IMMEDIATE creation lurks?"***

#### The Term *Generation* in the Ancients vs. in Later Scholars

Of the ancient and most used signification of generation among the Ancients, it is this: namely as it says ***mutation from potential to actual being***, or (what comes to the same) ***mutation of potential substance into actual***. Aristotle's generation requires only the terms (potential being, actual being), potential-being being neither mere nothing nor actual-being (***nothing comes to be from pure nothing, nothing is generated from pure nothing***) — matter itself is ***the very potential entity***, which is in its own genus an actual entity, and already before (hidden in actual entities) imports a certain determinate actual entity. Yet as not-yet-outside-all-causes it is denied to be ***actual entity*** in Aristotle's definition. Potential entity proximately signifies ***aptitude to be actual***, yet simultaneously tacitly says ***privation of act***.

In this ancient sense, the ***common ratio of generation*** is thus: production from potency to act in natural bodies. ***Supernatural generation*** (production from inhabile matter) is only ***δευτέρως / secundarily*** generation; and ***creation*** is likewise ***δευτέρως*** said of production from inhabile matter, and ***πρώτως*** said of production from mere nothing.

Hence Veltheim's resolution:

> ***Creation and Generation are each ***commons to one***. Each of them primarily (πρώτως) is said of its proper ratio (creation of ex-nihilo; generation of ex-potentia-ad-actum in habile matter), and secondarily (δευτέρως) is said of the mixed case — production from inhabile matter — which can be called ***creation secunda sive mediata*** (so-called from its approach to the ex-nihilo pure-creation condition since inhabile = quasi-nothing), or equally can be called ***generation supernaturalis*** (so-called from its being still a production ex-subjecto, though inhabile).***

So the apparent dilemma (either creation or generation strictly, no middle) collapses: both terms are ***commons to one*** admitting a middle case which is called by either name per analogy.

#### Note IV of § 3 — Hundreds of Other Common-Formal-Reason Questions

**IV.** By the same method it is now easy to respond to six hundred other questions. For as in other disciplines many, so far more in all and every practical discipline, do there occur [notions] which indeed receive some common ratio formalis before descent is made to distinctions into inferiors. But the more accurate Doctors judge such ratio formalis as ***imperfect and rude***, and the definition answering to it, if compared with the exact definitions of other things, they judge as similar to a mere ***umbratile pictura*** (shadow-painting). Thus for example to the questions ***what formaliter is MORALITY? what VIRTUE? what LAW? what OBLIGATION? what WAR? what CIVIL POWER? what MAJESTY? what DOMINION? what RIGHT in THING?*** etc., eruditely can be answered before morality is distinguished into morality-of-divine-action and -of-created-action, into honestas and turpitudo; virtue into intellectual and moral; law and obligation into natural and voluntary; civil power (likewise majesty) into plenary and less-plenary, likewise into perpetual and temporary; war into merely-public, private, and mixed; dominion into plenary and less-plenary; right in thing into *ius in re* and *ius ad rem*. Such responses are like ***σκιαγραφίαι***, which as in painters' tables shadows show what the image represents, yet not perfectly as the painting does — so they teach what the things formaliter are, in an imperfect mode.

The ***maximum number of such ὀρισμῶν σκιαγραφικῶν*** (shadow-definitions) exists. Therefore it belongs to the suitable cultivators of all Faculties and disciplines to inquire: ***does one and the same ratio formalis belong to several things equally or unequally?*** If the former, to the question ***what formaliter is this or that?*** it can be answered through a ***λόγος εἰς μίας*** (speech into one). If the latter, at least a ***δρισμὸς σκιαγραφικός*** (shadow-definition) holds the place of response; and then the chief care to lead oneself and others happily to solid erudition is to know accurately how to make perspicuous to oneself and others the reason of that inequality, and in what it consists.

#### Note V of § 3 — The Reduplication Objection

**V.** What may be responded to the Scotistic reason that was pressed earlier (that the inequality by which two or several participate the same formal reason unequally is outside the common formal reason — e.g. accident, although posterior to substance, is not posterior ***in the formal reason of ens*** or *qua ens*, since otherwise every being would be posterior) — the ***Greek Philosophers*** reply: the reduplication which is wont to be made with the little word ***qua*** (or another similar) is to be received otherwise in univoca strictly and in rigor so-called, otherwise in commons to one. Let it suffice to have touched this with a little word, since the more prolix and fuller treatment pertains to the Analytic.

#### § 4

> ***Commons to one which come closer to AEQUIVOCA agree with aequivoca strictly so-called in this: that according to the common name they do not have the same formal reason. They differ from aequivoca strictly and in rigor so-called in this: that these [aequivoca] according to the one and common name have DIVERSE formal reasons, those [commons to one closer to aequivoca] by no means.***
>
> ***For example: a certain species of worm is called ERUCA and a certain species of herb is called ERUCA, and they have according to this common name plainly diverse formal reasons. On the contrary, animal is called HEALTHY, urine is called HEALTHY, medicine is called HEALTHY — yet only to animal does the formal reason of healthy belong, nor is anything besides animal judged healthy by intrinsic appellation. For intrinsically healthy is called what has health in itself. And what health is must stand from Physics. For the rest, whatever besides animal is denominated healthy, these are so called by secondary and extrinsic denomination; yet simultaneously can be sufficiently shown the habitudo to that primarily and intrinsically denominated such, by force of which they undergo this denomination.***
>
> ***Thus URINE is extrinsically denominated healthy, because it says a habitudo of SIGN to the healthy animal as the signified: namely health in certain cases can be known from urine, and then urine is a sign of health in the animal. Likewise MEDICINE is called healthy only by extrinsic denomination (if you call it healthy), inasmuch namely as it says a habitudo of EFFICIENT CAUSE to the health of the animal, and so to the healthy animal as EFFECT.***

#### § 5

> ***In commons to one which come closer to aequivoca, that saying has most place: "Qui bene distingvit, bene docet" ("Who distinguishes well, teaches well"). For in defining things of this kind nothing other is left than, by enumerating the significates — both PRIMARY and INTRINSIC, and SECONDARY and EXTRINSIC (or if there be several, the remaining extrinsic and secondary significates) — to look upon the FORMAL REASON of the primary and the HABITUDO of the secondary (or secondaries) to it. For example: when Physicians and Medics teach what formaliter is health, and how one thing has health in itself, another has not health in itself but indicates the animal's health, another effects it, another augments it, another conserves it, etc. — so they teach in common what healthy is, which otherwise (as of animal, urine, medicine, and many others) is said not only ἀλλῳ καὶ ἀλλῳ (differently) but also ***ἑτέρως καὶ ἑτέρως*** (in another and another way).***

#### Notes

**I.** Not to be confused here: ***extrinsic denomination*** and ***improper denomination***. Thus if someone pointing to a medicine should say to a sick man: ***"This is health, I bring you health"***, he would surely use an improper predication. If however he said: ***"This is healthy, which I bring you"***, perhaps one could doubt whether this response is improper predication — though no one would doubt that it is an extrinsic predication. Otherwise it is evident that extrinsic and improper predications greatly differ. For example: this predication ***"girl is loved"*** is a most true predication, is also a proper predication, yet an extrinsic one. It is proper because no word of it departs from native and genuine signification; it must be called extrinsic because the form denominating (namely love) whence the girl is denominated with truth saved is not in the girl nor in any part of her, but uniquely in the appetite of the lover.

**II.** Let one example be sought from Theology. Thus ***God*** is said to have ***supreme authority***, and ***Sacred Scripture*** too is judged to have supreme authority. Surely he would betray his ***ἀπαιδευσία*** that Student of Theology who desired a definition of ***supreme authority*** or ***having supreme authority*** in common which could be attributed to God and to Sacred Scripture. Nor however must it on that account be said that of Sacred Scripture it is only improperly or equivocally said that it is of supreme authority. The accurate Doctors and Preceptors of Theology, to teach that Sacred Scripture is of supreme authority, in their auditors require first the notion of what absolutely authority is called — which can and must stand from Philosophy. Surely we estimate the authority of a Writer or Author from his perfection. Two things are required in an author or writer that he can be said of some authority: ***can and will*** (i.e. ***potency*** to lead the one for whose sake he writes into decent notice of the thing; ***will*** to perform this). Then they call to notice ***the perfection of the Supreme Numen***: for not only from Sacred Scripture but also from the light of nature it stands sufficiently that God is omniscient, that God is infinitely good. Therefore God never can be deceived (since He is of infinite knowledge); God never can deceive (since He is of infinite goodness). Therefore it is necessary that Sacred Scripture, since it is the Word of God, be such a Scripture that God neither could nor willed, nor could-will to deceive us. Whence whatever Sacred (Canonical) Scripture teaches is infallibly true; and since it teaches those things which must be believed and done for eternal salvation, Scripture must be ***sufficient*** in all those things necessary for knowledge for salvation, must also be ***perspicuous*** especially in those places which treat of things necessary of knowing and doing. Now we learn: ***that primarily and absolutely supreme authority belongs to GOD; secondarily and in order to God's authority, authority is attributed to Sacred Scripture***. For to use a crude comparison: healthy primarily was called animal, healthy secondarily was denominated urine, from healthy animal; such that health never is in urine itself.

**III.** Let us take another example: ***moral action*** is called that which is the object of natural law, and that which is the object of positive law. The former is called such ***primarily and intrinsically***, as that to which the formal reason of morality belongs; the latter secondarily and by extrinsic denomination. E.g. per se and intrinsically moral action is ***obeying the magistrate***; but per se the formal reason of morality does not have ***bearing a sword***, which however is denominated moral in so far as by the authority of a Superior commanding this act to the subjects, it becomes the object of a per-se-moral action, and in this sense is denominated moral.

**IV.** Innumerable examples of commons to one coming closer to aequivoca occur everywhere in Moral doctrine and in that of any department of law — chiefly where contracts, likewise delicts and penalties, are treated.

#### § 6

> ***Commons to one which are nearly altogether MIDDLES between univoca and aequivoca agree with univoca in this: that according to the same name they have the same formal reason (albeit furnished with fewer notes); and with aequivoca in this: that according to the same name they do not have the same formal reason absolute in all its numbers. They differ from UNIVOCA in that these have the same formal reason absolute in all numbers equally according to one name, those do not; and from AEQUIVOCA in that these have formal reasons in all numbers diverse according to one and common name, those have them in some numbers the same.***
>
> ***For example: demonstration ***ὅτι*** is more imperfect and furnished with fewer notes, yet is a demonstration. NATURE is attributed to a heavenly body and to sublunary ones; primarily however it is said of these. The same judgment is to be had of GOOD in respect of honest, pleasant, and useful; likewise of CITIZEN in Politeia, Aristocracy, and Monarchy.***

#### § 7

> ***The greatest use of commons to one nearly middling between univoca and aequivoca exerts itself if what primarily is such is placed as a quasi IDEA and EXEMPLAR of the other or of the rest, to whose reason others strive — yet so that those which do not attain it in every part are not therefore rejected from that genus of things.***

#### Notes

**I.** On the one hand ***demonstration ὅτι*** is equally a demonstration as ***demonstration διότι***, since each says premises from which a necessary and certain conclusion is inferred, so that we certainly know that the thing is such and cannot have itself otherwise. On the other hand, demonstration ὅτι is not a demonstration, since by it no one comes into notice of the simpliciter proximate, genuine, and domestic cause. However much therefore from demonstration ὅτι some science is had — namely science ὅτι — it is still imperfect science: since anyone seeking science of some thing, if its simpliciter proximate, genuine, and domestic cause can be had, does not rest until he has made perspicuous to himself ***why*** the thing is such and ***why*** it cannot have itself otherwise. Therefore demonstration ***διότι*** and ***science διότι*** are more perfect demonstration and par excellence such in all numbers; on the contrary, demonstration ***ὅτι***, likewise science ***ὅτι***, is furnished with fewer notes, yet is a demonstration, is science.

**II.** So in Politics the most perfect norm of the remaining citizens in any Republics is a citizen in a popular Republic — that is, an associate of the city who can be partaker of the suffrages (or deliberations) and of the Magistracy and judgments, and of the right of determining about the Republic. If however any of these be lacking to a citizen, for that reason the name and part of every definition must not be denied him, nor truly can be. Why many have exploded, rejected, or at least not been able to grasp this definition of citizen handed down and praised by ***Aristotle, Giphanius, Piccartus, Scherbius, Contanno, Clymbert, Sigonius, Conringius***, the supreme and most celebrated Politicians — we do not wonder, being sufficiently certain of this: that at least ***the ignorance of commons to one in some non-whole practical Philosophy runs upon the little words of certain unskilled persons***.

**III.** The ***commons to one*** of which here there is treatment are those which ***Thomas de Vio Cajetanus Cardinalis*** peddled as ***middle analoga attributionis*** between ***analoga attributionis intrinsecae*** and ***extrinsecae***, and claimed himself their first inventor — on which matter his whole tract ***De Nominum Analogia*** stands, which in the volume of all his *opusculorum* is of the third tome, treatise 5.

**IV.** This however must simultaneously be given warning: such ***commons to one***, although usually they signify ***the chief and quasi most perfect species***, sometimes also argue the whole complex of the remaining quasi more-imperfect species. Thus for example of ***sublunary bodies*** it is excellently said that they have nature — chiefly of those in which motions of all genera can be perceived. Thus however it also often happens that ***natural body*** is divided into ***heavenly*** and ***sublunary***, although in the heaven and in the heavenly things (especially in heaven itself) scarcely any motion can be known or perceived, except that the parts of the heaven are locally moved, and to the heaven itself ***ἐντελέχεια*** is attributed simple. Therefore ***nature*** is of the number of commons to one which are altogether middles between univoca and aequivoca.

**V.** Accurately speaking and most properly that is called ***common to one*** which to several in order to one, and so unequally, is attributed. Thus for example most rightly ***ens*** is called common to one with respect to substance and accident. Use however (which has the right of speech) carries that commons to one are also called those by which with reason and respect of one, one and the same name is attributed. Thus for example substance and accident are called commons to one with respect to being, since one and the same name — and one and the same nature noted by this name — is attributed to them with truth saved: to substance primarily and absolutely, to accident secondarily and in order to substance; so that nothing is called ens unless it be substance or says order to substance.

**VI.** Hence the Scholastics distinguished between ***analogum analogans*** and ***analogum analogatum***, so that they could more easily distinguish ***common to one*** from those with respect to which the common to one is said. For as in the Schools ***univocum univocans*** is wont to be called what according to the same name and same formal reason belongs to several equally, and ***univoca univocata*** are called those to which according to the same name and same formal reason that which is called univocans equally belongs — so ***analogum analogans*** will be the common to one itself, and ***analoga analogata*** those will be called to which that common to one belongs. However, we are not yet led to approve this mode of speaking, by which analoga are confused with those our commons to one; the reasons which terrify us we touched above. Nor however do the Scholastics themselves dissent in this. ***Cajetanus*** in the cited tract ***De Nominum Analogia*** expressly testifies that the name analogon is not very commodious to those which to Aristotle are called ***commons to one***, nor fitting from Aristotle's mind nor otherwise, as from chapter 1 of the said tract is plain — nor only in that but in the following chapters he manifestly acknowledges the abuse of the vocable.

#### § 8

> ***Commons to one — both those which come closer to univoca, and those which come closer to aequivoca, and those which are nearly altogether middles between univoca and aequivoca — agree with each other in this: that according to one and common name they say HABITUDINES to one formal reason. They differ in this: that in the latter (nearly altogether middles) one is the IDEA and EXEMPLAR of the other or others; in this they differ from the second kind (closer to aequivoca) — that these spit out the same formal reason according to the common name, and only through demonstrated habitudo to the one is it said what formaliter they are. Finally they differ in this: that commons closer to univoca have the same formal reason according to the common name (not however rigorously and par excellence so-called) according to all numbers (i.e. in all modes) unequally common; those nearly altogether middles have the same and in unequal reason common, but not according to all, however in fewer than all notes.***

#### Note

**I.** These two must be accurately distinguished: ***to say according to one and common name a habitudo to one formal reason***, and ***to have according to one and common name the same formal reason***. For the latter, as we have said hitherto, rigorously speaking belongs only to univoca strictly and in most rigorous signification so-called. Of commons to one it can in some way be said, yet not of any — but precisely of those which come closer to univoca, or which nearly altogether are middles between univoca and aequivoca (more of those former commons however than of these). But of commons to one which come closer to aequivoca, it cannot with truth saved be said that they have the same formal reason according to one and common name — equally as to aequivoca such repugns. Yet it remains most true that ***all commons to one***, and so also those which come closer to aequivoca, say ***according to one and common name a habitudo to the same formal reason***. For example: healthy animal, healthy urine, and healthy medicine say according to one and common name ***healthy*** a habitudo to the same formal reason, namely to the formal reason of health — the one because the formal reason of health belongs to it; the next because from it the formal reason of health belonging to the animal is noted; the last because it brings it about that the formal reason of health belongs to some.

**II.** One thing is for one formal reason unequally to be common to two or more; another, for one formal reason not in every mode to be common to two or more. For from this to the former the consequence always holds, not from the former to this.

#### Notes continued — The Grand Promissionum Example

**III.** To many cultivators of Philosophy and of other faculties the doctrine of commons to one which are nearly altogether middles between univoca and aequivoca appears very difficult, since they cannot easily attain by what reason it can come about that several things have one formal reason common — not however each in every part. But the more difficult and useless to many this doctrine appears, the more useful and necessary it stands — and this the suitable doctors and cultivators of the practical disciplines and higher faculties (as they are commonly called) daily experience with great emolument.

We shall adduce one example in place of a thousand, that of this signal doctrine's use it may more rightly stand to the Cultivators of Theology, Jurisprudence, and Morals. Let us take the ***noble matter of promises***. In it one who wishes to be happily and fruitfully conversant must know that ***three most distinct genera of promises are given***, which however so have themselves that the notes of the first genus belong to the whole second and third genera, and the notes of the second genus to the whole third genus, but not conversely. And this is the cause why we say ***promise*** is of the number of commons to one which are nearly altogether middles between univoca and aequivoca.

For to all promises properly so-called one formal reason belongs, but ***unequally***; and the single promises of all three genera are properly and intrinsically promises, furnished with the same notes — meanwhile the second with fewer, and with still fewer the first genus is absolved.

[The three genera unpacked:]
- **First genus**: promise with ***reserved right of changing the will*** — minimal notes; even so, if the promisor dies before changing his mind in due solemnities, the thousand imperials go to the promissee (the promisor had willed yet could not execute the change) — not quite a promise in Jurists' and Philosophers' strict sense, yet carries real effect.
- **Second genus**: promise where the promisor ***renounces the right of changing his will*** — more certain hope sustains the promissee.
- **Third genus**: promise where the promisor ***additionally transfers the right of vindicating the promise-claim to the promissee*** — absolute and in all numbers perfect, the ***idea and exemplar*** of promises.

**Hence the solid demonstration of divine-promises-sanctimony and human-promises-sanctimony communality**: Both God when He promises and man when he becomes promisor renounce the right of changing their will. But anyone of sounder judgment attains spontaneously that it would be manifestly unjust if someone wished to use a right to which he had renounced. Therefore from the nature of promises of the second genus we demonstrate the reason by which the ***sanctimony of divine promises*** and the ***sanctimony of human promises*** communicate with each other — which reason is also in promises of the third genus, although to this third genus divine promises can by no means be referred. More fully to pursue this matter does not at all suit our institute. Yet this we attempted in our ***Introduction to the Work of Hugo Grotius, through the whole chapter XI of lib. II***.

**IV.** More things about commons to one and their signal and necessary use may be seen below in the chapter on ***universals***.

— ❦ —

## Caput Septimum

### Of Principle and Principiatum, Likewise of Order

#### § 1

> ***PRINCIPIUM is called that WHENCE SOMETHING PROCEEDS. For example: a shoe proceeds from a shoemaker when it is made by him; therefore the shoemaker is the principle of the shoe. Thus man proceeds from an organic body and a rational soul: when he becomes, because he becomes from an organic body and a rational soul; and when and as long as he is, because when and as long as he is, he consists of organic body and rational soul; whence organic body and rational soul are and are called principles of man.***

#### Note

In all Metaphysics no doctrine more necessary and useful occurs — and which can more be commended to the cultivators of the ***higher Faculties*** (as they are called) — than that which in the preceding three chapters we have expounded, and that which is ***de causis*** (on causes), a most noble matter indeed, to which we now deservedly approach. The order of treatment altogether demands that we first make duly perspicuous to ourselves the most common notion of ***principle*** — since nothing surely is cause unless it be principle, although not every principle is cause.

And although otherwise most Metaphysicians are wont first to treat of ***potency and act***, to us however (with the better judgment of anyone saved) this order has pleased. For either by ***potency*** is understood ***potency of existing***, and so in chapter two we treated of it, when there was treatment of ***ens-potentia*** and ***ens-possibile***. Or there is signified the ***potency by which something can be cause*** — which the Scholastics call ***potentia causativa*** — which however does not lie as wide as that by force of which something can be principle (for not what can be principle can immediately be cause). And so ex professo (as far as the plan of our institute suffices) of potency in the most noble doctrine on principles and causes, both in this and in the following chapters, there will be treatment. The same must be judged of ***act***: either ***act entitativus*** (which is the Scholastics' diction) — that is, existence is indicated, whose doctrine was expounded in the preceding chapter three; or (as the Scholastics speak) ***act formal*** — although ***second act*** considered in its latitude lies far wider than ***formal act***; and so about act in the following chapters a necessary and most useful treatment, in its own place, will by no means be omitted.

#### § 2

> ***PRINCIPIATUM is called that which proceeds from elsewhere. Thus for example a shoe is called the principiatum of a shoemaker, because it proceeds from a shoemaker when it is made by a shoemaker; man is a principiatum with respect to organic body and rational soul, because man thence proceeds — for man becomes and consists of organic body and rational soul.***

#### Notes

**I.** The Scholastics are the authors of this name ***principiatum***. For as the Scholastics (as we shall see in its place) use these actives ***causare*** and these passives ***causari***, so also these voices ***principiare*** and ***principiari*** — little solicitous of Ciceronian hands, who however will forgive us if we have explicated these doctrines and locutions in so far as among the Doctors of other Faculties as among Philosophers they have been received by use and are still approved.

**II.** These two must not be confused: ***something to proceed from elsewhere*** and ***something to proceed thence***. For it can happen that something proceeds from elsewhere, and yet what proceeds from elsewhere is not another from that or with respect to that whence it proceeds — of which more things in the following.

**III.** If anyone wishing to philosophize more accurately with Scholastic terms would in philosophical rigor rightly distinguish between ***that which is principiated*** and the ***principiatum***: thus when a shoe is being made by a shoemaker, it does not yet merit the name ***principiatum***, but of ***that which is principiated*** (i.e. which proceeds from the shoemaker); but after the shoe has been made and the shoemaker's working has ceased, we more rightly attribute the notion of ***principiatum*** to the shoe in order to the shoemaker. The Scholastics by ***principiatum formaliter*** — that is, considered according to its formal reason — understand that which is principiated in so far as it is principiated — i.e. they signify ***proceeding-from-elsewhere qua such***. Thus for example when the axiom is adduced ***"POSITO PRINCIPIO PONITUR PRINCIPIATUM, et contra"*** (with the principle posited the principiatum is posited, and conversely), the sense is: with that posited which principiates (that is, whence something proceeds), there is necessarily also posited that which is principiated (that is, which thence proceeds); and conversely. Thus for example: with it posited that a shoe is being principiated from a shoemaker (i.e. is proceeding from the shoemaker), it is necessarily also posited that the shoemaker principiates it (that is, is its principle).

**IV.** These terms ***principiare*** and ***principiari***, if the cultivator of Metaphysics makes them perspicuous to himself, for that reason he does not sin; nevertheless he must abstain from them, since other terms are at hand likewise received by use, and more elegant: ***the shoemaker is the principle of the shoe***, and ***the shoe has the shoemaker as principle***, we express as: ***from the shoemaker the shoe proceeds***, likewise ***the shoe proceeds, that is, [has] the shoemaker and the shoe which thence (namely from the shoemaker) proceeds***.

#### § 3 — The Two Requisites of Principle

The requisites of ***principle*** are two:

**First** is required the ***habitudo*** of that which is called principle to that which with respect to it is called ***principiatum*** (which habitudo is called ***relatio originis***). E.g. the shoemaker says a habitudo to the shoe, because the shoemaker regards the shoe as that whence it proceeds — that is, as that which has elsewhere its first origin.

**Second** is required ***priority***: nothing can be called principle, truth saved, unless it is prior to that of which it is and is called principle. Thus the shoemaker, when he is called principle of the shoe, altogether says a priority — which is a Metaphysicians' manner of speaking: for the shoemaker is naturally prior to the shoe.

#### Notes on § 3

**I.** One of these requisites without the other does not suffice for something to be called principle.

**II.** ***Prius*** is said in many modes indeed; but since we now look upon ***principle*** as it says its most common notion, there is as yet no need to expound the various modes of priority. ***Boethius*** had regard to this when he defined principle: ***that whence something in whatever mode proceeds***.

#### § 4 — The Two Requisites of Principiatum

The requisites of ***principiatum*** are likewise two:

**First** is the ***habitudo*** of the principiatum to that which is called its principle: thus the shoe has a habitudo to the shoemaker, as to that whence it proceeds elsewhere.

**Second** is ***posteriority***: because nothing is formally called principiatum unless it is posterior to that in respect of which it is called principiatum: thus the shoe is (by nature) posterior to the shoemaker.

#### § 5 — Where Prius and Posterius, there Order

> ***Where there are given a prior and a posterior, there order is given: for this is what Philosophers call ORDER, in which prior and posterior obtain their place.***

Thus for example a double order of cognition is given between cause and effect, because here a double priority is given, a double posteriority: for as to ***confused cognition***, effect can be called prior, and cause posterior to effect; as to ***distinct cognition***, cause is always prior to effect, effect posterior to cause. For effect in distinct cognition proceeds from cause; cause in confused cognition proceeds from effect.

Thus order is given between the ***Persons of the Most Holy Trinity***, namely the ***order of natural enumeration*** (as it is called by Theologians), because the Father is the first Person, not the second, nor the third; the Son is not the first, nor the third, but the second; the Holy Spirit is not the first, nor the second, but the third.

#### Notes

**I.** Orders certainly vary, and diverse orders of the same things can be given simultaneously; which above all must be noted — in ***our mode of conceiving*** very often an order is given which nevertheless has its foundation in the truth of the thing. Thus in our mode of conceiving it is prior that Adam's lapse was going to be than that the same was foreknown by God; or, as the Scholastics speak, the ***futuritio*** of the Adamic lapse was prior to the divine foreknowledge of that lapse. For this proposition is not a true causal proposition: ***"Adam's lapse was going to be, because God had foreknown the lapse"***; but this is a true and simultaneously causal proposition: ***"God had foreknown Adam's lapse, because it was going to be."***

**II.** ***David Pareus***, among the other arguments by which he did not blush to defend that one having supreme authority can be punished by an inferior magistrate, used also the following argument: Even of the inferior Magistrate it is said, **Rom. XIII** [:3-4]: ***He is the minister of God to you for good, nor for a terror to good works but to evil, nor does he bear the sword in vain, but as the avenger of wrath against him who does evil***; and so the inferior Magistrate must be judge of the superior if the superior does evil, and must then also strike him with capital penalty. To this argument we believe it can be best answered if the Metaphysical doctrine of ***order*** be called to our aid: just as in Dialectics an ***intermediate species***, if you regard the genus, is species; if you regard the species placed below, is genus — so that Magistrate, with no account had of inferiors, is not private; but if he be considered toward the superior, he is private. While therefore Pareus himself expressly confesses, in his book of commentaries, that on account of this assertion there posited he was ***publicly burned at Oxford by hand of hangman by decree of the King***, [and still asserts] that subjects not private but constituted in the inferior Magistrate can inflict the capital penalty on the superior — he contradicts himself. For subjects in order to the supreme cannot be given, unless they are in respect to him ***merely private***.

**III.** The use of the Metaphysical doctrine of ***order*** will be shown more at length in the axioms belonging to this chapter.

#### § 6 — Principium Cognoscendi vs Principium Essendi

> ***Principle is distinguished into PRINCIPLE OF KNOWING and PRINCIPLE OF BEING. PRINCIPIUM COGNOSCENDI is called that whence something in its cognition proceeds, or whence the cognition of some thing proceeds: thus e.g. when the Physician from urine knows a disease, the principle of knowing with respect to the disease is called the urine, because the cognition of the disease proceeds from the urine; thus when fire is known from smoke, smoke is called principle of knowing with respect to fire.***
>
> ***PRINCIPIUM ESSENDI is called that whence something in its being proceeds, or whence it has or accepts its essence: e.g. the shoe in its being proceeds from the shoemaker when it is made by the shoemaker, whence the shoemaker is the principle of being; likewise the leather can be called principle of being with respect to the shoe.***

In acts of will, because they depend on the will, the principle of knowing is the will; so that it cannot be judged by anyone whether this or that act of the agent can be imputed in the ***genus of morals***, unless of the agent's will it is established. E.g. I cannot know, in the case of a private man who had killed another man, whether the killing can be imputed to penalty, unless I have first known: whether the mind of killing was present, and with what mind someone has killed — whether to defend himself, or to punish, or to offend? Likewise the will of acts which depend on the mind, when they are produced ***from the true will of the agent***, is the ***principle of being***. Thus will is the principle of being with respect to civil law, testament, pact, contract, etc. For it is of such manner of acts, which depend on will by their nature, that by a new act of will one can withdraw from them: whether from one part only (as in law and testament), or from both at once in conjunction (as in contracts and pacts).

#### Notes

**I.** ***Principium cognoscendi***, accurately speaking, is not principle of the thing which is known, but of the cognition of the thing: and this and nothing else do they will, and can will, who say the principle of knowing is the principle of the thing ***as it is known***. E.g. urine is not the principle of the disease, but of the cognition of the disease: for not the disease, but the disease's cognition, proceeds from urine.

**II.** In ***Analytics*** the principle of being is taken otherwise than in Metaphysics, as will be taught ex professo in its place.

#### § 7 — The Parallel Division of Principiatum

> ***As principle, so principiatum also is twofold: PRINCIPIATUM COGNOSCENDI, which proceeds from elsewhere in its cognition; or, as others say, cognition of something proceeding from elsewhere: e.g. fire is principiatum of knowing with respect to smoke; disease, with respect to urine.***
>
> ***PRINCIPIATUM ESSENDI, which proceeds from elsewhere in its being: as the shoe with respect to the shoemaker, likewise with respect to leather.***

Thus civil law, testament, pact, contract, in order to the will, are rightly called ***principiata of being***. Likewise no act in the ***genus of morals*** can be imputed to anyone, truth saved, unless the principle of being be the will of him to whom it is imputed. Hence always ***Moral Doctors*** should look narrowly into the ***mind of the agent*** — with what mind someone has acted; and likewise ***Jurisconsults*** indicate [the same] when with ***Ulpian*** they say: ***voluntas distinguit maleficia*** (the will distinguishes crimes).

#### § 8 — Principium Cognoscendi: Absolute vs Exclusive

> ***Each principle — and so each principiatum (namely both of knowing and of being) — admits various distinctions of things, of which it pleases us to adduce the chief. And (1) indeed, PRINCIPIUM COGNOSCENDI is taken either ABSOLUTELY or EXCLUSIVELY, as the Scholastics speak.***
>
> ***It is taken ABSOLUTE when it is so taken that even any principium essendi can be called principium cognoscendi: thus e.g. the matter and form of any natural body are rightly called principles of knowing, however much also they are principles of being. Likewise since every cause of a thing contributes to the cognition of the thing — nay every principle of being contributes to the cognition of that of which it is heard to be principle of being — hence every principle of being, likewise every cause, can be called principle of knowing.***
>
> ***On the contrary, PRINCIPIUM COGNOSCENDI is taken EXCLUSIVE when nothing is called principle of knowing except what, with respect to the same thing as to which it is called principle of knowing, is not simultaneously principle of being — i.e. principle of knowing taken exclusively is that which is principle of knowing and not simultaneously principle of being: as smoke with respect to fire; urine with respect to some certain disease, which is known thence.***

#### Notes

**I.** We scarcely count it necessary to explicate by peculiar formulas what ***principiatum cognoscendi*** absolutely or exclusively taken is called — since to anyone it is easily perceived, by changing what must be changed, that what has just now been applied is repeated: ***absolute*** is taken principiatum cognoscendi, if it is so taken that even every principiatum of being can be called such; on the contrary, ***exclusive*** is taken principiatum cognoscendi, if nothing be called principiatum cognoscendi which is simultaneously principiatum essendi.

**II.** That ***principium cognoscendi, absolute*** taken, is so taken that every principle of being is principle of knowing — this is easy to say: for as a thing has itself in its being, so also it has itself in its being-known (as they speak), i.e. in its cognition. For true cognition of a thing is that by which the thing is known as it is in itself. Now if a thing proceeds elsewhere in its being, it has a principle of being; wherefore, for the perfect cognition of a thing, the cognition of this principle of being is necessary; and so the principle of being will be principle of knowing.

**III.** One thing is for ***the thing which is in the meantime principium essendi*** to be called ***principium cognoscendi***; another thing to call ***principium essendi qua tale*** a principle of knowing. For principium essendi ***formaliter***, i.e. in sensu composito, is not principle of knowing. For just as these differ — ***cognition of a thing and the thing itself*** — so also do these differ: principium cognoscendi and principium essendi. For principium essendi, qua such, is ***that whence the thing is***; principle of knowing, qua such, is ***that whence the cognition of the thing proceeds***.

**IV.** In ***Morals and Politics***, whoever teaches uses principles of being and simultaneously principles of knowing. The same obtains in Theology, so also in Jurisprudence, and in all other disciplines and Faculties. But of this matter it will be treated below ex professo.

**V.** An illustrious example of a ***principle of knowing exclusively taken*** the Holy Spirit Himself furnishes to us in the ***first chapter of the Epistle to the Romans***, when He expressly asserts that ***from the visible works of the world the eternal power of God and divinity itself (or the divine essence) can be known by man, who after his lapse is left uniquely to his natural powers, and so even without any special revelation made by God***. Thence one may argue: ***That whence the cognition of a thing proceeds is in this sound sense rightly called principle of knowing. But cognition of God proceeds from Creatures. Therefore.*** The Major is the definition of principle of knowing, admitted ever by all sounder Philosophers. The Minor is manifestly clear, since expressly at the cited place, in the ***nineteenth and twentieth verses***, it is said: ***"What may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them. For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead, so that they are inexcusable."*** A signal lapse of judgment do they commit, and gravely err, who assert: ***God has a principle***, and go about to prove it from this, that He has a principle of knowing. For there is no consequence here: ***"God has principle of knowing. Therefore: God has principle."*** For as was warned in the preceding, ***to have a principle of knowing*** is the same as ***to be able to be known from elsewhere***. Nay, those who say ***God has principle of knowing taken exclusively*** will this and nothing else: that God, essentially considered, is plainly from Himself — i.e. that the divine nature does not proceed elsewhere in its being, and yet the natural cognition of Him proceeds from the natural cognition of the creature; since expressly the Gentiles are therefore called ***inexcusable***, that they could have known the true God, since ***the eternal power of God*** and the ***θειότης*** can be known from the visible works of the world. But what sort of consequence is this: ***"God can be known from the works of the world. Therefore: God, speaking absolutely, has a principle"***? This certainly, and nothing else, follows: ***Therefore: the natural cognition of God acknowledges its principle***. For these must not be confused: ***the thing itself and the cognition of the thing***.

**VI.** Let us take another ***Theological*** example. Thus e.gr. when it is asked: ***What is the principium cognoscendi with respect to the Most Holy Trinity?*** By orthodox Theologians it is answered: ***Sacred Scripture***. The reason is: that God is Triune in Persons, this cognition touches us uniquely and solely from Sacred Scripture. But Sacred Scripture is principium cognoscendi ***exclusively taken***: for the Most Holy Trinity is indeed known from Sacred Scripture, yet does not proceed in its being from Sacred Scripture — because God does not have it, that He be Triune in Persons, from Sacred Scripture, but the Most Holy Trinity was ***from eternity***, Sacred Scripture only in time; nay rather, the Most Holy Trinity is the ***author of Sacred Scripture***. Whoever therefore calls Sacred Scripture ***principium cognoscendi exclusively taken*** with respect to [the Most Holy Trinity], wills this and nothing else: that the Most Holy Trinity is known to us from Sacred Scripture; and this no one of sound mind will deny.

**VII.** Let there be one example, ***Juridico-Politico-Moral***, in place of many. Effects of right which depend upon the mind cannot yet follow upon the sole act of the mind, unless that act be indicated by certain ***signs***. For to attribute efficacy of right to bare acts of the mind would not have been fitting to the nature of man, who cannot know acts except from signs. But signs have no ***mathematical certainty*** about the acts of the mind: for men can speak in words other than what they will and feel, and dissimulate in deeds. Yet the nature of human society does not suffer that there be no efficacy to acts of the mind sufficiently indicated. Therefore ***what is sufficiently indicated is held as true against him who has indicated***. Thus therefore those signs are ***principles of knowing taken exclusively***.

**VIII.** Questions by which it is asked ***whether something is*** (***an sit?***), in all disciplines and Faculties, we can decide from principles of knowing taken ***exclusively***. For these questions can be expedited also by arguments received merely from an effect or from some sign.

**IX.** In Theology and so in Jurisprudence altogether most numerous principles of knowing occur which are simultaneously principles of being. Thus e.g. when it is asked: ***Why does everyone believing in Christ have hope of eternal life?*** Rightly it is answered: ***Because he is justified***: surely justification, in order to hope of eternal life, is simultaneously principle of knowing, and is also cause, and so principle of being. Likewise when it is asked: ***Why is Christ to be loved above all things, and in Him all our trust to be placed?*** It is answered through principle of knowing simultaneously of being, if it be answered: ***because Christ by His merit redeemed us from the power of sin, of the Devil, of death, and ours [the power] from theirs***. More ***Theological*** examples — not only, but also ***Juridical, Moral, Political***, and those drawn from the other parts of Philosophy — we adduced above in chapter 7 from p. 377 up to p. 381, which may be reduced hither if it please. So often indeed do Theologians, Jurisconsults, Ethicists, Politicians, Doctors of all disciplines use ***principles of knowing and of being simultaneously*** as they teach ***accurately***, i.e. hand down things through their ***genuine causes***.

#### § 9 — Principium Cognoscendi: Proper vs Common

> ***Principium cognoscendi (1) is either PROPER or COMMON. That is called proper which is proper to that in respect of which it is called principle of knowing: thus e.g. the principle of knowing proper to Physical Science is: EX NIHILO NIHIL FIT (from nothing nothing comes). The principle proper to Moral Science is: EX SUA NATURA HONESTUM (TURPE) EST EXPETENDUM (FUGIENDUM) (what by its nature is honest/base is to be sought/shunned). That is called common which is common with others, namely to that in respect of which it is called principle of knowing: so that in respect of others also it is principle of knowing. E.g. principle of knowing common to all Faculties and disciplines is: IMPOSSIBILE EST IDEM SIMUL ESSE ET NON ESSE. QUODLIBET EST VEL NON EST. NIHIL EST CAUSA SUI IPSIUS, etc.***

#### Notes

**I.** Maximum use this distinction has in all and singular disciplines and faculties: for every one rejoices in domestic or proper principles; every one also delights in common principles.

**II.** Cultivators and Doctors of a more accurate doctrine ought to know this: that in Metaphysics many axioms occur which by consideration are proper to Metaphysics; by use, however, they become ***quasi-proper*** to any faculty or discipline. Thus e.g. when the Politician restricts certain Metaphysical axioms by praxis to persons, things, business of the civil order, they thus become ***quasi-proper*** principles of Politics. The Ethicist restricts the same principles to moral duties, and so they become proper to moral discipline. The same judgment stands of the Theologian and of the Jurisconsult. Thence it has come about that the most accurate doctors — those most versed in the Practical disciplines and those of the laws — distinguish between ***principia propria*** and ***principia quasi propria***, such that from those [propria] the primary doctrines and demonstrations are derived, from these [quasi propria] the secondary doctrines and demonstrations of a lesser class; and to this second or lesser class the ***Metaphysical axioms*** pertain in the sense which we have indicated.

**III.** It pleases us to adduce one or another example of a Metaphysical Axiom, so that even the rude auditor may more easily grasp by what reason they become quasi-proper to a certain discipline or faculty. Thus e.g. the Theologian teaches accurately why every one believing in Christ has hope of eternal life; and he teaches this from the fact that he is justified. Let anyone ask: ***on what principle does the Theologian rely?*** Surely it cannot be denied that the whole Theological discourse and the whole of this doctrine goes back into that principle common to all disciplines and faculties, by consideration proper to Metaphysics: ***POSITA CAUSA PONITUR EFFECTUS*** (with the cause posited the effect is posited). For justification is the cause of hope of eternal life; and so, with it posited that one is justified, altogether one has hope of eternal life. With it posited that one believes in Christ, justification is posited, since faith in Christ is cause of justification, and on this account faith is called ***justifying***. But if you further consider ***whence the Theologian is apprised of this matter*** — that every one believing in Christ is justified, and that the justified (before God) has hope of eternal life — certainly it cannot be otherwise answered than that this uniquely stands from Sacred Scripture, which affirms both with manifest words. Here now the Theologian uses a ***truly proper principle***, namely this: ***Whatever Canonical Sacred Scripture says, is infallibly true***. Again, the Jurisconsult teaches accurately that the heir ought to defend, approve, and make good the deed of the deceased — and he teaches this from the fact that he has succeeded into his whole right: the whole discourse again rests on the same axiom. More examples we do not wish now to adduce, since inspection of the axioms (whose practical use and abuse we have demonstrated) sufficiently and amply indicates [the matter] for the plan of our institute.

**IV.** That which floats on many lips — ***"Philosophers use reasons, we (devoted to Theology and Jurisprudence) use mere authorities"*** — is most truly said, so long as it be understood and received ***cum grano salis***: namely that the discussion be of the ***proper and simultaneously ultimate principle*** of Theology and Jurisprudence — of which above in the Preliminary Chapter from § 41 and following, pp. 26 ff., and nearly to the end of said chapter, we have taught at length, and here these things merit repetition.

#### § 10 — Principium Cognoscendi: Ultimate vs Non-Ultimate

> ***Principium cognoscendi is either ULTIMATE or NON-ULTIMATE. The former acknowledges no other principle; the latter does. E.g. an ultimate principle of knowing is this: IMPOSSIBILE EST IDEM SIMUL ESSE ET NON ESSE. A non-ultimate principle is: QUODLIBET EST VEL NON EST — because its truth can be known if one attends to the fact that it is impossible for the same thing simultaneously to be and not to be.***

#### Notes

**I.** This distinction is especially current and received in disciplines and faculties; and chiefly it is attributed to ***complex principles***.

**II.** The non-ultimate principle is sometimes called by Metaphysicians the ***proximate*** — such however that ***proximate*** be said in this sense: because it is not ultimate. Thence we believe it has come about that non-ultimate principle is distinguished into ***immediate*** and ***mediate***. E.g. the ultimate principle in moral jurisprudence is this: ***by its nature the honest is to be sought***. Now when I wish to demonstrate this proposition, ***promissum est servandum*** (what is promised must be kept), surely a closer principle is given, namely this: ***the right which has been acquired to each must be left to him***. And still a closer one is given, from which it is demonstrated that from a promise a right is acquired to the other, whether perfect or imperfect.

#### § 11 — Ultimate: Simpliciter vs In-a-Certain-Genus

> ***An ultimate principle of knowing is either SIMPLICITER such, or IN A CERTAIN GENUS. E.g. the simpliciter ultimate complex principle of knowing is this: IMPOSSIBILE EST IDEM SIMUL ESSE ET NON ESSE. On the contrary, e.gr. in Theology the ultimate complex principle of knowing is: QUICQUID SCRIPTURA S. CANONICA DICIT, ILLUD INFALLIBILITER VERUM EST. In Jurisprudence: QUICQUID JUS CIVILE SANCIT ET APPROBAT, HOC CIVILITER JUSTUM EST, i.e. has the effect of civil right.***

#### Notes

**I.** Let those things be reduced hither which we disserted above in the Preliminary Chapter § 47 ff., pp. 38 ff., inasmuch as they ex professo belong here also.

**II.** ***Ultimate*** principle in another sense can be called ***first***: ***ultimate***, because the cognition ultimately goes off into it and is resolved into it; ***first***, because it is the first fount of cognition. Thence it comes about that ***Metaphysics is said to hand down the first fonts of any whatever cognition***.

#### § 12 — Complex vs Incomplex

> ***Principium cognoscendi is either COMPLEX or INCOMPLEX. The former is an integral proposition: as the Major and Minor in a Syllogism. The latter is by no means [an integral proposition]: as the middle term in a Syllogism.***

#### Notes

**I.** Not every principle of knowing which is a complex something is therefore a complex principle of knowing. Thus e.g. when in the place of the middle term in a Syllogism the ***definition*** is put, [and in the place] of the major term the ***defined***, so surely the definition is principle of knowing (inasmuch as placed in the position of the middle term), and is a complex something — yet is not a ***complex principle***, because it is not an integral proposition, but an extreme of a proposition.

**II.** It is wont to be asked: ***Is Sacred Scripture, with respect to Theological dogmas, principle of knowing INCOMPLEX or COMPLEX?*** The response is easy: because Sacred Scripture is a complex of many propositions, from which we know ***the essence and will of GOD***, the dogmas of faith as of morals (whose cognition suffices for our eternal salvation) — rightly it is called ***principium cognoscendi complexum***. But in the meantime if you argue: ***"Whatever Sacred Scripture says is infallibly true, and must likewise be believed. But Scripture says this [X]"*** — the Major proposition there is surely a complex principle: but here that complex term which is had in the Major — namely ***Scripture itself***, the term which is repeated in the Minor — is rightly in its sense called ***principium cognoscendi incomplexum***. And this is what Theologians will, when they call this proposition ***"Whatever Sacred Scripture says is infallibly true"*** the ***principium cognoscendi ultimum complexum*** with respect to Theology; so however that Sacred Scripture is by the same called ***principium cognoscendi incomplexum*** with respect to Theology.

**III.** Let the same be the judgment when it is asked of the ultimate principle of knowing with respect to forensic jurisprudence. For ***civil right (jus civile)*** is now taken precisely for one civil law, this or that; now for the complex of civil laws; and so now one, now more propositions it notes — such that in a Syllogism ***jus civile*** can be made part of the premises, and in this sense can be called ***principium incomplexum***.

#### § 13 — Principium Essendi: Wider vs Stricter Signification

> ***Principium essendi admits various distinctions equally as principium cognoscendi. And (1) indeed, principle of being is now taken in a WIDER, now in a STRICTER signification. Taken in the FORMER mode, every one is called principle of being whence something proceeds into being — whether it merely proceeds thence while it is being made, or also thence proceeds after it has already been made. E.g. the shoe, both when it is being made and when it has already been made, so long as it is, proceeds from leather: for it comes to be from leather, and is from leather. On the contrary, the shoe proceeds from the shoemaker only when it is being made; afterwards it is and can be a shoe, though the shoemaker has long since departed to the many.***
>
> ***Taken in the LATTER mode, principle of being is only that from which not only something comes to be but also proceeds when it has already been made and so long as it is. In this sense, leather is principle of being with respect to the shoe; the shoemaker is not.***

#### Notes

**I.** Metaphysicians have the rule: ***Whence a thing has its essence when it has already been made*** (so, namely, that the essence of the thing, after it has been made, still proceeds thence) — ***thence also the thing was proceeding in its coming-to-be, thence also it was being made***. Thus since an animal has its essence when it has already been produced from organic body and sentient soul, therefore thence also the animal was proceeding in its coming-to-be. Organic body and sentient soul were therefore ***principles of the animal in fieri***, and now are ***principles of the animal in facto esse***. Yet the animal, once begotten, no longer has its essence from the ***generans*** (begetter); therefore the generans was principle of being only in the ***former mode*** taken. On this account they distinguish between ***principium entis in fieri*** and ***principium entis in facto esse***. For from the latter to the former, but not conversely from the former to the latter, they say the consequence holds.

**II.** This distinction is of principium essendi which is simultaneously ***a true cause***.

**III.** ***Gravely do they err*** who in divine matters call the Father ***principium essendi*** with respect to the Son — since nevertheless they define principium essendi thus: ***principium essendi is that whence a thing not only depends while it is being made, but also when it has already been made***. Indeed to all, even to the simplest, from our ***Symbolic Books*** it cannot but stand that ***no Person of the Divinity is either made or created***. But of this matter more things will be treated in the following chapter.

#### § 14 — Principium Essendi: True-and-Real Ens vs Non-Ens

> ***Principium essendi (2) is either a true and real Ens — as the Physician in respect of the medicine he administers — or a non-ens, as health not yet existing, for the sake of which however the medicine was administered. For rightly both the really existing Physician and the non-existing health are called principles of the administered Medicine.***

#### Note

In the doctrine on causes it will be demonstrated at length that many causes are given in various genera of causes which can simultaneously be ***non-entities and true causes***. But every cause is principle of being: thus therefore ***true principles of being can be non-entities***.

#### § 15 — Principium Essendi: Internal vs External

> ***Principium essendi (3) is either INTERNAL or EXTERNAL. Internal, which enters the constitution of that in respect of which it is called principle of being: as leather in respect of the shoe; matter and form in respect of the composite. External, which does not enter its constitution: as the shoemaker in respect of the shoe; agent and end in respect of the composite.***

#### Notes

**I.** This distinction is wont to be applied by the vulgar of Metaphysicians uniquely to ***causes***, and indeed to causes which are ***true entities***.

**II.** Not rarely however it is applied in this sense also to ***non-Entities***, inasmuch as of a non-Ens it cannot be said that it enters the constitution of that of which it is principle.

**III.** There are learned Men who attribute the notion of ***internal principle*** even to non-entities. For thus they feel, as many as teach in Physics that principle is ***privation***, not indeed taken in abstract, but ***in concrete***: ***For from non-ens comes ens, from non-man a man, from non-plant a plant***.

#### § 16 — Principium Essendi: Causal vs Non-Causal

> ***Principium essendi (4) is either CAUSAL, i.e. a true cause — as David is called causal principle of Solomon — or NON-CAUSAL, i.e. not a cause: e.gr. the TERMINUS A QUO is called principle of a journey, the POINT [principle] of the line, the DAWN [principle] of the day; and yet these are not causes.***

#### Note

The use of all and singular of these distinctions of principium essendi will be faithfully shown in what follows.

#### § 17 — The Parallel Transfer to Principiata

> ***It will now be easy for any Reader, even of less experience, to transfer the distinctions handed down about principles of knowing and of being, with the necessary changes, to PRINCIPIATA of knowing and of being.***

## Caput Octavum

### Of Cause and Causatum, and of the Necessary Requisites of Each — the Primary as the Secondary. Likewise of the Notion ALIUD

#### § 1

> ***CAUSA in common is called that WHENCE ANOTHER THING (ALIUD) in its being PROCEEDS, and has or accepts its essence. E.g. the shoe accepts its essence from the shoemaker, whence the shoemaker is called cause of the shoe. Likewise the shoe, when it comes to be, comes to be from leather, and so long as it is, is from leather; wherefore the leather is called cause of the shoe.***

#### Notes

**I.** By these words — ***unde essentiam accipit et habet*** — it is signified that ***cause is principle, and indeed principle of being***. All things therefore which have been said in the preceding chapter about principle, and about principle of being, must sedulously be recalled to memory here, since otherwise it is not granted to progress happily in the doctrine on cause.

**II.** With special study we distinguish between ***to accept essence*** and ***to have essence***. E.gr. the shoe has essence, though no longer the shoemaker exists who effected it; but the shoe does not ***accept*** essence unless the shoemaker effect it.

#### § 2 — The Two Requisites of True Cause

> ***Two things therefore are required for a TRUE CAUSE: (1) that it be principle of being, i.e. that it be that whence SOMETHING in its being proceeds; (2) that it be that whence ANOTHER (ALIUD) in its being proceeds. For not whence SOMETHING in its being proceeds does immediately ANOTHER THING in its being proceed thence.***

#### Notes

**I.** With special study, in the definition and requisites of ***CAUSE***, mention was made of the word and notion ***ALIUD***. For by this word is sufficiently distinguished ***cause*** from ***principium essendi***, since in the preceding [chapter] § 16 p. 523 it was said that not every principium essendi is cause. For to be a cause, it is not enough if something accepts and has essence thence, or if it be that whence something in its being proceeds — but it is further required that that which accepts and has essence from it, that which thence proceeds in its being, be ***ALIUD***, as will presently be shown at length.

**II.** There are those who thus define cause in common: ***it is principle whence ANOTHER has or accepts its essence***. But this word [***principium***] could safely be omitted, inasmuch as the particle ***unde*** (namely, ***whence another has or accepts essence***) subintends it.

**III.** Whether in the meantime the word ***principium*** be expressed or omitted, anyone sees the notion of cause to be so common that an exact definition of cause in common can neither be had nor be urged. For the variety of modes by which another is said to accept or have its being ***from something, out of something, through something, on account of something, around something, by the impulse of some one, by imitation of some one*** — and who could at once enumerate all the modes — this variety (I say), weighed, means that these modes are not distinct by whole genus. So that no small cause is given why, with ***Suarez Metaphysical Disputations volume I, Disputation 12, section 2 § 1***, in the investigation of the one concept of cause in common, as formal as objective — since from the modes by which another receives or has its being from it, the vulgar call diverse ***genera of causes*** — [the position] can and must be abstracted, so that not only from some ***proportionality metaphorically***, but from ***a proper, true, and real convenience*** the common concept be abstracted. [On this] we are unwilling to tarry — nay rather to die upon — as if bound to ***Ixion's wheel***.

**IV.** By the word ***principium*** the common concept, which answers as it were to the genus, could be signified: by the words ***unde (ALIUD) essentiam habet aut accipit***, a certain intermediate and quasi-generic difference is indicated, if the word placed in parenthesis — ***aliud*** — be not attended to. For it is the same as if it had been said: ***cause is (principle) of being***. For ***whence something*** (yet these must not be confused: ***aliquid*** and ***aliud***) ***has or accepts its essence*** — this is called principium essendi, as from what was said above is clear. By this therefore cause differs from ***principium cognoscendi exclusively taken***. The ultimate and quasi-specific difference, however, the word ***aliud*** indicates. For not whence something has or accepts its essence is cause, but it is further required that what thence accepts essence be ***aliud*** from that of which it is called cause — on which matter a little later it will be treated more distinctly.

**V.** We have explicated the ***Metaphysical notion of cause in common*** by simple and clearer words, nor perhaps is anything else expressed by that most known formula: ***causa est principium per se influens esse in aliud*** (cause is a principle per se flowing being into another), which belongs to the ***Conimbricenses lib. II Physicorum c. 7 q. 7 a. 1***, and which the ***Pope of the Metaphysicians*** (as ***Jacobus Revius*** calls ***Suarez***) has canonized. On which [definition] Revius himself (who in the book which is inscribed ***Suarez Repurgatus Disputatio 12 Sectio 3***) more freely passes judgment in these words: ***"This definition is, first, improper, as is clear. Second, averse to the rules of syntax, whence it comes that it signifies no sound sense. For it is not aptly said: 'I flow being into another,' as neither does a man flow water into a vessel but pours it, nor does a river flow water into the sea but discharges it. Therefore to flow (which is absolute) must necessarily be explicated through a transitive, namely through 'make-to-flow,' i.e. (as we have said) 'infuse.'
