Now see how feverish this cause-definition is: Cause is that which pours being into another. Is this to define a thing or to involve it?"*** Thus far Revius at the cited place, p. m. 164. Should anyone meanwhile desire to know with what success that ***giant among this century's Scholastics*** (for ***Rodriguez de Arriaga***, in the preface of his ***Course of Philosophy***, adorns Suarez with that elogium) defended the common and received definition, inspection of the section on the common reason of cause (which is the second in the Suarezian 12th Disputation) will suffice. Revius himself in his senile age admitted it, and on p. 15 promises he will use it — a definition however which he reprehends in many modes.

**VI.** Since therefore, as we have just now admonished, the word ***ALIUD*** distinguishes cause from any other principle whatever, and so much importance is placed in the consideration of this little word, we shall more distinctly explicate ***what by the notion ALIUD here is signified***.

#### § 3 — ALIUD: In Sensu Negante vs In Sensu Affirmante

> ***ALIUD in Metaphysics is wont to be taken in two modes. (1) IN SENSU NEGANTE, and so ALIUD is called a TRUE AND REAL ENS WHICH IS NOT OF THE SAME NUMERICAL ESSENCE WITH THE ENS WITH RESPECT TO WHICH IT IS CALLED ALIUD. Thus e.g. the shoe is ALIUD with respect to the shoemaker, because the shoe is a true and real ens which is not of the same numerical essence as the shoemaker. ALIUD is the act when someone uses medicine with respect to the health which is still desired, because [the act] is a true and real ens, which with the health is not of the same numerical essence [— for health does not yet exist].***
>
> ***(2) IN SENSU AFFIRMANTE, and so ALIUD is called a TRUE AND REAL ENS WHICH HAS AT MINIMUM A NUMERICALLY DIFFERENT ESSENCE FROM THE ESSENCE OF THAT TRUE AND REAL ENS WITH RESPECT TO WHICH ALIUD IS DENOMINATED. E.g. ALIUD also in this sense is the shoe with respect to the shoemaker, because the shoe has its essence (since it is a true and real ens), and the shoemaker has his essence (since he is a true and real ens), yet by no means of the same species, and much less of the same numerical essence are the essences of shoe and shoemaker. Contrariwise, when a sick man uses medicine, the act by which he uses the medicine cannot in sensu affirmante be called ALIUD with respect to the health which does not yet exist — because health which does not yet exist is non-ens, and so has no essence whatever. For ESSENCE (as it is here taken) and EXISTENCE really do not differ. Let it therefore be noted that in the definition of CAUSE the word ALIUD must be received in the former sense, i.e. in sensu negante.***

#### Notes

**I.** Two mere ***non-entia*** can also be called ALIUD and ALIUD. E.gr. ALIUD is ***blindness*** and ALIUD is ***ignorance***, which however are mere non-entia, namely mere privations. Nor is it difficult to say why they are called ALIUD and ALIUD: for ALIUD is ***sight***, and ALIUD is ***knowledge***; but blindness is nothing other than ***absence of sight*** from a capable subject, and ignorance nothing other than ***absence of knowledge*** from a capable subject. For according to Aristotle (and the truth of the thing) ***the essence of privation is absence*** (***privationis essentia est absentia***). Easily therefore can be perceived in what manner ALIUD is called blindness, and again ALIUD is called ignorance: namely not primarily and intrinsically, in themselves and in respect of themselves (for thus they are purely and simply nothing), but secondarily and extrinsically, in respect of the true and real entities which primarily and intrinsically, in themselves and in respect of themselves, are ALIUD and ALIUD — because other is the essence of sight, other the essence of knowledge. It is said: ALIUD and ALIUD are called also pure absence of sight and privation of sight, since they tell of the absence of the same positive. ***Response:*** Even less properly can pure negation and privation of the same positive be called ALIUD and ALIUD. Yet thus far this appellation finds a place inasmuch as they regard the true ALIUD and ALIUD primarily so called. For the former [i.e. pure negation] notes an incapable subject, the latter [i.e. privation] a capable subject; and so they connote subjects of diverse essence.

**II.** In the present passage ALIUD is taken ***absolutely and in its primary signification***, such that the notion of ALIUD is not attributed except to a true and real ens — i.e. nothing is called ALIUD unless it be a true and real ens. This acceptance also the words indicate: ***unde ALIUD essentiam suam habet aut accipit***. For what has or accepts essence is ens, since ens is that which has true and real essence (or, which in this place is the same, existence).

**III.** Nor do we leave this untouched: that ALIUD in this place is received by Metaphysicians ***per modum substantivi*** (in the manner of a substantive).

**IV.** In the meantime ALIUD ***in sensu affirmante*** is by no means by this bidden to be absent from the definition of CAUSE — as if CAUSE could not be called that whence ALIUD-in-sensu-affirmante proceeds in its being. For it is abstracted from that sense, not excluded as repugnant: because cause is given whence ***ALIUD IN SENSU AFFIRMANTE*** has or accepts its essence; and cause is given whence ***ALIUD IN SENSU NEGANTE*** (which could in no way be received in sensu affirmante) has or accepts its essence. The whole difficulty consists in attending to this: that ***one cause is a true and real ens, another cause is indeed a true cause but not a true and real ens***. Of which in what follows it will be treated.

**V.** From ALIUD in sensu affirmante the consequence holds to ALIUD in sensu negante, but not conversely. This is: whatever have numerically different essences, those do not have the same numerical essences; but whatever do not have the same numerical essences, do not thereby immediately have different numerical essences, since it can come about that one of these may have no essence whatever — if, namely, it be non-ens. These expressions however must be understood of ALIUD in sensu negante ***absolute***, not ***exclusive***, taken. For from ALIUD in sensu affirmante there never holds consequence to ALIUD in sensu negante exclusively taken (i.e. such that it altogether excludes the affirming sense). Which distinction becomes easy to recognize if those things be repeated which in the preceding chapter § 8 p. 505 were said of ***principium cognoscendi absolute*** vs ***exclusive sumto***.

**VI.** By this little word ALIUD the ***Theological Scholastic Doctors*** know well to use, when, namely, in the discrimination of the supreme mysteries — the mystery of the ***Most Holy Trinity*** and the mystery of ***the Incarnation*** — they explain [the matter] in the following mode: that in the Trinity-mystery ***alius, alius atque alius***, ***ἄλλος, ἄλλος καὶ ἄλλος***, [are given] — not ***aliud, aliud atque aliud***, ***ἄλλο, ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο***. But in the Incarnation-mystery ***aliud et aliud***, ***ἄλλο καὶ ἄλλο*** [are given] — not ***alius et alius***. By which they intimate that in the Trinity-mystery one numerical ***being*** is given of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — i.e. one and the same numerical essence or divine nature — three really distinct Persons however in one and the same numerical essence. But in the Incarnation-mystery there is one numerical person — the Person ***τοῦ θεανθρώπου*** (of the God-Man) — yet two really distinct essences or natures: namely the divine nature of Christ, which He had from eternity, and the human, which in time He assumed. And to add this in passing: the ***Scholastics*** chiefly placed the word ***ALIUD*** in the explication of the notion of CAUSE in order that the divine persons, by reason of ***actions ad intra*** (as in the Schools they are called), might be excluded from the number of causes. See on this matter ***Suarez Disputationes Metaphysicae tom. I Disp. 12 sect. 2 § 1 p. m. 243 ed. Mogunt.*** For Theologians teach that ***the Son of God has from God the Father his essence through eternal generation***, and ***the Holy Spirit has from the Father and the Son his essence through eternal spiration***. Yet because there is one numerical essence of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — and so Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are not ***aliud, aliud atque aliud*** — therefore in divine matters neither to the Father in respect of the Son, nor to Father and Son in respect of the Holy Spirit, can the notion of ***ALIUD*** be attributed. For although the ***Fathers*** are read sometimes to have used this notion — as also ***Augustine*** somewhere is believed to have admitted priority of nature in God, when he called the Father prior to the Son by nature — yet the usage of the ***Theological Schools*** repudiates this locution as too broad and less safe. For the rest, that cause and that of which it is cause can have one specific essence, yet the latter be called ALIUD with respect to the former — this is clear from the father-and-son example in human things.

#### § 4 — ALIUD in Sensu Affirmante: Adequate vs Inadequate

> ***ALIUD in sensu affirmante taken is again twofold: ALIUD ADEQUATE and ALIUD INADEQUATE. ADEQUATE ALIUD is called in sensu affirmante when from the ens with respect to which it is called ALIUD it differs NEITHER AS INCLUDING, NOR AS INCLUDED — i.e. it neither includes the other ens, nor is included by it. Thus e.gr. ADEQUATE ALIUD and ALIUD are the shoe and the shoemaker. INADEQUATE ALIUD is called in sensu affirmante when from the ens with respect to which it is called ALIUD it differs either AS INCLUDING or AS INCLUDED. E.gr. INADEQUATE ALIUD and ALIUD are the shoe and the leather, because the shoe differs from leather as ens-including from ens-included.***

#### Note

Thus inadequately ALIUD and ALIUD are: ***homo*** and ***mens hominis***. Whence they ineptly define man who most accurately think they define him through ***mens***, saying: ***"homo est mens"***, etc. Surely not only do they really inter se differ, but also they are ***Ens aliud and Ens aliud***; and neither of them is predicable of the other, in nominative case and truth-saved and properly, nor accordingly can be defined through it. You will say: ***"Someone often possesses many fiefs, and nevertheless from one alone (because it is of greater estimation) is denominated hereditary."*** We respond: ***"This is to trifle splendidly, as everyone knows against his mode of defining rightly and accurately."*** You will except: ***"But by the consent of all, denomination is made from the more worthy (a potiori)."*** We respond: ***"This is perversely to re-sing the Logical canons from itch of novelty."*** For to all the learned (nay even to boys of Logic) it is clear that this canon ***denomination is made from the more worthy (a potiori)*** has not had, nor has, this sense: that the ***accurate definition of a thing totally and essentially physical*** (as they call it) should be made ***through the more worthy essential physical part*** — inasmuch as such [a part] always really differs from the whole of which it is called essential part. For ***definition essential and the defined never really differ***, which could and ought have been known even to the beginning students. Nay more: if every ***essential definition must be a complete essential predication*** (i.e. in which the predicate explicates the whole essence of the subject), by what reason could it be said (without manifest absurdity) that one essential part of man — and indeed placed in the nominative case — could absolve the accurate definition of man? But of this matter more distinctly will be treated below in the chapters on the composite, and on the whole and parts. The proper place of its disquisition is in ***Analytics***, which perhaps, if God wills, will be made public elsewhere by us and subjected to the censure of the learned. We in no way doubt that this labor would be easy and could be exceedingly profitable to the Academies' students, if the ***offices and vices of teachers and learners*** — and how the former ought to be fulfilled and the latter avoided — be reduced into the form of a discipline. And if ever, perhaps at this time this practical treatment would have been to the convenience and advantage of studies.

#### § 5 — ALIUD: Absolute vs With Determination (Cum Determinatione)

> ***It will aid also to adduce this distinction of ALIUD: when ALIUD is taken sometimes ABSOLUTELY, sometimes WITH DETERMINATION. Hitherto there was treatment of that which is called ALIUD simpliciter, absolute, and without determination.***
>
> ***This distinction must also be especially commended to Theological Students. Thus absolutely, simpliciter, and without determination, NO PERSON OF THE DIVINITY with respect to another Person of the divinity can be called ALIUD, because simpliciter nothing is called ALIUD with respect to that with which it has the same numerical essence. But one Person of the divinity with respect to another Person of the divinity CAN be called ALIUD SUPPOSITUM, and so WITH DETERMINATION ALIUD. For the three Persons of the divinity have the same numerical ESSENCE, but not the same numerical SUBSISTENCE, since three really distinct subsistences are in divinis, and so three really distinct SUPPOSITA — which however remain one numerical ens, one in essence GOD.***

#### Notes

**I.** Cultivators of Theology ought to know: ***ALIUD and ALIUD ENS is not given in divine matters, yet ALIUD and ALIUD SUPPOSITUM is given***. For three really distinct supposita between themselves are one true and in essence one God.

**II.** Signal use this doctrine presents ***against the Antitrinitarians***. For from them there are some who thus argue: ***Either the Son of God is ALIUD SUPPOSITUM from God the Father, or He is not. If so, they are not of the same essence, since it is impossible that two of the same numerical essence be simultaneously ALIUD and ALIUD and yet not be ALIUD and ALIUD. If not, they are not really distinct Persons, since two really distinct Persons are ALIUD and ALIUD SUPPOSITUM.*** To this argument the ***Orthodox Theologians*** respond by denying that a true contradiction obtains when the Son of God is said to be ALIUD SUPPOSITUM and GOD THE FATHER is called ALIUD SUPPOSITUM, and simultaneously however it is denied that God the Father and the Son of God are ALIUD and ALIUD. For a true contradiction requires that affirmation be of the same singular subject ***simpliciter, according to the same, to the same, in the same mode, and at the same time***. But now, when it is said: ***the Son of God is ALIUD suppositum and God the Father is ALIUD suppositum***, and simultaneously it is affirmed that the Son of God is ***not ALIUD from God the Father***, thus opposites are not simpliciter affirmed of the same singular subject — because it is affirmed that the Son of God is ***not ALIUD from God the Father*** and this is simpliciter affirmed, such that by ALIUD is understood ***absolutely and simpliciter ALIUD*** in sensu affirmante (i.e. ALIUD ***ens***), as if it were said: ***"The Son of God is not ALIUD, i.e. not ALIUD ens from God the Father, but God the Father and the Son of God are one numerical ens, one in essence GOD."*** When however it is simultaneously affirmed that the Son of God is ALIUD suppositum from God the Father (or, which in this place returns to the same, ***alia persona***), thus it is not simpliciter affirmed that He is ALIUD (as previously was simpliciter affirmed that He is non-ALIUD from the Father), but it is affirmed only that He is ***WITH DETERMINATION*** ALIUD — i.e. not ALIUD *ens*, but another ***person*** (and because every person is a suppositum, though not every suppositum is a person) ALIUD ***suppositum***; and thus the subsistence is determined, and it is signified that the subsistence of the Son of God is not the subsistence of God the Father, nor the subsistence of God the Father the subsistence of the Son of God; and three really distinct subsistences are of the three Persons of the divinity — yet so that one numerical essence remains of all three Persons of the divinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

And this is what the ***Scholastics*** willed when, in their Theology using the barbaric term, they distinguished between ***ALIETAS essentiae*** and ***ALIETAS subsistentiae***, and denied that the consequence holds from the latter to the former.

#### § 6

> ***SUPPOSITUM CAUSAE EST CAUSATUM*** (the suppositum of the cause is causatum).

#### Notes

**I.** Let those things be repeated which we said above on ***principiatum***, p. 495 ff.: for every ***causatum*** is ***principiatum***. The Scholastics, the inventors of this barbaric name, understand by ***causatum*** that of which something is a true cause, or (as they themselves explain) ***id quod causatur*** (that which is being caused). To be noted once again: in the doctrine on cause they use these voices — ***causare*** and ***causari*** — such that the verb ***causare*** is active, and conversely the verb ***causari*** is passive. Thus according to these Scholastic Doctors ***the architect is said to CAUSARE the building***, when he has erected it; and ***the building is said to have been CAUSATUM by the architect***, because it was built by him.

**II.** And indeed no verb occurs among classical authors which, placed separately and alone, suffices to express and sufficiently explicate what the Scholastics indicate by one word, using the voices: ***causare*** and ***causari***.

**III.** Just as elsewhere ***amari*** and ***amatum fuisse***, ***extrui*** and ***extructum fuisse*** differ greatly, so if even ***causari*** be taken as passive, yet ***causatum*** is not accurately called relatively opposed to cause, but rather ***id quod causatur*** is opposed to it. For although it is true, with cause posited (i.e. with that posited which causes), that ***id quod causatur*** is also posited — yet not therefore immediately is ***causatum*** posited. And conversely, with ***causatum*** posited (i.e. with that posited which has been caused), ***cause is not necessarily posited*** (i.e. that which causes). Thus e.gr. with it posited that the architect builds a house, not therefore immediately is the building posited; and with it posited that the house has been erected, often no longer is posited what was the efficient cause of the house, and if posited, is not posited as efficient cause. Meanwhile in the Schools it has obtained that by ***causatum*** in this place be understood not ***quod causatum est*** but ***id quod causatur***.

#### § 7 — Formal Definition of Causatum

> ***CAUSATUM is Ens which proceeds from elsewhere in its being, so however that it be ALIUD with respect to that whence it proceeds in its being. E.gr. the shoe is causatum with respect to leather and shoemaker.***

#### Notes

**I.** It is one and the same, and suffices for causatum, that it be ***aliud proceeding from elsewhere in its being*** — whether that whence it proceeds in its being be ***non-ens*** or ***verum ac reale ens***. E.gr. ***verum ens*** is the shoemaker, ***ens*** is the leather, ***adequate aliud ens*** is the shoe from the shoemaker, ***inadequate aliud ens*** is the shoe from the leather. Thus when the shoemaker makes the shoe with this mind — ***that he may sell it, that the buyer's foot may be covered by the shoe*** — thus the shoe is called ***aliud quid*** from the future sale, although the future sale is non-ens.

**II.** ***Causatum*** must be ***aliud*** — i.e. not of the same numerical being with that in respect of which it is called causatum. Here again we must beware not to confuse ***aliud suppositum*** with ***aliud ens***. For something can be ***aliud suppositum*** such that simultaneously it be ***aliud ens***; and something can be ***aliud suppositum*** such that nevertheless it be not ***aliud ens***. E.gr. ***aliud suppositum and aliud suppositum*** are Peter and Paul, and they are also ***aliud ens and aliud ens***. On the contrary, in divine matters the three Persons of the divinity are ***aliud suppositum and aliud suppositum and aliud suppositum***, yet remain ***one numerical ens***, nor can they be called ***aliud, aliud atque aliud***.

**III.** The notion of each — both ***CAUSAE*** and ***CAUSATI*** — can better stand if the requisites of each be duly attended to; which we shall now without delay hand down.

#### § 8 — Two Genera of Requisites of Cause

> ***The GENUINE REQUISITES OF CAUSE are of a twofold kind: some are called PRIMARY or MORE WORTHY (potiora); the others are called SECONDARY.***

#### § 9 — Three Primary Requisites

> ***The primary and more worthy requisites of CAUSE are three: (1) MATERIAL of cause (materiale causae); (2) REASON OF CAUSING (ratio causandi) — also called the FIRST FORMAL of cause; (3) CAUSALITY (causalitas) — which is also wont to be called the SECOND FORMAL.***

#### Note

Every cause of every thing requires these three — all and singly — such that where these three requisites are not simultaneously present, cause has no place. And indeed, from any Student's or Doctor's standpoint (of whatever faculty he be), it is of fruitful good use to weigh these requisites rightly and to know how to apply them decently to the cause which one considers or hands down. And this must be so much the more thought necessary and commended, the more certainly it stands to all lovers of solid erudition that the ***most difficult questions*** in any whatever disciplines and faculties — especially in practical disciplines — are of one, or more, or all causes, and so also of the primary and more worthy requisites of one, more, or all causes. These questions are decided more happily and accurately in proportion as these ***genuine and more worthy requisites*** of every cause are duly weighed beforehand.

#### § 10 — Materiale of Cause

> ***MATERIALE of cause is called that which can be and be called CAUSE, truth saved. E.gr. ***Peter*** can be cause of a building — not however if he be precisely considered as ***Peter***; wherefore ***materiale*** on the side of the cause of the building is called Peter.***

#### § 11 — Materiale of Cause: Twofold

> ***MATERIALE of cause is twofold. One ***materiale*** of cause is a REAL ENS, as ***Peter*** when he is called cause of a building. Another ***materiale*** of cause is NON-ENS, as ***inhabitation***, when it is called cause of a building being erected — since that inhabitation does not yet exist, nor perhaps will exist (for it can come about that the erected building be immediately consumed by flame and perish, and never be inhabited).***

#### Note

***An ens can be a true cause; a non-ens too can be a true cause.*** Of this matter we shall see especially when we treat of final, impulsive, and objective causes.

#### § 12 — Reason of Causing (Ratio Causandi)

> ***RATIO CAUSANDI is that by which something is APT to come to be or to be CAUSE. It is called also in the Schools POTENTIA CAUSATIVA, because it is the potency by which something can be cause, or (if we may use the barbaric Scholastic term) by which something is ABLE TO CAUSE. It is also called (as we have mentioned) the FIRST FORMAL of cause; and FIRST ACT; and (again a barbaric vocable) CAUSATIVITAS. Thus e.g. the ratio causandi on the side of the efficient cause of a house is ***architectural art***; on the side of the efficient cause of the sun's light, the ***potentia illuminandi*** in the sun. On this requisite more will be treated in the following chapter.***

#### Notes

**I.** Nothing exists unless it can exist: so nothing is cause unless it can be cause, or (as the Scholastics speak) ***unless it can cause***. And on this account the Scholastics called ***potentia causativa*** that potency by which something is apt to come to be or to be cause.

**II.** Just as the Scholastics distinguished between ***actus entitativus*** (by which namely something exists) and the act by which something ***can exist***, so they are wont to distinguish between ***the act by which something can be cause*** and ***the act by which something causes***.

**III.** Again, as above was distinguished between ***ens potentia*** and ***ens actu***, so now it is distinguished between ***causa potentia*** (i.e. what is not cause but can be) and ***causa actu*** (i.e. what truly is cause).

**IV.** Finally, just as ***ens possibile*** differs from ***ens potentia***, so ***causa possibilis*** differs from ***causa potentia***: for ***causa possibilis*** lies wider than ***causa potentia***.

**V.** Meanwhile the ***Scholastics***, seeing that what is not cause can either be cause or not be cause, distinguished between ***actus primus*** and ***actus secundus***, and called ***actus primus*** that whence something has this, that it be ***causa possibilis*** — not attending whether it be actu cause or not. ***Actus secundus*** they called that by which something is ***true cause***. And since something has this (that it be ***causa possibilis***) formaliter from ***ratio causandi*** (which if it could not be attributed to it, it would be ***causa impossibilis***, i.e. could not be cause); and this (that it be ***vera causa***) it has formaliter from ***causalitas***; and (which must simultaneously be noted) ***prior*** is for something to be ***causa possibilis***, ***posterior*** for it to be ***actu cause*** (since actus secundus always presupposes actus primus) — thence we see and easily collect why ***ratio causandi*** is called ***formale primum***, and ***causalitas*** is called ***formale secundum*** of cause.

#### § 13 — Causality (Causalitas)

> ***CAUSALITAS is that by which something is a TRUE CAUSE. It is called also absolutely the FORMAL of cause; item CAUSATIO; item CAUSATIO ACTIVA; ACTUS SECUNDUS; the ACT OF THE CAUSE absolutely. E.gr. ***aedificatio*** is the causality on the side of the efficient cause of the house; ***illuminatio*** as it proceeds from the sun is the causality on the side of the efficient cause of the sun's light produced in the air.***

#### Notes

**I.** Just as something, through existence (i.e. while it actually exists), is ***ens, ens actu***: so through ***causalitas*** (i.e., if you will speak with the Scholastics, while it really causes) it is ***vera causa, actu causa***.

**II.** Thence it is clear why it is called ***actus secundus***, item ***formale secundum*** on the side of cause. Let what was noted on the preceding § be compared.

**III.** Whence just as nothing is formaliter cause unless it be actu cause, so it is easy to perceive why ***causalitas*** is called the ***formale of cause***, item ***actus***.

**IV.** And just as the ***actus primus or ratio causandi*** was called ***potentia***, so ***causalitas*** is named ***actus***; item, because ***causalitas*** is that by which something causes, it is therefore called ***causatio***. For as through ***aedificatio*** someone is building (***aedificans***), so through ***causatio*** (as the Scholastics speak barbarously) something is ***causans***.

#### § 14 — Secondary Requisites: Causa Sine Qua Non

> ***SECONDARY REQUISITES of cause are NECESSARY CONDITIONS on the side of the cause, which however can be judged neither CAUSE, nor RATIO CAUSANDI, nor CAUSALITAS truth-saved. E.gr. for the sun to illuminate a chamber whose windows had been shut by valves, the removal of the valves is altogether necessary — for unless the valves had been removed from the windows, the chamber could not have been illuminated by the sun, nor could the sun have illuminated it. Meanwhile, the removal of the valves cannot be called cause of the light and of the illumination, nor ratio causandi, nor causalitas — because the removal of the valves does not illuminate the chamber, nor is it the potency of illuminating, nor is it illumination itself. These secondary requisites of cause are called CAUSAE SINE QUIBUS NON.***

#### Notes

**I.** Two things therefore are required for a secondary cause-requisite (or ***causa sine qua non***): (1) that it be necessary ***on the side of the cause*** — i.e., required on the side of that in respect of which ***causa sine qua non*** is called. (2) That it be neither cause of it, nor ratio causandi on the side of it, nor causality. One of these requisites without the other by no means suffices.

**II.** It was first required that it be ***on the side of the cause*** of which it is called ***causa sine qua non*** necessary. For they err and are ignorant of solid Philosophy who call ***however-necessary*** immediately ***causa sine qua non***, provided it be not cause, nor ratio causandi, nor causality. For one thing is ***to be necessary***, another ***to be necessary on the side of the cause***. Thus to the architect a heart is necessarily required, since no one saw an architect building who lacked a heart; yet he would be inept who would call the heart ***causa sine qua non*** with respect to the building, since it is not required on the side of the cause ***on the side of the ens*** which is called ***materiale*** of cause.

**III.** For the other requisite — namely that which in the second place was required to the causa sine qua non — the distinction between ***causa quae*** and ***causa qua*** makes it better understood. For thus the Scholastic Doctors distinguish by mutilated terms. Namely: that which has ratio causandi which now exerts itself (so that already causalitas is given) is called ***causa quae***, which precisely, absolutely, and ultimately is called cause. Thus the Sun has the potency of illuminating, which it now exerts while it produces light in the chamber; and thus causalitas is given which is ***the action***, namely ***illumination***, whence ***causa quae*** is given. On the contrary the potency of illuminating in the Sun as it now exerts itself (or as it is deduced into second act), likewise the second act itself (namely illumination itself exerting itself in the Sun), are called ***causa qua*** — because the potency of illuminating exerting itself in the Sun around the chamber, and the illumination itself as it proceeds from the Sun, are those by which the Sun is efficient cause of the light in the chamber.

**IV.** When vulgarly it is said that ***causa sine qua non*** is ***that which does not flow being into the causatum, nor perhaps has the force of flowing in, yet without which the causatum cannot be or come to be*** — this is to be understood in a sound sense. For it is the same as if it had been said: ***causa sine qua non*** is indeed necessary on the side of the cause, not however the cause [itself]. Whence unless ***causa quae*** and ***causa qua*** be understood simultaneously, the adduced formula of definition deceives. Thus the illumination which proceeds from the Sun is not cause of the light, yet without it the light could not come to be; meanwhile illumination ***is causa qua***, for it is causalitas itself.

**V.** Often in Practical disciplines, especially also in Theology and Jurisprudence, the ***name of causa qua*** comes into use, inasmuch as ***causa qua*** notes causalitas. Thus when in Ethics it is said that the ***cause of virtue is not nature but action*** — frequent action and consonant with right reason — then the sense is that causalitas on the side of the efficient cause of virtue is action. Likewise when in Politics we say that ***consensus is the efficient cause of marriage***, item when the Jurisconsults ***with Ulpian*** say: ***"NUPTIAS NON CONCUBITUS SED CONSENSUS FACIT"*** (marriage is made not by concubitus but by consent) — we understand ***causa qua***, namely causalitas on the side of the efficient cause of marriage. Nay rather often does this happen in the practical disciplines, especially when about the efficient cause itself there is no difficulty. Thus no one is ignorant that of ***human virtue*** the ***causa quae*** is man; of ***marriage*** the causae quae are male and female while they make themselves husband and wife. Of this therefore the question is: ***what is the causalitas by which man is efficient cause of virtue, male and female efficient causes of marriage?*** Thus in a sound sense it can still be said: nature is cause of virtue — if by cause you understand ***causa qua***, and indeed ratio causandi as it now exerts itself: for when rational nature in man frequently acts as right reason imbued with the sense of natural law prescribes, by it man is efficient cause of moral virtue.

**VI.** Therefore, that the more accurate Philosophers call ***causa sine qua non*** nothing of which, truth saved, can be said that in respect of that of which it is called ***causa sine qua non*** it is true cause, ratio causandi, or causality — thus anyone rightly knowing and wishing to appraise Metaphysical doctrine easily grasps this very determination ***sine qua non*** whenever added by the more accurate Metaphysicians to the voice ***causa*** — ***it removes the signification of the voice CAUSA***, and indeed removes it altogether; and so is a ***determinatio alienans***, i.e. such that it renders the signification of the voice ***causa*** altogether foreign. For although of a true cause it can be said that without it the causatum could not have been made nor made, this once received produces no prejudice to sound philosophizing — since usage is the best master of philosophizing, and reference must uniquely be had to it, when certainly in sound Metaphysics it is nowhere received in usage that true cause be called by the name ***causa sine qua non***. Metaphysicians have their notions and their terms, whose signification we ought to appraise not from popular usage, nor from grammatical origin, but ***from the usage received in the Schools***. For we would say the same of Metaphysics which ***Cicero*** most truly said of Dialectics in the ***first book of Academics***: ***"Dialecticorum verba nulla sunt publica"*** (the words of the Dialecticians are not public) — i.e. the people hardly grasp them, and hardly even that — and this is common to nearly all arts (i.e. disciplines and faculties). In the vocables of the arts therefore, which the vulgar scarcely grasps, the prudent-persons-of-each-art's definition must be employed.

#### § 15 — Causati-Side Requisites

> ***On the side of CAUSATUM the same requisites are given, both primary and secondary. The primary requisites are: (1) MATERIALE of causatum, i.e. that which is apt to undergo the denomination of causatum: e.g. from non-shoe a shoe can be made, whence it is called POSSIBLE CAUSATUM; so long as a shoe is not yet made from it, it can be called CAUSATUM POTENTIA; when now actually a shoe comes to be from leather, it becomes CAUSATUM ACTU. (2) RATIO CAUSANDI PASSIVA, i.e. that by which something is apt to become causatum: e.g. when I consider leather sufficiently disposed, it is apt indeed to become causatum, namely a shoe; that aptitude therefore is called PASSIVE REASON OF CAUSING. (3) CAUSALITAS PASSIVA, i.e. that by which something comes to be or is causatum: e.g. the effecting of the shoe considered as PASSION is causalitas on the side of the shoe.***

#### Notes

**I.** When we distinguish between ***active*** and ***passive ratio causandi***, we must not think that active ratio causandi is the same as ***potentia activa causativa*** (which is only given on the side of the efficient cause). We with the more accurate Philosophers require on the side of every cause ***ratio causandi actively considered***, as we shall examine at greater length. Whence we altogether admit those who distinguish between ***potentia activa*** and ***potentia active-spectata***. Thus e.g. the passive potency of matter, insofar as it is passive, is still ***active-spectata*** when, namely, it is considered that matter ***can cause*** (i.e. ***can be cause***), since ***causare*** is taken actively by the Scholastics. Just as therefore ***causare*** lies wider than ***agere*** — nay also ***pati est causare*** (passion also is to cause), since when matter receives form it causes, i.e. is cause of the composite — so ***ratio causandi active-spectata*** lies wider than ***ratio causandi activa***.

**II.** Let the same judgment be of ***causalitas active-spectata***, which lies wider than ***action***, since passion — nay the causality of any cause — can be actively-considered, and on the side of the cause must be.

**III.** When we attend to the requisites on the side of the causatum, this can be done in two modes. (1) Thus e.g. while we consider that ***air*** can be rendered luminous or illuminated, we consider the materiale on the side of the causatum. When we further attend that the air says a potency by which it can be illuminated, we consider ratio causandi. We consider also causalitas when we recognize that the air is illuminated, i.e. the ***passive illumination***. (2) In this mode: light inasmuch as it can be produced in the air is called the ***materiale of the effect*** (and so the materiale of the causatum); the potency whence the light has this (that it can be produced) is called ratio causandi; production so considered, inasmuch as it produces light, is called causalitas on the side of the causatum.

#### § 16 — Causa: Materialiter vs Formaliter Spectata

> ***For the rest, a true cause is considered either MATERIALITER or FORMALITER. Materialiter is considered a cause when there is considered that which is true cause, yet not qua-such is true cause. E.gr. ***a MUSICIAN BUILDS A HOUSE***, and on that account is most rightly called and is true cause of the house, yet is not true cause of the house INASMUCH AS HE IS MUSICIAN, since Music is not the ARS οἰκοδομική (architectonic art). A cause materialiter considered is also called ***CAUSA PER ACCIDENS on the side of the cause***.***
>
> ***Contra, FORMALITER is considered a cause when there is considered that which qua-such is true cause. E.gr. ***an ARCHITECT builds a house***, and on that account is most rightly called and is true cause of the house, and is true cause of the house INASMUCH AS HE IS ARCHITECT, since architectonic art is the ARS οἰκοδομική and the PERFECTA RATIO CAUSANDI (perfect reason of causing).***

#### § 17 — Causatum: Materialiter vs Formaliter

> ***Likewise a true causatum is considered either MATERIALITER or FORMALITER. ***Materialiter*** is considered a causatum when there is considered that which is true causatum but not qua-such is true causatum. E.gr. when a ***doctor is son of a rustic***, the doctor is called true causatum of the rustic — yet is not true effect, and so not true causatum of the rustic ***qua doctor***.***
>
> ******Formaliter*** is considered a true causatum when there is considered that which qua-such is true causatum. E.gr. a ***house*** is a true causatum with respect to the architect, because the house qua-such is from the architect. The ***son in human things is a true causatum, because qua-son he is from the father***, who is true cause. Causatum materialiter considered is called ***CAUSATUM PER ACCIDENS on the side of the causatum***; causatum formaliter considered is called ***CAUSATUM PER SE on the side of the causatum***.***

#### Notes

**I.** The accurate doctrine of ***cause per se and per accidens***, with its practical use, we reserve to a peculiar chapter.

**II.** But also this must be noted at this place: that the ***practical use and decent application*** of both the primary and the secondary requisites of cause and causatum we shall demonstrate (as we hope) in a peculiar chapter and more convenient method only after some [intervening] chapters.

## Caput Nonum

### Of Potency and Act — Especially That Potency Which They Call CAUSATIVE, and That Act Which They Call CAUSALITY. Likewise of First Act and Second Act, and of Various Useful Distinctions Pertaining Thereto

#### § 1

> ***For the present chiefly serviceable is the distinction of POTENCY into CAUSATIVE and NON-CAUSATIVE. CAUSATIVE POTENCY is that by which something is APT to come to be or to be true CAUSE. Thence it can easily be collected which potency is called non-causative.***

#### Note I — The Multiple Significations of POTENTIA

The vocable ***potentia*** is of the number of those which are ***multifariam dicuntur*** (said in many ways):

**(1)** It notes a certain ***non-repugnance***, which ***B. Stahl*** and others vulgarly make ***triple***: ***MATHEMATICAL, LOGICAL, and OBJECTIVE***. They teach that these agree in being ***non-repugnances***; they render them distinct in that:
- ***Mathematical*** is deduced into act through ***termination of quantity***, from which a certain figure results;
- ***Logical*** through the ***operation of the intellect***;
- ***Objective*** through the ***external action of an efficient cause***, by which that which does not repugn to be is actually produced.

Of this ***Aristotle*** makes mention when in ***Metaphysics V, c. XII*** he says: ***καὶ μεταφορά ἐστι, ὡς ἡ ἐν τοῖς γεωμετρικοῖς δύναμις*** (it is also by metaphor, as the potency in geometrical things); and the same there he declares egregiously enough by an opposite example in the preceding words. Of that other [sense] he joins mention in the same place in these words: ***τὸ γὰρ δυνατόν ἐστι τρόπον τὸ μὴ ἐξ ἀνάγκης ψεῦδος σημαίνειν, ἕνα δὲ τὸ ἀληθὲς εἶναι, ἕνα δὲ τὸ ἐνδεχόμενον εἶναι*** (for ***the possible*** is in a mode that which does not necessarily signify what is false; another is to be true; another is to be contingent).

Marvelous indeed is it that many among the learned should think there is nothing else to be understood by ***potentia logica*** than ***non-repugnance of terms*** (through which, namely, one can be truly predicated of another) — when nevertheless the description here labors under the gravest disease of ***narrowness***. For, that from the immense cumulus of examples we may at least adduce some by way of instance: who would deny that the non-repugnance by which it does not repugn to an ***exponible proposition*** that, on account of its obscurity, it be expounded through two or more more-known simple notes, comprehended in one composite enunciation — likewise that by which it does not repugn to a true ***converted proposition*** that from it there follow a true converting — likewise that by which it does not repugn to Syllogisms of the second and third figure that from them be made Syllogisms of the first figure — is ***logical non-repugnance***, to which however the adduced definition does not fit?

This the ***Scholastics*** hand down; by whom (especially if we speak with the Scotists) ***potentia OBJECTIVE*** is formally the ***non-repugnance according to which something is apt to be the object of an active potency, that through it it may come to be***. And commonly they call it ***the potency of Scotus*** — either because ***Johannes Duns Scotus*** discovered it, or because he is at least the inventor of the name, or because the disciples of Scotus used this acceptance of potency more than the rest of Philosophers against the ***Thomists***, to whom the term ***potentia objectiva*** is extremely hateful. ***Scotus*** himself in these same words defines it in ***2. dist. xii. q. 1***, with this distinction: that he defines it at least ***in ordine ad potentiam divinam***. Nor incongruously. For every ens, before it be created by God, does not have a true and real entity in itself, whence neither is it formally in GOD; it is however in His potency — partly ***eminenter***, inasmuch as by God (as its equivocal cause) it is causable (as the Scholastics speak); partly through ***formal concept*** or ***express species*** in GOD, i.e. according to intelligible being. See ***Johannes de Rada, Aragonian Bishop of Padencia, Controversiarum Theologicarum inter Thomam et Scotum, part II, controv. 1, artic. 2, not. 2, p. m. 11***. The same was taught by ***Augustine***, as the same [Rada] transmits in I. dist. 36 — namely in ***book 83 of Questions, question 46***, and in many other places, where [a passage] is thought by others especially notable, which is ***XII de Civitate Dei c. XII***. The same the ***Angelic Doctor Thomas Aquinas*** felt, in ***part prima, question 25, article 4, ad primum, p. m. 95***, and elsewhere in clearest words.

And although there are those who hold ***potentia Logica*** and ***potentia objectiva*** to be the same — among whom ***Franciscus Suarez*** and ***Thomas Comptonus Carletonus*** are more celebrated — it would nevertheless be most easy to refute the same from ***Rodrigo de Arriaga***, perhaps also from Scotus himself, if the reason of our proposal would allow. The same censure deserve those who teach that ***potentia Objectiva coincides with passive*** [potency], not without the mark of confusion. That the acceptance of ***potentia objectiva*** is less proper is nearly in confessed [agreement] among all.

**(2)** ***Potentia*** is taken for ***any force or form*** by which the thing is ***plainly immutable, or not easily mutable for the worse***, as Aristotle at the cited place speaks.

**(3)** The voice of ***potentia*** sometimes notes the same as ***natural principle***, whatever that may be — as from the same place of Aristotle and many others it stands.

**(4)** ***Potentia*** is received for ***habit***. Thus Aristotle, in ***book 9 Metaphysics c. 2***, teaches ***δυνάμεις*** (potencies) to be sometimes ***ἄλογοι, rationis expertes*** (irrational, devoid of reason), sometimes ***δὲ λόγου (cum ratione)*** (with reason), and immediately adds: ***διὸ πᾶσαι αἱ τέχναι καὶ αἱ ποιητικαὶ ἐπιστῆμαι δυνάμεις εἰσί*** (whence all arts and productive sciences are potencies). And a little after: ***αἱ μὲν μετὰ λόγου πᾶσαι τῶν ἐναντίων αἱ αὐταί*** (those with reason are all of them of opposites).

Of this place, as to the former words, various render variously: ***Bessarion Cardinal Nicene*** thus renders: ***"Wherefore all arts and productive sciences are potencies."*** In the same way ***Johannes Argyropoulos Byzantius***: ***"Wherefore all arts and all effective sciences are potencies."*** ***Ernestus Sonerus, Noric Professor, p. m. 489*** renders thus: ***"Hence it comes about that all effective arts and sciences are counted among potencies."*** "I think moreover," says Sonerus, "that by the vocable of art and science ***Aristotle understands all acquired habits which are exercised in another inasmuch as it is another***." Some collect from these and from the following words (which can be seen at the cited place) that according to Sonerus's mind this is to be received only of practical or effective sciences — so that by this very fact it is thus specifically brought about in them that they be ***rational potencies***, since they can be directed to effecting either contrary.

Whatever be the mind and exposition of others, it pleases us ***Alexander of Aphrodisias's interpretation***, which in his Commentaries (edited by the interpreter ***Johannes Genesius Sepulveda Cordubensis***) we discerned, which runs thus: ***"Therefore all arts — both effective, as the art of building a house or ships; and also sciences — are faculties. By a more common vocable (Aristotle) called sciences arts; for they are principles of moving in another."*** And immediately in the following: ***"The reason indeed why faculties endowed with reason are producers of opposites is this: that science is a certain reason, i.e. a faculty with reason, a certain cognition (so to speak) scientific; and reason and scientific cognition show and know not only the thing and the habit, but also the privation,"*** etc. See more at the same place.

And this ***Αλεξάνδρειαν*** (Alexandrine) explication approves ***Dn. Dreierus disput. in primam Philosophiam decima tertia § 4 et seqq. p. m. 228***, and firmly suggests that the vocable ***δυνάμεις*** should be taken amplately, so that it include sciences too — from ***Eustratius*** and ***Alexander*** at another place; nay rather from ***Aristotle Metaph. 3 c. 2, book 2 c. 3, book 10 c. 4*** he most clearly evinces that according to Aristotle's mind all sciences are of contraries. Many interpreters try from this place to evince the liberty of each potency of the rational soul, both of intellect and of will — but certainly they labor in vain, since it never came into Aristotle's mind to treat there of intellect and will.

And indeed we could adduce far more acceptances of ***potentia***, if signal utility would allow us (who wish to be briefer in less necessary matters). Let him approach ***Aristotle*** who wills, who in many places indicates various acceptances of potency. For us, in that one chapter ***c. 9 lib. V Metaphysicorum***, where he treats ex professo of the various signification of this notion, we have been able to apprehend ***seven distinct significations*** recounted by him there.

#### Note II — Potentia Causativa vs Non-Causativa: The Eternal-Generation Application

Not without fruit and necessity have we adduced the distinction of ***POTENTIA*** into ***NON-CAUSATIVE*** and ***CAUSATIVE***. For it is very different, ***to be potency*** and ***to be causative potency***. The former is wider than the latter, because every ***causative*** potency is ***potency***, but not conversely — i.e., not every potency is causative. For even that ***incomprehensible force and fecundity*** by which (as it is supposed from Theology) ***GOD the Father from all eternity, from His own substance, generated the Son, [and] by which the Father and the Son spirated the Holy Spirit*** — is ***potency***, yet not ***causative***.

We do not fashion this notion from our own brain. It was long since employed by ***Theologian Scholastics***. The same ***Scotus*** uses in ***Quodlib. quaest. 7***; likewise ***Johannes de Rada*** in ***Controv. Theol. inter Thomam et Scotum part. 1, controv. 1, artic. 2 ad 1, p. m. 149***. The same can be seen in ***Hurtado de Mendoza, Disp. Phys. sect. 14 subf. 2 § 101 p. m. 350***, and elsewhere; in ***Franciscus Toletus 1. Phys. q. 2 quaest. 14 conclus. p. m. 252***; in ***Petrus Fonseca Lusitanus lib. V Metaph. c. 1 quaest. 4 sect. 4 p. m. 526***, and in many others.

We shall not grow weary of adducing the words of the Bishop of Padencia [Rada], which have themselves thus: ***"POTENTIA ACTIVA can be received bifariously: FIRST, PROPERLY, for POTENTIA CAUSATIVA, whose object is the possible, as it is opposed to being simpliciter necessary — such are all beings other than God, which are not simpliciter necessary, since they can be and not be; whence everything other than God is the object of potentia activa properly so called. SECONDLY, potentia activa can be received LESS PROPERLY, for POTENTIA PRODUCTIVA, whose object is every producible, whether other than God or God Himself. But these two potencies differ: (1) as superior and inferior — every potentia activa in the first mode (which is called causative) is potentia productiva, but not conversely: for the eternal Father has potentia productiva with respect to the Son, not however potentia causativa or active in the first mode. For the Father is not CAUSE of the Son, though He is His PRINCIPLE. (2) They differ in this: potentia causativa regards an object OTHER in nature from that of which it is [the potency], because cause and effect cannot be of the same numerical nature. Potentia productiva, however, can be with respect to a product existing in the same numerical nature as that of which it is the potency — as is clear in divine matters, of the potency of the Father with respect to the Son."***

#### Note III — On the Potentia Generandi Debate

We shall not here dispute whether ***the POTENTIA GENERANDI by which GOD the Father from all eternity, from His own substance, generated the Son, and by which the Father and the Son spirated the Holy Spirit*** — can be called ***active***. ***B. Stahl*** and others constantly deny this, because by such a potency what is produced is not ***aliud*** [another thing], but at most ***alius, aliud suppositum, alia persona*** — having the same numerical essence with the producer. Others however (as even from ***Johannes de Rada*** stands) hold that this locution can be admitted in its mode, since those ***generation*** and ***spiration*** are called ***ACTIONES AD INTRA***, item ***ACTUS PERSONALES***, by others also ***ACTUS NOTIONALES*** (because from them the persons of the divinity are made known to us).

From Theology it stands that ***the Son and the Holy Spirit have been produced neither from any subject nor from nothing*** (since whatever is produced in either mode is a creature); but that each has been produced ***from the substance of the producing principle*** — the Son from the substance of the Father, the Holy Spirit from the substance of the Father and the Son — such that each Person has essence not from Himself, but the Son from the Father, the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, through ***true, real, and actual communication***. Since however the divine essence is ***one, simplest, and plainly indivisible***, it could not but be that the Son of God was so produced from the substance of the Father, and the Holy Spirit from the substance of the Father and the Son, that ***the Son received the same numerical essence which is in the Father, and the Spirit the same numerical essence which is in the Father and the Son — and this [essence] whole and undivided*** — as the Theologians accurately teach.

Whatever therefore it be — whether such potency can be called active or not — this is certain: that it can in no way be called ***causative***. But of ***potentia causativa*** we now speak. From what has thus far been said it abundantly stands by what reason not only the Theologian ***Scholastics***, but also our own [Lutheran] Theologians, judge the distinction between ***POTENTIA NON-CAUSATIVA*** and ***POTENTIA CAUSATIVA*** most useful and necessary to know.

#### Note IV — Suarez's Common Definition of Potentia Causativa + the Scholastic Alius-vs-Aliud Trinity Precision

***Suarez*** and the ***Scholastics***, whom most of today's Metaphysicians follow, commonly define potentia causativa in this mode: ***"Potentia causativa is nothing other than the potency itself FLOWING BEING INTO ANOTHER (influens esse in aliud)."*** ***Influere esse*** here is held to be received not strictly (as it alone fits an efficient cause causing through active causative potency), but widely — so that ***to flow being*** is nothing other than ***to give and communicate being***. By ***aliud*** they do not say except ***an ens which is not of the same numerical essence with another***. Thus Peter is ***aliud quid*** from Paul: for although the nature of Peter and Paul is one — as it is denuded of the singular properties and individuating differences (as they call them) of Peter and Paul and abstracts from them (by which reason Peter and Paul are said to have one nature, namely by essential and specific unity, and so are not essentially distinguished) — yet Peter and Paul still differ in ***singular essence***, and are ***aliud and aliud*** inasmuch as the nature of Peter and of Paul is considered, as each is contracted and individuated by singular differences (as the Scholastics speak). For it cannot be said that one numerical essence or nature is in Peter and Paul — for the nature in Peter and Paul is numerically divided, since really in them it is multiplied or plurified, such that it is not one numerically in many, but many in many, i.e. such that in Peter and Paul there are two distinct natures, which however are called one nature in species, on account of one and similar ratio which human nature obtains in Peter and in Paul.

Hence [the Scholastics] teach it can easily stand why the potency by which God the Father from eternity produced the Son, and the Father and the Son from eternity produced the Holy Spirit, ***cannot be called causative*** — because namely the three Persons of the divinity cannot be called ***aliud, aliud atque aliud***. Thus ***Thomas, 1 part., question 25, article 1, ad 1, p. m. 148***, and ***Cajetanus in his commentary on the same place***, testify that on this account among the Latin Doctors the name ***CAUSA AD INTRA in the Trinity*** was never admitted, because ***causa importat diversitatem substantiae*** (cause imports diversity of substance). ***Vazquez 1 p. d. 131 c. 1*** shows from the common sense of the Fathers that ***aliud*** uttered neutrally signifies diversity in nature. Whence the ***Council of Ephesus***, the ***Toledan***, and the ***Lateran c. Damnamus de summa Trinitate*** admitted in the Trinity ***alium et alium***, not however ***aliud et aliud***. Although therefore ***aliud suppositum in Trinitate*** be admitted, not however ***aliud simpliciter*** [is admitted]. For ***aliud et aliud simpliciter*** argues distinction in essence; this distinction however ***aliud et aliud suppositum*** does not argue — since ***aliud simpliciter*** is the same as ***alia natura*** or ***essentia***. Of this matter also we treated in the preceding chapter.

For although the divine essence is common to several really distinct [persons], it is not however common ***with its own multiplication*** — since in the three persons it remains ***one in number***. Nay rather, nor to every singular nature (what? — nay not even to every singular suppositival singularity) does ***communicability*** repugn. For not every communicability of nature effects ***universality***, but only that which is conjoined with its own multiplication — by one name, ***communicability multiplicative***; this suffices for universality; that this can stand with singularity of nature is ***impossible***. Most eruditely did ***Johannes Baptista Alonsorius Valentinus Bocairentanus*** treat this matter in his ***Pandectae de universis***. We have gathered these from the Scholastic doctrines; whoever desires a more copious explication may approach ***Franciscus Suarez tom. 1 Disp. Metaph. Disp. XII sect. 2 pp. 171, 243, et 244***. As to Aristotle himself: ***Franciscus Suarez*** and ***Mendoza l.c.*** state that he did not define ***potentia causativa*** in common; and this is the common opinion of the Scholastic Doctors.

#### Note V — Potentia Objectiva as Potency-but-not-Causative + the Eternal-Creation-Possibility Defenders Chain

We have seen an illustrious enough example of ***potentia non-causativa*** commended not only by the Theologian Scholastics, but also by our own [Lutheran] Theologians. We wish still to add another, the notice of which promises no slight use to Philosophers of the First [Philosophy] and to cultivators of Theology. Namely, there is also given ***POTENTIA OBJECTIVA***, which likewise is a true potency, yet not causative.

For by the unanimous consent of the more accurate Metaphysicians and of orthodox Theologians: ***the creatures, before they were produced out of nothing, were in the best and greatest God — not however as things actually existing, but as POSSIBLE EFFECTS, or as ***possible effects to be in the virtue of their cause***. We notably say ***not as actually existing***: for this is diametrically against the Sacred Scriptures.

Nor (which we note in passing) ***according to specific likeness*** — as otherwise is caused that which must be caused by a univocal cause: for before it be caused, it is said to be formaliter in its univocal cause, since when it is caused, it is one and the same as its cause by essential ratio. Thus e.gr. ***fire***, before it was generated, was said according to essential unity to be in the fire from which now it has been generated; just as in human things the Son, before he was caused by his Father, was said to be in his Father according to specific ratio. For thus God would be made ***a univocal cause of creatures***, not without great absurdity. For a univocal cause is a cause which causes a causatum of the same species. But now God under such a species (which is precisely indicated in the description of a univocal cause) is neither contained, nor can be contained in any mode. For by it is understood only the ***species specialissima*** (most special species), since otherwise even an equivocal cause can cause a causatum of the same species (namely subalternate), and so there would be no discrimen between univocal and equivocal cause. But to the divine nature it absolutely repugns to have a most-special species above itself.

But we have said: ***as possible effects in God Himself, or producible by God, as equivocal cause***. Nay, there are Philosophers and Theologians of great name who defend that ***the creatures from eternity have had POSSIBLE BEING in God*** — or, which comes to the same, that they could have been produced from eternity by God.

Thus: ***Augustine XII de civ. Dei c. 15***; ***Ambrose lib. 11 Hexaem. c. 3***; ***Athanasius orat. 2 contra Arianos***; ***Cyril of Alexandria VI.6 thes. c. 2***; ***Damascene lib. 2 fidei orthodoxae c. 8***; ***Hugo of St. Victor lib. 3 de Sacr. c. 10***; ***Albert the Great in his paraphrase on ch. 1 of book 2 of the Summa Theologiae***; ***Bonaventura in 2 dist. 1 artic. 2 quaest. 2***; ***Marsilius quaest. 1 art. 2***; ***William of Paris lib. 1 de Universo***; ***Henry of Ghent Quodlib. 1 quaest. 7 et Quodlib. 9 quaest. 17***; ***Eugubinus lib. 1 perennis philosophiae***; ***Nicolaus Cusanus in lib. de venatione sapientiae c. 38***; ***Raymundus de Sabunde in Theologia naturali th. 22 et 23***; ***Philoponus, the gravissimus Peripateticus, in lib. adversus Proclum de mundi aeternitate c. 3***; and innumerable others cited in ***Didacus Massus, Vallesius, Toletus in comment. in cap. prior. 8 physicae lib. Arist.*** and in ***Bonaventura Baro Hibernus Clonmeliensis*** — have adduced in the contrary direction an almost innumerable number of reasons, whatever ***Aegidius Romanus in 2 dist. 1 in quaest. de hac re***, ***Johannes Duns Scotus in 2 dist. 1 quaest. 3***, and ***Pererius lib. 15 c. 13*** have said, who think it can be responded to the arguments of each side, and resolve nothing other than that the matter is doubtful.

The chief argument which is wont to be urged by them for the affirmative is this: ***No repugnance is given why creatures could not have been produced from eternity*** — neither on the side of God the Creator, nor on the side of the creatures, nor on the side of the action or production; and besides Creator, creature, and creation here nothing is found. ***Not on the side of God the Creator*** — because it does not repugn that effect be able to be simultaneous with its cause (as is clear from the sun and its rays, which are wont ever to exist simultaneously with the sun; and if the sun had been from eternity, from eternity would have been the rays, true effects of the sun). Nay rather, since God through His immense potency with which He is powerful can also do all and singular things which do not imply contradiction and which He wills — therefore He could also, if He had so willed, have produced the creatures themselves from eternity. ***Nor on the side of the creatures*** can any repugnance be given: for there is one and the same numerical entity (as to the matter) by which someone produces and something is produced; if therefore God could from eternity produce creatures (as has now been shown), creatures also could have been produced from eternity by God. ***Nor finally on the side of the production or action*** can any repugnance be given: for since it does not repugn that God could produce from eternity, it also does not repugn that production could have been given from eternity, since no real discrimen can be dreamed between ***to produce*** and ***to exercise production***.

From the ***Scholastics*** this view is defended by ***Thomas Aquinas 1 part., quaest. 46, artic. 2; in 2 dist. 1 quaest. 1 artic. 2; quaest. de potentia artic. 14; and in his opuscula, opusc. 27 which is De Aeternitate Mundi contra Murmurantes***; ***Durandus a Sancto Portiano 2 dist. 1 quaest. 2***; ***Argentina quaest. 1 art. 3***; ***Capreolus***; ***Dionysius Cisterciensis***; ***Henricus Palatinus*** ibid.; ***Bassolis quaest. 3***; ***Gabriel Vazquez part. 1. summ. Disp. 177***; ***Baconinus***; ***Gabriel Biel***; ***Guglielmus Occam***; ***Suncius***; ***Javellus***; ***Soto***; ***Villalpandus***; ***Aquarius***; ***Ferrariensis***; ***Isidorus de Isolanis lib. 2 de aeternitate mundi contra Averroystas***; ***Rodericus ab Arriaga Disp. 17 physic.***; ***Franciscus Suarez Disp. Metaph. 26 sect. 6***.

#### Note VI — Scotus's Formal Definition of Potentia Objectiva

Let us see therefore what ***potentia objectiva*** is. ***Scotus*** in ***book of 2 Distinctions, dist. 12 quaest. 1*** expressly defines it thus: ***"POTENTIA OBJECTIVA is nothing other than that non-repugnance according to which something is apt to be the OBJECT OF DIVINE ACTIVE POTENCY, that through it it may come to be."*** Let us thus suppose, e.gr., that God today still wills to produce some angel who does not yet exist: here surely no repugnance is given why such an Angel cannot be produced by God. That non-repugnance therefore, according to which that Angel (who does not yet exist) can be put forth to the creative potency of God, and through it come to be, is called ***potentia objectiva***.

#### Note VII — The Massive Thomist-vs-Scotist Controversy

The genuine sense and truth of this assertion can perhaps be more conveniently perceived if we recount and examine the ***reasons by which Promachus [the champion] of the Thomists, after Thomas, [and] the supreme Leaders — Thomas de Vio Cajetanus and Johannes Capreolus, Thomists (most, though not all) — impugned potentia objectiva***, so as to make things more difficult for ***Scotus and his Disciples*** who, all and each with most-joined forces, with ***Johannes de Rada*** as standard-bearer, defended and championed potentia objectiva strenuously.

But first let us see ***why Thomas was so hostile an enemy to potentia objectiva***. The occasion of the fight was that controversy risen between Thomists and Scotists: ***Whether PRIME MATTER is Ens actu, existing through its own existence; or whether it is ens potentia, not existing through its own, but through another existence?*** The former the ***Scotists*** affirmed constantly and the latter denied and exceedingly denied; the latter the ***Thomists*** defended and rejected the former. The chief battering ram by which the Thomists used against the Scotist foundation was: ***"If matter qua such does not have form, matter qua such does not have act. The former is true. Sc. the latter."*** That the Scotist leader [Scotus] might shake this, he distinguished in many places between ***potentia objectiva*** and ***subjectiva***: distinguishing the former against the ***actus entitativus*** (or ***existentiae***); the ***objectivo*** (as ***Aegidius Romanus*** speaks), ***transcendentally or presential existence*** (as Magister Johannes Magister, Scotist, calls it); the latter however [he distinguished] against the ***formal act*** or ***form***. The army of Scotus denied all ***formal act of matter qua such***, yet saved the ***entitative act of matter qua such***. Indignant Thomists, that they might not lose all effort, sounded the open battle-trumpet against the Scotists, defenders of this distinction, holding ***as nothing and void that which is the sign of potentia objectiva***. By what art and by what Mars they obstructed the subtle Leader's forces, is taught by the following arguments of theirs — the most powerful certainly, by which they displayed their hostile assaults:

**(1)** Every potency really existing is either ***active*** or ***passive***. The potentia objectiva of Scotus is neither active nor passive. Therefore: Scotus's potentia objectiva really is not given.

**(2)** Every real potency has a real respect to act. Scotus's potentia objectiva does not have real respect to act. Therefore: Scotus's potentia objectiva is not real potency. The ***Major*** they prove because potency and act are relative: with one of the related posited, there is posited its respect to the other. The ***Minor*** they demonstrate because if Scotus's potentia objectiva had respect to act, then it would either be ***productive of act*** (and so active) or ***receptive of act*** (and so passive) — both fight against the Scotist bands.

**(3)** If through Scotus's potentia objectiva something can be the object of really-existing active potency, it follows that Scotus's potentia objectiva is itself really-existing active. But the consequent routs the Scotists, who contradistinguish potentia objectiva itself from active and passive. Therefore the antecedent, and consequently potentia objectiva, is not any real thing — it is nothing.

**(4)** Whatever formally says negation is nothing. Scotus's potentia objectiva formally says negation: for it is ***non-repugnance***, the negation of ***repugnance***. Therefore: Scotus's potentia objectiva is nothing.

**(5)** Whatever does not exist really is ***Ens rationis, chimera, λόγιος minutus [little word]***, nothing. Potentia objectiva does not exist really. Therefore.

Nor indeed were the ***unwarlike Thomists*** destitute of auxiliary troops: from the ***Nominalists*** some stood on their part — nay the very ***Prince of the Nominalists, Gabriel Biel 2 dist. XII q. 2*** [stood on their part]; and that we may be silent on many others conspiring with the Thomists, we yet name one Scotist enemy who, without strength, was most vehemently angry — the illustrious Count ***Jacobus Zabarella***, who in ***lib. 2 de rerum materia c. 2 p. 185*** holds it as manifest that potentia objectiva is not given.

But indeed the reasons which stand behind the Scotists exceed the Thomistic reasons by many parasangs. Among them are the following:

**(1)** Whatever formally says ***non-repugnance*** is formally a positive thing. Potentia objectiva formally says non-repugnance. Therefore. ***Major*** proved: because repugnance formally is a negative thing (for it says nothing other than negation, by which one cannot be the other). But now repugnance and non-repugnance are opposed to each other by ***contradictory*** opposition; and contradictorily opposed things always differ as ***positive*** and ***negative***. ***Minor*** per se evident.

**(2)** Whatever formally does not say negation, nor depends on the operation of the intellect, that is a ***real and positive thing***. But potentia objectiva &c. Therefore. ***Major*** evident. ***Minor*** cannot thence be denied: for just as it does not depend on the operation of the intellect, nor says negation, that the Angel is produced ***in second act*** by God, so neither says negation nor depends on the operation of the intellect that the Angel ***can be produced*** by God.

To the Thomist arguments it is not difficult to respond without entangling oneself in war.

To (1): respond by conceding the whole, if indeed the conclusion is rightly inferred by the Thomists. The ***Major*** had itself thus: ***"Every potency really existing is either active or passive."*** It can be subsumed: the ***informative potency of form***, as it is in act a ***formal cause***, is no less a potency really existing than active or passive is — and yet it must be called neither active nor passive. For if it were active, the form (as it is formal cause) would not be formal cause but efficient; if passive, then it would be material. Let the Major stand. The ***Minor*** was this: Scotus's potentia objectiva is neither active nor passive. This proposition was always confessed by the Scotists. The conclusion ought therefore to be inferred thus: ***Therefore: Scotus's potentia objectiva is not really existing***. Thus the whole argument is not against Scotus, who with his own grants that potentia objectiva is not really existing. But if the conclusion be thus inferred: ***Therefore: Scotus's potentia objectiva is not a real thing*** — the argument shows the sole of its foot, since one thing is the ***real***, another the ***really-existing*** (let the axiom in c. 1 above adduced be seen). The same sentence is defended by Scotus and his disciples, as the most learned Scotist ***Johannes de Rada part. 2 controv. Theol. inter Thomam et Scotum controv. 12 art. 2 notab. 4 p. 379*** testifies.

To (2): respond by denying the ***Minor***. For expressly this Minor proposition contradicts the truth. ***Never did Scotus hold that potentia objectiva has no real respect to act***, but rather he everywhere in his writings asserts and strives to defend with all his powers that it itself has respect to ***actus entitativus*** or ***aequalis existentia***.

To (3): respond by denying the consequence. For it does not follow: ***"If through potentia objectiva something can be the object of a really-existing active potency, then even potentia objectiva itself will be active."*** They differ by the whole heaven between themselves: ***to be able to be object of active potency through potentia objectiva***, and ***for potentia objectiva itself to be active***. Who would bear him who said: ***"Through the shoemaker's art leather can be the object of the shoemaker. Therefore the shoemaker's art is the shoemaker himself"***?

To (4): respond by denying the Minor. The contrary stands from reasons adduced in the contrary: for if repugnance is negation, non-repugnance cannot but be a positive thing, since everything which is opposed to negation contradictorily is a positive thing. To the proof — when it was said that through non-repugnance repugnance is negated — it must be said: it does not thence follow that non-repugnance is formally the negation of repugnance. Thus ***immutability*** and ***immortality*** in God negate mutability and mortality; nor however are these divine attributes (immutability, immortality etc.) formally a negative thing — unless you were also willing to call ***non-stone-ness, non-lion-ness*** divine attributes, since they also negate those imperfections from God. ***Non-repugnance*** formally does not say negation, but rather an aptitude by which one can be another, though it connotes negation.

To (5): respond by denying the Major. Its falsity can be grasped by the hands. The Thomist sword's knot (if one is present) can be dissolved thus:

> ***What does not really exist is Ens rationis.***
> ***The essences of things did not really exist from eternity.***
> ***Therefore: The essences of things from eternity were entia rationis.***

The conclusion is against the Thomists; Minor and Major are the Thomists'. Thus the ***Thomists contradict themselves***.

#### Note VIII — The Three Scotist Requisites of Potentia Objectiva + Final Defenders List

For something to be ***in potentia objectiva*** with respect to God, ***with the Scotists we require three things***:
1. **That that which is said to be in potentia objectiva do not exist in the nature of things apart from the operation of the mind** — e.g., angel, dog, lion, since they now actually exist, cannot be in potentia objectiva.
2. **That there be no subject out of which it comes to be**.
3. **That it be able to be produced** — for if it could not be produced, by what reason could possible-being be attributed to it?

The same teaches ***Johannes de Rada part. 3 above-cited controv. 2 de potentia creandi, art. 1 p. 32***. Those whom we mentioned above accommodate the doctrine on potentia objectiva to their view thus:
1. The creatures were not actually in the nature of things from eternity, since neither does right reason dictate this, much less does the Sacred Codex (which testifies the contrary).
2. From eternity there was no subject from which they came to be from eternity.
3. It did not repugn that they be produced through God's creative potency.

Whoever desires to know more on potentia objectiva, let him approach ***Scotus*** at the place cited. The matter has been copiously set forth by three most-strenuous followers of Scotus: ***Petrus Tataretus, Parisian, in 1. Phys. c. 5 q. 1 p. 17***; ***Antonius Trombeta, Paduan, in Tract. de formalitatibus Scoti sent. art. 1 p. 32***; ***Magister Johannes Magister, Parisian, in 1. Phys. q. 2 not. 1 p. 57 b***. To these let be joined: ***Antonius Siretus in formalitatibus modernioribus de mente Scoti p. 23***; ***de la Fuente, Toledan, 1. phys. q. 2***; ***Bartholomaeus Mastrius Disp. Phys. 2***; ***Johannes Ponsius Carmina Hibernus l. 11 phys. disp. 3***; ***Bonaventura Baro Hibernus Clonmeliensis in his Scotus Defensus tom. 2 apolog. 2 act. 4 p. 251***; and he who was first to be named after Scotus — the most studious Scotist, ***Johannes de Rada, Aragonian, Bishop of Padencia, part. 2 controv. 12 artic. 2 p. 379 and artic. 3 p. 385***. To these, if needed, we could add others: ***Vazquez, Greg. de Valentia, Franciscus de Oviedo, Franciscus Bonae spei, Rodericus ab Arriaga, Durandus, Hurtadus de Mendoza, Gregorius de Arimino, Franciscus Victoria, Dominicus de Soto***, and innumerable others. From our own [Lutherans] we cite ***B. Stahl Instit. Metaph. cap. 9 § 16 p. 185***; ***B. Slevogt Disp. de esse possibili p. 157 ff.*** and ***Disp. de ratione formali entis finiti sect. 1 et 2 de esse essentiae et existentiae p. 136 ff.***; and ***D. Petrus Musaeus Instit. Metaph. c. 4***.

#### § 2 — Causative Potency: Complete vs Incomplete

> ***POTENTIA CAUSATIVA is distinguished into COMPLETE and INCOMPLETE.***

#### Notes

**I.** Here it merits to be well noted that it is one thing [to speak of] potentia causandi ***precisely as it is potentia causandi***, another [to speak of it] ***as it is complete or incomplete***.

**II.** Metaphysicians dispute: ***Is potentia causativa in common the entity itself of the cause absolutely conceived, or an ens superadded to the cause absolutely conceived?*** Some assert the former, others the latter, many bid us walk the middle way. But all are deceived. For even to mere non-entities true potencies causative can be ascribed, since (as we mentioned above p. 526, and will be sufficiently shown in what follows) many true causes can be non-entities, to which no entity can truth-saved be attributed; so neither can the potency of causing (which is attributed to them) be said to be either the entity of the cause itself or an ens superadded to it. Added to this: the potentia causativa which belongs to a cause as true and real ens does not really differ from the ens itself, and so cannot be said to be the entity of the cause absolutely conceived. For although something can exist without an existing causatum, yet it cannot cause unless the causatum be possible, since to the impossible there is no potency. Whence if (per impossibile) nothing could be caused e.gr. effected, no potentia causativa could be given either — since from potency something is called ***powerful (potens)***, but nothing is called powerful unless it be powerful ***of something***. ***Suarez*** and ***Arriaga*** treated this matter at length. For us it suffices to have said: a true potentia causativa qua such is sometimes a ***non-ens***, sometimes a ***true and real ens***; and this latter — the true and real ens — is again either really the same with the cause to which it is attributed, or really distinct and really superadded.

**III.** These two do not involve contradiction: ***something to have true potentia causativa, and nevertheless not to be able actually to be true cause***.
