For something is not immediately deprived of the potency of causing because it cannot actually be cause; but for something not actually to be cause, nor to be able actually to be cause, it can suffice that the potency of causing not be complete. E.gr. ***Peter*** has sight, and while he has sight, has potency of causing (namely of seeing); often however it comes about that he cannot exert sight on account of ***defect of the pellucid and perspicuous medium***. Thus the ***Sun*** has potency of causing while it has potency of illuminating the chamber, yet cannot actually be cause of light in the chamber unless the valves by which the chamber's windows were covered be removed. One thing therefore is for something ***to be able to be true cause so far as in it lies***; another, ***to be able actually to be true cause***. For the former the sole potentia causativa suffices; for the latter it is required that potentia causativa be complete. Meanwhile, so long as potentia causativa is incomplete, we call its efficacy ***pendent***. Thus e.gr. he who is continuously detained in darkness, to him it is as if he had no potency of seeing (because he cannot exercise it, i.e. he cannot see — not because of defect of the potentia causativa, but because of defect of the requisite on the side of the potentia causativa).

#### § 3 — Formal Definition of Complete Causative Potency

> ***POTENTIA CAUSATIVA COMPLETA is a potentia causativa to which ALL ANTECEDENTLY REQUISITES are simultaneously present. Contrariwise, POTENTIA CAUSATIVA INCOMPLETA is a potentia causativa to which not all antecedently requisites are present. Examples let be sought from the next immediately following §.***

#### Notes

**I.** In two modes it can come about that some potentia causativa is not a potentia causativa to which all antecedently requisites are present: (1) If none at all of the antecedently requisites be present. (2) If one or more antecedently requisites be present, not however all. Whence we shall not oppose anyone if he wills to call every such potentia causativa ***incomplete*** — whether all antecedently requisites are lacking, or antecedently requisites are lacking (not however all). Meanwhile apparent contradiction will arise if someone else wills to call that potentia causativa — to which all and singular antecedently requisites are lacking — ***neither complete*** (since not all antecedently requisites are present) ***nor incomplete*** (since no antecedently requisites are present). For each, if a different mode of speaking be attended to, can be defended: both ***that every potentia causativa is complete or incomplete***, and ***that there is given a potentia causativa which is neither complete nor incomplete***. In whichever mode anyone speaks, it remains most certain that ***potentia causativa in itself can be considered without any respect had to antecedently requisites***, such that one does not attend whether they be present or absent, whether all are present or not all; and if the latter, whether one be lacking or more.

**II.** The present § needs to be more distinctly explicated, because what ***potentia completa*** is, and what ***incompleta***, cannot be sufficiently understood unless we know what are called ***antecedently requisites***.

#### § 4 — Antecedently vs Concomitantly Requisite

> ***Metaphysicians distinguish (in the present doctrine on the necessary requisites of potentia causativa) between ANTECEDENTER REQUISITA and CONCOMITANTER REQUISITA. And indeed antecedently requisite they call those which (as the Scholastics speak) HOLD THEMSELVES ON THE SIDE OF POTENTIA CAUSATIVA. Contrariwise, concomitantly requisite they call those which HOLD THEMSELVES ON THE SIDE OF CAUSALITAS.***
>
> ***E.gr. on the side of SIGHT, if it be considered as potentia causativa, these are antecedently required: OBJECTUM, MEDIUM, and ORGANON. The OBJECT is color and light. The MEDIUM is a perspicuous [thing] — e.gr. air, water, crystal, glass, etc. The ORGANON is the eye. Whence unless all these be present on the side of sight, sight is called an INCOMPLETE potentia causativa; but if all antecedently requisites be present, sight is a COMPLETE potentia causativa.***

#### Notes

**I.** The antecedently requisite must not be confused with the concomitantly requisite. Thus e.gr. he would be inept who would deny that man's will is on that account not free from necessity in acting — namely because, with the action posited, it cannot not act, and without the action posited, it cannot act. For anyone endowed with sounder judgment easily perceives this: that it is ineptly to confuse ***concomitantly requisite*** with ***antecedently requisite***. ***For with concomitantly-requisites posited, no potentia causativa is any longer INDIFFERENT to acting and not-acting — whether that potency be natural or free.*** That it is no longer indifferent, concomitants-posited, is proved thence: concomitantly-requisite are requisite of ***causality itself***; and causality determines potentia causativa so that that to which potentia causativa is attributed ***causes***, or (what is the same) actually comes to be or is cause.

**II.** This the ***Scholastics*** had in view when they teach that some requisites of potentia causativa are ***extrinsic to causality***, others ***intrinsic***: those come under the name of ***antecedently requisite***, since potentia causativa can be without causality; the latter belong to the ***concomitantly requisite***.

#### § 5 — Causative Potency = First Act (Latius vs Angustius)

> ***POTENTIA CAUSATIVA and ACTUS PRIMUS (as here taken) differ as WIDER and NARROWER. For every actus primus is potentia causativa; but not every potentia causativa is actus primus — since potentia causativa is called actus primus only when it is COMPLETE.***

#### Notes

**I.** It is studiously said: ***actus primus as here taken***. For the ***Scholastics***, and not a few among the Recentiores (who follow them), also call certain ***causes*** actus primus. E.gr. the ***soul***, inasmuch as it is cause of a natural animated body, of a plant or animal, they say to be ***actus primus***, and to it they attribute potentia causativa. But this signification does not belong to the present place, nor is otherwise sufficiently commodious or accurate — of which matter will be said in its place.

**II.** ***Vulgarly in the pamphlets of the Metaphysicians actus primus is wont to be defined as: a form or nature inasmuch as it can be the principle of operation.*** But this definition is far narrower than its defined. For: **(1)** If ***operation*** be taken precisely as it says ***action***, even form or nature can be called actus primus inasmuch as it can be principle of ***passion***: for there is given ***agens in actu secundo***, and there is given ***patiens in actu secundo***. **(2)** Because not only is there given efficient cause in actu secundo and material cause in actu secundo, but also formal cause and final cause are given in actu secundo — nay however many causes are given, so many causes in actu secundo are given. Therefore anyone sees the adduced formula labors under narrowness. **(3)** To say in few words what the truth of the thing requires: ***actus primus and actus secundus lie as wide as CAUSE and CAUSATUM lie***. For wherever (namely) cause and causatum can have place, there is also place for the distinction between cause in actu primo and cause in actu secundo, likewise between causatum in actu primo and causatum in actu secundo. We therefore rightly and deservedly call ***every complete potentia causativa actus primus***.

#### § 6 — Actus Secundus Defined

> ***To ACTUS PRIMUS as taken in this place, ACTUS SECUNDUS is contra-distinguished. ACTUS SECUNDUS is that by which something ACTUALLY COMES TO BE OR IS A TRUE CAUSE. Let those things be reduced [hither] which were said at Chapter 8 § 13 pp. 548 and 549.***

#### Note

There are most learned Men who define ***actus secundus*** thus: ***it is that through which the potentia causativa IMMEDIATELY EXERTS ITSELF***. Which formula, if rightly understood, can be tolerated. Thus e.gr. when fire is cause of heat in water, or (as the Schools speak) causes heat in water, the complete potentia causativa in the fire immediately exerts itself through the act of ***heating*** or ***calefactio*** (the heating-act); whence ***calefactio*** is called ***actus secundus***. For the rest, potentia causativa never exerts itself unless it be actus primus — i.e., complete potentia causativa.

#### § 7 — Distinctions Pertaining to This Matter

> ***Some distinctions pertaining to this matter must now be noted. And (1) indeed: ACTUS PRIMUS and THAT WHICH IS CALLED SUCH IN ACTU PRIMO must not be confused. Likewise ACTUS SECUNDUS and THAT WHICH IS SO CALLED IN ACTU SECUNDO are distinguished mutually. For ACTUS PRIMUS is potentia causativa; but THAT WHICH IS CALLED SUCH IN ACTU PRIMO is not potentia causativa, but THAT WHICH HAS potentia causativa. Nay, actus primus can be given, yet nothing be given which is called such in actu primo: ACTUS PRIMUS is RATIO CAUSANDI; THAT WHICH IS SUCH IN ACTU PRIMO is CAUSA POTENTIA or CAUSATUM POTENTIA.***
>
> ***E.gr. in the Sun, the complete potency of illuminating the chamber is ACTUS PRIMUS. The Sun, if indeed at midday itself the chamber's windows be obstructed, is not actus primus — yet is CAUSE OF LIGHT IN ACTU PRIMO. And when the Sun, with the valves removed, illuminates the chamber, there is still given actus primus (namely the complete potency of illuminating); yet there is no longer given cause of light in actu primo, but in actu secundo. The complete potency of illuminating in the Sun itself is ratio causandi; the Sun however, when considered as cause of light in actu primo, is CAUSA POTENTIA.***
>
> ***Nor is it difficult to show the reason of the distinction between ACTUS SECUNDUS and WHAT IS SUCH IN ACTU SECUNDO: for ACTUS SECUNDUS is that by which cause is cause, or that by which causatum is causatum; what is such in actu secundo is the cause itself, or the causatum. E.gr. the illumination of the chamber effected by the Sun is actus secundus; but the Sun illuminating the chamber is not actus secundus — it is cause of light in actu secundo; and the light which is produced in the chamber is causatum in actu secundo.***

#### Notes

**I.** A difficulty arises here: ***Given this explication of actus primus, and of that which is said to be cause or causatum in actu primo, can natural cause be given in actu primo?*** Studiously is it asked of a natural cause; for of a free cause there is no difficulty. For free cause, with all antecedently requisites posited, can exert its potentia causativa and not-exert it: thus e.gr. the architect, with all antecedently requisites posited, can build and not-build; and it comes about that, with all antecedently requisites posited, now he builds (and thus is cause in actu secundo), now does not build (and thus is cause in actu primo). The difficulty therefore is of ***natural or necessary cause***. Either all antecedently requisites are present, or not: if the latter, natural cause is neither in actu secundo nor in actu primo (since for cause in actu secundo and also for cause in actu primo, it is always required that all antecedently requisites be present, as from what has been said stands); if the former, natural cause will always be cause in actu secundo. For by this is natural cause (i.e. necessary) called: that with all antecedently requisites posited, it cannot not actually be cause (i.e. necessarily is cause in actu secundo). E.gr. the ***Sun is natural (necessary) cause of light produced in the chamber***. It seems however as if the Sun could never be called cause of light in actu primo. For either all antecedently requisites are present (and so it necessarily illuminates the chamber, and so is cause of light in actu secundo); or one or another of the antecedently requisites is lacking (and so in the Sun the potency of illuminating the chamber is incomplete, and so because that potency is not actus primus — inasmuch as actus primus is always complete potentia causativa — nor will the Sun, so long as not all antecedently requisites are present, be called cause in actu primo truth-saved).

**II.** To remove this difficulty, a distinction is needed. Namely, this locution has a twofold sense if it is said: ***potentia causativa is complete***. First this can be the sense: ***All antecedently requisites are present which hold themselves on the side of potentia causativa ACTIVELY CONSIDERED*** — i.e. those which are antecedently required for something to be able to cause another. Second it can be understood thus: ***All antecedently requisites are present, both those which hold themselves on the side of potentia causativa active, and those which hold themselves on the side of potentia causativa PASSIVELY CONSIDERED*** — i.e. both those required for something to be able to cause, and those required for something to be able to be caused.

If the ***latter*** mode of understanding the assertion be received, it is false that natural or necessary cause can be given in actu primo. For when in this mode all antecedently requisites are present, natural or necessary cause cannot not be posited in actu secundo. E.gr. when all those are present which are antecedently required for the Sun to be able to illuminate the chamber, and for the chamber to be able to be illuminated by the Sun — then necessarily the Sun is cause of light in actu secundo.

But if the ***former*** mode be the discourse, altogether natural or necessary cause in actu primo can be defended. Thus e.gr. when someone at midday itself obstructs all windows and chinks, lest the chamber be illuminated, we most rightly say the Sun is then cause of illuminating the chamber ***in actu primo*** — because on the side of potentia causativa actively considered all antecedently requisites are present (i.e. nothing is lacking of those which are antecedently required on the side of the Sun for the Sun to be able to illuminate the chamber), although on the side of the chamber not all antecedently requisites are present (since for the chamber to be able to be illuminated, it is necessary that the valves be moved from the window-glass).

**III.** Antecedently requisites on the side of potentia causativa can be taken ***in three ways***: (1) on the side of potentia causativa actively and passively considered simultaneously (cf. not. I to § 3, cap. 8, § 15 p. 536); (2) on the side of potentia causativa actively considered only; (3) on the side of potentia causativa passively considered only. In the second mode are antecedently requisites taken when there is distinguished between ***what is thus true cause in actu primo*** and ***what is really cause in actu secundo***.

#### § 8 — Habens Actum Primum vs Id Quod Tale Est In Actu Primo

> ***(2) These differ: HAVING ACTUS PRIMUM and that which IS SUCH IN ACTU PRIMO. For the consequence holds from the latter to the former, but not from the former to the latter immediately. For whether something be CAUSE or CAUSATUM in actu primo, whether it be CAUSE or CAUSATUM in actu secundo, it is always said [to have reference] TO ACTUS PRIMUS. E.gr. the potency of illuminating the chamber in the Sun can be complete, and thus the Sun HAS ACTUS PRIMUM — although the Sun be only CAUSE of light IN ACTU PRIMO. There is also given in the Sun complete potency of illuminating the chamber WHEN the Sun actually illuminates the chamber, i.e. when it is CAUSE of light IN ACTU SECUNDO.***

#### Note

That to which potentia causativa is attributed is most rightly distinguished into cause ***in actu primo*** and cause ***in actu secundo***.

#### § 9 — Cause in Actu Primo vs Actu Secundo

> ***(3) CAUSE IN ACTU PRIMO and CAUSE IN ACTU SECUNDO differ as ***that which is not true cause*** and ***that which is true cause***. Let the same be the judgment of the discrimen between CAUSATUM in actu primo and CAUSATUM in actu secundo.***

#### Notes

**I.** What above in c. 1 not. 2 p. 52 we said of the discrimen between ***ens possibile*** and ***ens potentia***, let that be said here of the discrimen between ***causa potentia*** and ***causa in actu primo***. Namely, just as every ***ens potentia*** is ***ens possibile***, but not every ens possibile is ens potentia — so every ***causa in actu primo*** is ***causa potentia***, but not every causa potentia is causa in actu primo. And just as ***ens possibile*** can simultaneously be ***verum ens***, so ***causa potentia*** can simultaneously be ***causa in actu primo***. For these propositions are true ***in sensu diviso***: ***"Ens possibile is ens"***; ***"causa potentia is causa in actu primo"***. Contrariwise, although of ***ens possibile*** it can be said in sensu diviso that it is a true ens, yet of ***causa potentia*** it cannot be asserted that it is true cause. For as one thing is ***ens possibile***, another ***ens potentia***, so one thing is ***causa possibilis***, another ***causa potentia***. And just as ens possibile can be true ens, and in its mode (as ***animal*** has itself to ***homo*** and ***brutum***) so it has itself to ens actu and ens potentia — so causa possibilis can be true cause, and in its mode (as animal has itself to homo and brutum) so it has itself to causa potentia and causa actu. For the rest, ***causa potentia*** is again distinguished into ***causa potentia incompleta*** and ***causa potentia completa*** (which is also called ***causa in actu primo***). ***Causa actu*** is also called ***causa in actu secundo***.

**II.** Of ***causatum possibile***, ***causatum potentia***, [and causatum] such ***in actu primo*** and ***in actu secundo***, in the immediately following chapter 10 it will be treated.

**III.** Antecedently-requisites are some ***absolutely necessary***, others ***by hypothesis***. E.gr. for the complete causative potency of burning stubble to be in fire, it is not absolutely and simpliciter necessary that fire be applied to the stubble, since fire can be cause of the combustion of stubble ***in actu primo*** although it be not applied; and is cause ***in actu secundo***, provided that the stubble be applied to the fire. ***By hypothesis*** however: for fire to be cause of the combustion of stubble ***in actu secundo***, it is necessary that fire be applied to the stubble — if, namely, we posit that it will never happen that stubble is applied to the fire. In the meantime, it is absolutely necessary for the complete potentia causativa to be given that one of the two be applied to the other.

#### Note IV — The Natural Knowledge of God: Notitia Dei Connata/Innata

**Amplest use does this doctrine find in all disciplines and Faculties**: for it extends itself as far as the use of the doctrine on causes and causata extends. Let it be allowed to illustrate the truth of this assertion by one or two examples, and let us first take a ***Philosophico-Theological*** example.

It is asked by Philosophers and Theologians of this and that part: ***Is there given in us some knowledge of God naturally implanted?*** The affirmative all orthodox Theologians defend, nor would any of the more accurate Philosophers easily deny it or call it in doubt. Nor is there doubt that, if the question be formed thus — ***Does some knowledge of God naturally arise in or arise with man?*** — the affirmative is of all orthodox Theologians. For all orthodox Theologians by unanimous consent affirmatively subscribe and constantly assert it, and prove it from various places of Sacred Scripture:

- Chiefly from ***Rom. 1:18 ff.***, where the Gentiles are said to ***detain in injustice*** the ***ἀλήθειαν (truth) and what is manifest of God in them***.
- Item from ***Rom. 2:14, 15***, where the Gentiles are said to ***do by nature what is of the Law*** and to show the ***work of the Law written in their hearts***.
- Third, from the ***testimony of conscience***, with ***thoughts mutually accusing themselves***, as treated in **Rom. 2:15**.
- Fourth, from the ***consensus of the ancient Fathers***: ***Tertullian de testimonio animae*** and ***Apol. adv. Gentes c. 17***; ***Arnobius lib. I adv. Gentes***; ***Jerome in Jer. c. XXVI.23 and in Ep. ad Gal. c. 1:15***; ***John of Damascus lib. I de Fide Orth. c. 1***. In which — from the midst of Gentilism — ***Epicurus apud Ciceronem lib. 1 De Natura Deorum*** and ***Cicero*** had anticipated, teaching the same: namely that ***nature itself has impressed on the minds of all the notion of the gods***.

Theologians call this ***knowledge of God implanted or innate***: some call it ***light and habitual perfection connatural to the knowing power or naturally implanted***; others ***a HABITUS or disposition*** — not indeed a habit properly so-called, but ***κατ' ἀναλογίαν, an imperfect habit, something analogous to habit — a certain τελειότης (perfection) of the intellectual potency remaining in man after the lapse, by whose benefit man can know God in some measure***. And in this they dissent from other Philosophers who, holding the intellective potency to be the proximate and complete principle, held it unnecessary to establish and defend that ***τελειότης*** and perfection or light connatural to the intellect.

In the meantime there is controversy on this: ***Whether, without all heterodoxy and its danger, it can be defended that there are given NO knowledges of God in actu primo which are connatural or naturally implanted to the human intellect — nor any knowledges of God in actu secundo which are connatural or naturally implanted?*** Although it is neither our office nor institute to adjudicate this Theological controversy — and nothing is less proposed by us now than to call this Theological matter under our disquisition's anvil — yet this stands most certain: every student of First Philosophy and of Theology, nay even a blind man, sees that those who wish to engage in such matters happily and rightly will either lose their effort or ill-place it, unless from the ***First Philosophy*** (to which it belongs ex professo) they have learned ***what ACTUS PRIMUS is, what ACTUS SECUNDUS, what is called such IN ACTU PRIMO, what called such IN ACTU SECUNDO***.

For the Physicus also, when he treats ex instituto and accurately — ***what is necessarily required for knowledge? what is knowledge IN ACTU PRIMO? what knowledge IN ACTU SECUNDO? is there given connatural knowledge in actu primo or in actu secundo?*** — must seek the distinction between that first [act] and second from Metaphysics, and apply it with suitable reason to his own dogmas.

Whence we do not marvel if someone not sufficiently expert in Metaphysical terms, from what he hears this or that Theologian defend — that there are no connatural or naturally-implanted knowledges of God in actu primo or secundo in the human intellect — immediately collects that there is defended a ***bare potency without any perfection or light connatural to the intellect and remaining in post-lapse man***, without ***any habit, properly or less-properly taken, by whose benefit man can know God in some measure***, with ***no discrimen admitted between the connatural knowledge of principles and the easily-acquired knowledge of conclusions***. Yet no one accustomed to solid Philosophical doctrine will collect this from that alone, unless he will manifestly err and establish [things] against the solid foundations and principles of First Philosophy.

For those who ***deny that there is given knowledge in actu secundo*** which is connatural to the human intellect give the reason of their negation thus: ***knowledge in actu secundo always argues an act of knowing elicited by the intellect — and so from man himself as efficient cause posited in actu secundo, and from his intellect as actus primus or complete causative potency in the genus of active potency, proceeding***. Which act, by this very fact (that it is really effected by man and his intellect) is not naturally implanted or connatural to the nature of man and his intellect.

Nor indeed do those who ***deny that there is given knowledge in actu primo*** which is naturally implanted or connatural to the intellect of man after the lapse — in denying this — immediately deny that there is given ***light ingenerate or naturally implanted to the intellect, or a naturally implanted or innate perfection of the intellective potency, analogous to habit, an imperfect habit, by whose benefit man can know God in some measure***. For they deny in this sense knowledges in actu primo naturally implanted or connatural, because — by the consent of the more accurate Metaphysicians and Physicists — ***actus primus says a causative potency, and that complete***, which certainly is never given unless all antecedently requisites be present. Among all the antecedently requisites for the intellect to be posited in actu secundo is also, by consent of all Philosophers, the ***species impressa*** (which vulgarly is wont to be called ***species intelligibilis***).

If therefore it can be shown that ***species impressa*** is among the antecedently requisites — and if it can simultaneously be solidly and sufficiently evinced that the species impressa (which is pre-required for eliciting the act of cognition) is naturally implanted or connatural — then: not yet, from the fact that someone denies the knowledge of God in actu primo connatural or naturally implanted to the intellect, can it be collected that he has understood by ***innate knowledge of God*** the ***bare potency of knowing*** and nothing beyond.

#### Note V — Further Theological Examples

By many other ***Theological*** examples the use of this distinction could be commended.

Thus when it is debated: ***Is Sacred Scripture perpetually efficacious, or not?*** Who does not see that distinction between actus primus and actus secundus — namely between the efficacy of Sacred Scripture ***in actu primo*** and ***in actu secundo*** — is needed? For if it be said that ***Scripture converts no one unless it be read or heard***, the orthodox Theologians respond that for efficacy ***in actu secundo*** it is required that legitimate use accede (i.e. reading and scrutiny), without which indeed no one is converted — not however for efficacy ***in actu primo***, which however cannot be separated from Sacred Scripture.

Again when it is asked: ***In what sense is the saying of the Savior at Mark XIII:32 to be understood — "De die illo [of the extreme judgment] NEC IPSE FILIUS NOVIT"?*** — especially when some believe that version better-sounding and more congruent to the text: ***"The Son of Man is ignorant of the day of extreme judgment"***? The Reformed from this saying try to prove that ***omniscience was not communicated to the human nature of Christ***. Yet certain Theologians hold that, employing the distinction between actus primus and actus secundus, every difficulty can easily be removed: namely, if it be said that ***actus primus — namely omniscience — altogether belonged to the human nature of Christ***, and that by this saying is indicated only ***the suspension of actus secundus during the time in which the Son of Man was in the state of exinanition***. Surely it is not our office now to treat of the genuine sense of this saying; but this anyone easily notices: that one laboring under ignorance of these Metaphysical notions which we now expound cannot bring judgment happily enough on the recounted interpretation of the adduced saying.

Again when in Theology it is disputed: ***Was the WISDOM created-together-with the first man in the state of innocence also actus secundus, or only actus primus?*** Anyone sees here is need of accurate notice of the distinction between actus primus and actus secundus.

Thus when some orthodox Theologians, against ***Bellarmine*** who agitates our Theologians (because they have numbered the inordinate motions of concupiscence (anteverting all use of reason) among original sin), teach that ***peccatum originis is taken doubly***, either in actu primo or in actu secundo. In actu primo it is nothing other than ***the mere privation [disposition] of concupiscence***; in actu secundo however it is ***those inordinate motions*** which, as fruits from original sin as from a tree, next sprout up — even with the will repugnant. How well these things stand, and whether concupiscence itself is original sin not only in actu primo but also in actu secundo, no one will rightly and decently judge, unless the Metaphysical distinction between actus primus and actus secundus (with all more accurate Theologians consenting) be rightly understood beforehand.

Thus by consent of all more accurate Theologians, ***justifying faith*** is now taken for actus primus, now for actus secundus. Far more examples could be adduced; but let it suffice, for the present scope, to have indicated these in passing and barely to have touched them.

#### Note VI — Juridical-Political-Moral Examples: The Grotius Citation

Let us also touch ***Juridical-Political-Moral*** examples. Jurists of great name — when (as the common view bids us believe about primeval community: namely that all things, with property wholly excluded, lay open to promiscuous use, and dominions themselves came to be at length by division and occupation — these [Jurists] denying this) — have objected to them ***L. possessio 1 et dominiumque 1 D. de acquirenda vel amittenda possessione***, where it is expressly asserted that ***the dominion of things originated from natural possession***, from which it would follow that possession could not have begun from dominion. They respond that the law is to be understood of ***actus secundus***, and so does not at all contradict the view of dominion ***taken for actus primus***.

Namely, for those Jurists who depart from the view of the ancient Jurists, ***dominion is nothing other than actus primus, i.e. the full power of occupying and possessing***, through which one comes into possession, and from possession into dominion (which is in actu secundo). And who does not see them using the Metaphysical distinction between actus primus and actus secundus, while they explicate the alleged law thus: ***"If Caius institutes Accius as heir, the dominion of the inheritance is directly and immediately transferred to Accius, without apprehension, immediately upon the testator's death — of actus primus; as soon as possession accedes, dominion in actu secundo begins. Therefore natural possession signifies nothing other than dominion in actu secundo, opposed to dominion in actu primo."*** Thus those celebrated Men — of whose view no one can felicitously discern anything unless he has rendered the Metaphysical notions and distinctions hitherto handed down more than sufficiently perspicuous to himself.

Innumerable ***Juridico-Politico-Moral*** examples ***Hugo Grotius*** most nervously comprehends in very few words at ***book 1 de Jure Belli et Pacis cap. III m. 24*** when he says thus:

> ***"It must be distinguished no less in empire than in dominion between RIGHT and the USE OF RIGHT, i.e. between ACTUS PRIMUS and ACTUS SECUNDUS. For just as an infant king has the right, but cannot exercise empire — so too a madman, a captive, and one who is in another's territory such that free actions regarding an empire situated elsewhere are not permitted him: in all these cases curators are to be given over them. Therefore DEMETRIUS, when he could not live sufficiently free in the power of Seleucus, forbade that his seal or letters be trusted, but willed that all be administered as if he were dead."***

Thus Grotius. Certainly if the discussion be of ***actus primus***, no doubt is given that such a King has Majesty. For if he did not have it, either in such a Republic there would still be true Majesty, or there would not be. The latter cannot be said, since it implies contradiction that a true Republic be given without Majesty. Nor will the former find place. For where would that Majesty be? Either it would be ***in the people***, or ***in the curator***. Not in the people, since to them is still left uniquely the ***glory of obedience***. Not in the curator, inasmuch as he rules everything not in his own name, but in the ***name of a curator***. Nay, though it be most true that e.gr. an infant king, a mad one, a furious one, etc. cannot exercise Majesty — and so Majesty, as it says ***actus secundus***, is most truly denied them by Grotius — yet to no one do we doubt attributing ***actual Majesty, or that opposed to governance in actu secundo***, as governance ***in actu primo***. For we also do what we do through others. Whence what is done through tutors and curators (who meanwhile sustain the person of the King) is to be estimated as if the tutor or curator acting had done nothing — but the King had acted through the tutor or curator what the latter was fitting to do.

## Caput Decimum

### Of the Possible, and Its Necessary and More Frequently-Used Acceptances and Divisions

#### § 1

> ***We treated in the preceding chapter of potency; whence, since nothing is nor truth-saved is called POSSIBLE except it say respect to potency, it will be not inconveniently treated in the present chapter of the POSSIBLE. Most of all does the name POSSIBLE merit [application to] that which says respect to CAUSATIVE POTENCY — this is, the POSSIBLE CAUSATUM.***

#### Notes

**I.** Here returns that question: ***Was there from eternity a possible causatum, or (what returns to the same) could any creature be caused from eternity?*** (The voice ***causari*** taken passively.) Certain [authors] there are, not only from the Scholastics but also (and especially) from the ***Fathers of the Church***, who deny it. Their most powerful arguments we shall in good faith recount:

**I.** If a creature (e.gr. an angel) had from eternity possible being in God — or, what is the same, could have been produced by God from eternity — it follows that it could have been created from eternity. But the consequent is absurd. Therefore the antecedent. The ***consequence*** is proved because there are only two modes of production: ***creation*** and ***generation***. But it implies contradiction that the angel, since he is Spirit, could be generated (since generation is production ***out of matter***, and the angel according to his essence is wholly destitute of matter). It is therefore necessary that the angel, when produced, be ***created***. The ***absurdity of the consequent*** stands clear: creation is ***production out of nothing***. If therefore the angel had been produced from eternity out of nothing — either he had been in duration prior under ***nothing*** than under his own ***being***; or he had not been in duration prior under nothing than under his being; or his nothing-ness and his being were simultaneous. If he had been prior-in-duration under nothing than under his being, then he was not produced from eternity, since eternity excludes all priority and posteriority of duration. If the angel had not been prior-in-duration under nothing than under his being, either (a) the nothing-of-the-angel and the being-of-the-angel were simultaneous (so that it would follow the angel in the same duration both was and was not — most absurd and the first of all impossibilities), or (b) the nothing-of-the-angel plainly was not, and so the angel could not be called produced ***out of nothing***.

**II.** If the creature from eternity was in ***objective potency*** with respect to God, it would follow that, if it had been produced from eternity, it must have been produced either ***successively*** or ***in a certain instant***. Not successively: for thus it would have had something ***prior to itself in duration*** (namely motion, which would have antecedent the creature as a term in duration), and consequently the creature would not have been produced from eternity. Not in an instant: for thus in a certain instant it would have been made so that before it was not, and so it would not have been from eternity.

**III.** If every creature which now actually exists was from eternity in objective potency with respect to God, surely if it had been produced from eternity, it would have been produced either ***when it was*** or ***when it was not***. If produced when it was, then every creature would be a ***successive ens***, and nothing in the world would be ***fixed and permanent***, since everything which existed would always be ***in fieri and in fluere***; nay nothing could have been conserved by God, but would always have been only ***created***. If it had not been always produced when it was, it would follow that it was indeed sometimes produced, and so was not produced from eternity, but in time.

**IV.** If the creature from eternity was in objective potency with respect to God, surely if it had been produced from eternity, either it would have been by nature ***posterior*** to God, or not. If not, then it would not be a ***creature of God***, since every causatum is naturally posterior to its cause. If so, then also [would have been] posterior in duration — since nature of God and duration of God, as to the matter, are one and the same in God: if therefore God had been prior by nature, He would also have been prior in duration.

**V.** If the creature were from eternity in objective potency with respect to GOD, surely if it had been produced from eternity, it would be ***God Himself***. Now a produced creature cannot be God. Therefore the creature could not have been produced from eternity. The consequence is proved: (1) because if it had been produced from eternity, it would have been ***eternal***, and so would have had the attribute of God — namely eternity. Now whatever has the attribute of God is God Himself. Nay rather, the Doctors of the true Church against ***Antitrinitarians*** use this maxim before others: ***"Whoever is eternal is true God"*** — to assert and defend the divinity of Christ. (2) Because if the creature had been eternal, it would have been immutable; now the immutability of a creature repugns.

**VI.** If the creature had been from eternity in objective potency with respect to God — or, if from eternity it had had possible being — surely from eternity it would have really existed. But the consequent is absurd. Therefore. The consequence is proved: (1) because ***potency and act divide true and real ens***; (2) because they would have had true being in the creative potency of God.

#### Note II — Responses to the 6 Arguments

Nor however are those few who ***maintain the affirmative***, relying on the reason which in the preceding chapter we noted. And according to their view, if responses have place, perhaps it would thus be answered to the arguments just adduced:

**Ad I.** Deny the ***absurdity of the consequent***. It is not absurd that the angel could have been produced from eternity out of nothing. To the proof it must be said: ***the nothing-of-the-angel plainly never was***. Yet it does not follow that the angel cannot be called produced ***out of nothing***. For it must be observed that the particle ***ex*** is otherwise taken in two modes:

**(1)** As it notes ***temporal succession*** or consecution of one to another: thus we say ***"ex mane fieri meridiem, ex nocte fieri diem"*** (from morning comes noon, from night comes day), because noon follows morning, and day succeeds night.

**(2)** As it notes ***matter***: for among all the genera of causes, it is proper only to matter that ***something comes to be ex it***: for matter is that out of which, with it placed within, something comes to be.

In neither mode is the particle ***ex*** here received, but ***to come to be ex nihilo*** here is the same as ***not to come to be ex aliquo as from a pre-existing matter***. For that ***creation***, properly and according to the common mode of speaking, notes the same as ***production ex nihilo*** — i.e. ex no pre-existing matter — teach:

- ***Augustine*** in his book ***de Genesi ad litteram c. 1 et 2*** and ***de Civitate Dei c. 25***;
- ***Justin Martyr*** in his ***admonitorio ad gentes***, where ***from Plato he distinguishes between opifex and creator***: ***opifex*** is he who produces something out of matter; ***creator***, however, is he who establishes something out of nothing;
- ***Anselm in Monologion cap. 6, 7, and 8***;
- ***Thomas 1 pars q. 45 art. 1***;
- The ***Master of the Sentences, Petrus Lombardus, Bishop of Paris, 2 dist. 1 book dist. 1, Cologne 1575 ed. p. 155***, where he expressly says: ***"CREATOR is he who makes something de nihilo: and CREARE properly is to make something de nihilo; FACERE however is not only to work something de nihilo, but also de materia: whence both man and Angel are said FACERE certain things, but not CREARE. And one is called factor or artifex, but not creator. For this name properly belongs to God alone, who both from nothing makes certain things and from something makes certain things: He therefore is CREATOR and OPIFEX and FACTOR; but the name CREATION He has properly reserved to Himself. In Scripture however OFTEN CREATE is received as FACERE, without distinction of signification."***

The same teach ***Scotus, Durandus, Herveus*** — in one word, ***all the Scholastics in this distinction***.

The consequence was: ***"If the Angel produced from eternity was never nothing, it follows that he is not produced ex nihilo — i.e. that he is produced from pre-existing matter."*** Who does not see the falsity of this consequence?

**Ad II.** [If the creature had been from eternity produced,] it would have been produced in an instant. When in the proof it was said: ***"If in a certain instant, then before it would not have been, and so would not have been from eternity"*** — to this ***Herveus in 2 dist. 1 q. 2 usque ad 7*** responds: ***instans is twofold: one is STANDING, which is without newness of being; the other FLOWING, which is with newness of being***. The consequence holds of the ***flowing instant***; but the creature which from eternity had been produced would have been produced in that ***standing instant***, of which the consequence does not proceed.

**Ad III.** We respond: ***"If the creature had been produced from eternity, it would have been produced when it was — i.e. in that duration in which it was."*** To both proofs it is wont to be responded.

**To the former** respond ***Capreolus and Durandus***, denying that the creature which is wholly produced in that duration when it is, is a ***SUCCESSIVE ENS*** — because a successive ens is not ***totum simul***, but has newness in the parts of its being which flow and which succeed each other mutually. We give an instance: ***If from eternity Peter had looked into a mirror, the whole image of Peter from eternity would have been projected onto the mirror; yet the image of Peter in the mirror would not have been a flowing and successive thing.***

**To the latter proof** ***Thomas Aquinas 1 pars q. 104 art. 1 and de potentia q. 5 art. 1***; ***Henry of Ghent quodlib. 1 q. 7 and 9 q.***; ***Aegidius Romanus in Tract. de esse et essentia q. 7***; ***Ferrariensis 3 contra gentes c. 65***; ***Vazquez part. 1 Summ. disp. 172 n. 11***; ***Becanus l. 1 Theol. Scholast. tract. 1 c. 18 n. 10***; ***Suarez disp. Met. 11 sect. 2*** respond at length, showing that ***CREATION QUOAD REM IS CONSERVATION ITSELF***. And most rightly: for ***conservation is nothing other than continued creation***. God could therefore have continued the creation of some creature made from all eternity into all eternity.

**Ad IV.** [If the creature had been produced from eternity, it would have been by nature posterior to God.] When in the proof it was collected thus: ***"If the creature from eternity made had been by nature posterior to God, it would also have been by duration posterior to God"*** — that collection is called ***vain***. Further, the proof whereby it is said ***the duration of God and the nature of God are one and the same in God*** — this evinces nothing other than that in the duration in which God is called ***eternal***, the creature cannot be called eternal. To make the matter clearer, we note (following the hand-leading of ***Thomas Aquinas*** in his ***opuscula*** — namely ***opusc. 27 de aeternitate mundi*** — and of ***Durandus of St. Pourçain 2 dist. 1 q. 2***) that the duration of a creature which from eternity would have been (if we posit it had been) can be considered in two ways:

**(1)** As to the ***common being*** (quoad esse commune), inasmuch as it involves something in which God converges with creatures: thus it is easily conceded that the creature's duration, if it had been from eternity, would have been the nature or essence of God itself — for thus the creature's duration is considered as an abstract something from both durations, God's and the creature's.

**(2)** As to ***proper being*** (quoad esse proprium), or as it is conceived in the creature to be restricted to the creature itself (or as it is such or such): thus it is absurd to say the duration of the creature, if the creature were from eternity, were the nature or essence of God itself. For just as this [duration of the creature] is not formally in God, so neither can it be the nature of God: for the creature's duration considered according to specific and proper being says such a duration by which the creature so endures that it is also ***able not to endure***; the duration of God, however (as it is God's duration), says such a duration by which God so endures that He is ***not able not to endure***. So these two stand: the creature can be simultaneously in duration with God; and the creature's duration, as such, cannot be God's duration as such.

The sense of each the ***Doctor Angelicus*** sets forth in the cited opusculum in the following words: ***"If it be understood that something besides God could always have been, as if there could be something eternal besides Him not made by Him, the error is abominable — not only in faith but also among the Philosophers, who confess and prove that everything which is in whatever mode cannot be unless caused by Him who most greatly and most truly has being. If however it be understood that something always was, and yet caused by God, this can stand"*** etc.

**Ad V.** Respond by denying the consequence, which was: ***"If the creature had been produced from eternity, it would have been God Himself."*** The first proof certainly does not proceed: ***"If the creature had had eternity, it would have had the attribute of God."*** For between ***aeternitas Dei*** and ***aeternitas creaturae*** a distinction is given — both formal and real:

- ***Eternity of God*** formally is that eternity to which ***it absolutely repugns not to be, not to have been, not to be in future***;
- ***Eternity of a creature*** is that eternity to which, absolutely speaking, ***it does not repugn not to be, not to have been, not to be in future***.

The eternity of a creature perpetually supposes something prior to the creature by priority of nature; but the eternity of God most simply excludes all priority of nature from which it would causatively depend. What therefore would follow if you collected thus: ***"If the creature had been eternal by the eternity of God, i.e. intrinsically and through essence, the creature produced from eternity would have been God"*** — the ***former*** is openly false. In vain is it also invoked [the testimony] of the Church. True and inconcussible stands this proposition of the Theologians: ***"Whoever really and actually is from eternity is true God"***; the Sacred Codex proves the same, when it asserts that any creature was really made ***in time*** and had actual beginning of its duration.

You say: ***"If whatever is actually eternal is true God, it follows that the creature — because it could be actually from eternity — could have been true God. The consequent is absurd. Therefore so is the antecedent."*** We respond with limitation: ***"If whatever is actually eternal INTRINSICALLY AND THROUGH ESSENCE is true God, it follows that the creature — because it could be actually from eternity — could have been true God"*** — the consequence is denied. For an ***aeternitas*** which denominates a creature intrinsically and through essence absolutely repugns to created nature.

The other proof is held for null, unless it had been stated under this limitation: ***"If the creature had been eternal INTRINSICALLY AND THROUGH ESSENCE, it would have been immutable; now a creature cannot be immutable; therefore it could not have been eternal intrinsically and through essence"*** — the whole argument is conceded: for it is not against us.

**Ad VI.** Respond by denying the connection and its double proof.

**Ad (1)**: respond that it is false that ***potency and act formally divide ens***. Either the discourse is of act and potency ***in recto*** (so that the sense be: ens is divided into act and potency) — but thus the division is ***maimed***, for ***a natural body is Ens***, yet is neither potency nor act, but ***something constituted from potency and act***. Or the discourse is of act and potency ***in obliquo*** (so that the sense be: ens is divided into ens-potentia and ens-actu) — but this division likewise is not good, since ***ens***, being that which exists, cannot be predicated of ***ens potentia***.

**Ad (2)**: respond that the sequela is null: for ***to have true being in the creative potency of God*** is nothing other than ***to be able to be created by God before it is created***. It is as if someone wished to argue: ***"Whatever can be created, but is not yet, really is."*** For whatever creature is, is at length through creation. Or we shall argue thus: ***Whatever is in the creative potency of God, is a true Ens. The angel who does not yet exist, but will be created three days from now by God, according to existence is in the creative potency of God. Therefore the angel who does not yet exist, but will be created three days from now by God, according to existence is a true Ens.*** The Minor is manifest; the Conclusion is false; therefore the Major will be false — but the Major was the adduced proof.

#### Note III — Paulus Voet contra ab-aeterno + Campanella

It would have been easy for us to adduce more arguments from the writings of various Scholastics, Reformed, and others. Thus among the Reformed Recentiores: ***Paulus Voet, son of Gisbert, Professor of Law in the Academy of Utrecht***, assigns to most of the Reformed (who are Theologians of some note) ***the negative*** [view], and judges, according to the ***more common view of the Reformed***, that it is ***altogether inconceivable that a creature be called co-eternal with God***. Hence in his ***Theologia Naturali Reformata c. 30 through the whole § 3 n. 7 p. 205 ff., edited in the year 1656***, he adduces ***thirteen arguments*** by which, if they stand, our defended view would go to ruin. Likewise ***Thomas Campanella*** adduces various reasons against the ***eternal possible-being of creatures*** in ***tome 4 of his works, i.e. of his Metaphysical Dogmas part 3 lib. 11 cap. 5 artic. 3 p. 25 et seq.***

But either from what we have thus far said the solution easily depends, or is hoped for in vain. [The solution] we would deliver most willingly, if space and time did not now persuade otherwise. Let it suffice to have said these things concerning the creature regarding the ***former mode of being*** in God from eternity.

#### Note IV — Slevogt on Deum-posse vs Deum-fecisse

Meanwhile, if what the matter is must be said: although by greater arguments and with all doubtation removed it cannot be affirmed that some creature could have been from eternity, yet neither must it be pertinaciously denied. For ***although in the substance which is intrinsically and through essence eternal, ESSE and POSSE ESSE do not differ, yet manifestly in that substance FACERE and POSSE FACERE differ. For it is not in God thus with His own ESSE as with His own FACERE: whence He can do all things that are possible, or that can come to be — but He does not do all those things.*** As is clear from the saying of Christ at ***Matt. 26:54***: ***"Do you suppose I cannot ask the Father, and He will provide me more than twelve legions of angels?"*** — where however neither did Christ ask, nor did the Father provide the angels. Thus ***Matt. 3:9 / Luke 3:8*** — ***"God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham"*** — which however we never read He did. Whereby it is made manifest: it is not necessary, nor does it pertain to the reason of God's potency, that if a possible creature was from eternity and God Himself could have produced it from eternity, He also would have produced it. Thus discourses ***B. Slevogt Vol. disputt. Academ. part. 1 disp. 9 § 18***.

#### § 2 — Causatum Possibile vs Causatum Potentia

> ***CAUSATUM POSSIBILE and CAUSATUM POTENTIA differ, because the consequence holds from the latter to the former, but not from the former to the latter — this is: EVERY CAUSATUM POTENTIA IS CAUSATUM POSSIBILE, BUT NOT EVERY CAUSATUM POSSIBILE IS CAUSATUM POTENTIA.***

#### Note

As ***ens possibile*** and ***ens potentia*** have themselves to ens, so ***causatum possibile*** and ***causatum potentia*** have themselves to causatum. Namely, what is a true causatum, if precisely considered as ***it can be causatum***, is called ***causatum possibile***; what can be causatum but ***is not yet***, is called ***causatum potentia***. Whence just as ens potentia is not true ens, so causatum potentia is not true causatum.

#### § 3 — Impossibile

> ***The opposite of ***possibile*** (if, namely, possibile is taken as noting the same as causatum possibile) is ***IMPOSSIBILE***. ***Impossibile*** is called a NON-ENS WHICH CANNOT BE CAUSATUM POSSIBILE.***

#### Note

Two things are required for ***impossibile***: (1) that it be ***non-ens***; (2) that it ***cannot be causatum possibile***. One of these without the other does not suffice, because this place treats of the ***impossibile*** as precisely considered in opposition to causatum possibile.

#### § 4 — Repugnance: On What Side?

> ***One who wishes to know both — the ***possibile*** and the ***impossibile*** (as taken in the preceding §§) — more rightly and distinctly must studiously discern ***ON WHAT SIDE*** that which is called impossibile says repugnance. For nothing is called impossibile unless it say repugnance.***

#### § 5 — Threefold Repugnance

> ***There is given a THREEFOLD such repugnance:***
>
> ***(1) EX PARTE CAUSATI: e.gr. a stone cannot be the son of a man — i.e. a stone cannot be called causatum possibile with respect to man as father, since generation ***passive*** (by which something has it, that it be called SON) repugns to a stone; since such generation always says the ORIGIN OF A LIVING THING FROM A LIVING THING IN A SUBSTANCE LIKE ITSELF.***
>
> ***(2) EX PARTE CAUSAE: e.gr. a stone cannot be father of a man — i.e. a stone cannot be called causa possibilis with respect to man as son (and so as causati possibilis), since generation ***active*** (by which something has it, that it come to be or be FATHER) repugns to a stone.***
>
> ***(3) EX PARTE UTRIUSQUE: e.gr. a stone cannot be the father of a stone, nor can a stone be the son of a stone.***

#### Note I — The Diligent Inquiry Required

The inquiry of such repugnances or non-repugnances often requires great ***diligence***, as from the doctrines of causes-in-species it will more rightly stand. For not only in the genus of ***efficient cause***, but also in the genera of all other causes, the use of this distinction exerts itself. Thus e.gr. in the genus of ***objective cause***:

- repugnance is given ***ex parte causae*** if we say that ***by a man endowed with the complete potency of seeing, taste or sound cannot be seen*** — because taste or sound is altogether not in the number of visibles;
- Contrariwise, if we assert that ***by a blind man colored and luminous cannot be seen***, this is not to be received as if colored and luminous are not visible, but because in the blind man there is no potency which can be extrinsically terminated to that which is otherwise the object of sight (i.e. the colored and the luminous);
- Finally, if I say ***it is not possible for taste to be seen by a blind man***, here repugnance is given ***ex parte utriusque***.

#### Note II — The MASSIVE IUS-NATURAE-IMMUTABILE Doctrine

**Chiefly in Moral Philosophy and Theology (both Natural and Revealed) does this doctrine have plainly a notable use.** Let us take one example of this matter: when there is treatment of ***Jus naturae*** accurately and rightly so-called, and it is established as ***so immutable by Philosophers, not only but also by Theologians and Jurisconsults, that not even by God can it be changed*** — we find ***too shallow appraisers*** of this assertion, who ***do not blush to put dust in the eyes of the inexperienced and to persuade*** as if this very [thesis] derogates divine glory and Majesty, since:

**[Objection 1 — Divine Eternity/Immutability]**: God alone is eternal, therefore God alone is immutable; so to assert the immutability of natural Law is to detract from divine omnipotence and to circumscribe it with certain limits, as if the hand of the Lord were abbreviated or shortened. For every human legislator (since he is the author of law) can change his own law if he wills; why not God, who is the author of natural Law, if He willed, change natural Law?

**[Objection 2 — Divine Omnipotence]**: Likewise this derogates divine omnipotence — the hand of the Lord cannot be shortened.

**[Objection 3 — Divine Liberty]**: They say this also derogates God's ***absolute and unqualified liberty***: since God, as He [made] all things, so also He condited man ***from His freest beneplacitum of will***. From this it is consequent that it is in His beneplacitum what nature He wills to assign to man; and so by no reason can right fall into man which — from intrinsic and absolute necessity, outside God's beneplacitum — would oblige him. For no actions are naturally honest or shameful to any man, except what the condition of nature (which man was allotted not from any immutable necessity but from divine beneplacitum) most required to be done or omitted. So the morality of actions, as those convenient or disconvenient to him qua rational and social, must be derived from the same source [i.e. divine beneplacitum]. So the saying ***"jus naturae is immutable"*** must be limited, lest that eternity be extended beyond divine imposition and the freest beneplacitum of divine will, or beyond the origin of the human race (which no one cannot ascribe to the freest will of God).

On this matter we shall not now dispute whether these men first persuaded themselves and then others of such things, or whether — against the proper testimony of conscience — they strive by trifles of this kind to blind the eyes of the incautious and inexperienced lighter-folk, that they may have occasion of cavilling against received doctrines and insulting most celebrated Men. Let it suffice at present to have supplied an argument by which suitable cultivators of Metaphysics may more easily appraise the ***ignorance of fitting instruments*** which men of this kind either affect or simulate.

**[Veltheim's main thesis]** Namely, when it is said that ***Jus naturae is so immutable that not even by God can it be changed***, so far is it from being derogated by this from divine glory and Majesty, that rather it is thereby abundantly confirmed by an ***illustrious and most evident argument***. For ***no repugnance is given ex parte DEI as cause***, who altogether could change natural Law if indeed it were mutable (i.e. could be changed) — just as no repugnance is given ex parte of a man endowed with perfect sight and all those things requisite for exercising sight that he could see taste or sound, provided taste or sound were in the number of visibles (i.e. could be seen). Therefore ***all repugnance is ex parte juris naturalis itself***, of which it is denied with the same truth that it could be changed, with which it is said of taste or sound that it cannot be seen. For who endowed with sounder judgment would say that any man labors in his eyes because no one can see this or that taste or sound? Why therefore shall we not say ***those labor in judgment*** who dream that any perfection is detracted from God if it be asserted that jus naturae is immutable? Certainly, as it in no way derogates from the perfection of sight that it cannot apprehend invisibles, so neither does it conflict with God's perfection that He cannot change immutables.

For the rest, the ***πρῶτον ψεῦδος*** (first falsehood) we believe is placed in this: that the contradictors either will not or cannot attain the true and genuine sense of this proposition — ***"Jus naturae is so immutable that not even by God can it be changed."*** For it has this sense, and no other: ***So true is it that natural Law cannot be dispensed with, nor can be derogated from, nor can be abrogated, that not even GOD can dispense with it, derogate from it, or abrogate it*** — i.e. ***so long as man exists*** and can use his reason and will (unless he will be an obstacle to himself), it cannot come about that there be removed from him the obligation to choose and commit (shun and omit) acts necessarily convenient (disconvenient) with his rational and social nature. For it implies manifest contradiction: for God to have given to man a rational and social nature with which certain acts necessarily converge, and yet to will that those acts be fled and omitted ***under the reason of that necessary convenience*** — which is the same as for God to will that ***aversatio from the good under the reason of good*** be given; and conversely, to will that acts necessarily disconvenient with rational and social nature be chosen and committed — which is the same as for God to will that ***appetitio under the reason of evil*** be given. Which absolutely and simpliciter is impossible. For although indeed it can happen that no appetition or aversion be made by a creature (if no creature endowed with the faculty of appetition or aversion be given), yet it is altogether impossible that appetition under the reason of evil, or aversion under the reason of good, be given — and this repugns equally to the uncreated will and to created appetite and will.

Vain therefore and frigid is this ***little persuasion*** when it is said: ***"Since God alone is eternal, therefore God alone is immutable, and so Jus naturae is not immutable."*** What shall we do with those disputants who do not understand the very terms they use for disputing? For who ever in this sense said Jus naturae is immutable — as if, namely, it also obliged those who never existed, do not exist, nor will exist? It is as if those urging such a reason would collect: ***"God alone had neither beginning of His duration nor will have end, so that He could not have had beginning or end (since He is destitute of all mutation). Therefore: it can come about that, although man can most fully use his reason and will, yet under the reason of necessary and accurately-and-sufficiently-known convenience with the rational nature he has from God, something can be shunned (nay must be); and under the reason of necessary and accurately-and-sufficiently-known disconvenience with rational nature, something can be sought (nay must be)."***

Nay, not a bit better is that too-shallow philosophy, when it is said: ***"No man exists except from the free beneplacitum of divine will — therefore it follows that the saying 'jus naturae is immutable' must not be extended beyond divine imposition and the origin of the human race."*** Frigid and shallow is this sophistication, similar to this: if you would collect: ***"No fire exists except from the free beneplacitum of divine will — therefore it follows that the saying 'fire is hot' must not be extended beyond divine imposition and the origin of fire."*** Who ever, I pray, said fire exists hot before it exists, or that there is given an immutable jus naturae before it is given? ***In few words: NECESSITY OF EXISTENCE is confused with NECESSITY OF ESSENCE***. It suffices that ***true fire conditioned freely by God cannot exist unless it exists hot***: it suffices that ***jus naturae cannot be given in actu in man freely conditioned by God unless it be immutable***.

The new Philosophers retort: ***"God can effect that no longer there be any Jus naturae which binds man, if no longer there were man; just as no jus naturae would have bound man had He not conditioned him."*** O miserable collection! As if indeed there were those who established the obligation of Natural Law ***in man before man existed*** who could be bound by Natural Law!

**[The Grotius citation]** We are provoked to the ***common consent of Philosophers, Jurisconsults, and Theologians***. All certainly, when they establish that natural Law in man is immutable such that not even by God can it be changed, pre-suppose both the ***existence of natural Law*** and the ***existence of man***. And they will this and nothing else: that so long as man exists (i.e. ***animal rationale ac sociale*** exists, whom God has obligated by Law of Nature — this is, as the contradictors themselves define it, ***by such a law as flows from the general condition of human nature, whose reasons must be sought from the universal condition of the human race, and which can be investigated and known and considered from the powers of ingenuity congenital to men and from consideration of human nature in general***) — so long also it cannot come about that man remain (i.e. that rational and social animal remain) and yet no longer be obligated to the Law of Nature. And this the contradictors themselves — whether willing or unwilling — must confess, nor find anything by which to palliate so open a matter.

For in express words writes ***Grotius lib. 1 de Jure Belli et Pacis cap. 1 § 10 n. 5***:

> ***"But NATURAL RIGHT is so immutable that not even by God can it be changed. For although God's potency is immense, yet certain things can be said to which it does not extend; for those things which are so said are only said — they have no sense expressing the matter but repugn to themselves."***

(This is: that God cannot change the Law of Nature — repugnance is not given ex parte Dei, who can change all things that are mutable, but repugnance is given ***ex parte objecti***.) Grotius continues:

> ***"As therefore even by God it cannot be effected that ***twice two should not be four***, so neither can it be effected that what is intrinsically evil should not be evil. This is what Aristotle signifies when he says: ἔνια εὐθὺς νομισάμενα συνειλημμένα τῇ πονηρίᾳ (certain things are at once judged bound up with wickedness). For as the ESSE of things, after they are and insofar as they are, does not depend from elsewhere, so also the PROPRIETATES which necessarily follow that esse. And such is the ***malice of certain acts compared to nature using sound reason***. Therefore ***GOD HIMSELF according to this norm permits Himself to be judged***, as is seen in ***Gen. XVIII:25, Isa. V:3, Ezek. XVIII, Jer. II:9, Mic. VI:2, Rom. II:6, III:6***."***

**[Novatores' critique of Grotius' point IV]** Meanwhile the following in no way frightens us [the critique]: ***"Grotius has not sufficiently weighed this matter, when among those things to which divine potency does not extend because they involve contradiction, he counts the malice of certain human acts. Indeed twice two cannot not be four, since both two and four really are one and the same (so that either they differ by name only, or they are only in a mode where contradictories simultaneously obtain in one and the same subject — for contradiction is the same simultaneously affirmed and denied of the same). But this contradiction does not appear in acts opposed to natural law. Whence the same [Grotius] soon derived this malice from comparison to NATURE USING SOUND REASON. But in the very vocable 'SOUND REASON', when attributed to man, is contained respect to the LAW OF SOCIALITY injoined by the Creator to man. Likewise he says in ibid. § 12 that something is of natural Right is proved from convenience or disconvenience necessary with rational and social nature. But social nature man was allotted not from any immutable necessity but from divine beneplacitum. Therefore the morality of actions — as those convenient or disconvenient to him qua social — must be derived from the same source. So these [moral characters] belong to acts not from absolute necessity but from hypothetical necessity, with that condition posited which God freely assigned to man above other animals. Nor is there any support for defenders of the other view in the sayings of Sacred Scripture adduced at the said place. For without doubt from the beginning God proclaimed to the human race that He will be the ***remunerator of the good and avenger of evil*** (Heb. XI:6), and that He will give to each according to his works (Rom. II:6); from which, since veracity does not permit Him to depart from His own, Abraham rightly appealed thus (Gen. XVIII:25, add. Ezek. XVIII:25, Rom. III:6). But how from this does it follow that morality is in human acts per se, apart from divine imposition? Nor does it yet appear how the same conclusion can be elicited from the saying at Isa. V:3 — that it is justly omitted to cultivate that thing in which oil and labor are lost. Finally at Mic. VI:2 it is indeed said that mortals understand from their own judgment that it is fitting that gratitude be rendered for benefits. But from this it is not permitted to collect: therefore, that men to whom there is sense of benefits ought to be grateful is not injoined to them by any law, but the same is necessary per se before all law."***

**V.** [Veltheim's defense] ***Grotius weighed this matter sufficiently***. For ***contradiction appears in acts opposed to the Law of Nature***, in virtue of which such acts can never by God be ***permitted or prescribed by any law to any agent*** who otherwise is capable of law. For (as was admonished before) it manifestly implies contradiction that an act necessarily disconvenient with rational nature be prescribed or permitted by a true law. The objection — that for something to be numbered among realities there is no need of a specific disposition of it, nor of any ***precept of a Superior***, but by the very fact that any thing exists it is one; and if beside this another exists, there are one and one (which for brevity's sake we call ***two***); and one and one, if taken twice, come to be one, one, one and one (which for brevity's sake we call ***four***); so that whoever denies that twice two are four denies the same to be the same; but to the ***turpitudo*** which is discerned in human acts opposed to nature, that it may result, there are required both that man's nature be formed in a peculiar mode, and that the law be posited as the ***norm of actions*** — from whose relation at length that ***moral quality*** arises; but for a thing to be numerable, nothing else is required than that it exist in whatever mode — to this the response is easy:

**(1)** Grotius never intended that ***by the same reason*** by which twice two are four, by that and no other reason jus naturae is immutable such that not even by God can it be changed. Rather his mind returns to this: ***just as God is not impotent by this — though He cannot effect that twice two should not be four (since this itself cannot be effected because it implies a true contradiction) — so neither is anything detracted from divine omnipotence if it is established that Jus naturae is so immutable that not even by God can it be changed, since it likewise implies a true contradiction*** (which contradiction we showed above). Therefore Grotius willed nothing else than to show that these two converge in this: ***twice two are not four***, and ***jus naturae is changed*** (i.e. abrogated, derogated, dispensed in it) — both cannot be done by God; not as if God were by this made impotent, but because God could effect both — both that twice two should not be four, and that Jus naturae be changed — if either could come to be. That this was Grotius' mind and no other, whoever cannot discern, must be of a very unhappy wit.

**(2)** As to the point that for ***turpitudo*** to actually adhere or belong to human acts opposed to Natural Law, there is pre-required a nature of man ***actually existing*** and ***formed in a peculiar mode by God*** — no one ever denied; and the same is signified by the common Metaphysical dictum: ***Agere praesupponit existere***. But what thence? It suffices that ***manifest contradiction can be shown*** on account of which, from man (i.e. rational animal), after he has been created by God, the obligation to omission of certain acts cannot be removed, so long as he exists (i.e. remains ***rational animal***). Meanwhile one thing is to treat of ***actual turpitudo of acts***, another of ***possible turpitudo of acts***: let what we expounded at length above at axiom I of c. 1 be repeated. It is attached to Grotius ***as if he had come to a better mind***, because soon he derived that malice ***from comparison to NATURE USING SOUND REASON***. But this is to commit a ***fallacy of division***, dividing what Grotius had conjoined, lest matter for cavilling be lacking. It is as if someone wished to deny that man and brute import contradictory reasons on the ground that such contradiction between man and brute is not of the sort as is given between ***ens and non-ens*** — since man and brute import contradictory reasons with respect to animal, with respect to which however there is no need for the sort of contradiction between ens and non-ens. For the rest, in what sense ***relation-to-the-law-of-nature*** can and should be posterior to morality was likewise shown above (in the practical use of axiom I of chapter I).

**VI.** That in the very vocable of ***sound reason***, when attributed to man, there is contained respect to the ***law of sociality*** injoined to man by the Creator — if this be received as if morality could not have itself ***antecedently to law taken for a decree of a Superior*** — this we refuted above at the same place. What more [they allege] on ***hypothetical and absolute necessity*** we discussed there. For the rest, as to the Scriptural sayings adduced: sufficient support do the defenders of the true view find in them. Most true is it that God proclaimed to the human race that He will be ***remunerator of the good, avenger of the evil***, and that He will give to each according to his works. Here however it is further asked: ***could God have proclaimed the contrary?*** And because God, truth-of-justice-saved, could not, therefore there is given altogether an ***immutable nature of justice common to God with men***. Therefore it easily stands how it follows that ***morality belongs to human acts apart from respect to the decree of a Superior***.

**[Isa. V:3 worked]** ***God Most Good Most Great*** asks of His actions judgment from men (as those He produced rational and capable of injuries, and such that between God and men justice should have place) — what remained to be done for the Jewish people which He did not do? For the Prophet compares the Jewish people to a ***vineyard***, and God to its ***cultivator***, showing: God supplied to the people all those things which are demanded of the cultivator of a vineyard, that the vineyard be said to be duly cultivated. Hence it is clear how frigidly it is asserted that nothing on morality can be collected from the view at Isa. c. V.

**[Mic. VI:2 worked]** Of similar tenor is the place at ***Micah c. VI:2***, where God — though by supreme right Lord of all — wishes nevertheless from men (that is, from ***worms of the earth*** if compared to Himself) to prove the equity of His actions. The words of the preceding text have themselves thus: ***"Hear what the Lord says: Arise, contend in judgment against the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Hear mountains the judgment of Jehovah, and firmaments [of the earth], prophet plead My cause against My people"*** etc. By ***montes and colles*** are understood the ***inhabitants*** of them (i.e. ***πατριάρχαι***, patriarchs), since the judgment of Jehovah with His people is the Lord's suit with His people — ***the Greeks say κρίσις τῷ Κυρίῳ***, and ***with Israel He will dispute***. Verse 3: ***"My people, what have I done to you, and in what have I wearied you? Testify against Me."*** How excellently indeed do the following things agree with these — which this ***new commentator*** adduces in this manner: ***"Finally Mic. VI:2 says that mortals understand from their proper judgment that it is fitting that for benefits gratitude be rendered"*** [etc.]. But let it suffice to have touched these in passing; their solid examination does not belong to the present place.

**VII.** [Theological examples closing Note II] So much on the adduced Moral example. It pleases to transcribe one or two ***Theological*** examples hither. Thus e.gr.:

**(a) John VIII:43** — Christ says of the Pharisees: ***"Why do you not understand my speech? Because you cannot hear my word."***

**(b) 1 Cor. III:1-2** — Paul says: ***"I, brothers, could not speak to you as to spirituals."***

By each saying an example of ***impossible matter*** is manifestly indicated. But to one wishing to know the ***repugnance*** by force of which each thing is called impossible, it will easily appear that it is ***not of one genus***. For in the former example repugnance is given ***ex parte potentiae***, not ex parte objecti; in the latter ***ex parte objecti***, not ex parte potentiae. For as to the former example: Christ's speech was altogether of the number of those which can be ***object of hearing***. That the Pharisees could not hear him came to pass because their hearing (or ***potency of hearing***) was impeded by ***hatred of truth***, as is indicated by the following verse 44: ***"You are from the Father, the Devil, and the desires of your father you wish to do; who is a liar and the Father of lies."*** Contrariwise, in the latter example, altogether to speak to the Corinthians ***as to spirituals*** was in the number of ***possibles in order to the potency of speaking by which Paul was powerful***. That he could not however speak to them as to spirituals — defect occurred ***ex parte objecti***: they were ***not yet capable of more solid food***, as he himself indicates vv. 2-3: ***"With the drink of milk I nourished you, not with food: for you were not yet able to bear it. Nay, not even now are you yet able. For you are still carnal."***

Let us take two more examples. Thus **(c) 1 John III:9** says: ***"Everyone born of God does not commit sin, nor is he even able to sin."*** Sin is altogether of the number of those possible to man. That however he who is born of God cannot commit it — something intervenes ***ex parte agentis***, and it is for this reason: because he is born of God and has His seed in himself, and so qua such not only does not sin but also ***cannot sin*** — since ***to have the seed of God and the Holy Spirit in oneself, and to follow His leading, and to sin and so not to follow the leading of the Holy Spirit, are contradictories***.

**(d) Gal.
