IV:15** — Paul writes contrariwise: ***"I bear witness, that if it were possible, you would have plucked out your eyes and given them to me."*** That it is possible for someone to pluck out his eyes, no one can deny; but that the Galatians could not pluck out theirs was impeded ***ex parte objecti***: because that was conjoined with their perishing. Behold the repugnance here ex parte objecti, there ex parte potentiae. Examples of this kind well-nigh innumerable occur in the Sacred [Scriptures].

#### § 6 — Possibile Physicum vs Logicum

> ***The chief distinctions both of the POSSIBLE and of the IMPOSSIBLE are the following. (1) Commonly Philosophers distinguish the possible into PHYSICUM and LOGICUM. The former they call that which is such IN ORDER TO FINITE POTENCY; the latter they name that which is such IN ORDER TO INFINITE POTENCY — that is, the OMNIPOTENCE OF GOD.***
>
> ***E.gr. ***Peter before he is generated can be generated***, and so is a possible something — but is called POSSIBILE PHYSICUM, because he takes his denomination from the ***potency of generating*** which his parents have before they beget, and this potency is finite.***
>
> ***Contrariwise, ***a GOLDEN MOUNTAIN***, which God perhaps has neither created nor will create, can be created by God, and so is a possible something — but is called POSSIBILE LOGICUM, because it is denominated from the ***creative potency of God*** which God has even before He creates, and which potency itself is the infinite [potency] of God.***
>
> ***From what has been said it easily appears what is called ***IMPOSSIBILE PHYSICUM*** and what ***IMPOSSIBILE LOGICUM***.***

#### Notes

**I.** This distinction has ***signal use in Moral Philosophy and in all Theology***, as will appear from the immediately following § at length. Nor can it otherwise come about than that those who entirely dismiss this distinction from their eyes often slip in judgment.

**II.** Regarding ***possibile Physicum*** let it be noted: that as in respect of that potency to which it says order it is possible, so in respect of another potency to which it does not say order, it is ***impossible***. E.gr. ***to fly*** is possible to a bird, since it has the potency of flying; it is not however possible to a man, since although he has the locomotive potency, he does not have [it] to flying. And ***to see whiteness*** is possible in respect of sight (or the visive potency), but not in respect of hearing (or the auditive potency). For just as it implies that what is not comprehended under the object of sight be seen, so by the same reason it repugns that what is not contained under the object of hearing be heard.

**III.** ***Possibile Logicum*** can be considered in two ways: (1) precisely as it says ***non-repugnance*** — i.e. that it is not yet (or is not), can however be or come to be, or does not imply contradiction for it to be or come to be; (2) as it ***connotes a habitudo to the potency of God*** by which it can be produced. Therefore ***Possibile Logicum says three things***: (1) that it is not; (2) that it can be or come to be; (3) that it can be or come to be ***by God***.

**IV.** Nor is this to be passed over: that ***possibile***, as it is distinguished into Logical and Physical, is for the most part taken in such a way that it is the same as ***potentia tale*** (what is in potency to such) — although otherwise the signification of the voice ***possibile*** is wider, as was admonished at § 2.

#### § 7 — Possibile with Respect to God vs With Respect to Creature

> ***It must be rightly noted: many things are possible which GOD CANNOT [do], but a CREATURE CAN; and conversely, many things are possible which GOD CAN [do], but a CREATURE CANNOT. E.gr. in respect of a creature it is possible to eat, drink, lie; in respect of God it is impossible. In respect of God it is possible to create (i.e. to produce something from simpliciter nothing), to raise up seed of Abraham from a stone; in respect of a creature it is impossible.***

#### Note I — Precision Required on *Possibile Respectu Dei*

It is worth the labor to weigh accurately what must be called ***possibile with respect to God***. For although ***Christ Himself*** professes at ***Matt. XIX:26 and Mark X:27***: ***πάντα δυνατὰ παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ*** (***that with God all things are possible***); and the ***Angel*** at ***Luke I:37*** says: ***οὐκ ἀδυνατεῖ παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ πᾶν ῥῆμα*** (that is, ***there is nothing impossible with God, every word***) — and these utterances of ***heavenly truth*** are altogether most true and cannot be denied by anyone of sound and pious mind — yet it is most certain that even among those things which are possible, certain things cannot be done by God, as will presently be demonstrated at length. So far indeed is this from any addition accruing to the ***infinite potency of God*** through this assertion, that rather by it that [potency] is more and more confirmed and more evidently demonstrated.

Meanwhile we cannot but gravely reprove the ***rightly-detestable boldness*** of those who seek some I-know-not-what glory in deciding ***superfluous and petulant questions*** on the potency of God — of which kind are those of the ***Scholastics***: ***"Could God in Christ's place have supposited a woman? Could God have supposited a pumpkin, and if He had supposited it, how would it have preached, how would it have performed miracles, how would it have been crucified?"*** — and six hundred others, whose ***vanity, petulance, and impiety*** no one does not most strongly detest. See ***B. Johann Gerhard***, Theologian of our Academy and of the whole Church of Christ far most-deserving, ***Methodus Studii Theologici c. 4 p. 302 ff.***

#### Note II — Class I: Quae Deus Non Potest = Contradictio-Implicans

**II.** Among those which with respect to God are not possible, ***first*** are those which simpliciter imply ***the most manifest and truest contradiction***, and so are ***simpliciter and absolutely impossible, in themselves and in their nature***. For they do not truly imply contradiction, unless which are absolutely impossible, i.e. in themselves such that they cannot come to be. By what reason, I pray, could those which are absolutely and simpliciter impossible fall under the potency of God? Surely if they fell under God's potency, they would altogether fall under some potency, and so because they would fall under some potency, they would not be absolutely impossible. ***As impossible therefore it is (with all the requisites of true contradiction applied and observed) that the same simultaneously be and not be, so impossible is it that those things which are simpliciter and absolute impossible be possible to God.***

This is the ***constant view of Metaphysicians and Theologians***. Let be seen ***B. Jacobus Martini Exercit. Metaph. lib. II exercit. IV theor. XX*** and ***B. Scheibl Opera Metaph. lib. II c. 3 tit. 16 artic. 3***. ***Thomas 1 pars q. XXV art. III*** discourses thus:

> ***"It must be said that commonly all confess GOD is OMNIPOTENT, but to assign the reason of omnipotence seems difficult. For doubt can be had on what is comprehended under this distribution when it is said: ***God can do all things***. But if one rightly considers (since potency is said in respect of possibles), when GOD is said ***can do all things***, nothing more rightly is understood than that He can do everything POSSIBLE, and on this account is called OMNIPOTENT. ***Possibile*** however is said in two ways, according to the Philosopher in Metaphysics. In one mode, by respect to some potency: as what is subjected to human potency is said to be possible to man. It cannot be said that God is called omnipotent because He can do all things possible to created nature — for divine potency extends to more. If however it be said that God is omnipotent because He can do all things possible to His own potency, there would be ***circulatio*** in the manifestation of omnipotence. For this would be nothing other than to say GOD is omnipotent because He can do all that He can do. It remains therefore that God is called omnipotent because He can do ALL ABSOLUTELY POSSIBLE THINGS, which is the other mode of saying ***possible***. Something is said possible or impossible absolutely from the ***habitudo of terms***: possible, namely, when the predicate does not repugn the subject (as ***Socrates to sit***); impossible absolutely because the predicate repugns the subject (as ***man to be an ass***). It must moreover be considered that, since every agent acts upon something like itself, to every active potency corresponds a POSSIBLE as its proper object according to the ratio of that act in which active potency is founded — as potentia calefactiva is referred as to its proper object to being-heatable. But the ***divine being***, upon which the ratio of divine potency is founded, is ***esse infinitum, not limited to any genus of being, but prehaving in itself the perfection of total being***. Whence whatever can have the ratio of being is contained under the possibles-absolutes with respect to which God is called omnipotent. Nothing however is opposed to the ratio of being except non-being. This therefore repugns to the ratio of possible-absolute (which is subjected to divine omnipotence): that it imply simultaneously ***to be and not to be***. For this is not subjected to omnipotence — not from defect of divine potency, but because it cannot have the ratio of a factible, nor of a possible. Whatever therefore does not imply contradiction, is contained under those possibles with respect to which God is called omnipotent. But those which imply contradiction are not contained under divine omnipotence, because they cannot have the ratio of possibles. Whence more conveniently it is said that ***they cannot come to be***, than that ***God cannot do them***. Nor is this against the word of the Angel saying: ***it will not be impossible with God every word***. For that which implies contradiction cannot be a word — because no intellect can conceive it."*** — Thus Thomas.

A good part of these words of Thomas ***B. Johann Gerhard*** adduced in his ***Exegesis of Tome I locus II de natura Dei et attributis divinis § 18***, finally adjoining this his ***ἐπίκρισις*** (judgment): ***"The implication of contradiction is nothing other than REPUGNANCE; but what repugns to come to be is impossible to come to be. We concede that GOD DOES NOT DO THOSE THINGS WHICH IMPLY CONTRADICTION, and which are simpliciter impossible."*** See at length at the cited place.

The same, after many other things pertaining excellently hither, finally discourses thus: ***"And from these it easily appears what great wantonness it is that the ***Photinians, following the footsteps of the Calvinians***, say that these imply contradiction and are simpliciter impossible: that God is one in essence, three in persons; that God from eternity generates the Son from His own essence; that the divine and human nature in Christ are personally united"*** etc.

#### Note III — Class II: Ex Hypothesi Impossibilia (Facta Non Fieri Infecta)

**III.** Second, with respect to God those are not possible but impossible which ***ex hypothesi cease to be possible***. E.gr. ***things done by GOD cannot be made or rendered undone***. For facta, qua such, cease to be possible from this: that otherwise what are true, by the very fact that they are true, would be false. For ***necessaria***, though they be such ex hypothesi, cannot not be. Whence what have been done cannot not have been done, by the reason by which they have been done.

Praises this very view (which he says was also Agatho's) ***Aristotle VI Nic. Eth. c. 2*** in the following words: ***"Quod factum est, qua factum sit, fieri nullo modo potest"*** (what has been done, qua done, can by no mode be done). On this account rightly did Agatho say:

> ***Μόνον γὰρ αὐτοῦ καὶ θεὸς στερίσκεται, ἀγένητα ποιεῖν ἅσσ' ἂν ᾖ πεπραγμένα***
> *(God alone is deprived of this one thing — to make unmade what has been done.)*

The same is denied also to ***time, parent of all things***, says ***Pindar in 2. hymn. Olympiorum***. See also ***Sophocles in Trachiniis***. Thence ***Eustratius Bishop of Nicaea*** illustrates Aristotle's place by this paraphrase: ***"It cannot be done that what is done not be done. Agatho was a tragic Poet, whom Aristotle here mentions because he wrote things agreeing with himself, whence he also praises his saying. For since (he says) these matters have themselves thus, on this account Agatho rightly said that so necessarily what is already done cannot be not done, that we even dare to say of God Himself that, though He can do all things (as cause of all things), He is deprived of this alone: that He cannot make what is done to not be done. For either God is cause even of the thing done — since of all things, both which are and which have been, He is cause — whence if He so should take away what has been done, that it was not done, He could also take away that He Himself were the cause of it. Or if He is not cause of the thing done, He will not be cause of all things, both of which [options] are absurd and in no way can be."***

Jurisconsults also treat this Metaphysical matter. Thus ***Decius ad L. verum est 31 D. de Reg. Jur. n. 2*** and ***Jason ad L. possessio 1 D. de acquirenda possessione*** dispute whether ***deflowered virginity can be restored?*** — and they approve the saying of ***Jerome in c. si Paul. 22 q. 5***: ***"I shall say boldly: although God can do all things, He cannot raise up a virgin after her ruin."*** This however other Jurisconsults deny, and will have Jerome to ***speak hyperbolically***. Thence they distinguish between the ***state of virginity of integrity*** and the ***state of dignity***: they judge that God can ***reduce the virgin to the state of integrity by the removal of all corruption*** — since nothing is impossible to Him. But He cannot revoke her to the ***state of dignity*** which consists in this: that she was never corrupted; for God cannot make the corrupted not to be corrupted, since this implies contradiction, and God cannot do contradictories. And hither they drag this [saying]: ***"God indeed is able to deliver from penalty, but He does not will to crown the corrupted."*** This contrary view defends ***Hieronymus Cagnol in cited L. verum est 31 D. de Reg. Jur.*** See also ***Scipio Centius 2. notis ad Apolog. Apuleji n. 511.*** and ***Kornmann l. 2 de jure Virginit. qu. 25***.

Whatever be of the arguments of either part (for this question — far be it that we make it our own), yet this anyone easily notices: that from each part is invoked the ***common and most true assertion of the Metaphysicians***, whose sum hitherto we have expressed.

#### Note IV — Class III: Deus Himself Cannot Fieri

**IV.** Third, although God is some ***possibile*** (inasmuch as namely He says no repugnance), yet ***GOD does not fall under omnipotence***, since God has been neither made, nor could be made, nor can be made — such that rightly it is said to be in the number of absolute impossibles ***that God be made***. And so again, with respect to God, it is also impossible ***that God be made***.

#### Note V — Class IV: Contra Perfectiones Dei Physicae

**V.** Fourth, with respect to God all those acts are impossible which ***fight with the perfections of God*** which Philosophers and Theologians in one and most true sense call ***PHYSICAL***. E.gr. ***it cannot be done that God EAT, DRINK, locally MOVE Himself***, etc.; item ***that He take NUTRIMENT, AUGMENTATION, DIE***, etc. — because all these fight with the perfections of God natural (or belonging to God in the genus of nature), such as ***aeternitas, immutabilitas, immaterialitas, immensitas*** etc., nay ***omnipotentia itself***. For if God could eat, drink, locally move, then He would be corporeal; if He could be nourished and augmented, He would not be immutable and immaterial; if He could die, He would not be incorruptible and immortal.

Whence those which are therefore called impossible with respect to God because they fight with God's perfection — they certainly ***simultaneously argue and confirm the infinite perfection of God***. God can however, perfection-saved, ***effect that such things happen in creatures*** in respect of whom they are possible: e.gr. God cannot eat, die; yet He can effect that ***man eat, die***, etc.

#### Note VI — Class V: Mediate-Creature-Dependent Operations

**VI.** Fifth, with respect to God certain things are said to be impossible insofar as, although they can be done by God, they ***cannot be done by Him without the creature***. E.gr. ***an act of created intellect, a vital operation in a creature*** — God can effect it, but not except by means of the ***vital potency*** (namely intellect). For it implies contradiction that an act of intellect be given, and yet it be done without an intellect: if it is not from intellect, certainly it is not an act of intellect.

This moved the more accurate Philosophers and Theologians to call those Theological virtues (such as ***faith, hope, charity***) not ***immaterial forms*** (such as is the soul of man as being of spiritual essence), but ***material forms*** — since indeed they cannot be produced by God except ***dependently on the subject***. E.gr. ***faith in Christ*** cannot be produced by the Holy Spirit except dependently on the intellect (inasmuch as it says ***notitia and assensus***) and dependently on the will (inasmuch as it notes ***fiducia***). For by no reason can it be done that the Holy Spirit excite faith in Christ the Redeemer in man except dependently on the rational soul of man.

#### Note VII — Class VI: Simul-et-Collective vs Sigillatim-et-Successive

**VII.** Sixth, with respect to God those things are impossible ***simul et collective*** which can however be done by Him ***sigillatim et successive***. Thus one and the same creature can by God be ***conservari*** and (which is the Metaphysicians' diction) ***annihilari***. Both however cannot simultaneously be done, because ***it manifestly involves repugnance***.

#### Note VIII — Class VII: Contra Perfectiones Dei Morales

**VIII.** Seventh, with respect to God those things are impossible which manifestly fight with the ***moral perfection of God***. E.gr. absolutely impossible is it that ***God LIE, God DENY HIMSELF, God FAIL IN PROMISE, act CONTRARY TO HIS OATH***, etc. — because such things and far more necessarily fight with the ***moral perfections of God***, i.e. those whose consideration pertains per se to ***Moral Theology, both natural and revealed***. Of this kind are the moral perfections of God: ***VERACITAS, IUSTITIA, MISERICORDIA, BONITAS, SANCTITAS***, etc.

For although these are possible to man — e.gr. ***possible is it for man to lie***, man can deny himself — yet they cannot be done by God. For if God could ***deny Himself, and so lie***, He would be ***the first and immutable Verity*** (by the very fact that He is God), and would ***not be the first and immutable Verity*** (by the very fact that He could lie). But that He be the first and immutable Verity, and not be the first and immutable Verity (as is manifest per se), implies contradiction.

Here we count it to be noted that with those which fight with the ***moral perfections of God***, matters are quite otherwise compared than with those which fight with the ***physical perfections of God*** (treated in the preceding fifth note). For those which fight with the physical perfections of God and so cannot be done ***immediately*** by God can still be done by God ***mediately — through a secondary cause or through a creature***. But those which fight with the moral perfections of God — these qua such can neither ***immediately nor mediately*** be done by God. E.gr. God can neither Himself lie, nor effect that man or angel lie; God can neither act against a promise or oath, nor effect that man act against promise or oath.

#### Note IX — Closing: Nothing Detracts from Divine Potency + Slevogt + Luke 1:37 Hebrew

**IX.** These — and perhaps innumerably many others — which with respect to God are not possible, no one endowed with sounder judgment will refer [to divine impotence]. Nor does anything thence decrease from divine potency, since the defect in this part is not in ***divine potency*** (which altogether remains infinite potency) but rather ***in the objects***. Whence more rightly we say ***they cannot be done*** than ***God cannot do them***. See what we adduced above at this present chapter's § 1 note 3 ff. p. 629 ff. at length.

***All things therefore with GOD are possible***, as ***CHRIST said*** — namely those which do not imply to-be-and-not-to-be, and so it does not repugn that they come to be. In that pronouncement of the ***Angel*** [Luke 1:37], as the mode of speaking is Hebrew, so also the sense must be elicited from Hebraism. For the Greek ***ῥῆμα*** (rhēma) answers to the Hebrew ***דבר*** (dabar), and sometimes signifies ***word or speech***, sometimes ***thing***. If taken in the former mode, the angel intimates that it is not impossible for God to do what He has promised and said He will do. If in the latter, this will be the sense: that no thing is impossible to God, provided it does not repugn to come to be.

Let be seen ***B. Slevogt's dissertation de esse possibili***, which is in the new edition part 1 at number VIII pp. 157 ff. Whose inspection will teach how far the footsteps of this most-praised man have been read by us.

#### Note X — Against the Indifferentismo-Novatores (opens)

**X.** Either he betrays ***crass rudeness and affected stupor*** or ***great malice***, whoever rejects the hitherto handed-down doctrine (which the common consent of accurate Philosophers and Theologians approves) as ***stupid or impious***, and lacerates with atrocious invectives. A specimen of such rudeness or malice, should anyone desire it, will perhaps be luculently supplied by the following words of a ***newly-born Philosophy***:

> ***"There is nothing in that doubt that should move anyone: If the morality of all human acts depends from law, could not God have formed the Law of Nature such that there were commanded the contraries of those [commands] which now are? Verbi gratia, that among the mutual duties of man there be ***to kill, to steal, to commit adultery, to calumniate***; among the forbidden [acts] ***to show gratitude, to keep covenants, to repay loan***, and similar things. For it seems ***SUPERFLUOUS AND PETULANT*** to ask what God could have done, when it stands what He has done."***

Everyone whose sound mind is in a sound body most easily notices that by this very [sentence] a useful and necessary Philosophical doctrine is ***defiled with invectives***.

**(1)** For first, if the ***mark of vanity and petulance cannot be escaped*** by him who asks what God could have done, when it stands what He has done, then the whole doctrine on ***potentia Dei absoluta ac ordinata***, on ***voluntate Dei antecedente et consequente***, on ***decretis Dei absolutis et ordinatis*** will be useless and void — the notice of which most useful and necessary dogmas, ***against the Reformed and those who lick their spittle***, suitable ***Philosophers and Cultivators and Doctors of Theology*** can in no way lack.

**(2)** Next, in those things even which God did, two questions altogether must be distinguished: ***"Did He do it?"*** and ***"Could He have done it?"*** No one will confuse these, nor will anyone call their discrimen superfluous and petulant, unless he does not blush to read the footsteps of those ridiculous men ***the Megarics***, who (as ***Aristotle IX Metaph. cap. 1*** authorizes) taught that potencies do not precede their acts, but only exist when their acts exist — as if ***he who does not laugh cannot laugh, but only he who laughs can laugh (when he laughs)*** — which view however ***B. Stahl exploded*** in his ***Reg. Philosoph. part. 1 disp. 2 reg. 1***, let it be seen.

**(3)** Third, these two questions are ***basely confused***: ***"What could God have done?"*** and ***"What could He have done ***otherwise***?"*** Nay, if anything else, surely this frivolous assertion (by which it is established as superfluous and petulant to ask whether God could, truth-of-justice-saved, have prescribed to man or left in man's freest arbitration the acts which Philosophers, Theologians, and Jurisconsults by unanimous consent call ***by their own nature and per se shameful***) ***furnishes patronage*** (whether willing or unwilling the patron of the assertion) ***to the frivolous and impious commentum DE INDIFFERENTISMO***, as they call it.

For if to someone pondering that ***among the mutual duties of man injoined by the Law of Nature*** are ***to show gratitude, to keep covenants, to repay loan***, and similar; ***among the forbidden*** are ***to commit homicide, to steal, to commit adultery, to calumniate***, etc. — thoughts of this kind cannot but arise: Is not the matter with the object of the Law of Nature equally compared as with the objects of other laws, so that just as other laws recognize for their matter acts per se and by their own nature neither honest nor shameful (i.e. neither per se and necessarily convenient with rational nature qua such, nor per se and necessarily disconvenient with it), but ***by their nature indifferent*** — so also the objects of the Law of Nature are such acts which in themselves and in their nature are ***indifferent-licit***, to which God has superadded necessity ***from His freest beneplacitum of will***, such that unless the ***freest will of God, placed above all justice***, had so seen it, it would have mattered nothing whether they came to be thus or otherwise?

Now if here it were not permitted to the Doctor of Morals to demonstrate the negative of this question — and indeed from this foundation: that ***on account of the intrinsic and absolutely necessary convenience or disconvenience of voluntary acts (of which the Law of Nature disposes) God could not have formed the Law of Nature such that contraries were commanded of those [commands] which now are*** (v.gr. such that among man's mutual duties were to kill, to steal, to commit adultery, to calumniate, etc.; among forbidden were to show gratitude, to keep covenants, to repay loan, and similar) — by what reason, I pray, could every peril (lest the Cultivator of Morals fall into the error of indifferentismo) be averted?

For what is said — that for averting this peril it suffices if it be shown that, now that man has been created by God as an animal which cannot be safe except by observation of the Law of Nature, it is in no way lawful to believe that God wills to abolish or change the Law of Nature so long as He introduces no change into human nature; and so, with the constancy of human nature posited, although it was so formed from the beginning from divine beneplacitum, the Law of Nature persists ***firm and unmoved*** — otherwise than laws which so depend on divine will that they do not seem thus necessarily to be demanded from the condition of men in general — [this] is said in vain. For the questions ***return***:

(α) Could God not have conditioned man rightly and properly so called, such that he could be safe apart from observation of the natural Law?

(β) Can GOD, with man remaining safe, introduce change into human nature? For unless it were impossible that there be given a man who is not rational animal, neither would it be impossible that GOD introduce change into human nature.

**(1)** Unless it were simpliciter and absolutely impossible that there be given a man who is not rational animal — surely the ***discrimen of the Law of Nature from other laws*** could not be placed in this: that the former [the Law of Nature] is necessarily demanded from the condition of men in general, [while] others are not.

**(2)** If it were superfluous and petulant to ask whether God could have formed the Law of Nature otherwise than it now is — most vain and most petulant would also be this question: ***whether the Law of Nature is thus necessarily demanded from the condition of men in general?***

**(3)** It was indeed placed in the divine will to produce or not to produce rational animal. But when such a consequence is knit together: ***"If it was placed in the divine will to produce or not to produce rational animal, it follows that it was placed in the divine will by the Law of Nature to prescribe to man this and prohibit that"*** — this either has the sense: ***"God by His free will could have effected that the Law of Nature actually bound no man, if, namely, He had effected that no man actually existed"***; or it leaves behind this sense: ***"God by His free will could have effected that there were commanded the contraries of those [precepts] of the Law of Nature which now are."*** In the former sense the adduced proposition is most true — but was adduced in vain, since there is no one who denied it. In the latter sense it remains most false, as even a blind man sees.

**(4)** Fourth, do not marvel that all solid Philosophy is distasteful to such a disputant — one who does not blush to ***correct the tongue of the Holy Spirit***:

- ***2 Tim. 2:13*** says expressly: ***"If we believe not, He abides faithful; ἀρνήσασθαι γὰρ ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται — HE CANNOT DENY HIMSELF."***
- At ***Hebr. 6:17-18*** the Holy Spirit calls the promise and the oath ***δύο πράγματα ἀμετάθετα ἐν οἷς ἀδύνατον ψεύσασθαι θεόν — TWO IMMUTABLE THINGS, IN WHICH IT IS IMPOSSIBLE FOR GOD TO LIE***.

Him who does not see that here by the Holy Spirit Himself the question is moved ***what God CAN DO*** — must be hedged with such thick darkness that he does not even seem to see those things from whose sight not even the initiated are prohibited. For does not He most rightly respond to these questions — ***"Can God deny Himself? Can God lie?"*** — who, using the words of the Holy Spirit, responds thus: ***"God cannot deny Himself; it is impossible for God to lie"***?

What then shall we do with that man, who in this controversy — in which nothing but a pumpkin blinks — believes himself alone to have conquered? Nor was it enough for him to reproach the ***ignorance under which he himself labors*** not only to Grotius but to many of our own Theologians and Jurisconsults; he even made the ***oracles of heavenly truth suspect***, and when he had nothing else, said: ***"That God does certain things, or does not always do all things, this is not from DEFECT OF LIBERTY, but from HIS OWN BENEPLACITUM."***

And this he finally explicated thus: ***"Since GOD is most-free and omnipotent, and the abyss of His potency and goodness is not yet exhausted, it is asked why He nevertheless does not do certain things, or does not always do things which otherwise do not seem to abhor from His perfection? I here have nothing else to respond than that the beneplacitum of God so bears it; and I count it more reverent to render this one simple reason and towards the divine majesty, than to adorn subtle inventions by which divine omnipotence is reduced to order and circumscribed by the straits of our judgment. And I think this reason rests not only on sound reason but also on the sayings of Scripture at Ps. 115:3, Eph. 1:11."***

Afterwards he added: ***"That however God is said not to be able to do certain things, this does not arise from any extrinsic impediment acceding — natural or moral — but from His own placitum, which we mortals conceive as tempered to His greatness and prominence."*** On which words he soon commentated: ***"Further I render the reason why God cannot do certain things — namely sins. Namely that God is said not to be able to sin — this is not from an extrinsic impediment acceding naturally (i.e. the force of a greater and more valid) nor morally (i.e. of obligation coming from a Superior) — for neither falls on Him who has no Superior. But it arises from the most-right placitum or will, which agrees with the greatest and most prominent being. Where (that I may have made mention of God's placitum or will, as of the supreme and most perfect being), I adduced this reason: that where discourse is of God's liberty, it seems more convenient to express His perfection by assigning the ***will — such as can fall into a most-perfect ens*** — as the principle of His own actions. Then that that perfection by which GOD is understood not to be able to sin be expressed as conjoined with the ***highest liberty***, and not held for such an impossibility of sinning as is in brutes and inanimate things (which can therefore not sin because they are destitute of rational will). Finally since in the divine attributes (which we are wont to conceive in some way according to analogy of faculties in man) a ***most-perfect union and as it were co-conspiration*** must be understood — so that the will of God can never repugn to His own greatness, prominence, justice, sanctity, goodness, and so must never be opposed to this."***

But rightly and deservedly here we repeat the words elsewhere opposed to the adversary by ***B. Slevogt*** in his praised dissertation ***de esse possibili***: ***"It repugns that something be done by God which can nevertheless be done by a creature. Thus Paul at 2 Tim. 2:13 writes: 'If we believe not, He abides faithful; ἀρνήσασθαι γὰρ ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται, HE CANNOT DENY HIMSELF.' And at Hebr. 6:18: 'It is impossible for God to lie.' These, although possible to man, cannot be done by God. For if God could deny Himself and so lie, He would be the first Verity (by the very fact that He is God), and would not be the first Verity (by the very fact that He could lie). But to be the first Verity and not to be the first Verity (as is clear) implies contradiction. And this is the most true reason why God can neither deny Himself nor lie — far more rightly assigned than we see done by the adversary, who, when he had nothing else, said HE CANNOT DENY HIMSELF is the same as HE DOES NOT WILL TO DENY HIMSELF."***

Nor do the following words of the ***calumniator*** frighten me: ***"To be noted by a word is the calumny of Veltheim, who fashions this proposition — 'It is impossible for God to lie' — as having, according to my mind, this sense: 'God does not will to lie.' But this is my sense: 'To lie repugns to the divine will of the most-perfect being Himself. It repugns to the divine perfection with which the divine will always co-conspires, and in such a way that it does not arise from any extrinsic impediment acceding, but so that nonetheless to Him the omnimodal liberty devoid of all bond stand firm.'"***

**For: (1)** What could be clearer than these words of his: ***"The omnimodal liberty, knowing no impediment or defect, falls on God Most Good Most Great alone — which is conceived as the noblest attribute of His essence. Which Himself admits no circumscription and is conjoined with omnipotence. Whence that God does certain things, or does not always do all things, this is not from defect of liberty but from His own beneplacitum. But that the same is said not to be able to do certain things, this does not arise from any extrinsic impediment acceding (natural or moral), but from His own placitum, which we mortals conceive as tempered to His greatness and prominence. In which sense must be interpreted that trite saying: God is law to Himself."***

Surely no one is so blind that he does not see that the discourse of the adversary was of actions ***which all sounder Philosophers and Theologians call impossible to God, because they fight with the perfections of God which are of moral and practical consideration***. For this is nothing new, but it is customary and perpetual with trifflers of this kind: ***against the proper testimony of heart and conscience and most manifest words, finally to assert something else*** — only that they may put dust in the eyes of the inexperienced, and also of men of some judgment to whom indeed the power is not given of inspecting and weighing those writings with a composed mind — and yet elsewhere to defend the contrary.

I pray let someone inspect what precedes and follows in the context, and he will easily see that the discourse is of ***those acts of God which sounder Philosophers and Theologians assert to repugn to God's perfection***. Nay if, in the following words — ***"that however the same"*** etc. — the discourse were of ***sins*** (whether God can sin?), [and] in the antecedent words — ***"That God does certain things"*** etc. — were treated only of those which otherwise do not seem to abhor from His perfection: where would remain those acts which are not sins but which otherwise fight with the physical perfections of God, or because they involve manifest contradiction, or for other causes which we touched in the preceding notes, [and so] cannot be done by God? And what has this to do with me?

For declining the calumny of which the calumniator accuses me, to forcefully repel [it], it suffices that he himself expressly posited what follows: ***"That God is said not to be able to do certain things arises from His own placitum."***

**(2)** Secondly we note: although the words are read adjoined — ***"from His own placitum, which we mortals conceive as tempered to His greatness and prominence"*** — these words nevertheless cannot free the author from most manifest absurdity. For here it comes into disquisition: ***what by greatness and prominence (to which he conceives God's proper placitum tempered) does he will to be understood?*** He himself responds that must be understood ***the perfection of God*** — so that the sense here is: ***God on account of His perfection cannot not do certain things, and cannot not omit certain things on account of the same***.

But now it is further asked: ***of what kind is that perfection? physical or moral?*** Following the more accurate Philosophers and Theologians, I say that perfection is ***moral***. For the question here is of ***actions considered in the genus of morals, or as of moral consideration***. For everyone of sound mind sees that in this place is asked about actions of this genus — such as ***to lie, to fail in promise, to commit perjury*** — such that the sense be: ***Can God, with His moral perfection saved, lie, fail in promise, become perjured?***

The adversary retorts: ***"Veltheim ill-calls some perfection of God moral — since all perfections in God are essential, and (as far as stands to me) by the usage of all Philosophers 'perfection moral' is called that which is acquired by usage and discipline, and inheres in the mind as a habit."*** But what, I pray, is easier than to respond to these reasons:

**First** it is said: by me ill is called some perfection of GOD moral, since all perfections in GOD are essential. ***But let the reason be given why a perfection essential in GOD cannot be called MORAL***, i.e. cannot be called such a perfection as is per se and directly of moral consideration. For by the unanimous consent of all — both of Moral Philosophy and of Theology Doctors — this consequence is good in the genus of morals: ***This or that act of God repugns to veracity, or justice, or goodness and sanctity. Therefore it displeases God, therefore God forbids it to be done, therefore it is against the eternal law of GOD.*** All (as far as I know) acknowledge the truth of this proposition: ***whatever voluntary action repugns to the moral perfections of God qua such, that cannot not be morally evil, be sin***. All Moral Philosophers (if we except the Sceptics and patrons of indifferentism) hold these propositions as ***reciprocal***: ***whatever fights with God's perfection in the genus of morals is morally disordered and disconvenient with rational nature qua such***; and ***whatever is morally disordered and disconvenient with rational nature qua such fights with God's perfection in the genus of morals***.

Nay, if even most we could not provoke to the unanimous consent of Philosophers and Theologians, the thing itself would nevertheless speak thus. I pray let a reader free from affections and lover of solid erudition judge, what the cause is: that from this — that ***to be able to lie, to be able to fail in promise, to perjure fights with the perfection of God*** — rightly it is inferred that ***man sins if he lies***; and not likewise from this — that ***to be able to eat and drink fights with the perfection of God*** — is it permitted to infer that man sins if he eats, drinks.

All the sounder [thinkers] hitherto responded that the cause is the ***diversity or double difference of the perfections of God***. ***To eat, to drink*** fight with the ***natural*** perfections of God (e.gr. with ***spirituality***, as they call it), because these are actions which cannot be done except in the matter of that from which they are done. But ***to lie***, item ***to fail in promise, to perjure***, are acts fighting with the ***moral*** perfections of God. Added to this: no one of the more accurate Doctors can say that the ***doctrine on God's justice, veracity, sanctity*** etc. (item on ***divine promises, divine judgments***, etc.) per se pertains only to ***theoretic Philosophy***. If therefore it pertains per se to ***Moral Philosophy*** — and in species to the ***doctrine of the eternal law and to Theologia naturalis practica or moralis*** — shall we therefore recede from the received and common view, and no longer distinguish between ***physical and moral perfections of GOD***, lest the adversary have occasion further to cavil at received and necessary-to-know most-useful doctrines?

Surely whatever of perfection is attributed to God, in this sense is ***essential***, and is so called by all the sounder confessing this: inasmuch as from God it was neither received, nor could be received, but as to the matter is God Himself (and so the very essence of God) — though formally it be distinguished in God from His essence — nor does it lose the name of ***essential perfection*** whether of Metaphysical or Moral consideration. Nay rather, ***the actions of God ad extra*** also come under the name of perfections of God — now ***natural*** (as: to create, to conserve), now ***moral*** (as: to keep pacts entered with men, to punish crimes) — which perfections however in God are not essential in that sense in which ***veracity, justice, sanctity*** etc. were called essential.

**Secondly**, shall we accuse the adversary of ignorance or impudence when he asserts that ***by the usage of all Philosophers no perfection is called moral except that which is acquired by use and discipline, and inheres in the mind as a habit***? But this is the adversary's ***ψευδὲς*** (falsehood). As far as stands to me, ***by the usage of all more accurate Philosophers and Theologians, moral perfection is called every perfection which qua such is of moral consideration — which qua such is a principle of actions necessarily and per se convenient with rational nature***; nay rather, any necessary convenience of voluntary acts with rational nature qua such (so long as not of physical but of moral consideration) is counted under the name of ***moral perfection***. Indeed the adversary's ***jejuno sophistications*** smile upon those who hate or rodent-gnaw all solid Philosophy, and find easy approval with them; but the multitude of the rude does not win patronage for rudeness. Let it suffice that by all cultivators and Doctors of more accurate Philosophy and Theology these matters are otherwise treated and estimated.

And what finally would the adversary say if we denied ***sapientia*** to be a perfection of God, and that God is ill-called wise, since by the usage of Philosophers ***sapientia is a habit inhering in the mind, acquired by use and discipline***? Beyond doubt he will bid us distinguish between ***created and uncreated wisdom***, and will call this a ***jejune objectiuncula***. But let him take this to himself in place of response to his own objection. For here also has place the distinction between ***uncreated moral perfections (which are God's) and created moral perfections (which are men's)***.

Yet the adversary still has what to retort: for he says that lying (he assumes only this example) repugns to God not inasmuch as it is a ***moral*** imperfection, but inasmuch as it is a ***physical*** [imperfection]. But this is most false. For whatever of imperfection is in lying — by whose reason to God it repugns to be able to lie — thence takes its origin: because lying is ***disordered from the evil and disordered intention***. If you remove that ***fallendi intentionem*** (intention of deceiving) and substitute a good intention (such as: that another may be taught that what is uttered is false), then to utter the false or express it by sign is in no way evil, nor does it in any way repugn to God. Let it therefore stand fixed and in confession that lying repugns to God's perfection ***not of physical but in the genus of morals***.

In passing we add this (perhaps not without cause, but to more easily ***cover his dust***): the adversary substituted this question: ***Why can God not sin?*** — namely so that he might have what to say, that it is in vain to ask why God cannot sin (i.e. transgress a law borne by a Superior), since He does not have a Superior from whom law could be borne against Him. Meanwhile it is not [the case] that anyone should think, as if the decision of the question — ***Why can God not lie?*** — had no commerce with that: ***Why could God not form the Law of Nature in man otherwise than it now is?*** For altogether ***the truth of the latter is founded in the former***, since God could not condition the human rational nature except by this reason: that ***whatever repugns to God's truth, justice, and other perfections in the genus of morals must also disgrace the intelligent creature***; and in man as in God reason cannot approve anything, cannot dictate anything to be done which it has seen to repugn to moral perfections qua such (likewise to God's perfections in the genus of morals).

**[CAPUT X § 7 NOTE X CLOSES]**

#### § 8 — Possibile II: Phyicum vs Morale

> ***POSSIBILE (second division) is distinguished into PHYSICUM and MORALE. The former respects ***δύναμιν*** — potency as it is of PHYSICAL consideration (taking the notion of ***Physical*** in opposition to ***moral***). The latter respects ***ἐξουσίαν*** — potency as it is the object of MORAL estimation, or in one word called ***POTESTATEM***.***
>
> ***E.gr. ***physically*** possible to a robber is it to despoil and kill an innocent and unarmed traveller; ***morally*** possible to the innocent and unarmed traveller is it to defend his life by the robber's slaughter. Thence is easily learned what is called IMPOSSIBILE PHYSICUM and what IMPOSSIBILE MORALE: e.gr. ***morally impossible to a robber*** is it to despoil and kill an innocent and unarmed traveller; ***physically impossible to an unarmed and innocent traveller*** is it, by the slaughter of an armed and robust robber, to defend himself placed in danger of life.***

#### Note I — Usage of the Terms

This distinction is in received use both among Theologians and among all Doctors of every Law. The most convenient vocables are: ***δύναμις and ἐξουσία*** — ***potentia Physica and potentia moralis*** — although ***δύναμις*** is sometimes wont to be received in a wider sense, as it is distinguished into Physical and moral. The Latins, following the Greeks, distinguished between ***potentia and potestas***. Therefore what ***potentia*** and ***potestas*** signify in the abstract, that ***possibile Physicum*** and ***possibile Morale*** (and ***physice possibile*** and ***moraliter possibile***) signify in the concrete.

#### Note II — Scriptural Examples

The order of our institute advises illustrating each distinction between possible and impossible (both physical and moral) ***by examples***. And (1) it pleases to adduce ***examples drawn from the Sacred***:

**(a)** When it is said at ***Gen. XLIII:32***: ***"The Egyptians cannot eat bread with the Hebrews, because this is abomination"*** — that ***non possunt Aegyptii*** is nothing other than ***non licet ipsis*** (it is not permitted to them) stands both per se and from the context. ***Vatablus Interpres*** confirms this by his own calculus, when he thus expresses this place: ***"It was unlawful for the Egyptians to eat with the Hebrews, for they thought such a convivium a human thing."*** And ***B. Luther*** likewise most knowingly renders ***τὸ non poterunt*** as: ***"Sie dürfen nicht"*** (they are not permitted). And the thing itself speaks: that the words of the Holy Spirit should be received of ***possibile morale*** (not physico): for ***physically*** [they] could have, there is no doubt; but when they are said ***non posse***, it must be understood ***with religion saved, or even with law saved***.

**(b)** Another example of the same sense is supplied by ***Paul 1 Cor. X:21***, when he writes: ***οὐ δύνασθε, NON POTESTIS to drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons: NON POTESTIS to be partakers of the Lord's table and of the table of demons***. Well does ***Flacius*** pronounce that ***NON POTESTIS*** should be understood thus: ***"non potestis scilicet juste"*** (you cannot, namely justly). He adds in place of better explication the following: ***"For de facto they could, and in the thing itself were doing it exceedingly. Therefore the Apostle there speaks not of the IMPOSSIBILITY of fact, but of RIGHT."***

**(c)** Another example occurs at ***Acts X:47*** where Peter says: ***μήτι τὸ ὕδωρ κωλῦσαι δύναταί τις — can anyone forbid the WATER, that these not be baptized, who have received the Holy Spirit as we too?*** Which words ***Flacius*** interprets thus: ***"Can anyone forbid them water? i.e. ***not justly and licitly can he***, [although] otherwise de facto he can."***

**(d)** An evident example again is had at ***Acts XXV:9-11*** where Paul — with Festus obliquely urging him to present himself for judgment at Jerusalem (which forum, by appeal to Caesar, he was declining), — says: ***οὐδεὶς δύναταί με τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις χαρίσασθαι — Καίσαρα ἐπικαλοῦμαι — NO ONE CAN give me (understand "to those to whom Festus wished to gratify") — I appeal to Caesar***. By these words the Apostle denied Festus ***moral potency or potestas***, denied that it was ***morally possible*** for Festus to give him to the Jews — i.e. that it could not be done ***justly*** that an innocent be handed by Festus to his adversaries. For otherwise Festus altogether could do this, if we spoke not of ***moral potency and right*** but of ***physical potency and fact***.

**(e)** Thus ***2 Cor. XIII:8***: ***οὐ γὰρ δυνάμεθά τι κατὰ τῆς ἀληθείας, ἀλλὰ ὑπὲρ τῆς ἀληθείας — WE CANNOT [do] anything against the truth, but for the truth*** — namely ***by right and justly, with God approving***.

**(f)** Again at ***Prov. XX:9*** is read: ***"Who CAN say: I have cleansed my heart?"*** — i.e. ***who can truly affirm this?*** Also by these words is indicated ***MORALITER IMPOSSIBILE***, since what is ***truly*** affirmed is ***justly*** affirmed.

**(g)** And hither we also altogether refer the passages mentioned above at note 8 of preceding § 7, p. 604, when the ***Holy Spirit*** at ***2 Tim. 2:13*** expressly asserts: ***ἀρνήσασθαι ἑαυτὸν οὐ δύναται — God CANNOT deny Himself***. And at ***Hebr. 6:18***: ***ἀδύνατον ψεύσασθαι θεόν — IT IS IMPOSSIBLE FOR GOD TO LIE***. We do not doubt that of each place the sense is this: ***With His veracity and justice saved, God CANNOT deny Himself, cannot lie***. If God denied Himself, if He failed in promise, if He acted against oath, God would be ***unjust***, and so would ***not be God***. I rejoice to have in this [matter] the best and orthodox Interpreters of Sacred Scripture consenting with me — that this discourse is of those [matters] which do not fight with the ***physical*** perfections of God but fight with the ***moral*** perfections of God.

Well ***B. Scharff***, Theologian signally deserving of the orthodox Church of Christ, [says]: ***"They say — but [this is] profane error and ridiculous delirium of those who judge and say: 'If God commanded this or that, He would be unjust'; but they themselves seem to be in delirium when they write these things. They seem not to know what is the ***SYLLOGISM δι' ἀδυνάτου*** (through-the-impossible), of which Aristotle in ***Prior Analytics II***. Just as rightly I conclude: ***If man did not have a rational soul, he would not even be man***; so also rightly I conclude: ***If God willed falsehood, crime, injustice***, etc., ***He would be unjust, and so would not even be God***."*** See ***Cent. Illustr. quaest. Theolog. disp. 50 de prima causa et natura mali quaest. 7 p. 420***. Let be conferred, if it please, those things which in the ***Introduction to Hugo Grotius' Opus de Jure Belli et Pacis book 1 chap. 1 quaest. 1*** we disserted of these Holy-Spirit-assertions, from the mind and counsel of the Venerable Orthodox Theologians, from pp. 209 to 214.

#### § 8 Note III — Corpus Juris Civilis Examples

**III.** From Sacred Scripture we have just adduced [examples]; it pleases now (2) to adduce testimonies and examples from the ***Corpus of Civil Law***. For each notion — ***POSSIBILE*** and ***IMPOSSIBILE*** — both in the physical sense and in the moral sense, is of frequent and received usage in civil law. Thus:

- ***Emperor Justinian, L. curare 32 Inst. de actionibus***: ***"The Judge must take care, as far as POSSIBLE for him, to render his sentence of a certain money or thing — even if about an uncertain quantity it has been treated among us."***
- ***Feudorum lib. II tit. VI***: ***"He who swears fidelity to his lord must always have in memory these six: SAFE, JUST, HONEST, USEFUL, EASY, POSSIBLE."*** And shortly after: ***"Lest the good which was POSSIBLE for the lord he make IMPOSSIBLE."***
- ***Ulpian L. ea quae 135 D. de regulis juris***: ***"Those things which are IMPOSSIBLE to be given, or which are not in the nature of things, are held for not-adjoined."***
- ***L. 1 Inst. de inutilibus stipulationibus***: ***"If someone stipulates to give a thing which is not in the nature of things or cannot be — such as Stichus who is dead, whom he believed to live, or a hippocentaur which cannot be — the stipulation will be useless."***
- ***L. 11 eiusdem tit.***: ***"If an IMPOSSIBLE condition is adjoined to obligations, the stipulation is of no force. An IMPOSSIBLE condition is held [to be] that to which nature is impediment to its existing — as if someone said: 'If I touch the sky with my finger, do you promise to give?'"***
- ***Macianus L. non solum 31 D. de obligationibus et actionibus***: ***"Not only are stipulations applied to an IMPOSSIBLE condition of no moment, but also the other contracts (such as sales and leases) interposed with an IMPOSSIBLE condition are equally of no moment — because in a matter which is done from the consent of two or more, the will of all is to be looked at, whose thought in such an act doubtless is that nothing is being done, with that condition appended which they know to be IMPOSSIBLE."***
- ***Paul L. 3 D. quae sent. sine app. rescinduntur***: ***"Paul responded that an IMPOSSIBLE command of a judge is of no moment. He responded that from a sentence to which the nature of things could not comply, there was appeal without cause."***
- ***Julian L. haec conditio 19 D. de conditionibus et demonstrationibus***: ***"This condition — 'if he shall have ascended the Capitol' — is to be received thus: 'as soon as he SHALL BE ABLE to ascend the Capitol.'"***
- ***Ulpian L. conditionum 2 eod. tit.***: ***"Of conditions some are those which sometimes CAN be fulfilled even while the testator is living (for example, 'if a ship shall come from Asia'; for whenever the ship came, the condition is seen to have been complied with). Some are those which only after the testator's death — 'if he gives ten'; 'if he ascends the Capitol' — for that someone be seen to have complied with the condition, even after death the condition inserted must be fulfilled, for if he does it by [other-than-prescribed] fact, he is not seen to obey the will."***
- ***L. obtinuit 3 D. eod. tit.***: ***"It has obtained that IMPOSSIBLE conditions ascribed to wills be held for null."***
- ***Celsus L. impossibilium 185 D. de Regulis Juris***: ***"OF IMPOSSIBLE THINGS NO OBLIGATION HOLDS."***

By innumerable other laws the same could be confirmed. In passing we add: ***Labeo in L. mulier 20 D. de conditionibus institutionum*** and ***Julian L. ab omnibus 104 § in testamento 1 D. de legatis 1*** — Jurisconsults who, though excellent in Latin, avoided the word IMPOSSIBILE and said ***ἀδύνατον***. Yet ***Quintilian l. 5 c. 10*** and other Jurisconsults have used it, as from what has been adduced is clear.

#### § 8 Note IV — Papinian + Gothofredus on Moral Impossibility

**IV.** Although from what has just been adduced the discrimen between ***physice*** and ***moraliter possibile and impossibile*** can abundantly stand, it will nevertheless appear more clearly if we confirm the signification of ***moraliter possibile*** and ***moraliter impossibile*** by illustrious testimonies of Jurisconsults. A signal testimony furnish the words of ***Papinian L. filius 15 D. de conditionibus institutionum***: ***"The son who was in [paternal] power, written heir under a condition which the Senate or the Princes disapprove, invalidates the father's testament — as if the condition were not in his power. For: QUAE FACTA LAEDUNT PIETATEM, EXISTIMATIONEM, VERECUNDIAM NOSTRAM, ET (UT GENERALITER DIXERIM) CONTRA BONOS MORES FIUNT: NEC FACERE NOS POSSE CREDENDUM EST"*** (things which when done wound piety, estimation, our modesty, and — to speak generally — are done against good morals: THESE WE MUST NOT BE BELIEVED ABLE TO DO).

On which law ***Dionysius Gothofredus, Jurisconsult***, thus commentates: ***"IMPOSSIBLE things are called those which we cannot [do] except with disgrace, which we cannot [do] with reputation and estimation saved. ***Paria sunt: IMPOSSIBILE et TURPE; IN NOSTRA POTESTATE NON ESSE et IN AUSTUM*** (impossible and shameful are equal; and 'not in our power' and 'in disfavor' are equal)."***

The same [Gothofredus] on words of ***L. avus 79 L. pater 1 D. de jure dotium***: ***"The father in his son's name promised 100 as dowry 'when it was most convenient.' On this Servius is said to have responded that it is owed 'as soon as it can be given without turpitude and infamy.'"*** [Gothofredus] notes: ***"POSSE implies HONESTUM; we CANNOT do what we cannot HONESTLY do."***

Thus ***Ulpian L. si vinum 1 § licet 3 D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae***: ***"It is permitted to the seller to pour out the wine, if he set a day for measuring and within the day it is not measured out. He cannot however immediately pour out, before by witness-attested notice he indicates to the buyer either to take the wine or to know that the wine will be poured out. If however, WHEN HE WAS ABLE to pour out, he does not pour out — he is rather to be praised. On that account he also CAN exact the hire of the vessels — but only if it concerned him that the vessels (in which the wine was) be empty, as if he had been about to lease them, or if he had to hire other vessels."***

In such a case therefore for the seller each is ***morally possible***: namely, morally possible is it for him to pour out the wine or sell it to another, and preserve it in itself for the buyer's sake. Likewise morally possible for him (if, as he preserved [it], it nevertheless concerned him that the vessels be empty) is it to exact the hire of the vessels, or to grant the grace of the hire.

#### § 8 Note V — Moral Possibility: Libertas vs Necessitas

**V.** ***Moral possibility*** is again twofold. One is ***conjoined with moral LIBERTY***, the other ***conjoined with moral NECESSITY***. The former is wont to be called ***licentia*** (and, qua such — i.e. inasmuch as conjoined with moral necessity — considered, it also comes under the name of ***moral debitum***). Hither pertains the ***Moralists' distinction between LICITUM and DEBITUM***. The former is also wont to be called ***ius in sensu negante tantum***; the latter ***ius in sensu affirmante***. E.gr. ***to promise this or that*** says moral possibility conjoined with moral liberty — i.e. ***to promise this or that is LICITUM***. Contrariwise, with the promise once made, ***to stand by the promise*** says moral possibility conjoined with moral necessity — i.e. ***to stand by the promise is DEBITUM***.

Each signification egregiously expressed ***Emperor Valentinian*** to his soldiers (who had made him Emperor) demanding what he did not approve: ***"That you should choose me to the imperium was in your potestas, soldiers; but after you chose me, what you ask is in my arbitration, not yours. To you as subjects it belongs to obey; to me to consider what is to be done."*** Thus the Emperor — to signify that it was ***morally possible*** for the soldiers to choose the Emperor, morally possible for them to obey the chosen Emperor; the former ***licitum***, the latter ***debitum***.

To this looked the Doctors of every Law when they distinguished between those constitutions whose effect perpetually depends on the will of those constituting, and those which from the beginning are of the will but afterwards have the effect of necessity — as a woman constitutes a husband for herself, that it be necessary ever to obey him. An example of moral possibility conjoined with liberty supplied ***Ulpian L. si vinum 1 § licet 3 D. de periculo et commodo rei venditae***; to which from the Sacred Pandects can be added ***1 Cor. VII:38***: ***"He who gives his daughter in marriage does well; he who does not give her in marriage, does better."*** Likewise the Apostle, though he had ***potestas*** (equally with the other Apostles) of living from the Gospel and from the Church's upkeep, nevertheless thought it ***satius*** not to use this potestas, as he teaches at length in ***1 Cor. IX***; just as at the following chapter v. 23 [i.e. 1 Cor. 10:23] he writes: ***"All things to me are LICIT, but not all are expedient; all things to me are LICIT, but not all build up."***

#### § 8 Note VI — Moraliter Possibile = Respect to Law

**VI.** For the rest, from what has been said it is clear that ***moraliter possibile*** and ***moraliter impossibile*** both say respect to law. As therefore laws vary, so the notion of each in turn varies. And indeed, most especially and primarily the name ***LAW*** deserves ***the Law of Nature***; so most of all is called ***moraliter impossibile*** that which cannot be done with the Law of Nature saved. For what cannot be done with another law saved, cannot be done with the Law of Nature saved either — since the Law of Nature prescribes obedience to positive laws; and a positive law which with the Law of Nature cannot stand (if we estimate the matter morally) ***is not law***. Likewise ***moraliter possibile simpliciter*** will be called that which can be done with the Law of Nature saved — although many things come to be morally impossible ***ex hypothesi***, inasmuch as it happens that they are prohibited by positive laws, which to obey the Law of Nature prescribes.

#### § 8 Note VII — Moraliter Possibile Citra-Respectum-ad-Legem

**VII.** If ***LAW*** be taken precisely for ***a Superior to whom you are subjected***, by whose prescription that one composes his actions — then altogether it must be said that there is given moraliter possibile and moraliter impossibile ***citra respectum ad legem***. E.gr. ***to lie, to deny oneself, to fail in promise, to act against oath*** — in a sound and true sense are said to be ***moraliter impossibilia*** to God, because they necessarily repugn to veracity and justice (which are indeed of moral consideration). Nor is there doubt that moraliter possibilia and impossibilia can be considered also for the rational creature qua such ***citra respectum ad legem*** — of which we treated above at chapter 1 axiom I.

#### § 8 Note VIII — Moraliter Possibile cum Libertate as Impunitas

**VIII.** This also we count worthy of note: that sometimes ***moraliter possibile cum libertate*** in the Schools of the Politicians and in the civil forum is received in such a loose signification that it comes under that name which indeed ***non licet***, yet with ***impune*** (as far as ***impune*** is the same as without danger of human penalty) it is ***LICIT***. Hither pertains that ***rule of Right*** which ***Paul the Jurisconsult*** commends at ***L. non omne 144 D. de regulis juris***: ***"Not everything that is permitted is honest."*** Civil laws sometimes do not render true right to a person but only ***impunity among men***. For there is no doubt that either kind of law can be made in certain cases; whether the former or the latter is willed must be understood partly from the law's words, partly from its matter. For if the law indulges only to grief, it removes the human penalty, not the vice — as in a husband who kills an adulteress wife or adulterer.

Also in this sense ***licit*** (as namely ***licentia*** notes mere impunity among men) has its ***degrees***. For the example of the highest licentia is the one supplied by ***Julia the stepmother to Antoninus Caracalla***, exposing her bosom; and when he said: ***"Vellem si liceret"*** (I would, if it were permitted), she responded: ***"Si libet, licet"*** (If it pleases, it is permitted). ***Spartianus in Antonino Caracalla***.

#### § 8 Note IX — Luke 9:1 δύναμιν et ἐξουσίαν Conjoined

**IX.** So much on this distinction between ***possibile physicum*** and ***possibile morale***. These notions ***δύναμις*** and ***ἐξουσία*** (in order to which they were defined) are of such frequent use. A notable place is at ***Luke IX:1***, where the Evangelist conjoins each notion: ***"Jesus called the twelve disciples, and gave them δύναμιν καὶ ἐξουσίαν — potency and potestas — over all demons, and that they might heal sicknesses."*** But of these and other significations of each notion (received in Theology and in every branch of Law) occasion to treat will be given in its place in the subsequent doctrine on the ***efficient cause and active potency***.

#### § 9 — Various Looser Significations of Possibile

> ***(III) Still various significations of ***possibile*** are given, confirmed likewise by use. Thus possibile sometimes is taken so loosely that itself (because it can be) is contained in the number of possibles. Not rarely ***possibile*** is the same as ***EASY, PLEASING, DECOROUS, CONVENIENT***, to which is opposed ***impossibile*** inasmuch as it signifies nothing other than ***DIFFICULT, TROUBLESOME, UNBECOMING, DISCONVENIENT***. These significations in the meantime, and several others, we now leave to their place.***

#### Note I — Scriptural Examples

Everywhere significations of this kind find approval in the Sacred [Scriptures]. It pleases to confirm this by one or two examples.

**(a)** ***Mark VI:5*** writes: ***οὐκ ἠδύνατο ἐκεῖ δύναμιν ποιῆσαι — HE COULD NOT there (Christ in His own country) do any virtue, except that laying hands on a few sick, He healed them.*** Was the hand of the Lord ***abbreviated***, or did the potency of doing miracles ***desert*** Christ among His own? ***Away with that!*** Therefore ***NON POTUISSE*** is said of what ***conveniently and without taedium He could not among incredulous men*** — and among whom He was in no honor, as from the preceding v. 4 is clear.

**(b)** Likewise at ***Luke XI:7*** the richer-man responds: ***"Trouble me not: the door is already closed, and my children are with me in bed; οὐ δύναμαι ἀναστὰς δοῦναι σοι — I CANNOT, rising, give to you."*** Absolutely speaking he could rise and give — but since he had given himself to rest with his own, and so all were closed, ***it was not CONVENIENT and FITTING for him***. He said therefore ***non posse*** of what ***conveniently and without molestation he could not***. More examples of Scripture we need not and have not leisure to adduce.

#### Note II — Juridical Examples

Nor indeed are there lacking Juridical examples.

**(a)** Perfectly to this makes ***L. Nepos Proculo 125 D. de verborum significatione***. ***Nepos*** writes to his Proculus: ***"From him who thus has promised you dowry — 'when it will be CONVENIENT, there will be for you a hundred gold-pieces of my daughter's dowry' — do you think dowry can be sought immediately on the marriage? And what if he had promised: 'CUM POTUERO (when I SHALL BE ABLE) will there be for dowry?' If the latter obligation has some force — the word POSSIT, how is it to be interpreted: whether with the alien-debt deducted, or [debt] standing?"***

***Proculus*** responds: ***"When someone has thus promised dowry — 'CUM POTUERO, there will be for you 100 of dowry' — I think the interpretation is to be reduced to what was done. For he who speaks ambiguously speaks what from those [things] which are signified, he felt. It is nearer, however, that I think he felt this: 'with the alien-debt deducted, I shall be able.' That signification can also be accepted: 'with my dignity saved, I shall be able.' Which interpretation is the more to be received, if it had been thus promised: 'when it will be convenient — i.e. when without inconvenience to me, I shall be able.'"***

The ***Gloss*** has the following: ***"And the promisor is understood to BE ABLE with alien-debt deducted. Otherwise, with alien-debt not deducted, the promissor is given [to be able]. For he who cannot except dishonestly does not seem to BE ABLE."***

**(b)** Thus ***Alciatus in his commentary***: ***"When someone promises himself about to give — 'WHEN HE SHALL BE ABLE' — we moderate the promise by interpretation, since he does not seem to have promised what he can do with highest inconvenience. When the Roman Pontiff says he CANNOT dispense, it is understood: 'except from just cause.' When he affirms NON POTUISSE his neighbors to be ignorant of what came to his notice, we take 'NON POTUIT' — i.e. ***NON POTUISSE is presumed***."***

**(c)** ***L. puto 1 D. de haeredibus instituendis***: ***"I think it is rightly generally defined: whether a condition was in his power, or not — if there is such a power. For this can be: 'if he shall arrive at Alexandria' — not to be in his arbitration; it can also be: if it was imposed on him who dwells at the first mile from Alexandria. It can also be: 'if he gives ten to Titius' — be in a difficult [state], if Titius travels on a long journey. For which reasons recourse must be had to the general definition."*** Cf. ***L. cum servus 39 et seqq.***

Hence also ***"difficile pene impossibile"*** is said by ***Ulpian at L. si familia 95 D. familiae erciscundae***.

**(d)** Perhaps to this (in its own mode) you may draw the response once given by the Andrians to Themistocles demanding money. For when he alleged that the Athenians were supported by two great Deities — ***Persuasion*** (***suadela***) and ***Necessity*** — those responded: ***"The island of the Andrians is never deserted by just so many propitious Deities, but these ever inhabit it — POVERTY and IMPOSSIBILITY. Obnoxious to these Deities, we shall not give money: for never shall the potency of the Athenians be stronger than the Andrians' IMPOSSIBILITY."*** ***Herodotus lib. 8 num. 217 p. 484***.

— ❦ —

#### § 9 Note III — Impossibile Ratione Existentiae vs Ratione Essentiae

**III.** If any further distinction of ***impossibile*** merits notice, it is that by which there is distinguished ***impossibile ratione EXISTENTIAE, EXERCITII seu CONTRADICTIONIS*** from ***impossibile ratione ESSENTIAE, SPECIEI seu CONTRARIETATIS***.

E.gr. it is asked: ***Is it simpliciter and absolutely impossible that adultery not be shameful?*** We respond ***affirming it***. There is one who, though the unanimous consent of Philosophers, Jurisconsults and Theologians approves this assertion, ***accuses it of stupidity and impiety*** — inasmuch as (he thinks) it ***removes God Most Good Most Great from the office of Creator***. For with this standing — that human acts are given which cannot not be shameful — he asserts as consequence that God in no way created man by free will.

Thus he [the censor]: ***"All confess that God, as all things, so also man, created by freest will. To which it is consequent that it was in His beneplacitum what nature He willed to assign to man. By what reason therefore can there belong to the action of man some affection which emanates from intrinsic and absolute necessity, outside the imposition of DIVINE beneplacitum? So that really all motions and actions of man, with every law removed (both divine and human), are indifferent; and some of them are called 'naturally honest or shameful' only on this account: that the condition of nature (which the Creator freely attributed to man) most required them to be done or omitted."***

Elsewhere: ***"God can form the law of nature thus and not otherwise, supposing the creation of a rational animal — which there is no one who does not ascribe to the freest will of God."*** Item: ***"That certain things are said necessarily impossible to man in the genus of morals — this must always be understood with relation to the nature of man as a rational and social animal, and consequently with relation to the will of GOD, which (as all things, so also man as such an animal) created by His freest will."***

Nay rather, on account of these [considerations], he does not hesitate to call the dogmas (by which it is handed down that it is simpliciter and absolutely impossible for God to form the law of nature otherwise than it now is — [and] that these propositions: ***adultery, homicide, theft are not shameful*** are simpliciter and absolutely impossible) ***frigid, most stupid, foul, most unjust, and horribly blasphemous***.

But what is easier than ***to wipe away the fogs cast over the true and (among all the sounder) received view***? Surely by employing ***one single distinction*** — which ought to have been known to any beginners — the whole difficulty expires. For when e.gr. it is said that it is simpliciter and absolutely impossible that ***adultery not be shameful***, that man not be bound by the Law of Nature by which now he is bound, that God does not bear the Law of Nature to man — this (as not even the boys of Metaphysics and Logic are ignorant) must be understood of ***simpliciter and absolute impossibile NOT by reason of EXISTENCE, EXERCISE, or CONTRADICTION, but by reason of ESSENCE, SPECIES, or CONTRARIETY***.

What then does our ***egregious censor*** [mean]: ***"Impossibility (he says) is not absolute but hypothetical, presupposing namely the creation of rational and social animal, which there is no one who does not ascribe to the freest will of God"***? As if the ***supreme man, Hugo Grotius*** (and all Theologians, Jurisconsults, and Philosophers) denied creation to be a free action of God! He has reduced the censor to such ineptitudes that he dares to discourse on absolute and hypothetical impossibility, when he does not even understand what discrimen there is between them. Let him then suffer himself to be taught this by us (or rather by all Logicians and Metaphysicians); or if he refuse, let him cease to lacerate with invectives those matters he does not understand. Let him not laugh at what he still must learn.

E.g. who is so inept, that having heard this assertion — ***"These propositions: 'homo est animal rationale'; 'ignis est calidus' — are propositions absolutely and simpliciter impossible"*** — would dare so to collect: ***"Therefore the defenders of this assertion do not ascribe the creation of rational animal and most-hot element to the freest will of GOD, and remove God from the office of Creator"***? Everyone knows ***in actu*** there is not (nor exists) rational animal, most-hot element, unless man and fire be freely created by God. But here is no question of ***impossibility of existence, exercise, or contradiction***, since it is not asked: ***"Is it simpliciter impossible that rational animal and most-hot element not exist?"*** For man ***actu*** would be rational animal, fire ***actu*** would be most-hot element, even if they were not made by God. But the question is of this: ***"Is it simpliciter impossible that a being of such essence or species be given, which we rightly and properly call man or fire, which is nevertheless not rational animal or most-hot element?"***

Nor is it [permitted] to object that these [examples] are not of ***moral consideration, but physical***, while here the discourse is of predicates and affections not physical but moral. Can you believe that a man can simulate such ***stupor***? Namely: just because when we say ***"fire is hot"*** here is no question of action (which could be referred to law) nor of moral predicate; while when we assert ***"adultery is shameful"*** here is discussion of an action (which the Law of Nature stands to prohibit) and of ***turpitude as a moral affection*** — on this account, I say, shall these two no longer converge in one third [respect], so that just as ***simpliciter and absolute impossibile*** remains it that fire not be hot — not by impossibility of existence, exercise, or contradiction, yet by impossibility of essence, species, or contrariety — so also ***simpliciter and absolute impossibile*** remain it that adultery not be shameful? Not by impossibility of existence, exercise, or contradiction (for if it plainly does not exist, neither does it exist shameful — just as fire, if it plainly did not exist, neither would exist hot nor cold); yet by that impossibility (as they call it) of ***essence, species, or contrariety***.

What then of acumen or ***ὀξύνοιας*** (sharp-wit) is in these words: ***"That Velthemius substituted another question to which this Metaphysical term does not fit — the fault is no fault of mine"***? What of candor or prudence in this assertion: ***"What follows, if most greatly, I accepted some Scholastic term otherwise than has been sanctioned by Stahlian tablets as if by eternal law of the Parcae?"*** Not only Stahl but ***all the erudite hitherto*** have now accepted the term otherwise than this new censor.

And what of probity, finally, in this utterance: ***"Was it however fitting on this account to insult a MAN in such acerb manner? Was it only to raise tumult, as if the salvation of Church and Republic were in question?"*** Was not he first — he who said that the view by which those propositions (***Adultery is shameful***; ***To worship God is honest***) are called simpliciter and absolutely necessary, and conversely those propositions (***adultery is not shameful***; ***to worship God is not honest***) are called simpliciter and absolutely impossible — ***was than which nothing more stupid could be feigned; from which a horrible absurdity follows, so that he (the censor) often marveled that not Grotius alone, but many of our Theologians, admitted that assertion everywhere without any doubt***? And how do these [his later soothing words] agree with those: ***"What they think or do not think, concerns me nothing"***?

#### § 9 Note IV — Examples of Impossibilia ratione Contradictionis

**IV.** Meanwhile it is easy for one desiring [them] to exhibit examples of ***impossibilia ratione existentiae, exercitii seu contradictionis***.
