Thus these propositions: ***God is impotent; God is finite***; etc.; ***God is unjust; God is a liar***, etc., are not only impious but also ***simpliciter and absolute impossibiles***, both with respect to contradiction and with respect to contrariety. Likewise this proposition: ***idem simul est et non est*** (the same simultaneously is and is not) is simpliciter and absolute impossibilis, both with respect to contrariety and with respect to contradiction.

Perhaps to this makes the example supplied by ***Marcianus the Jurisconsult*** at ***L. si Titius 16 D. de conditionibus institutionum***: ***"If Titius will be heir, let Seius be heir; if Seius will be heir, let Titius be heir. ***Julian writes the institution is useless, since the condition cannot exist***."*** Another perhaps exhibits ***Pomponius L. si Titius 9 D. de verborum obligationibus***, where that is said to be perplexed and so ***impossible***: ***"If I promise you a farm, if I shall not have given it to Titius; and I promise the same farm to Titius, if I shall not have given it to you."*** Similar to which is this case: ***"Titius has promised by oath to give Caius 100, if Sempronius shall not likewise give him the same. But also Sempronius has sworn to give Caius 100, if Titius gives him nothing at all. For since these conditions perpetually recur upon themselves, they cannot seem to have an exit."***

**[CAPUT X CLOSES]**

## Caput Undecimum

### Of the Metaphysical Notion of Cause — Its Genuine Discrimen from the Analytic Notion. Likewise of CAUSA VIRTUALIS, as it is Called

#### § 1

> ***The notion of CAUSE is TWOFOLD: one METAPHYSICAL, the other ANALYTIC. The former was expounded above in chapter VIII, when CAUSA IN COMMUNI was called "that WHENCE ANOTHER IN ITS BEING PROCEEDS." The latter is the ***RATIO A PRIORI*** by which an ***ANALYTIC RESPONSE TO A SCIENTIFIC QUESTION*** (that is, a solid and in-all-numbers absolute proof) can and must — from the whole — satisfy one desiring it.***

#### Notes

**I.** This matter must be treated by us the more diligently because — when less understood — it has produced all ***ἀκρίβειαν*** (loss of precision) and has left so many perverse estimators and cultivators of every genus of doctrine. And this will be able to stand in the progress of this chapter: that of this twofold notion rightly and solidly perceived, those also must be especially solicitous who affect ***solid erudition and moral and political science***, and so of the universal prudence of natural law and of nations (that I say nothing of the science of civil law and of Theology). Chiefly for this reason are such [matters] here treated by us.

Also in Morals and Politics (namely) ***tum demum vere aliquid scimus, quando rei cujusque moralis et civilis causam plene cognoscimus*** — then at length do we truly know something, when we know the cause of each moral and civil matter plainly — as judges ***Hermann Conring***, man of greatest judgment, in his golden book ***De Prudentia Civili c. 10 p. m. 200***. ***"As in other sciences, so in Morals and Politics all things have themselves most well, when we understand the causes of moral duties and civil events through DEMONSTRATIONS"*** (p. 206). ***"If you except the one question AN SIT (whether it is), all the rest in the single disciplines (even in Morals and Politics) treat either of all those four causes in general, or of some of them. For when it is asked AN QUID EXISTAT (whether anything exists), it is not immediately asked of some one of the causes: whence this question can be expedited even by an effect or by some sign only received. Such questions in Morals and Politics are rarer: of others there is an immense number"*** (p. 209). ***"Besides questions on causes, no [question] of moral and political use can be adduced in Morals and Politics; and whatever question falls, by no difference of time, inquires about all or some cause. Likewise every doubt is at least of some cause: ever however I except the question or doubt whether a thing is. To questions all consultation also is to be numbered. For although not every question is consultation, consultation is nevertheless question. For he who consults asks."*** And p. 214: ***"Suitable principles for demonstration and solid doctrine are not readily at hand, but only ***verisimilia*** — which however most well and conveniently can be sought from the places of each cause. Thus indeed ***probabilis collationes*** can be most greatly akin to demonstrations. Which to observe is in truth's interest."*** See the whole chapter X of the praised book.

The same must be judged of the solid doctrines of Theologians and Jurisconsults — which Doctors of Theology and Jurisprudence endowed with more accurate judgment will not unwillingly pronounce.

**II.** The former notion — namely the ***METAPHYSICAL*** of cause in common — we expounded in the said superior chapter. And since it is of interest to the students of any discipline and Faculty, especially of those Faculties which vulgarly are called ***superior***, we approach the latter notion of cause in common — i.e. the ***ANALYTIC*** — to dwell on its explication somewhat longer.

Since in Analytics cause (as we just said) is called the ***GENUINE AND SOLID RATIO*** by which a Doctor can satisfy from the whole an Auditor seeking solid science, and generate solid science in his mind: before we teach what kind that ratio should be, there must altogether be premised something about the ***QUAESTIO*** itself. For if to the Auditor asking there be responded such a ratio (which the Masters of Analytics call ***CAUSA***), the Doctor who responds is judged to have solidly taught; the auditor to whom he responds is judged to have solidly learned; each is judged able to congratulate himself on solid erudition and science.

For whoever seeks ***solid information***, desires the ***scientia*** of the question (or, if you prefer thus to speak, of that which is in question). For if to the question (before being informed) he had known how to respond rightly and solidly (i.e. ***through CAUSA analytically taken***), there would have been no cause why he sought information. The Auditor prepared to respond to questions in the manner of a Doctor is said to have ***completed the numbers of his own perfection***. Where there is no place for question, there is place neither for solid doctrine, information, or science. For although not every question is scientific, science nevertheless ***pre-supposes question***.

**III.** Before all things therefore let it be observed that ***every question is absolved by these two things***: by that ***which is asked***, and that ***about which it is asked*** — i.e. (as the Schools love to speak) by ***PRAEDICATUM and SUBJECTUM***. One must beware (as elsewhere, so also in practical disciplines) that none take the terms (from which questions are made) ***as he will***, but ***as usage permits*** — which is the arbiter, right, and norm of speech. For who will compel those loving solid moral or political science to be bound (as regards the mere intelligence of a question) to accept terms in a signification which someone has previously fashioned according to his own arbitration? Only so that to him who would play with new acceptances of terms, the spur must be added that he not be heard. Let him speak in the usual [way], and in [the manner] which the men most expert and most prudent in this science have received, approved, and preserved — modestly, if he will be heard and understood, if he will not be led into suspicion of insidious contention over modes of speaking or other machination.

Of ***things*** are questions made, not of terms; we use terms in questions only ***as notes of things***, as ***Aristotle*** cleverly discourses in ***1 Elench. Sophist. c. 1***. Let us therefore use terms as the ***usage of speech*** (lord and best master) admits. And since we rightly rejoice that this is the common view of all (who teach true Analytics and love solid philosophy — also of all our Preceptors; nay of whomever prefers to be solidly erudite rather than to seem, as could easily be shown by invoking the suffrages of the prudent of each faculty), we are sure of this: if anyone has imposed on words and questions an inconvenient and in-no-use-received signification, he will experience at his own peril (and perhaps not without anxiety) how perilously full of hazard a work he undertakes, if first he will escape the just censure of the Logicians, and avoid the mark of ***ἀπαιδευσίας*** (ill-education); practically, if the question be moral, [to escape] from the moral forum.

For Grammarians use their own terms, moral Philosophers theirs — and this indeed is common to nearly all arts, as ***Cicero*** most truly says in ***Academicarum primo***. Beware also that none use ***terms savoring of the barbarism of an unhappy age*** without necessity or scholarly profit. In general however it must be noted and firmly held that ***such predicates must be as are permitted by their subjects, and such subjects as are permitted by their predicates***.

**IV.** These are the matters on questions, whose parts must be previously known so that (elsewhere as also in Morals and Politics, in Theology and Law) Doctors and Auditors know what is to be taught and learned. For questions and responses do not differ as to matter and terms: for the same parts which are of the question, are of the response.

Thus a ***moral question*** on the ***obligation which arises from the nature of a promise***: ***An promissa naturaliter, seclusis pactis ac legibus, quae volunt duas partes concordare, obligent?*** (Do promises naturally — pacts and laws (which wish two parties to agree) excluded — oblige?) — i.e.: ***An huic actui, quo servare quis promissum dicitur, insit necessitas moralis adeo, ut per se ac suapte natura sit debitus absoluteque necessarius in genere morum?***

Let the ***political question*** be on the ***citizen primarily and simpliciter so-called***, whether the right of suffrages is owed him — i.e. ***num in civitate, cujus socius est, suffragiorum particeps esse debeat?*** — such that he is not a true citizen unless he be admitted to public deliberations with suffrages?

If to these questions an erudite and prudent Master of Morals should put forth these to Ethics and Politics students, or in their favor he himself move them, in the matter and in the terms the responses to such questions do not differ from the questions. For these are the questions: ***An promissa ex natura sua obligent?*** and ***An civis debeat esse suffragiorum particeps?*** The responses: ***Promissa ex natura sua obligant***, and ***Civis debet esse suffragiorum particeps***. The same terms of questions, the same of responses; the same matters signified on each side.

This discrimen is permitted to observe: no question affirms or negates anything; response, however, formally affirms or negates, since it is a formal affirmation or negation. Likewise no question is formally true or false; every response, however, is formally either true or false — and indeed a ***solid response is true***.

**V.** Responses therefore are ***propositions which affirm or negate (truth-saved) that which was in the question***. It merits further to be noted: analytic responses are not accommodated to scientific questions or to auditors wishing science, unless they are (as ***Piccartus*** speaks) ***LARDATAE*** — i.e. ***brought forth together with the RATIO***. For here most of all has place what the Philosophers say: ***veritas non pendet a subjecto, sed ab objecto***. Of whatever erudition and authority the one is who responds to the proposed question — if he respond without the genuine and solid ratio adjoined — he leaves no demonstrative scientia, and therefore no doctrine and no solid erudition, in the auditor's mind; nor does he rightly fulfill the office of a genuine doctor. The same is proved by the authority of the Logicians: for ***arguments destitute of art*** are called by them those arguments ***not drawn from the question itself, but extrinsically assumed*** — of whatever authority the argument finally sustain the office.

#### Note VI — Ratio Must Be Propria (Syllogism-Formable)

**VI.** And this ratio — with which a proposition must stand, that it be called a ***solid response*** (satisfying the auditor from the whole) — we have at present called ***CAUSA***, and have in our mode determined. But that the analytic notion of CAUSA may better be understood, let us somewhat more accurately say how it should be constituted.

And first indeed in place (and this especially of all merits notice): this ratio must be ***PROPRIA***. That ratio we call ***propria*** which has itself so that it ***can be included in a syllogism*** (we say: ***can be included*** — whether it be included or not. For to include all rationes in syllogisms (though possible) is not however absolutely necessary, nor usual, nor becoming — since it would seem to argue that he for whose sake syllogizations are instituted is of slow wit and less exercised). The ratio must be such that ***its effect*** (i.e. the conclusion or response adduced by the Doctor) is such that the ***syllogism*** (which here signifies the same as the ***premises*** — for it is part of the syllogism, as from Logic is clear, [whereas] the conclusion is not [part of the syllogism]) pertains to the ***same genus of doctrine*** as the conclusion.

For example: We said above that a scientific moral question is this: ***An promissum ex sua natura obliget?*** The Moral Doctor responds scientifically when he responds: ***"Altogether a promise by its own nature obliges, because to the ***promissee*** (as they call him — the one to whom the promise was made) by the promise qua such a right has been acquired against the promisor."***

Now if, in favor of the less-exercised cultivator of Morals, we reduce the ratio into syllogistic form, it will easily appear to anyone that it is ***propria***. Let the argument be such:

> **Major**: ***From whatever qua such — all pacts and positive laws excluded — a right has been acquired to another, this [thing] by its nature obliges him against whom the right has been acquired.***
> **Minor**: ***But from a promise qua such — all pacts and positive laws excluded — against the promisor to the one to whom the promise was made a right has been acquired.***
> **Ergo**: ***a promise by its nature obliges the promisor.***

The ***Major*** rests on the principle of natural right most known per se: ***"Unicuique suum ius tribuendum est"*** — and so the Major by itself pertains to the Moral [sphere].

The ***Minor***, as it is proper to moral philosophy, can be sufficiently proved from it, perhaps in the following mode:

> **Major**: ***By a sufficiently signified will, a right to transfer right has been acquired.***
> **Minor**: ***But by a promise qua such a will is sufficiently signified.***
> **Ergo**: ***from a promise qua such a right against the promisor to transfer right has been acquired.***

The ***Major*** is vulgarly said to be of natural right. For it is in the very nature of right (full right, namely) that he who has it can transfer it, in whole or in part. ***Of natural right*** it is in this sense: that of this right ***reductively*** (as the ***Schools*** love to speak) are said to be those [matters] also to which natural right does not repugn.

Now again we could argue:

> **Major**: ***Into whomever by a sufficiently signified will a right has been transferred, to him by a sufficiently signified will against another a right to transfer right has been acquired.*** (For from singular experiments of rights, by induction made, it is clear: he who justly can the greater, can also the lesser which is comprehended under the greater. He who therefore can transfer right, why could he not transfer the right of transferring right?)
> **Minor**: ***But into another (e.gr. the ***donatarius***, as they call him) by sufficiently signified will — e.gr. by donation — right has been transferred, all admitting this, especially if the delivery of the thing has acceded.***
> **Ergo**: ***against another (e.gr. the ***promissee***, as they name him) by sufficiently signified will (namely by PROMISSION), a right to transfer right has been acquired.***

A ***promission*** indeed signifies nothing other than ***the signification of our will made about a future thing for another's sake***, and it is absolute in all its degrees and numbers, giving to the other (namely, him to whom the promise was made) ***full right*** to exact the promised from the promisor (whether willing or unwilling).

For either the promise was ***to give*** or was ***to do***. The former says a right to alienate the thing; the latter argues a right to alienate liberty or a particle of it.

There are given however also promises such that ***obligation be in the promisor and no right in the promissee***— i.e. of such a nature that they oblige indeed the promisor, so that he (natural equity saved) cannot change his will, nor however can the one who promised be compelled by natural right to fulfill his pledge, nor can from such promission the promisor's thing be retained against his will — which vulgarly are called ***promissa secundi gradus***.

What of this: that someone could have promised with ***the right of changing his will reserved to himself*** — just as often a testator reserves to himself the right of changing his will (and not rarely changes it, with the rules of moral duties saved) — which [promises] are called ***promissa primi gradus***. And they scarcely merit the name of promissions, since for them, that they be free of vice, the ***veritas cogitationis*** suffices.

#### Note VII — The Full Political Example

**VII.** So much on the moral example of ***propriae*** propositions. Let us assume the other (and that a political). The question was: ***Num civis debeat esse particeps suffragiorum in civitate?*** This response: ***"Altogether he ought to be partaker of suffrages"*** (which however is not to be received as if all citizens of all businesses ought to bear suffrages, since this would require both immense labor and more leisure than falls promiscuously on any; but there can be committed by citizens, in some businesses — especially of lesser moment — the ***power to some persons*** of defining and deciding, who armed with that authority represent the whole people).

The reason why the citizen ought to be partaker of suffrages in the city is given thus: ***because he is bound by means and counsel to help the salvation of the city with his powers***.

Now if you include this ratio in a syllogism, you will find the premises as well as the conclusion to be of altogether one and the same genus of doctrine. The argument will be such:

> **Major**: ***Whoever is bound to help the salvation of the city by means and counsel according to his powers, he must be partaker of the suffrages of the city.***
> **Minor**: ***But the citizen is bound to help the salvation of the city by means and counsel according to his powers.***
> **Ergo**: ***the citizen must be partaker of the suffrages of the city.***

Each of the premises is most easily proved — nor indeed can it be proved from elsewhere, except from the genus of Political doctrine. The ***Major*** rests on this ***Political axiom***: ***NECESSITAS FINIS FACIT IUS IN POLITICIS*** (the necessity of the end makes right in Politics) — or (what returns to the same): ***he who has right to the end, has also right to the means altogether and simpliciter necessary to that end***. For those matters which lead to an end in moral matter take their intrinsic estimation from the end itself. Hence those things necessary for pursuing the end of right (necessity taken not according to physical subtlety but ***morally***) — to those we are understood to have right. But in what way will he give aid to the Republic who is ignorant of its diseases? And in what way would someone be heard as a member of Society, who were not admitted to the stating of judgment on things pertaining to the Society? The ***Roman plebs***, before it was admitted to suffrages and honors, complains at ***Livius ch. 35*** that it was not permitted to it to be in the ***consortio*** or ***societas*** of the Republic.

The ***Minor*** proposition likewise can be sufficiently taught [as being] proper to Politics. For civil society is instituted ***for guarding tranquility***, and the true citizen is bound to turn all his effort, thoughts, goods, and finally even his blood for the use of his city — as from every example of society entered among men is clear. The more therefore and more a citizen is able to help the salvation of the city with his means and counsel, the more and more does he deserve the name of ***perfect citizen***.

Many indeed there are (and among them most-learned Men) who, so far from holding this ratio for ***genuine and propria***, utterly reject it — judging that the right of suffrages can be absent from citizens. But these indeed will scarcely be able to escape every mark of ***ἀπαιδευσίας*** (ill-education). For to one well-versed in Analytics it must be known that ***citizen*** is in the number of the ***commons to one (πρὸς ἕν)***, and indeed of those about which ***Grotius*** writes it is most certain: the name of the ***genus*** often peculiarly adheres to the ***species*** (especially to the more-excellent). The Analytics express it thus: ***"Commune absolute positum stat in significatu famosiori"*** (A common thing absolutely placed stands in the more-famous signification). Therefore it was not asked ***of citizen taken in any way***, whether he must be partaker of suffrages, but of ***the perfect citizen complete in all his numbers***. For those who do not know how to attain this ratio look not so much at the thing itself and the perfection of citizen defined by ***Aristotle***, as at the ***norm of their own city*** or even at the ***vulgarly-used custom of speaking***. To not a few certainly the state of the Roman Republic has imposed: so that deceived by its splendor and magnitude, they have not blushed to vend ***its morals as common and universal precepts***.

#### Note VIII — The Difficulty of Unius Generis + Medium Terminum as Form

**VIII.** Now we would progress to the other requisites — did we not fear that a difficulty may press the reader (and perhaps has pressed many hitherto, more than that we strive to remove it according to our strength). The plan of our institute demands [this]. Namely, we have taught thus to be constituted: that ratio which is adduced (either elsewhere or in Morals and Politics) can be called ***CAUSA*** in the Analytics, if it be ***propria*** — i.e. such that reduced to Syllogistic form, it argues such a syllogism as is proper (i.e. whose premises and conclusion ***per se, not per accidens***, pertain to one and the same genus of doctrine).

Here there is present a difficulty perhaps not easily expedited: namely, whence can it sufficiently stand that the premises and conclusion are of one and the same genus? For commonly in the Schools, to the question — ***"Whence can Auditors and Doctors in Analytics know PRIUS the things which were adduced and perceived to be ***propria***?"*** — it is wont to be responded that this stands from this: if the premises and conclusion are of one and the same genus. But they leave this difficulty: ***whence stands it that the premises and conclusion are of one and the same genus?*** For this is ***πρότερον-ὕστερον*** (prior-posterior reversal); and prior indeed must have been defined this very [point] — namely, whence it stands that the premises and conclusion are of the same genus.

And the more intimately this question must be weighed, inasmuch as its happy or unhappy decision has hitherto been (and still can be) the mother of so many inequities and iniquities — as no one wishing rightly to estimate solid erudition and solid Academic studies fails to see. For whence [come] so many complaints, so many indignations, so many often sinister judgments — while one lays complaints about the faulty leaps of another from genus to genus, flinging them back and forth; the other accuses the former of ***πολυπραγμοσύνης*** (meddling) and curiosity, that he has exceeded the limits of his object and sent his sickle into another's harvest, or danced outside the choruses? Whence you may see bitterness of minds, hatreds, contentions. By the solid and right decision of this question it could be provided that no just complaint could be — for everyone has what to attend to at home.

Whoever sedulously weighs the nature of ***conclusion*** easily admits that it has this (that it is conclusion) ***a priori***, whence conclusion is vulgarly called ***effectus syllogismi*** (as here saying ***praemissas***). But premises have (this, that they are premises) from no other source than ***from that RATIO which stands in the place of the MIDDLE TERM, as it is known as middle term***. Just therefore as premises and conclusion (this, that they are premises and conclusion) have [it] from the ***middle term***; likewise this, that they are ***TRUE premises and TRUE conclusion***: so [it is] consequent to this that, if you wish to judge rightly of the whole syllogism (as it says premises and conclusion together), whether it stand from ***propria*** — you must judge from the ***medium terminum***. Just as this syllogism is ***per se moral***, whose middle term per se pertains to ***Moral Philosophy*** and thence was sought; this ***political***, whose middle term per se [pertains] to ***Political Philosophy***; this ***Theological, Juridical***, etc., whose middle term per se is drawn from ***Theology or Jurisprudence***.

#### Note IX — The Three Propositions: Medium Terminum = Forma Syllogismi

**IX.** We shall endeavor to persuade this by its reasons. Therefore we assert the following:

**[First]**: ***MEDIUM TERMINUS IS THE FORM OF THE WHOLE SYLLOGISM***. For the conclusion — not considered as it looks to the middle term — is a bare proposition, no conclusion. The same must be judged of any of the premises considered separately. Just as a wall has this (that it is white) from ***whiteness***, so from the middle term premises and conclusion have this: that they are a perfect syllogism. ***For FORM GIVES BEING to a thing***.

**[Second]**: ***The medium terminus must be regarded as that from which the ratio of premises and conclusion — especially the habitudo of what is concluded to that of which it is concluded — depends***; for in this reason it is middle term.

**[Third]**: ***The medium terminus must be reduced to that fundamentum which is of that genus of which the whole argument (i.e. premises and conclusion) is said to be***. In this ***turns the hinge of the matter***, nor will you easily overcome the difficulty raised, unless you recur to the ***fundamentum of one and the same genus*** to which premises and conclusion ought to belong.

For example: let the two questions handed down above be recalled to memory — one ***Moral***, the other ***Political***. The ***Moral*** was: ***"Cur promissum ex sua natura obliget promissorem?"*** In the place of middle term was placed: ***"quia promissario (i.e. ei, cui promissio facta est,) ius adversus promissorem quaesitum est"***. In the decision of the other question — ***"Cur civis debeat esse particeps suffragiorum suae civitatis?"*** — this middle term was adduced: ***"quia salutem suae civitatis ope consilioque pro viribus iuvare tenetur."***

When you say that the arguments brought in through these middle terms were — the one ***mere morale***, the other ***mere politicum*** — you say truly indeed; but you may not yet rest in this, if on this ground you call the former ***mere morale*** and the latter ***mere politicum***: namely because the premises and conclusion of the former pertain to ***the genus of Philosophy which expounds every natural right*** (i.e. of Moral Philosophy); the premises and conclusion of the latter to ***the genus of civil Philosophy, which they call Political***. For of this you must have been most certain: that those premises pertain ***uniquely*** to the former, these only to the latter genus of Philosophy. But (as we have said, with better judgment saved) it can appear by making the ***reduction of the premises to the genuine and solid fundamentum*** by which that genus of doctrine stands.

Thus this is the ***true and genuine fundamentum of universal philosophy which expounds every natural right***: ***that there be given a per se and from its own nature HONEST; item a per se and from its own nature SHAMEFUL; and that the per se and from its own nature honest is to be sought, the per se and from its own nature shameful is to be shunned***. Whence it follows: whatever propositions enunciate only of the per se and from its own nature honest, or of the per se and from its own nature shameful, cannot not be numbered among propositions ***propriae to Moral Philosophy***. Now ***per se and from its own nature honest*** is (to all endowed with sounder judgment, [when] it does not escape their notice) ***to render his own right to another***. Likewise from Moral Philosophy it is clear that the ***nature of a perfect promise*** consists in this: ***that it ground a right acquired to transfer right***. Who then would doubt further that this syllogism (by which this question — ***"Num promissum ex sua natura obliget promissorem?"*** — was inferred through this middle term, ***"quia promissario, i.e. ei, cui promissio facta est, ius adversus promissorem quaesitum est"***) is ***purely moral***. For the Major proposition was the notice of natural right (i.e. of an act per se and by its nature honest and so owed). The Minor proposition was the notice of promise. So that at length thence it might be concluded that ***to keep a promise is an act per se and by its nature owed***.

Likewise [this is] the true and genuine ***fundamentum of the Philosophy on civil prudence***: that ***even a perfect society is instituted for αὐτάρκειαν and εὐδαιμονίαν (self-sufficiency and happiness), and that all those are just which per se contribute to the obtaining of αὐτάρκειας and εὐδαιμονίας*** (with the latter being mother of the former). Since therefore the citizen cannot sufficiently happily, and in a way just and fitting his office, procure either end, and cannot dextrously perform his duties (of the citizen ***κατ' ἐξοχήν*** the discourse was), unless he be admitted to deliberations of great moment and to bearing suffrages — thence was deduced this ***mere politica*** conclusion: ***that the citizen must be partaker of suffrages***. [And] which is given to recognize as merely political from this: that the premises (from which this conclusion was elicited), and the ratio itself (holding the place of middle term, whence the union of the extremes of this conclusion depended), ***goes off into the genuine and adequate fundamentum of universal political doctrine***.

Ex professo this matter and in a manner worthy of the dignity has been treated by the Man of exquisite and greatest judgment ***D. Johannes Musaeus***, in his altogether excellent book ***De Usu Principiorum Rationis et Philosophiae in Controversiis Theologicis contra Vedelium***, book 2, in the whole first chapter — let it be seen and consulted.

#### Note X — Second Requisite: Necessary and Certain Truth

**X.** And so much on the first requisite. We hasten to the rest. Secondly it is required that the ratio be so constituted that, included in a syllogism, it argues premises and conclusion to be ***true, and indeed NECESSARILY and CERTAINLY true***. The conclusion must be ***true***, since if someone judges that which is false to be true, he is not ***knowing*** but ***deceived or ignorant***. Nay rather, of what is false there can be ***opinion***, never ***scientia***. The conclusion must be ***necessarily true***, for a scientia complete and perfect in all numbers will not be given of that which can be otherwise. The conclusion must be ***certainly true***: for if scientia could be had of the uncertain, why not also of the false? And is it not by common consent that cognition most deserves the name of ***scientia*** which excludes ***all fear of the opposite***?

Most especially we have distinguished these two from each other: ***necessarily true*** and ***certainly true***. For the ***determination and necessity*** of truth or falsity regards the ***object***; contrariwise, ***certitude*** regards the ***subject*** (i.e. him who either himself effects the proposition or perceives it effected by another). Thus a necessarily-true proposition is called ***certainly true*** when to someone it ***infallibly stands*** of the necessary conformity of the proposition with its object.

Now since the conclusion must be true, therefore also the ratio included in the premises [must be true] — for truth does not follow from false. In every properly-so-called syllogistic consequence, no consequent is posited unless the antecedent is posited; so with the consequent removed, the antecedent is removed. In few words: ***From that whence truth must follow, that itself must be true***. From the ratio (which we have called ***CAUSA*** in the Analytic sense, included in the premises) truth must follow. Therefore the ratio (which we have called CAUSA) must be true.

Furthermore, since the conclusion must be ***necessarily*** true, therefore also the premises. For if from the ***contingent*** infallible scientia could be concluded, why not also from the ***false*** (since the contingent can be false)? ***Aristotle*** discourses thus: ***"If what we certainly know cannot be otherwise, it surely follows that only the necessary falls under demonstrative scientia: But we obtain demonstrative scientia only when we attain the demonstration itself; wherefore demonstration will be a ratiocination which necessarily consists of necessaries"*** — ***1 Posterior Analytics c. 4***.

Likewise, since the conclusion must be ***certain***, the ratio included in the premises (which we call CAUSA) must be ***certain***. For whenever I wish to prove something ***certainly***, I must be certain of it; I wish to prove something certainly by scientific premises; therefore I must be certain of the scientific premises; and of what I must be certain, that must be certain — for if from the uncertain certain [could follow], why not also from the contingent necessary, from the false true?

Indeed it cannot be denied that many are given (elsewhere as also in Morals and Politics) rationes and conclusions ***not necessarily and certainly true***, whose number of considerable magnitude can nevertheless be made closely akin to scientific rationes (and the conclusions corresponding to them). For first, it is better to infer a conclusion from ***verisimilia*** than from no propositions, when ***true causes*** (which Analytics otherwise requires for demonstration) are not at hand. Then, that CAUSA is of inferior order which, reduced to syllogistic form, argues premises mostly true, or a necessarily-true conclusion, so long as the premises remain true. For nothing hinders that of ***contingents (as to most, inasmuch as they are contingent as to most)*** a determined truth may be had. Just as in ***Physics*** a ratio can be given why sometimes it happened otherwise (since we know it happens thus mostly) — so the same obtains in ***Morals and Politics***, where often it suffices for a conclusion closest to scientia if you can teach or learn that these [actions] mostly bring forth losses, dangers, corruptions — resting on this axiom: ***"Omne, quod rei damnum infert, periculum, ipsum interitum, vitandum est"*** (Everything which brings loss, danger, or ruin to a thing must be avoided).

#### Note XI — Third Requisite: Immediate

**XI.** Thirdly it is necessary that the ratio (which in Analytics must be called CAUSA) be ***immediata***. For what is certain is no longer doubted of. The ratio called CAUSA in Analytics is certain. Therefore it is no longer doubted of. Of whatever is no longer doubted, that does not need proof. Whatever does not need proof, that is ***first***. What is first does not have anything prior by which it is proved, since for the first nothing prior is given. What does not have anything prior by which it be proved is ***immediatum***. Therefore the ratio (which reduced to syllogistic form is called DEMONSTRATION) is ***immediate***.

Here we count must at the same time still be noted that CAUSA analytically taken can be called ***immediata in two modes***:
- **First**, inasmuch as it is a ratio ***propria***, necessarily and certainly true, which proximately simpliciter satisfies the auditor seeking solid scientia of what was in the question — so that no closer and more certain ratio can be given.
- **Second**, inasmuch as that propria, necessarily-and-certainly-true ratio cannot [be inferred by another], nor can the scientific conclusion be inferred through another ratio which should claim for itself the name of true analytic CAUSA.

If CAUSA ***immediata*** be taken in the former mode, surely every ratio (which the Analytics call CAUSA) is immediate. If in the latter mode, it is not necessary that every CAUSA analytically so-called be immediate. For CAUSA analytically taken is of two kinds: one does not have another analytic CAUSA; the other acknowledges another analytic CAUSA. This is: every ratio of this kind either must be known through another ratio, or cannot be known through another ratio but is known either from ***singular experiments by induction made***, or ***per se sufficiently manifest***.

#### Note XII — Fourth Requisite: Doctor-Certainty + Imprudentia-Docendi Polemic

**XII.** Finally it is necessary that he who wills to leave solid scientia in his own or another's mind be ***sufficiently certain*** that this ratio (which he adduces in the place of the analytically-so-called CAUSA) is ***propria, necessarily and certainly true, and immediate***. For if even most he knew or adduced the ratio from which the proposed question follows, and that ratio is ***domestic, certain to others, necessarily true, immediate*** — yet if ***he himself or the auditor does not know that ratio to be domestic, certain, necessarily true, immediate*** — surely that ratio cannot be ***CAUSA Scientiae***; it cannot generate scientia in his or the auditor's mind.

Thence it comes that often one suffers ***filing-shavings for silver*** to be objected to himself, if neither the one willing to teach, nor the auditor, knows how to discern ***the contingent from the necessary, the probable from the certain, the common from the genuine, the immediate (in whatever mode) from that by which simpliciter and from the whole he is satisfied who seeks solid scientia*** — [and so suffers] simultaneously ***ἀναισθησίας*** (dullness). Repeatedly it comes about that those who ***labor from imprudence of teaching*** (like bad cooks who confound the best juices) so set forth even the most solid and most necessary doctrines to their auditors that from them, as they say, no juice and no blood can be elicited. For often those who teach accurately ***do not teach accurately***, because they do not know what they have taught, nor that by teaching others they teach themselves — and ***amid teaching, they willed to learn***.

Very often it happens that an ***ἀναίσθητος*** (dull-witted) auditor cannot grasp a doctrine most rightly, conveniently, and appositely enough handed down; and that he prefers to the most prudent [a teacher] less wise and in whose tongue sits the greatest treasure of erudition. What of this: that Moral auditors especially — the ***ἀναισθητωτέροι*** (duller) — most frequently, having heard the voices ***demonstratio moralis, demonstratio politica***, fashion to themselves such ***monstra*** as they can overcome? As in civil affairs the best cause is lost by acting badly, so day by day it happens that scientia, doctrine, labor, study go ill — now from the teacher's, now from the learner's ***imprudence***.

Nor let it any longer be a wonder why ***prudent disciples and masters*** (i.e. those endowed with ***prudence of learning and teaching*** — which those who have, know exactly how singular things prudently, i.e. perspicuously, orderly, consonant to the matter, must be taught and learned) can accomplish in ***one year*** as much as others (who are ignorant of that prudence) cannot accomplish in ***three or more years***.

#### Note XIII — Closes § 1

**XIII.** More indeed could now be adduced on the analytic notion of CAUSA, especially against the ***Recentiores*** (who wish to seem Aristotelians yet are not). For by what reason these same often slip in judgment while they vaunt the Aristotelian Analytic doctrines (which not even by dream had entered Aristotle's mind), and how, by their perverse example, the Cultivators of the practical disciplines (who follow and admire them) institute fallacious ***ἀναλύσεις*** (analyses), losing their time and effort — this ***Dn. Conring***, in his manner (i.e. succinctly and accurately), has taught in his book ***De Prudentia Civili c. 10 p. m. 197 ff.***, which should be read with judgment. But since our one purpose was ***to indicate the discrimen of CAUSA metaphysically-taken from the analytic notion***, enough and more will seem to have been done for the plan of our institute.

#### § 2 — Notio Causati: Metaphysica vs Analytica

> ***Since a double notion of cause is given — METAPHYSICAL and ANALYTIC — there is no doubt that a double notion of causatum must also be admitted. And what the ***METAPHYSICAL*** notion of causatum is, we believe is abundantly clear from chapters 8 and 7. ***But causatum analytically taken is nothing other than the CONCLUSION WHICH IS DEMONSTRATED***.***

#### Notes

**I.** Let the examples be repeated from the Notes to the preceding § 1 of this chapter.

**II.** In this matter we have as our forerunner ***Dn. D. Friedemann Bechmann***, who in his manner (i.e. with greatest perspicuity) expounds the true view and simultaneously Aristotle's mind in ***Institutiones Logicae lib. 4 c. 1 § 15***: ***"To this — that someone know — the Philosopher requires that the thing known cannot be otherwise; which words are to be understood of the CONCLUSION WHICH ONE DESIRES TO KNOW: so that the sense is that he who wills accurately to know something must be certain, and the CONCLUSION OF WHICH HE INTENDS SCIENTIA is necessary and cannot be otherwise — or that the predicate of the conclusion necessarily belongs to the subject. ***That this is Aristotle's mind*** is shown thus: for Aristotle's institute is ***to hand down certa, immota, constans scientia***; to which is required that what is known is constant such that it cannot be otherwise. ***But what is known IS CONCLUSION***. Therefore of the conclusion must be understood that it cannot be otherwise."*** Add ***lib. 2 c. 7***.

In this solid judgment we deservedly acquiesce. The same view is defended at length by ***D. Petrus Musaeus***, and he discourses nervously on it from ***Fonseca and Mendoza*** in ***Institutiones Metaphysicae c. 20 § 14***.

**III.** In the meantime it is not denied: if the ***subject of the conclusion*** is a being ***simpliciter necessary and immutable***, that a ***more perfect scientia*** can be generated.

**IV.** This is the common and received view of the most-approved Analytical Doctors, to deduce which would be ***to pour out light to the sun itself***.

#### § 3 — Requisites of Analytic Cause: Materiale = Medium Terminus

> ***Further, just as cause metaphysically taken, so also cause analytically received acknowledges its necessary requisites. What is called MATERIALE CAUSAE in the Metaphysical sense stands from chapters 10 and 11. But the MATERIALE CAUSAE IN THE ANALYTIC SENSE will be that which can be ***MEDIUM***, from which (as from a proper, certain, necessary, true, and immediate principle) the union of the extremes of the conclusion (whose scientia is sought) can depend.***

#### Notes

**I.** It pleases to recur to the examples adduced in the Notes to § 1. Thus, because from what is asserted of a promise — that it can ground a right acquired against the promisor — can be deduced the ***moral obligation of the promise*** (by which the promisor can be called obligated) — such that it can be medium, from which (as from a proper, certain, necessary, true, and immediate principle) the union of the extremes of this conclusion ***"Therefore: a promise by its own nature obliges the promisor"*** can depend — thence we wish to be present the ***materiale of the Analytic notion of CAUSA***. Let the same judgment be of this, which can be affirmed of the citizen (that he is bound by means and counsel to help the salvation of the city according to his powers), in order to this proposition: ***"The citizen must be partaker of suffrages."***

**II.** Just as at chapter 8 § 11 it was noted, the materiale of cause metaphysically-taken can be ***ens or non-ens***: so here we count must be noted that the materiale of CAUSA analytically-taken can be ***affirmative or negative*** — although affirmatives prevail over negatives. See ***Dn. Conringius De Prudentia Civili c. 10 § igitur cum multiplex p. m. 194 and § quum porro p. 214 and the following § p. 215***.

**III.** What of this: that particular rationes sometimes can be in the place of medium, which compared to universal rationes cannot deserve the ***Analytic denomination of CAUSA***? Just as elsewhere ***negative and particular*** are called ***weak parts***, so if they can be the cause of any scientia, they will be causes of ***imperfect and weak scientia***.

#### § 4 — Ratio Causandi: Metaphysica vs Analytica

> ***RATIO CAUSANDI on the side of cause considered in the Metaphysical sense was explicated in chapter 8 § 12. Of that, however, of which something can be CAUSE analytically-taken, this [analytical] ratio consists in this: ***SI POSSIT SOLIDAM SCIENTIAM QUAERENTI EX ASSE SATISFACERE*** (if it can satisfy from the whole him who seeks solid scientia).***

#### Notes

**I.** From what [criteria] such aptitude can be judged, we have more copiously disserted in the Notes to § 1 of the present chapter.

**II.** In ***Metaphysics***, what plainly says no ratio of causing (or qua such does not say it) either plainly is not — or qua such is not — a true cause metaphysically received. Likewise in ***Analytics***, what is plainly not apt to be or to come to be ***MEDIUM of DEMONSTRATION*** (or what qua such is not fit for demonstration), to this the true analytic notion of CAUSA cannot belong.

For example: If someone, from what was said — ***that from a promise there was acquired to the one to whom the promise was made a right against the promisor*** — should will to infer and demonstrate that ***even the promisor, in the case where the other (to whom the promise had been made) released him, is bound to stand by the promise***. In this act — although otherwise natural law disposes concerning the promise — a certain ***imago of mutation*** deceives the incautious, so that he thinks: otherwise, if it is pronounced [that the promisor is released], natural law is changed. But really this conclusion of Natural Law — ***"a promise by its nature obliges the promisor"*** — is not changed; rather the ***promise*** (concerning which natural law constitutes something) also receives mutation. For if he to whom I promised releases me from the promise, I am no longer bound to keep the promise — not because natural Law has ceased to prescribe that what I promise be kept, but because what I owed from the promise has ceased to be owed.

#### § 5 — Formale Causae: Metaphysica vs Analytica

> ***FORMALE CAUSAE in the Metaphysical sense was explicated in chapter 8 § 13. In ***ANALYTICS***, cause is cause ***by this***: that it SATISFIES FROM THE WHOLE a solid response to a scientific question to one seeking.***

#### Note

For the rest, just as in ***Metaphysics*** many things occur which (though they are neither cause, nor ratio causandi, nor causality) are nevertheless necessary for something actually to come to be or be cause: so in ***Analytics*** various indeed are given ***requisites and GRADUS*** (as they are called) ***of propositions***, of which can be seen ***Aristotle in the books of the Posterior Analytics***; ***Dn. D. Zeidlerus in Analysi, book 1, from chapter 3 to chapter 15***; and ***Dn. D. Bechmann Institutiones Logicae book 4 chapter 2 and 3***. Nor do we doubt that some of these requisites deserve to be called ***primary***, others ***secondary*** — which [note it suffices] to have touched in passing. Namely, these matters ex professo belong to Analytics.

#### § 6 — Causa Virtualis

> ***CAUSA VIRTUALIS by the Metaphysical Doctors (who indeed use this notion) is commonly defined thus: ***CAUSA VIRTUALIS is that which REALLY does not differ from that of which it is called causa virtualis — YET AS TO OUR MODE OF KNOWING, it has itself such that IF it were REALLY distinguished from it, it would be its TRUE CAUSE***.***
>
> ***Example: GOD, the immutability of God, the eternity of God are ***a parte rei one and the same numerically*** — because they are in God, and whatever is in God is God Himself. Yet if (***per impossibile***) the eternity of God, God Himself, and the immutability of God were really distinguished from one another — such that it would be one thing (though no one is thinking it) to be God, another to be eternity in God, another the immutability in God — by this hypothesis (made ***per impossibile***) altogether the immutability in God would be the cause of eternity in God. Hence [the Scholastics] call ***immutabilitatem causam virtualem aeternitatis***.***

#### § 7 — Causatum Virtuale

> ***What CAUSATUM VIRTUALE should be said to be from the mind of these Doctors is manifest per se. Namely this: ***that which really does not differ from that which is called its CAUSA VIRTUALIS, yet as to our mode of knowing has itself so that if it were really distinguished from it, this itself would be its cause***. Let be recurred to the example proposed in the preceding §. For if it were granted — which cannot be [given] without the greatest falsity — that eternity in GOD is NOT immutability in GOD, nor Himself God, then it would be ***causatum*** by comparison to immutability, and on account of this positing (made ***per impossibile***) they call it ***causatum virtuale***.***

#### Notes

**I.** In this sense the ***Scholastics*** in God, in Angels, and in souls (as and inasmuch as they are of spiritual essence) call the essence [the virtual cause] of each attribute, and one attribute the virtual cause of another. E.gr. in God, ***independence as the virtual cause of infinity***, ***infinity of absolute simplicity***, ***absolute simplicity of immutability***, ***immutability of eternity***, etc. Nor do they acknowledge such virtual causes only in simple substances, but also in composites: e.gr. in man, ***rationality as the virtual cause of docility***; in quantity, ***extension of divisibility***, etc. What of this: that are found Men of no vulgar erudition who hold that ***all proper*** (***ἀκρίβως*** and in strict rigor so-called) are ***causata virtualia*** — i.e. can be referred to those by whose comparison they can be called ***causae virtuales***?

**II.** Nor do the Scholastics only in the place and comparison of essence [designate] attributes as ***causata virtualia*** and virtual causes, but ***in divine matters*** they also call this or that ***internal action*** the virtual cause of another. E.gr. the ***cognition*** by which from eternity God knew Himself as the highest, most-perfect, and infinite good, they call ***the virtual cause of the LOVE*** by which from eternity God loved Himself. And the ***prevision of final faith in Christ*** [they call] the virtual cause of ***eternal election*** of the man finally about-to-believe in Christ.

**III.** By what reason the causa virtualis in the Schools is wont to be distinguished into ***causa per emanationem virtualem*** and ***causa citra emanationem***, we shall say in the doctrine on form.

#### § 8 — Four Discriminations Causa Virtualis vs Causa Formaliter Talis

> ***Thence it is easy to recount the various discriminations of ***causa virtualis*** from ***causa formaliter talis***, which have been noted here and there by the Scholastic Doctors:***
>
> ***(a) CAUSA VIRTUALIS does not differ really from the CAUSATUM VIRTUALE; the CAUSA FORMALITER TALIS differs really from the CAUSATUM FORMALITER TALE.***
>
> ***(b) CAUSA VIRTUALIS and CAUSATUM VIRTUALE are not ALIUD and ALIUD; the CAUSA FORMALITER TALIS and the CAUSATUM FORMALITER TALE are (as the Scholastics' locutions have it) ALIUD and ALIUD.***
>
> ***(c) CAUSA VIRTUALIS is not a TRUE CAUSE, because it does not really differ from that of which by comparison it is virtual: ***nihil enim est causa sui ipsius***. The CAUSA FORMALITER TALIS is a true cause of that of which it is and is called a causa formaliter talis.***
>
> ***(d) CAUSA VIRTUALIS (as the Scholastics' locutions are) ***does not cause the thing, but WOULD cause it, if the thing could be caused by it***. CAUSA FORMALITER TALIS actually causes the thing — for the thing is such that it can be caused by it.***
>
> ***The same discrimina between CAUSATUM VIRTUALE and CAUSATUM FORMALITER TALE must be observed, with the necessary changes made.***

#### Notes

**I.** The notion of ***causa virtualis*** and the notion of ***causatum virtuale*** owe their origin to the ***Scholastic Philosophy***. The first author (as far as I know) of the distinction between ***causa formaliter talis*** and ***causa virtualis*** (likewise between causatum formaliter tale and causatum virtuale) is ***Thomas de Vio Cajetanus Cardinalis***, who should be seen at ***1 Posterior. Analyt. c. 2***. On causa virtualis before others have treated ***Paulus Soncinas IV. Metaph. quaest. 15 and XII. Metaph. quaest. 28***; ***Johannes Sanchez comm. Log. tom. 1 quaest. 7 proemio***. To whom let be joined ***Franciscus Suarez Disputationes Metaphysicae 1 sect. 1 n. 27***; ***Michael Zanardus Bergomas ex Urgnano commentator in Logicam Aristotelis — and indeed on 1 Posterior Analyt. c. 2 lect. 9 n. 3***; and ***Bernardus Morisanus, Ferensis Hibernus, on 1 Posterior Analyt. quaest. 4***.

**II.** From our own [Lutheran] Doctors, the doctrine of this distinction (that we might more rightly attain the mind of the Scholastics) have proposed in the ***Institutiones Metaphysicae***: ***Stahl c. III concl. 2*** and ***Petrus Musaeus c. 13 § 10 ff.***

**III.** By what occasion this distinction was devised can perhaps be conjectured. Namely: because Cajetanus had seen that through a cause ***virtualiter talis*** one could respond ***as solidly*** to a scientific question as if it were a cause ***formaliter talis*** — nor could anyone respond more accurately and sufficiently, even if (what we posit ***per impossibile***) a cause formaliter talis had held place — he willed to call ***causa*** that through which accurately and solidly it could be responded to a scientific question, ***whether (as Cajetanus loves to speak) it caused, or not***.

For example: a scientific question: ***An Deus sit aeternus?*** It is responded: ***"Altogether, God is eternal, because He is immutable."*** Thence flows such an argument, whose premises and conclusion are of the same genus (namely they pertain to Metaphysics). For we argue thus: ***Every immutable is eternal, and indeed by intrinsic eternity. God is immutable. Therefore God is eternal.*** The middle term in this demonstration is ***causa*** because it is a ratio ***necessary, certain, propria, immediate***, through which it is responded. Yet it is not ***causa formaliter talis***, but ***virtualis***. For the immutability of God and the eternity of God do not really differ from each other, nor do they really differ from God; the immutability of God however is ***the virtual cause of the eternity in God***, because — if (NB. ***if***) the immutability of God were not quoad rem God Himself, nor were the eternity of God quoad rem God Himself (and God however were immutable) — then immutability would formally cause eternity in God, and would be formally the cause of eternity. Thus from Cajetanus' mind.

We wish to be present other examples: Thus, as in Morals so in Theological Schools received is this proposition: ***"Because God Himself and Himself alone knows Himself as the highest, most-perfect, and infinite good, therefore He loves Himself above all things."*** It is said then (as Note II to § 7 taught): the ***cognition*** by which God knows Himself as the highest/most-perfect/infinite good is the ***virtual cause of the LOVE*** by which God loves Himself above all. Surely if someone of the Morals or Theology Cultivators should wish to know ***why man using right reason loves God above all***, he will accept as response this reason ***a priori***: ***"because he knows God as the highest, most-perfect, and infinite good."***

These two propositions, therefore — ***"Because God Himself and Himself alone knows Himself as the highest/most-perfect/infinite good, therefore He loves Himself above all. Because man using right reason knows God and God alone as the highest/most-perfect/infinite good, therefore he loves God above all"*** — are by all Ethicists and Theologians properly called ***causales***. But this discrimen stands between the two: in the former the ***cognition*** by which God knows Himself as the highest/most-perfect/infinite good does ***not really differ*** from the love by which God loves Himself; in the latter the cognition by which man using right reason knows God as the highest/most-perfect/infinite good ***really differs*** from the love by which man loves God above all. Whence in the former, neither is the cognition the ***cause formaliter talis*** of love, nor is God the cause formaliter talis of cognition and love; in the latter, both the ***cognition is the causa formaliter talis of the love***, and ***man is the causa formaliter talis of cognition and love***.

Meanwhile, since each proposition expresses a true, necessary, certain, immediate, and proper ratio, each is rightly and deservedly called ***causalis*** both by the Moral Philosopher (who draws it from the light of nature) and by the Theologian (who draws the same ratio from the light of Sacred Scripture).

Likewise, if we consult the Theologians, all and singular by unanimous consent will pronounce these predications ***as causales received to the maximum degree in the Schools***: ***"Because God from eternity foresaw these or those about to believe in Christ unto the end of life, therefore He elected them. Because from eternity He foresaw few about to believe in Christ unto the end of life, therefore He elected few."*** But because in this also the Theologians consent — that the decree of ***election*** or ***predestination*** (as they call it) is an ***internal action of God*** (and indeed of the divine WILL), and that ***prescience or prevision*** likewise is an internal action of God, namely of the divine INTELLECT — and the ***internal actions of God*** (now the discourse is of God's internal actions considered in opposition to the ***actions ad intra***) ***do not really differ from each other, nor from the divine essence***: therefore not in that mode in which in a rational creature the action of intellect is said to be cause of the action of will can [this be said in God]. For in a rational creature it is one thing (though no one is thinking of the rational creature) [to be] the action of intellect, another to be the action of will; and the former is truly and formally the cause of the latter.

Whence as to our mode of knowing, prior in God is the ***prevision of faith*** than ***election***; and to the question — ***"Why did God elect from eternity for eternal salvation men about-to-believe in Christ unto the end of life (that salvation finally about to be bestowed on them)? Why did He elect few?"*** — these responses ***solidly satisfy***: ***"Because God from eternity foresaw them about-to-believe in Christ unto the end of life"***; ***"Because God from eternity foresaw few about-to-believe in Christ unto the end of life"*** — not otherwise than if in God prevision of final faith in Christ were causa, causa formaliter talis, from eternity of ELECTION. Whence since in all Theological Schools we have said these propositions are received as ***causales***, and this cannot be unknown nor should be to any Theology Student, everyone can attain from what has thus far been said in what sense we have called ***the prevision of final faith the VIRTUAL CAUSE of predestination or election to eternal salvation***.

**III.** When this doctrine (as in Theology, so in other disciplines, both ***Theoretic*** and ***Practical***) matters: Thus e.gr. in ***Morals*** the ***reatus of moral sin*** is demonstrated from ***moral culpa***; the ***obligatio coactiva*** (as they call it) from the ***obligatio directiva***. Thus e.gr. in ***Politics*** the obligation of civil law is demonstrated from the ***decree of the Magistrate***. Thus in ***Jurisprudence*** e.gr. from the ***contract of buying-selling*** is demonstrated the ***obligation to transfer dominion*** and to pay the price.

#### § 9 — Discrimen Causa Metaphysica vs Analytica

> ***To more rightly perceive the discrimen between CAUSA METAPHYSICA and CAUSA ANALYTICA, let the following be noted. Sometimes ***CAUSA METAPHYSICA and CAUSA ANALYTICA COINCIDE***. Exempli gratia: the ***true METAPHYSICAL cause*** of a saw is iron, since surely a saw is made from iron. True also is the ***ANALYTIC cause*** why a saw is hard: because it is made from iron. Likewise the ***true Metaphysical cause*** of a saw is the ***section of woods***, inasmuch as the saw is for the sake of [cutting] them; the ***Analytic cause*** too of why the saw must be hard is: because it is for the sake of the section of woods.***
>
> ***Sometimes ***CAUSA METAPHYSICA is NOT at the same time CAUSA ANALYTICA***. E.gr. the Metaphysical cause of the journey that Titius makes on foot is: Titius setting out, his soul and feet. But Titius setting out, his sensitive soul and feet are not the Analytic cause — for to the question ***"why does Titius make the journey?"*** it cannot be responded as by a ratio a priori: ***"because Titius setting out, his sensitive soul is the principle of the journey; and he completes the journey with his feet"***.***
>
> ***Sometimes ***CAUSA ANALYTICA is NOT at the same time CAUSA METAPHYSICA***. E.gr. ***immutability in God*** is the ANALYTIC cause of eternity in God; the METAPHYSICAL cause it is not; and because it is the Analytic cause but not simultaneously the Metaphysical cause, it is therefore by many Doctors of Theology (both natural and revealed) called by the name of ***CAUSA VIRTUALIS***.***

#### Note

The use of this doctrine will be placed before the eyes of the benevolent reader and the suitable cultivator of Metaphysics in the following chapter 14 ***on the Analytical use of all and singular genera of causes***. For his interest especially concerns (unless all judgment entirely deceives us) that such matters be rendered maximally perspicuous to himself.

#### § 10 — Pointer Forward: Examples CLOSES Caput XI

> ***We have adduced examples of METAPHYSICAL causes in the preceding chapters 8 and 9; many more will occur in the single chapters on the single genera of causes — this is the most important matter of the whole prior part and the chief scope of our proposal. Examples of ANALYTICAL causes meanwhile — if it please — may be sought from chapter 4, from p. 373 to p. 383, and let them be reduced hither.***

**[CAPUT XI CLOSES]**

## Caput Duodecimum

### Of Cause Per Se and Per Accidens. Likewise of Causatum Per Se and Per Accidens

#### § 1

> ***CAUSA IN COMMUNI is distinguished into ***CAUSA PER SE*** and ***CAUSA PER ACCIDENS***, and this distinction is in received use among all suitable Doctors of First Philosophy and has found their approval.***

#### Notes

**I.** That this distinction, known to students of ***Practical Philosophy, Law, and Theology***, is maximally necessary and most useful — chiefly in the ***Doctrine on the Efficient Cause*** — will be demonstrated.

**II.** With special study it is said that CAUSA ***IN COMMUNI*** is distinguished into per se and per accidens. For we shall not detain those who ***restrict this distinction to the efficient cause***, and so consider it in too narrow a signification; since this distinction wanders through all genera of causes.

**III.** The progress of the chapter will teach that ***division*** of cause into per se and per accidens is tossed about in vain, if ***causa per accidens*** be considered in its ***widest yet genuine and received signification***. On this account we said CAUSA in communi is ***distinguished*** (not ***divided***) into per se and per accidens.

#### § 2 — Likewise for Causatum

> ***Likewise the distinction of ***CAUSATUM IN COMMUNI*** into ***CAUSATUM PER SE*** and ***CAUSATUM PER ACCIDENS*** the common usage of suitable Doctors of Metaphysics admits and approves.***

#### Note

By the same law which was noted on § 1, [the same] cannot be repeated here, so far as the reason of the opposites is the same.

#### § 3 — Each Divides into Ex Parte Causae / Ex Parte Causati

> ***CAUSA PER SE is again distinguished into causa per se ***EX PARTE CAUSAE*** and causa per se ***EX PARTE CAUSATI***. In the same mode CAUSA PER ACCIDENS must be distinguished into causa per accidens ex parte causae and causa per accidens ex parte causati.***

#### Note

This distinction is unshaken in the eyes of him who, asked ***why he holds any causa per accidens as true cause***, responds: ***"because it really influences into the effect — e.gr. when a Musician heals a man, he truly influences and produces health; but the Musician in order to healing is causa per accidens."*** Who does not see that by this proof nothing more can be evinced than that ***causa per accidens EX PARTE CAUSAE is true cause***? But by ***the whole heaven*** causa per accidens ex parte causae and causa per accidens ex parte causati differ, as will soon be demonstrated.

#### § 4 — Causa Per Se / Per Accidens Ex Parte Causati

> ***Causa per se ex parte causae and causa per accidens ex parte causae were defined above at chapter VIII § 16. Let us see what are called causa per se ex parte causati and causa per accidens ex parte causati.***
>
> ***CAUSA PER SE ex parte causati is ***that which is the TRUE CAUSE OF ANOTHER, and indeed of another QUA SUCH***. E.gr. the ARCHITECT is causa per se of the building ex parte causati, because the architect is the TRUE cause of the building ***qua such*** (i.e. as building). The FATHER is causa per se of the son ex parte causati — i.e. as of son.***
>
> ***Contrariwise, CAUSA PER ACCIDENS ex parte causati is ***that which is the TRUE CAUSE of another, but NOT of another QUA SUCH; or plainly is NOT a true cause of that of which it is called causa per accidens ex parte causati, but is only the true cause of something which is CONJOINED with it (of which it is plainly not true cause) or which FOLLOWS it***.***
>
> ***E.gr. the ARCHITECT is true cause of a yellow building, yet not as yellow — for thus the cause was not the architect but the ***painter (tinctor)***. The FATHER is true cause of the Roman Pontiff, yet not as Pontiff, but as of son. Likewise a FATHER who sends his son to a wedding at the time when he knew nothing other than that the way was safe enough from robbers — nor had he to know otherwise — is called causa per accidens of his son's death, if on the way he be killed by robbers.***

#### § 5 — Convergence and Divergence

> ***Causa per se ex parte causae and causa per accidens ex parte causae ***converge*** in this: that each is a true cause. They ***differ***: because the former is true cause ***qua such***, the latter is not true cause ***qua such***. Exempli gratia: an architect through the act of building is true cause of a building — and indeed an architect ***as he is such***. The Musician too (through building) is true cause of a building, if, namely, the same person is simultaneously Musician and Architect — for otherwise the same would be simultaneously true cause of a building and NOT true cause of a building. Yet the Musician is NOT true cause of the building as he is Musician. By so much, therefore, as ***ars architectonica*** and ***ars Musica*** differ in order to building — though both may inhere in one and the same mind — by so much stands the discrimination between causa per se ex parte causae and causa per accidens ex parte causae.***

#### § 6 — Convergence and Divergence Ex Parte Causati

> ***Causa per se ex parte causati and causa per accidens ex parte causati ***converge*** in this: that each is a true cause of some causatum. They ***differ***: because the former is true cause of a causatum ***ut est tale***; the latter is true cause of a causatum — not however of that causatum of which it is called causa per accidens ex parte causati, but of another causatum which however is ***conjoined with*** or ***consequent upon*** that causatum of which it is true cause. Or if at times it can in its mode be said true cause of that causatum of which it is called causa per accidens ex parte causati, it will not with saved-truth be called true cause of it ***qua that causatum is such***, but only ***as it stands otherwise*** — i.e. as another causatum is united or conjoined with it, whence it takes the denomination of ***such*** or ***such a causatum***.***
>
> ***Exempli gratia***: The FATHER who sent his son to the market was called causa per accidens ex parte causati of the ensuing death of the son — where the son's death cannot in any way be called a causatum with respect to the father; nor can the father be called true cause of that death. For the father contributed plainly nothing to the son's death except that he had sent the son forth; and he was supposing — with saved conscience — at the time, that the way was safe from ambushes and least-infested. In the meantime, because the son, going abroad by the father's mandate and progressing further, fell among robbers and was slaughtered, the father is called causa per accidens ex parte causati of the son's death (which, namely, followed the father's mandate): yet the father was causa per se ex parte causati of the ***mandate***, just as the robber was causa per se ex parte causati of the ***slaughter***.
>
> So of a yellow building ***qua yellow*** the causa per se ex parte causati was the ***painter (tinctor)***; but of a yellow building the causa per accidens ex parte causati can be said to be the ***architect***, because though this building — insofar as it is yellow — does not have its yellow from the architect as from true cause, nevertheless this very building (which is yellow) received its essence from the architect; and because afterward the yellowness was united with the building, and the yellow-building ***as yellow*** was called causatum with respect to the painter, hence the architect is called causa per accidens ex parte causati of the yellow building — and indeed ***qua yellow***. So of the Roman Pontiff the causa per se ex parte causati were they who had elected and constituted him Pontiff; and of this same man — who afterward was created Pontiff — the father was causa per se ex parte causati; but the same father of the Pontiff ***qua Pontiff*** was causa per accidens ex parte causati.

#### Notes

**I.** Because the doctrine of causa per se and per accidens — both ex parte causae and ex parte causati — has given occasion to many errations in causes, and still is wont to do so, therefore greater diligence in its treatment is needed; and it comes commended more to the students of the practical disciplines and of the higher Faculties (as they call them). Let it be allowed, as we have begun, to pursue it from the foundation.

**II.** And indeed in the first place we made mention of causa per se ex parte causae and causa per accidens ex parte causae. If, then, we wish rightly to know the nature of each — and our purpose be to judge whether ***this*** or ***that*** can and ought with saved-truth to be named ex parte causae causa per se or causa per accidens — it will concern us to look into TWO things:

**(1)** Whether to that about which the question is: *whether ex parte causae it can with saved-truth be named causa per se or causa per accidens* — a true ***potentia causativa*** or ***ratio causandi*** can be attributed in order to that in-respect-of-which the question is instituted (i.e. whether we may call it its causa per se or causa per accidens). For if to anything no potentia causativa or ratio causandi in order to another belongs, this is a most-certain token that it ***can neither become nor be*** either its true causa per se ex parte causae or causa per accidens ex parte causae. But if with saved-truth potentia causativa in order to another can be attributed to it, then there is no doubt that it is fit to undergo the denomination either of causa per se ex parte causae or causa per accidens ex parte causae — and indeed with respect to that in order to which it argues potentia causativa or ratio causandi.

**(2)** It must further be looked into whether there be given a true ***causalitas*** through which it becomes or is a true cause of that of which the question is: *whether in its respect to another it be causa per se ex parte causae or causa per accidens ex parte causae*.

For these two propositions are of perpetual truth: ***Whatever does not say ratio causandi in order to another, that cannot be of another either causa per se ex parte causae or causa per accidens ex parte causae***; and ***whatever does not argue causalitas in order to another, that is not of another either causa per se ex parte causae or causa per accidens ex parte causae***. For (as we have demonstrated) nothing is of anything causa per se or causa per accidens ex parte causae unless it be true cause of that of which it is called such; hence nothing can be anyone's causa per se or causa per accidens ex parte causae unless it be ***able to be its cause***. Therefore, that we may render accurately clear to ourselves whether this (which we have known to be true cause of another) be causa per se ex parte causae or causa per accidens ex parte causae, nothing further do we have to see except this: ***Was this (which is true cause) true cause ut tale — or not ut tale?*** If the former — causa per se ex parte causae; if the latter — causa per accidens ex parte causae.

***Exempli gratia***: Suppose some man to be both Architect and Musician. Here surely there is no doubt that he enjoys potentia causativa or ratio causandi with respect to a building: for he who is skilled in the architectonic art is altogether apt to become or be efficient cause of a building, and so true cause. Suppose further that he is now actually erecting a building: here is present also *causalitas*, namely the very act of building. Now because ***it is impossible for the same to be and not-be at the same time***, surely it remains most-true that he who is at once Architect and Musician, while he erects the building, is true cause of the building — such that both propositions remain true: ***The Architect is true cause of the building***, and ***The Musician is true cause of the building***. This granted, it is easy to judge whether this man as ***Musician*** or as ***Architect*** be cause of the building. The former no sane-minded man would assert — because the art of Music carries plainly no respect to building; the latter is clear per se. Therefore when I say ***the Architect builds***, I propose an example of causa per se ex parte causae; when I form with saved-truth this proposition ***the Musician builds***, I adduce an example of causa per accidens ex parte causae.

**III.** Now any man can carry judgment upon this: ***Whether causa per accidens ex parte causae be true cause?*** To this question it must be responded that it can be taken in a twofold use:

**(1)** In ***sensu materiali seu diviso*** — as though the question had been: ***That which is called causa per accidens ex parte causae, if it be NOT considered as causa per accidens ex parte causae, is it true cause?***

**(2)** In ***sensu formali seu composito*** — such that the question is: ***That which is causa per accidens ex parte causae, insofar as it is causa per accidens ex parte causae, is it true cause?***

In the **prior sense** the affirmative is most-true — i.e. everything which is causa per accidens ex parte causae, ***if it be not viewed as causa per accidens ex parte causae***, is true cause. The reason: the ***formale causae*** — that is, *causalitas* in order to that causatum in-respect-of-which it is called causa per accidens ex parte causae — is present.

Let the argument be such: ***Whatever truly says ratio causandi of another, and true causalitas in order to that very thing, that both can be and is its true cause. But that which is anyone's causa per accidens in order to that of which it is causa per accidens ex parte causae (of which alone is now the question) says true ratio causandi and true causalitas. Therefore, that which is anyone's causa per accidens ex parte causae both can be and is its true cause.*** The Major is clear. The Minor likewise needs no fuller proof. Let anyone reduce any proposed example into the form of a syllogism: ***The Musician, when he builds, is true cause of a building, and so true cause. The Musician, when he builds, is efficient cause of a building per accidens ex parte causae, and so causa per accidens ex parte causae. Therefore some that is efficient cause of a building per accidens ex parte causae is true efficient cause of a building — and so some that is causa per accidens ex parte causae is true cause.*** For the rest, of all causae per accidens ex parte causae one is the account — i.e. in this all converge: that ***in sensu materiali seu diviso they are true causes***.

But though the affirmative in the prior sense (i.e. ***materiali & diviso***) is most-true, in the **posterior sense** (i.e. ***formali & composito***) it remains most-false — i.e. it remains most-false that ***causa per accidens ex parte causae qua it is causa per accidens ex parte causae is true cause***. The genuine and solid reason: because that which is causa per accidens of some thing ex parte causae, insofar as it is causa per accidens ex parte causae, does not say *causalitas* — nay, not even *potentia causandi* — in order to that thing of which it is called causa per accidens ex parte causae.

Let the argument again be such: ***Whatever qua such says no true causalitas, that qua such is not true cause. But causa per accidens ex parte causae qua such says no true causalitas. Therefore causa per accidens ex parte causae qua such is not true cause.*** The Major is clear from the terms: for if that which says no true causalitas at all is in no way true cause, it follows that also that which qua such says no true causalitas is qua such not true cause — i.e. ***so far forth not true cause as it does not say true causalitas***: for in both cases the reason is equal.
