The Minor is clear from the proposed example, which it is agreeable to reduce into the following form: ***The Musician who builds, insofar as he is Musician, is not true cause of the building. The Musician who builds, insofar as he is Musician, is cause (of the building) per accidens ex parte causae. Therefore causa per accidens ex parte causae*** — that is, something, insofar as it is causa per accidens ex parte causae — ***is not true cause***.

**IV.** Likewise for one looking into ***causa per accidens ex parte causati*** — whether it be true cause — it will be most-easy to attain that it is now ***plainly not true cause***, now ***indeed true cause***, but ***never qua such*** — that is, insofar as it is called causa per accidens ex parte causati — is it true cause. The reason: causa per accidens ex parte that causati is so-called because in its own being either ***it in no way proceeds from*** that which is called causa per accidens ex parte causati, OR if it does proceed from it, ***not however qua such*** does it proceed from it. We can argue in this mode: ***Whence a true causatum either does not proceed in its being, or qua such does not proceed in its being, that is not true cause — or so far forth as the causatum qua such does not thence proceed in its being, is not true cause. But causa per accidens ex parte causati is that whence a true causatum (namely that in-respect-of-which another is called causa per se ex parte causati) either plainly does not proceed in its being, or qua such does not proceed in its being. Therefore causa per accidens ex parte causati either is plainly not true cause, or so far forth as the causatum ut tale does not proceed from it in its being, is not true cause.***

**V.** Singular caution is to be employed here, lest we confound ***causam per accidens ex parte causati SIMPLICITER talem*** with ***causa per accidens ex parte causati SECUNDUM QUID***. For it can happen that something be, in a certain genus of cause, causa per se ex parte causati — yet in a certain [other] genus (if-one-may-so-speak-badly) of the ***same genus*** with saved-truth be held as causa per accidens ex parte of the same causatum.

**Thus**: he who ***splits wood*** and from behind, by invincible ignorance and against all intention, wounds one standing behind, is true cause of the involuntary laesio and wound: for he is true efficient cause of the laesio. Nor yet can it be denied that he is still ***in his own mode causa per accidens*** of it. For a certain quasi-species, or (so-to-speak-badly) peculiar mode of ***causa efficiens*** is ***causa libera*** (for free efficient-cause and natural efficient-cause are of the same ***genus*** — that of efficient cause — yet not of the same ***order***). Whence if you ask: ***Is the wood-splitter (fiffor lignorum) ex parte causati true cause per se of the splitting of wood as also of the laesio?*** we judge it to be most-rightly answered that he is true causa per se ex parte causati of ***each***, because both the fissio-lignorum ut tale and the laesio-of-the-one-standing-behind ut tale truly proceed from him: for he both splits the wood and wounds the one standing behind.

But if the question be put not so nakedly and crudely, but with the eye fixed on a certain genus of cause — so that this be the question: ***Is this wood-splitter ex parte causati true efficient cause per se of the inflicted laesio and of the wound dealt to the one standing behind?*** — here again we judge, rightly and meritoriously, that it must be responded that he is altogether ex parte causati true efficient-cause per se of the inflicted laesio and of the wound. But in this a cultivator of solidly-sound Philosophy by no means ought to acquiesce; for it is incumbent on him to descend to the modes or quasi-species of causa efficiens, and now more amply, sedulously and probely to ponder: ***Is the wood-splitter ex parte of this causatum — namely of the laesio done by himself — causa libera?*** We are certain that, this rightly pondered, each will spontaneously confess that the wood-splitter is indeed ex parte causati ***causa libera*** of the ***splitting***, but ***NOT causa libera*** of the ***inflicted laesio and wound***; and so in a sound sense can be said ex parte causati ***causa per accidens*** of the inflicted laesio and wound.

Nor is there room for the objection: *If the wood-splitter still be ex parte causati true cause of the wound, he cannot simul be said ex parte causati causa per accidens of the wound — since it implies contradiction that ex parte of the same causatum he be both causa per se and NOT causa per se*. For ***diversitas respectus tollit omnem contradictionem***. Certainly, just as it is no true contradiction for one-and-the-same thing simul to be true efficient-cause and yet NOT to be ***free*** efficient-cause: so neither does it imply true contradiction that something be ex parte causati causa efficiens per se, and simul with respect to one-and-the-same ex parte causati ***causa per accidens libera***.

Whoever has rightly cultivated Moral and Juristic studies cannot — and must not — be ignorant that in moral and civil forum ***usage has long obtained*** that this agent, who was not free agent, be held *for non-agent*, and that the cause of a non-free action be, by moral-and-forensic estimation, held ***for non-cause***. For ***voluntas distinguit morales, civiles, forenses actiones***. But of this matter it will be treated more amply in the doctrine of ***causa efficiens***.

**VI.** Let these things said meanwhile concerning causa per accidens in communi suffice. For the reason of our undertaking does not suffer us to tarry in refuting those [opinions] which are wont to be adduced against received-and-true opinions — especially when the contest is carried on NOT by weight but by *number* of reasons, if only that it may be imposed upon the less-experienced. For our purpose now is to deliver Metaphysica *positive* (as they call it), not polemic. Otherwise nothing would have been easier than to show that this mode of philosophizing — which it is pleasant to have now touched upon in passing — stands conjoined with ***affectata ignorantia***, if, namely, to show that ***causa per accidens qua talis is true cause***, the following should be assumed as foundation, never to be called into doubt or impugned: ***CAUSA PER ACCIDENS EST PRINCIPIUM INFLUENS IN EFFECTUM NON INTENTUM*** — for to *per accidens* and *indirectly* influence is, ***according to our natural manner of judging***, to influence *citra intentionem*.

For who is so stupid as not to advert that, even if causa per accidens in communi could be defined, nevertheless this formula could by no one who possesses and wishes to use natural judgment be peddled as the definition of causa per accidens qua such and in communi? For once this definition were admitted, ALL causes — ***efficient, material, formal, final***, nay of whatever genus they finally be (provided we except only ***causae agentes ex intentione***) — would be causae per accidens, and qua such would be causae per accidens — because *all and single* causes, if you except *causae agentes ex intentione*, are *principia influentia in effectus non intentos*: e.gr. ***fire*** when it burns straw is principium influens in effectum non intentum; ***the matter and form of a stone*** influence into effects not intended; ***health*** influences into an effect not intended. But who, even if he most-wanted to err, would dare defend so absurd a sentence?

Here it could be excepted: perhaps this definition is not peddled for causa per accidens *in communi* but only for the definition of causa per accidens in-genere-causae-efficientis. But the contrary teach the sequels [of those authors]: ***Of causes concur distinctions (1) in-genere, (2) in-specie. Among the general distinctions concerning causes is this — when cause in-genere is said to be some per se, some per accidens. The former per se and ***directly*** influences into the intended effect: e.gr. one who cuts wood with respect to the act of cutting. Causa per accidens too influences into the effect, but ***per accidens and indirectly***: as when one who cuts wood *citra intentionem* inflicts a wound on one standing behind, whom he knew not to be there.***

Moreover, if the adduced formula be not peddled for the definition of causa per accidens in communi, pray — by what natural manner of judging would it be permitted to argue from causa efficiens per accidens to causa per accidens in communi? Is not causa efficiens per accidens ***ex parte causae*** true cause — yet causa efficiens per accidens ***ex parte effectus*** NOT true cause, namely with respect to that of which they are called causae efficientes per accidens — as we have demonstrated in the preceding? If, then, from ONE causa efficiens per accidens (which is true cause) it is not allowed to argue to EVERY causa efficiens per accidens, as if every one were true cause, much less will this consequence hold: ***Causa efficiens per accidens is true cause. Therefore every causa per accidens is true cause. Therefore causa per accidens in genere is true cause. Therefore the distinction between causa per se and per accidens is a general ***division*** of cause.***

It is absurd to want to divide cause in genere into causa per se and per accidens, because causa per accidens often is not cause of that of which it is called causa per accidens; and ***always qua such*** is not cause of that of which it is called causa per accidens. Whence this division would be similar to this one: as if someone wished to divide ***homo in genere*** into ***homo vivus*** and ***homo mortuus***.

Excepted: ***Where plainly there is no influence, how there, pray, can there be cause — even per accidens? Whoever conceives causa per accidens, conceives also some causalitas.*** Response: this fares just as if someone said: ***Where plainly there is no human nature, how there, pray, can there be a man — however dead? Whoever conceives homo mortuus, conceives also some human nature.*** Retorted: that the word *mortuus* takes away the signification of *homo* — anyone sees who knows that *homo* is ***corpus animatum sensitivum rationale***. But whence, pray, is it clear that similarly *per accidens* takes away the signification of *causa*? Can not something influence into an effect, and exercise *causalitas proprio modo*, however *per accidens* — i.e. indirectly?

To this response again is easy: ***none of the more-accurate Philosophers has gone against this*** — that something can simultaneously be causa per accidens AND true cause. But they have denied this: (a) that every causa per accidens, with respect to that of which it is called causa per accidens, is true cause; and (b) that causa per accidens *qua such* is true cause. Now if it can be shown by solid reasons that causa per accidens often is NOT true cause of that of which it is called causa per accidens, anyone who sees this demonstrated also sees that one can conceive a causa per accidens with respect to that of which — by reason of it — ***no causalitas*** is conceived. Certainly it is most-true: cause cannot be where plainly there is no influence. But if something can be causa per accidens ex parte of that of which it plainly is not cause, what prevents us from conceiving a causa per accidens of some thing, such that ex parte of that which with saved-truth is called *causa per accidens*, no causalitas be conceived in order to that thing? Likewise if ***causa per accidens qua such ex parte causae*** and ***causa per accidens qua such ex parte causati*** (so-far-as qua tales) are not true causes, undoubtedly *per accidens* — as in the present this determination is taken — nowise infers *causalitas*.

With these things so observed, we wish all who possess any prudence of judging to judge whether that argument which is so commended has anything in reserve: ***Quicquid habet nomen causae, illud merito habetur pro vera causa, si non possit monstrari praegnans ratio nomini rationem deferendo. Atqui causa per accidens habet nomen causae. Ergo.*** [Response]: Let that argument stand firm, as long as that pregnant reason — by which the name's reason urges deposition — is not shown; but such reason has not hitherto been shown. Without any affect we say and believe that it has been sufficiently-evidently demonstrated by all more-accurate Philosophers. For if by arguments stronger-than-every-exception it was demonstrated that this proposition — ***causa per accidens qua talis non est vera causa*** — is of perpetual truth, and this predication — ***because this qua such is causa per accidens, therefore this qua such is NOT true cause*** — contains a true, necessary, germane, and immediate reason whence it must be causally denominated: there is no doubt that *in sensu composito ac formali* this proposition remains most-true: ***nulla causa per accidens est vera causa***. For the rest, those who said *per accidens* an ***alienating determination*** of the voice *causa*, having so added that these two: *to be causa per accidens of a thing* and *simultaneously to be true cause of that same thing* — in no way could simul stand — these, as far as we know, spoke of ***causa efficiens per accidens ex parte effectus simpliciter sic dicta***. But of this there is no doubt that, with respect to that of which it is called causa per accidens, true cause it cannot be said — whether in *sensu composito* or in *sensu diviso* it be regarded — of which more things will be dealt-with in the doctrine of ***causa efficiens***.

#### § 7 — Causatum Per Se / Per Accidens Ex Parte Causae

> ***Hitherto we have treated of causa per se and per accidens, and of each's distinctions. Now we must treat of ***causatum per se*** and ***causatum per accidens***. What causatum per se ex parte causati and causatum per accidens ex parte causati be, was defined above at chapter VIII § 17 (p. 561). It remains, therefore, that we explain what causatum per se ex parte causae and causatum per accidens ex parte causae be.***
>
> ***Causatum per se ex parte causae is causatum ***which from another QUA SUCH receives or has its essence*** — i.e. of which the cause is another ***qua such***. E.gr. the building is causatum per se ex parte causae with respect to the architect, because the architect ***qua such*** is true cause of the building.***
>
> ***Causatum per accidens ex parte causae is causatum ***which from another receives or has its essence, but not qua such*** — i.e. of which the cause is another, but not ***qua such***. E.gr. the building is said to be causatum per accidens ex parte causae with respect to the Musician, because the Musician (if, namely, he be simultaneously Architect) is cause of the building, yet the building from him is not qua such.***

#### Note

The phrase ***"from another qua such to receive or have its essence"*** is here taken in a ***wider*** signification, such that it notes not only the ***efficient*** cause but any other cause whatever — and is the same as ***to proceed from elsewhere in one's own being***.

#### § 8 — Convergence / Divergence Ex Parte Causae

> ***Causatum per se ex parte causae and causatum per accidens ex parte causae ***converge*** in this: that each is a true causatum in order to that in-respect-of-which it is called causatum per se or per accidens; they ***differ***, because the former proceeds from another ***qua such***, the latter proceeds from another ***not qua such***. E.gr. a building is true causatum both in respect of the Architect and in respect of the Musician, if, namely, the same man be simultaneously Musician and Architect: but from the Architect it is ***qua such***, from the Musician ***not*** qua such.***

#### § 9 — Convergence / Divergence Ex Parte Causati

> ***Causatum per se ex parte causati and causatum per accidens ex parte causati ***converge*** in this: that each acknowledges a true cause of itself; they ***differ***, because the former is a true causatum ***qua such***, and indeed in order to that in-respect-of-which it is called causatum per se ex parte causati; the latter in order to that in-respect-of-which it is called causatum per accidens ex parte causati ***is either plainly not causatum, or if it be causatum in respect of it, yet NOT qua such is it causatum***.***
>
> ***Exempli gratia***: a building is true causatum in respect of the architect, and is such ***qua such*** causatum in respect of the architect. ***But a Doctor, who is a rustic's son, is causatum in respect of the rustic — but not as Doctor***. ***And in respect of the Father who had sent the Son to the market at the time when he had believed, with safe conscience, that the way was safe from robbers, the slaughter of the Son perpetrated by robbers is rightly called ***causatum per accidens ex parte causati*** — and plainly is NOT causatum in respect of the Father***.

#### Notes

**I.** That ***causatum per accidens ex parte causae is always a true causatum*** is clear thence: because it is so called in respect of that of which it is true cause, though not as such. Hence is born this argument: ***That of which another is true cause, this is true causatum. But of every causatum per accidens ex parte causae, that in-respect-of-which it is called causatum per accidens ex parte causae is true cause. Therefore every causatum per accidens ex parte causae is true causatum in order to that in-respect-of-which it is called causatum per accidens ex parte causae.*** The Major is manifest, because ***with cause posited, causatum is posited*** — hence of which another is true cause, this very thing in respect of the other will altogether be causatum. The Minor is clear from the definition of causatum per accidens ex parte causae.

**II.** But that ***causatum per accidens ex parte causati is NOT always true causatum*** in order to that in-respect-of-which it is called causatum per accidens ex parte causati — and that if it be true causatum, ***yet never qua such*** — is clear from this: that that of which it is denominated causatum per accidens ex parte causati either is plainly not cause of it, or is not cause of it ***as it is such causatum***. The argument: ***That of which another is plainly not cause, or [not] of it as such, this in the other's respect either is plainly not causatum, or qua such is not causatum. But of causatum per accidens ex parte causati, that in-respect-of-which it is called causatum per accidens ex parte causati either is plainly not cause, or of it as such is not cause. Therefore causatum per accidens ex parte causati, in that other's respect, either is plainly not causatum, or qua such is not causatum.*** The Major is manifest, because ***with cause taken away, causatum is taken away***. The Minor's truth stands from the definition of causatum per accidens ex parte causati.

#### § 10 — Causa Per Accidens vs Causa Sine Qua Non

> ***Finally, let it be allowed to note the discrimen that stands between CAUSA PER ACCIDENS — both ex parte causae and ex parte causati — and the ***CAUSA SINE QUA NON***, as they call it. And indeed the discrimen between causa per accidens ***ex parte causae*** and causa sine qua non can be easily observed: For causa per accidens ex parte causae ***always is true cause*** of that of which it is called causa per accidens ex parte causae — though not as such — and so is true cause; but causa sine qua non simply is NOT true cause.***

#### Nota

Let there be compared §§ 5 and 6 note II of this chapter, and § 14 together with the notes to the same chapter.

> ***But ***causa per accidens EX PARTE CAUSATI*** and ***causa sine qua non*** differ in various modes.***
>
> ***(a) Causa per accidens ex parte causati is ***NOT necessary*** to that causatum in-respect-of-which it is called causa per accidens ex parte causati; but every causa sine qua non is ***necessary*** to that causatum in-respect-of-which it is called causa sine qua non.***
>
> ***(b) Causa per accidens ex parte causati, when it is necessary to the causatum, ***qua such*** is not necessary; but causa sine qua non is necessary to the causatum, ***and qua such is necessary***.***
>
> ***(c) Causa sine qua non is a ***necessary condition***; but in vain would you have said this of causa per accidens ex parte causati.***

#### Notes

**I.** These things so standing, we cannot but modestly dissent from the following assertion:

> ***"One who ***removes a door-shutter***, and one who ***separates sand from a cutting rope***, etc., are indeed true, real causes of removal and dissection; because however this neither illuminates the sun, nor the medicament restoring health, nor the stone's motion downwards, etc., positively and causally helps — nor does it actively produce illumination itself, or health, or the downward fall: therefore they can be called neither associate causes, nor true causes of those effects, but only ***causae sine quibus non***, i.e. [causes] such that the proximate and direct causes could not exercise their causalities, had not something such been conjoined."***

More clearly: some causa sine-qua-non can be referred ***to two things***: e.gr. one who removes a door-shutter can be referred (1) ***to the removing itself***, i.e. the action proceeding from himself as such; or (2) ***to that which proximately follows it, joined with the true and physical cause*** — e.gr. the sun — ***which, without that removing, could not causally produce the effect*** (e.gr. the illumination). In the ***prior*** consideration it is not so much a causa-sine-qua-non as a true, real, physical cause. In the ***posterior*** consideration it properly obtains the name of causa-sine-qua-non; and in the mode which pertains to this consideration is the present discourse.

Perhaps such things do less than clinch the matter: for one thing is the one-who-removes-a-door-shutter, another the removal-of-a-door-shutter in respect of illumination. The one-who-removes-a-door-shutter, though not true physical cause of the illumination, is yet true physical cause of the removal — whence he is wont to be called ***causa physica per accidens*** of the illumination. For he does something to which another follows, namely the illumination. But the removal of the door-shutter cannot be called ***causa physica per accidens*** of the illumination. Nor are we persuaded by what follows to change our mind.

And this is still further to be noted here: that ***causa sine-qua-non*** seems to hold great kinship with ***causa per accidens ex parte effectus***. And indeed it happens that something be simultaneously such a causa per accidens and a causa sine-qua-non. ***Aristotle*** certainly expressly names as ***causae per accidens*** him who ***causes the columns of the roof to fall*** and him who ***removes the stone from the wineskin*** — which same, that they can also be called ***causae sine-quibus-non***, no one indeed will doubt. ***Why not?*** Nay rather, we certainly do not doubt — but rather expressly ***deny*** [that they are such], on the reasons just given. The same account holds concerning the removal of door-shutters and of purulence, etc., with which — as effects-per-se — other effects (e.gr. illumination and health) are conjoined ***per accidens***. Altogether the same account: whence, just as he who submoves the columns of a house and he who removes a stone from a wineskin are not causae sine-quibus-non, nor physical causes per se, but ***causae physicae per accidens ex parte of their causata*** (namely of the house's ruin, and of the wineskin's upward motion); so also he who removes door-shutters and he who removes purulence are not causae sine-quibus-non in order to the illumination and the healing of the wound, nor are they physical causes per se, but ***causae physicae per accidens***.

And how these words agree with those which immediately follow:

> ***"Yet there occurs not altogether no discrimen. For causa per accidens ex parte effectus in genere naturae — or by reason of ***influxus*** — is always true cause of some per-se effect, with which per accidens another is conjoined; and so is called causa per accidens only in respect of this ADJUNCT effect, into which the true cause itself had not flowed. But causa sine-qua-non as such is not always true cause of some real effect — as, e.gr., the medium stands, which is causa sine-qua-non of vision: but per se, however, nothing it causes."***

Altogether much discrimen between causa per accidens ex parte effectus and causa sine-qua-non occurs, as is clear from the text of the §. But as to what is said — ***that causa sine qua non as such is NOT ALWAYS true cause of some real effect*** — we should say (with the saved judgment of any better one, and with unimpaired authority of him who asserts the contrary) that ***causa sine qua non as such is NEVER true cause of any real effect***. To say nothing of this: that causa sine qua non and causa per accidens ex parte causati extend far more widely than that they should be restricted to the one genus of ***causa efficiens***. More things below in the doctrine of ***causa efficiens***.

**II.** The ***practical use*** of this doctrine we reserve, with good right, and with the benevolent reader's peace, to the following ***chapter XIV***.

## Caput Decimum Tertium

### Of the Genera of Causes

#### § 1

> ***Four GENERA OF CAUSES are commonly set up: ***EFFICIENS***, ***MATERIA***, ***FORMA***, ***FINIS***.***

#### Notes

**I.** Some put forth these four genera of causes thus, so that they call one cause ***causam sine qua***, another ***causam ex qua***, another ***causam per quam***, and another ***causam cuius gratia***.

**II.** To confess ingenuously what the fact is: these four notions of causes, enumerated just now, must be extended to a vast degree — whether this can be done conveniently and with the laws of discipline unviolated, let others judge; or more than four genera of causes must altogether be admitted. Thus, e.gr., to ***Matter*** or the genus of ***causa materialis*** are wont to be referred the ***Subject*** and the ***Object*** — though these are plainly diverse rationes causandi and causalities, so that you must believe Subject and Object to differ (while remaining Subject and Object) from each other almost as if by whole genus, and also from the ***Materia ex qua*** (as it is called) itself. Again, to the ***Form*** is referred the ***causa exemplaris***, though differing almost by a whole-genus from Form. Likewise no erudite man is unaware what dissensions this not-less-difficult-than-noble matter concerning the ***causa impulsiva*** — both ***προηγουμένη*** [antecedent] and ***προκαταρκτική*** [initiating] — has brought forth: some have wished both referred to that [one genus]; others this one to that [genus] and that one to this; some this to this and that to that — and perhaps they would not sin so greatly who, for the sake of a more easy and more useful doctrine, would assign to it a peculiar genus of cause. Other examples we now pass over in silence.

**III.** And surely there will be much need of circumspect ***reduction***, if we wish to set up ***four*** Genera of Causes, and in this quaternary number — because it is more received — to acquiesce.

**IV.** Mindful of our purpose, we shall not now inquire into the subtlety and rigor of that division which we have just-now handed down — or rather, recounted. The ***QUATERNARY NUMBER OF CAUSES*** is surely received by use, and today by almost all is held as ***sufficient and adequate***. In the meantime we shall so temper ourselves: that in distinct chapters we shall first of all treat of the ***four Causes properly so-called in rigor***; then in peculiar chapters we shall deal with the ***other causes***, and simultaneously show in what mode by the Vulgo of Metaphysicians, or even by the more celebrated Metaphysicians, the remaining Causes are wont to be reduced to the said four Genera of Causes — so that we may seem both to have served our time and simultaneously to have offered the remaining equitable and benevolent reader and judge the occasion of judging whether such reduction be precisely needful, or whether it would be more consistent with the use of Academic studies to hand down more than four Genera of Causes.

#### § 2 — Tot Genera, Tot Rationes Causandi, Tot Causalitates

> ***But however many Genera of Causes are inquired-after or set-up, exactly so many — beyond all doubt — must be sought and assigned ***rationes causandi***, and so many ***causalities***.***

#### Notes

**I.** The ***ratio causandi*** was above (chapter VIII § 12 p. 546) called ***potentia causativa***. Just as therefore in that same place — and in almost the whole of chapter IX — we have prolixly taught that ***potentia causativa is that by which something is fit either to become or to be a cause***: so each will easily attain this — that, just as with potentia causativa taken away cause is taken away, so with ***this*** or ***that*** genus of potentia causativa taken away ***this*** or ***that*** genus of cause is taken away. There will be therefore so many genera of rationes causandi as there are genera of causes; and unless you admit this, you will at length be bound to confess that more causes exist, and more genera of causes, than can exist — than which nothing is more absurd.

**II.** Likewise ***causalitas*** at the cited chapter VIII § 13 p. 549 we have said is ***that by which something is true cause***. Therefore there will be given as many causes as there are given causalities, and vice-versa.

**III.** Whence you may wonder why it is Vulgo taught that only ***two*** potentiae causativae are given — namely ***active*** and ***passive*** — and yet at the same time four genera of causes are defended. Surely, if more Genera of Causes are given besides ***causa efficiens*** and ***causa materialis***, more Genera of ***Potentiarum Causativarum*** must also be given. For either ***Form*** and ***End*** — if indeed they be peculiar causes and constitute peculiar genera of causes (as surely they do constitute) — [are such] ***through active and passive potency***, [so that they] be peculiar causes and peculiar genera of causes; or ***through no potency at all***; or ***through plainly other potencies, and ones distinct in genus, from active and passive potency***. Not the first — because thus they would not be peculiar causes and peculiar genera of causes. Not the second — because thus they would plainly not be causes. Therefore more than two genera of rationes causandi are given. Nor is there anything in saying that ***potentia causativa realiter existens*** is thus divided; for even that potency through which Form properly-so-called is Form is surely really extant. And if you take exception — that this potency ex parte formae does not really differ from the Form — [it suffices to say] certainly, whatever is the case, let it be enough that we have just now rejoined that neither does ***active potency*** really differ from ***causa efficiens***.

#### § 3 — Four Genera of Potentiae Causativae

> ***The FOUR GENERA OF POTENTIAE CAUSATIVAE in the Schools are otherwise wont to be set forth thus: ***Potentia Effectiva***, ***Potentia Passiva***, ***Potentia Informativa***, ***Potentia Allicitiva*** or (metaphorically) ***Motiva***.***

#### Nota

Potentia ***Effectiva*** corresponds to ***causa efficiens***; Potentia ***Passiva*** to ***Causa Materialis***; Potentia ***Informativa*** to the ***Formal***; Potentia ***Allicitiva*** (or, metaphorically, ***Motiva***) to the ***Causa Finalis***.

#### § 4 — Four Genera of Causalitates

> ***The four genera of ***Causalitates*** themselves are handed down by the Doctors of the Schools thus: ***Vera et realis EFFECTIO***, ***PASSIO***, ***INFORMATIO***, ***METAPHORICA MOTIO***.***

#### Notes

**I.** Because the opinion received among Aristotle and most Philosophers is — as we admonished at § 1 — that there are given four genera of causes:

1. ***ἀρχὴ τῆς κινήσεως***, i.e. ***the source of the first motion***, or ***the Efficient Cause***.
2. ***ὕλη***, i.e. ***MATTER*** and ***Subjectum ex quo*** out of which something comes to be.
3. ***τὸ τί ἦν εἶναι***, i.e. ***the what-it-was-to-be***, or ***the FORM***.
4. ***τὸ ἕνεκα*** and ***τὸ ἀγαθόν***, i.e. ***that for the sake of which*** and ***the good***, or ***the FINAL CAUSE***.

(See Aristotle himself at *Metaphysics* I.3 and V.2; likewise *Physics* II.7 text 68. Let there be compared, if it please, ***Conimbricenses*** *Metaph.* I. c. 7 q. 1; ***Carolus Franciscus d'Abra de Raconis*** disp. 12 p. 2 art. 1; ***Petrus Fonseca*** *Metaph.* I. c. 7 q. 1 § 4) — chief among whom after Aristotle must be named ***Franciscus Suarez*** *Disp. Metaph.* 12 sect. 3. On this account they call ***effectio*** that by which ***causa efficiens is efficiens***, i.e. ***the causality of the efficient***; ***passio***, i.e. the ***reception*** of form and its ***retention***, that by which ***causa materialis is materialis***; ***informatio***, that by which ***causa formalis is formalis***, i.e. ***the causality of the form***; ***metaphorica motio***, that by which ***causa finalis is finalis***, i.e. ***the causality of the end***.

**II.** But what must be judged of these can more rightly stand clear from the doctrines of the single causes.

#### § 5 — Dichotomy: Interna / Externa

> ***To not a few the ***dichotomy*** pleases, whence they first divide cause into ***INTERNAM*** — which enters the ***constitution*** of that of which it is cause; and ***EXTERNAM*** — which does not enter the constitution of that of which it is cause. To the former they afterward refer ***Matter*** and ***Form***; to the latter, ***the Efficient Cause*** and ***the Final***.***

#### Notes

**I.** This division is received by use. By the formula ***"this enters another's constitution"*** nothing else is signified than ***that it stands that the other is composed from it***.

**II.** You may commonly see it said that there are two ***internal*** causes — namely ***Matter*** and ***Form***; and two ***external*** causes — ***Efficient*** and ***Final***. For truly, if you wish to refer to Matter (or the causa materialis) those things which, by the patrons and defenders of the quaternary of Causes, are reduced thereto, ***the Causa Materialis in its full latitude cannot be held as causa interna***. For:

(a) ***SUBJECT*** is also called the matter of that of which it is subject — yet the subject is not ***in*** that of which it is subject; rather, that of which it is subject is ***in*** that which is called subject. E.gr. a wall is the subject of whiteness: yet it is not that the wall is in the whiteness, but the whiteness is in the wall.

(b) Likewise ***OBJECT*** is not intrinsic to that of which, in Philosophical rigor, it is called the object; rather, extrinsically it ***terminates*** that of which it is called object. E.gr. the object of vision is a wall: a wall, however, extrinsically terminates the seeing.

(c) To say nothing of the ***matter*** which is attributed to ***material forms*** and whence they are denominated ***material***: for Matter never enters the constitution of a material form — otherwise the form would not be ***simple***; of which more things in the doctrine on form.

(d) Thus to ***Form*** is wont to be referred the ***exemplar***; but the exemplar does not enter the constitution of the ***exemplatum***, as it is called.

(e) Thus — men of great judgment and most-celebrated — some refer each ***causa impulsiva***, both ***προηγουμένη*** and ***προκαταρκτική***, to the ***causa efficiens***; others, the former to the causa efficiens and the latter to the causa finalis; yet again others reduce the former to the ***causa formalis*** and the latter to the causa finalis. Yet both these, those, and these others divide causa impulsiva into ***interna*** and ***externa***, and they call ***προηγουμένη*** causa impulsiva ***interna*** and ***προκαταρκτική*** causa impulsiva ***externa***.

**III.** For the rest, concerning the other causes in common — both as to their divisions and as to their bare distinctions — we have decreed to deal only after the doctrine of the single causes; and perhaps this method will seem not so inconvenient, inasmuch as these divisions and distinctions wander through the single genera of causes.

## Caput Decimum Quartum

### Of the Practical Use of the Doctrine on the Genera of Causes in All Disciplines — Chiefly in the Practical [Disciplines] and in the (so-called) Higher Faculties

#### § 1 — General Programme

> ***The use of the doctrine on the four genera of causes consists in the ***convenient, sufficiently decent, and genuine application*** of the notions occurring in the doctrine of causes ***to the subject-matter of disciplines and of faculties***.***

#### Notes

**I.** All those things come here to be repeated which at the ***Caput Praeliminare*** § 29 ff. were said concerning general and special use, so far as they can chiefly be drawn hither; likewise what we have discoursed throughout the ***eleventh*** chapter on the genuine discrimination of the Metaphysical notion of cause from the Analytical notion — chiefly at ***Note I to p. 701-702***.

**II.** Most rightly and most-properly so-called are the four genera of causes attributed to ***natural substances*** — which in the Schools are called ***natural bodies***. For if you consider a natural body — e.gr. a man — thus is given the ***matter*** of man most-properly so-called, namely the body; is given a ***form*** most-properly so-called, namely the soul: likewise it is easy to name a most-properly so-called ***final cause*** (that for the sake of which man was generated), and a most-properly so-called ***efficient cause***.

**III.** For the rest, if we would weigh the matter rightly on the balance of truth, nowhere else will you find all and each of the four genera of causes in such a rigorous signification simultaneously.

**IV.** Let the Cultivators of Morals, Jurisprudence, and Theology now judge: there is surely no doubt but that, by their own judgment, they will attain this — that an ***analogical*** treatment of causes is needed if in Morals, Theology, and Jurisprudence we wish to call any matter back to the four causes. Indeed I confess that there can be set-up and admitted — whether of ***acts*** or of other ***business and works*** Moral, Political, likewise those which are of Juridical or Theological consideration — ***FOUR CAUSES***, by imitation of the four causes in Natural [sciences] or Physics; but it must be done with ***applied limatum iudicium***, if we wish not only to find, perceive, hold in memory, and hand down to others — with such dexterity and ***ἀκρίβεια*** as is suitable — a similar ***efficient***, but also ***material*** and ***formal*** cause of Moral, Civil, Juridical, Theological actions, affairs, and works.

#### § 2 — The Praecipuus Labor of Academic Studies

> ***But because to ***learn (teach) rightly*** is ***to perceive (hand down) rightly*** the causes of things, therefore the chief labor and the chief care of Academic studies is absolved in the ***investigation, cognition, consideration, and explication*** of the ***single causes*** of each matter — e.gr. of Theological, Juridical, Moral, Political matters, etc. No doctrine, therefore, occurs in the whole of First Philosophy which can be said either ***more ample*** or ***greater in commendation*** than that which is of the present argument.***

#### Notes

**I.** When we assert that ***all science is from causes***, we suppose it sufficiently clear to all that the discourse here is of ***demonstrative science***, which can and must ***be had from priors***.

**II.** Nor is it [an objection] that we said the notion of cause is to be received otherwise in Metaphysics, otherwise in Analytics — thereby injecting a scruple, as if perhaps one or another less-exercised student may believe that these very things which we are now about to propose by no means pertain to Metaphysics (a difficulty which the daily inspection of books (which are exposed to all beginners' eyes and handled by their hands) could easily augment). For we believe testimony-greater-than-every-exception to be ***this***: that of all Academic Professors and Doctors (to whom the salvation of Academic Youth, as it tends toward higher and more solid things, is at heart and the subject of their care) by unanimous and continuous consent — out of the dignity and chief most-present commodity of any Academic Student fit for a cultivator of prudence idoneously tending toward solid erudition — it has been, as long as the orb of most-learned Men and suitable Professors and Doctors has stood, still is, and in no time to come will not be, ***to know the mode of felicitously reducing any suitable and solid doctrine, of whatever argument it finally be, to a certain genus of causes — to one or many, as the indoles of the doctrine demands***. For causes in Metaphysics are received, and ex professo the notions of them pertain to First Philosophy. These things I would not have willed to commit to public types unless I knew for certain that this matter must most-diligently be commended and inculcated to the Students of any Faculty and Discipline, chiefly however of Theology and Jurisprudence (likewise of Morals) — because the confusion of its sense, and the account of this doctrine, (where plainly not understood, or less-felicitously grasped) has given, to many Academic damages and already a sorrowful and ***irreparable*** loss of golden Time, and in posterity will give.

#### § 3 — The Testimony of Prudent Professors and Doctors

> ***In this I surely rejoice: that any ***prudent*** and ***cordate*** Professors and Doctors, and single most-learned Men of exact judgment, I have always had — and in posterity shall have — as going-before-me and consenting, in this: that if we except the one question ***An sit?*** [Whether it is?], all the remaining questions — such as ***Moral, Political, Juridical, Theological*** questions — [which] in the Schools by suitable and approved Doctors can and are wont to be proposed, must be able to be understood either of the four causes in universum or of some one of them.***

#### Nota

And let this chiefly be known, and have the having-of-it as commended to them, by those who in the Academies strive to carp the fruit from their studies.

#### § 4 — The Threefold Use

> ***Therefore the ***USE*** of the doctrine on the genera of causes — both in other disciplines and in the Practical and Higher (as they are called) Faculties — chiefly ***unfolds itself in three ways***:***
>
> ***(1) The ***FIRST*** is: that the learners (or teachers) in the Academies are bound to render to themselves (and others) decently and solidly ***perspectum*** this — ***QUAE RES SIT HUIUS VEL ILLIUS GENERIS CAUSA?*** [What thing is cause of this or that genus?]***
>
> ***(2) The ***SECOND*** is: that it is incumbent on them to call into notice the ***MODE OF PROVING, THROUGH A CAUSE OF THE SAME OR OF ANOTHER GENUS, A CAUSE OF THIS OR OF THAT GENUS***.***
>
> ***(3) The ***THIRD*** is: that they must be solicitous about the ***MODE OF DEMONSTRATING THROUGH A CAUSE THE CONCLUSIONS WHICH TREAT OF THE GENERA OF CAUSES***.***

#### Nota

Because by these three moments a great part of Academic erudition — and the whole of demonstrative Science — is absolved, it will be our [task] to hand down each of the three requisites of the Academic Student (or Doctor) with a little more distinctness, and to illustrate them with easy, most-clear examples.

#### § 5 — The First Use Unpacked: Three Sub-Requisites

> ***The ***FIRST USE*** was: to render ***perspectum*** to oneself (and to others) ***what thing is cause of this or that genus***. For this therefore to be rightly perceived, three things again are required:***
>
> ***(a) It is needful that there be a ***decent and suitable*** [grasp] of the notions of each cause, rightly and sufficiently understood.***
>
> ***(b) It is needful that there be an ***application*** of the solidly-known ***requisites*** on the part of each cause — all and single, both the ***primary*** and the ***secondary***.***
>
> ***(c) It is needful that there be ***notice*** of the various questions wont to be employed in the Practical Disciplines and in the (as they are called) Higher Faculties — questions in which now it is a matter of a certain genus of cause, now of a certain requisite on the part of a certain genus.***

#### Nota

These we shall again ponder each a little more intimately, nothing doubting but that our labor can be neither plainly useless nor so ungrateful to the benevolent Studiosus.

#### § 6 — The Practical Reduction Schema

> ***For a decent and suitable application of the notions of each cause, we have said that the Students of Morals, likewise of Jurisprudence and Theology, need a prior right and sufficient cognition of the notions themselves of each cause. Now, because the common opinion of the ***quaternary number of causes*** has struck roots almost in the minds of all — far be it from us to disturb beginners' concepts; rather we shall help them, laying up the memory of the distinction by a more useful method. Namely, in the Practical Disciplines and in the (as they are called) Higher Faculties, ***Efficient***, ***Final***, ***Matter*** and ***Form*** are thus explicated:***
>
> ***EFFICIENT CAUSE*** = ***the AGENT himself***, or ***the PERSON of the Agent*** — as the Doctors of the Practical Disciplines and of the Laws and of Theology love to speak.***
>
> ***FINAL CAUSE*** notes ***that for the sake of which the act or business occurs***.***
>
> ***MATERIAL CAUSE*** = ***the OBJECT***, i.e. ***that about which the act, business, or work is engaged***.***
>
> ***FORMAL CAUSE*** = ***the formal ratio*** or ***MODUS of the action or business***.***

#### Notes

**I.** Not only Ethics and Politics (in one word, the whole of Practical Philosophy), but also the whole of Jurisprudence and Theology, chiefly turn ***around acts***: Moral Philosophy turns around moral acts; Politics around civil acts (which of them are to be exercised, which omitted, which permitted). Likewise forensic Jurisprudence turns around forensic acts and business; Theology is occupied around Theological acts and business.

**II.** But all other and single [things] which, by whatever account, come at length into Moral and Political, Juridical or Theological inquiry, are — as by their nature or per se ***ordered to*** Moral and Civil, forensic or sacred (or by another account Theological) acts, and ***exist on account of*** such-mode acts and business — thus desired and come to be called into Moral, Political, Juridical, and Theological consideration ***chiefly on account of those acts and business***.

#### § 7 — The Four Causes in Every Act

> ***Let the Students of Moral and Civil Philosophy, likewise of Jurisprudence and Theology, be most-certain that ***an Efficient, a Final, a Material, and a Formal Cause*** is to be found also in ***all acts*** — Moral and Civil, forensic or Theological — and that for the full science of any action or business the cognition of all (and the single [causes]) of it is required.***

#### Notes

**I.** Here we cannot but — without any study or affect of parties — note by the way: that not rarely are found private ***manuductores*** who indeed (what is to be praised) inculcate seriously to their auditors that ***full science of any thing is constituted in the cognition of all its causes***; yet so they explicate and apply the common uses of causes (which is to be lamented, and worthy not of refutation but often of sad commiseration) that it would sometimes have been better and more consulted-for by their admirers to have in the meantime learned ***nothing*** — because once things have been grasped in by the consent of their Doctors and fellow-Students, it is more difficult to ***un-learn*** than to learn. These men indeed first impose on themselves, and then on others — perverted ***αὐτοδίδακτοι*** [self-taught] [as they are] — they come to this: that only ***while teaching***, i.e. while they struggle to hand down all the causes of a thing, do they begin to learn what this cause is, what that is, what is some other cause. For the Metaphysico-Analytical doctrine of causes, as ***Eustratius*** is author, offers to those wishing-to-teach nearly the same use that ***a rule and a plumb-line*** offer to the architect.

> ***"This therefore is the beginning of depraved dogmas — not to have first contemplated of causes, but at once-with to inquire into causes and (as if-you-knew what causes are and demonstrations from causes) to try to bring demonstration" ***— as ***Galen*** accurately judges, who elsewhere most-severely notes the arrogance of those who, without the Metaphysical and Analytical doctrine of causes, attack sciences and (as they are called) higher Faculties — and commemorates many inconveniences, into which it is necessary that those should run who philosophize without this light, ***blind leaders of the blind***: for ***"they neither assume what is known, nor demonstrate the unknown; but like legislators, they set up what pleases; finally, in the progress of discourse, after the manner of a Euripus, they bring forth the summit of inconstancy."***

**II.** Nor is there [a point] in saying that it is a matter not so-greatly-weighty, but almost ***puerile***, to render to oneself ***perspectum*** the four words of the genera of causes. For:

**(1)** Suppose the Metaphysical doctrine on the four genera of causes is not so-great in moment and is almost puerile — what else, pray, do those who so judge do than ***flagellate their own ἀπαιδευσία*** [untutoredness], and in those things which they had held for puerile, so-easily prostitute themselves? Surely the first rule of Grammar which schoolmasters inculcate upon their boys is: ***"Adjective and Substantive agree in the same genus, number, and case."*** Should ***Priscianus*** then by right and merit be flogged — as many times as, wishing to teach, he sins against this rule? Will a Doctor of this sort be able — in a Grammatical forum, against Priscianus, who was pressing an action against him — to except that it is a matter not so weighty, but almost puerile, to render to oneself ***perspectam*** the rule ***"Adjective and Substantive"*** etc.? Verily, ingenuous shame prohibits me from daring to demonstrate what otherwise could be demonstrated by most-easy effort: by what account Students, incautious and imprudent, if they fall into manuductores of this kind, often take ***bare phantoms of things, and shadows of causes***, for the things and the causes of things. For we know it to have happened not nowhere: that someone, promising to his admirers in the first chapter of his method on ***the efficient cause of a thing*** (whose accurate treatment he had taken-up upon himself) about to propose and solidly explicate [it], had in antecedent warned that he was ***now about to treat of the efficient cause — that is, of GOD alone***. Another, however, promising to treat solidly and artificially of the efficient cause ***of any Republic***, both of the mutations of any Republic and of its ***interitus*** [downfall], said that the efficient cause of all these is ***GOD*** — and besides this, nothing. Does this not reek of ridicule — when, about to narrate the ***material*** causes of an act or business, he hands down those things which ***impelled the person of the agent*** that he might exercise this or that act, or complete this or that business? Perhaps because ***OBIECTUM*** and ***OB QUOD AGITUR*** meet in two letters (***ob***), or because, while treatment of causes is being instituted, they themselves become the matter of treatment. What is more frequent — among many [of them] — than to ***confound causae impulsivae with causae finales***? E.gr. it is asked ***OB QUOD?*** — and the response is given through the ***final cause***: as though ***ob quod?*** and ***cuius ergo?*** were questions which never must be said of the same cause. How many lapses of judgment are allowed to be adverted-to — while many, leaning on natural Metaphysics and Analysis, strive to inquire into the ***form*** of a thing! Surely because they have firmly impressed on their minds that ***Matter and Form are internal causes***, hardly can it be said in words how much molestation they create for themselves and theirs ***in investigating and handing down*** the ***internal*** causes — as if the ***body*** and as if the ***soul*** of this or that act or business — since often ***they wash a brick, and by understanding they bring it about that they understand nothing***.

**(2)** And to confess ingenuously what truth demands: it is a matter not of so-small moment, nor puerile, to know the ***Metaphysico-Analytical*** doctrine on the causes rightly and decently. For the notice of the ***four words*** does not suffice; rather, it is simultaneously needful [to have] the suitable and accurate cognition of ***so many divisions and subdivisions***, of ***so many requisites*** (primary and secondary), of ***so many reductions*** to the certain genera of causes, of ***so many modes of demonstrating through causes*** — which (as ***Piccartus*** discusses) ***maxime inhabit*** the Practical Disciplines and the (as they are called) Higher Faculties — so that the most-clear and most-learned Men may always find how it may profit them more and more to teach ***briefly, perspicuously, in order, and congruently with the matter — in one word, prudently***; and the Auditors, how to admit the doctrine ***rightly and conveniently handed down***. For it ought not to raise a business for us: that many who have themselves accurately learned nothing of all these things, deny there is need of so-great apparatus. For ***the imperiti*** (the words are Aristotle's at ***Sophistical Elenchi I.1***) ***"gaze at all things only from afar; and to them the exquisite ratio of teaching is a molestation — whether because they cannot grasp the matter, or because they judge that diligence excessive. For such a thing has what is accurate; whence it happens that, just as in contracts, so in disputations, this seems to some ***illiberal*** — as the Philosopher again says at ***Metaphysics II.3***."***

**III.** Let us therefore cease to wonder, why so few hitherto have brought a sufficiently suitable notice of causes from the Metaphysics to the ***τὰ πρακτικά*** in universum — accustomed [as they are] to ***proletarian*** doctrine, or to ***testimonies and historiolae*** heaped together from here and there: men of that order whom ***the author of the Metaphysics Minor*** (whether he be ***Pasicrates***) noted at ***c. 3***, who ***admit no one lightly unless he uses examples or produces some witness***, and whom therefore he calls ***λοῖδοροι*** [abusers] — and this ***on account of the imperitia of Metaphysics and Analysis***. Many of them hold it a scruple of religion to pronounce ***without a witness*** that twice-two is four, yet do not shrink from vanquishing all with false or unsuitable witnesses. For one may often see the testimonies adduced [to be] either where there was no need of probation at all, or where the matter demanded ***a cause, not a testimony***, or where the thing to be proved has nothing at all in common with that testimony which is adduced except one or another little word. In one word: ***their testimonies are not rarely empty — plebeian bird-catchings of unlearned praise, not weights and arguments of things and causes***.

Tot-ergo erunt genera-rationum-causandi quot-genera-causarum; aliter *plures-causae-essent-quam-esse-possint*. **Note II**: causalitas = quo-aliquid-vera-causa (c. 8 § 13 p. 549); tot-causae tot-causalitates. **Note III = ANTI-VULGO POLEMIC**: Vulgo-doceatur duas-potentias-causativas (activam + passivam) + tamen-quatuor-genera-causarum — ***oportet-dari-plura-potentiarum-causativarum-genera***. *[T106 — **Caput XII § 10 + Nota + ex-parte-causati-vs-sine-qua-non differences + Notes I-II CLOSES Caput XII**. **§ 10 discrimen causa-per-accidens vs causa-sine-qua-non**: sub-ex-parte-causae: ***causa-per-accidens-ex-parte-causae SEMPER vera-causa*** (licet non-ut-talis), ***causa-sine-qua-non ne-plane-non-vera-causa***. **Nota bibliographic**: cross-refs §§ 5 + 6-Note-2 + § 14. **Sub-ex-parte-causati — THREE differences**: (a) causa-per-accidens-ex-parte-causati NON-necessaria vs causa-sine-qua-non SEMPER-necessaria; (b) when-necessary causa-per-accidens-ex-parte-causati qua-talis non-necessaria vs causa-sine-qua-non et-qua-talis-necessaria; (c) causa-sine-qua-non = necessaria-conditio, frustra-de-causa-per-accidens-ex-parte-causati. **Note I = THE MASSIVE ARISTOTLE ANTI-POLEMIC**: Veltheim modeste-dissentit from the adversary's assertion that ***removens-valvas et secernens-arenam-a-dissecando-funem*** = verae-reales-causae-remotionis-et-dissectionis + non-causae-illuminationis/sanitatis/lapsus-deorsum, sed-tantum ***causae-sine-quibus-non***. **Veltheim's *Clarius* worked disambiguation**: causa-sine-qua-non referri-potest ad-DUO — (1) ad ipsam-remotionem-seu-actionem-a-se-ut-tali-provenientem (= vera-realis-physica-causa); (2) ad id-quod-eam-proxime-consequitur-iunctam-cum-vera-physica-causa (sole) quae-effectum sine-illa-remotione-causaliter-producere-nequiret (hoc-modo = proprie-causa-sine-qua-non). ***Aliud removens-valvas, aliud remotio-valvarum respectu-illuminationis***. Removens-valvas = vera-physica-causa-remotionis + ***causa-physica-per-accidens-illuminationis*** (facit-aliquid ad-quod-aliud-consequitur); remotio-valvarum NON causa-physica-per-accidens-illuminationis. **The Aristotle citation**: ***ruentem-columnas-tectum*** + ***submoventem-lapidem-ab-utre*** = causae-per-accidens-expresse-nominat; nemo-ambiget-causae-sine-quibus-non-dici-posse. ***Cur non? *[T105 — **Caput XII § 7 close + §§ 8-9 + § 9 Notes I-II**. § 7 definition close: *aedificium ab eo non est ut tali*. **Nota**: *phrasis "ab alio qua tali essentiam accipere"* taken in laxiori-significatione — not restricted to efficient but any cause-genus; = *aliunde in esse suo procedere*. **§ 8 convergence/divergence ex-parte-causae**: both verae-causata; differunt — illud procedit-ab-altero-ut-tali, hoc procedit-ab-altero-non-ut-tali; aedificium = verum-causatum tum-respectu-Architecti tum-respectu-Musici (si idem simul = Musicus et Architectus) but ab-Architecto ut-tali, a-Musico non-ut-tali. **§ 9 convergence/divergence ex-parte-causati**: both agnoscunt-verum-sui-causam; differunt — illud = verum-causatum-qua-tale; hoc aut-plane-non-causatum aut si-causatum non-ut-tale. **Three worked examples**: (1) aedificium-respectu-architecti verum-causatum-qua-tale; (2) ***Doctor-rustici-filius = causatum-respectu-rustici sed non-ut-Doctor***; (3) ***pater-mittens-filium-ad-nundinas viam-tutam-a-latronibus-crediderat → caedes-filii-a-latronibus = causatum-per-accidens-ex-parte-causati, et plane-non-causatum-respectu-Patris***. **Note I**: ***causatum-per-accidens-ex-parte-causae SEMPER verum-causatum*** — syllogism *cuius-alterum-vera-causa, hoc-verum-causatum; omnis-causati-per-accidens-ex-parte-causae illud-vera-causa, cuius-respectu causatum-per-accidens-ex-parte-causae dicitur; ergo omne-causatum-per-accidens-ex-parte-causae verum-causatum*. Reason: ***posita-causa-ponitur-causatum***. **Note II**: ***causatum-per-accidens-ex-parte-causati NON-semper verum-causatum***, et si-verum nunquam-qua-tale — parallel syllogism ***sublata-causa-tollitur-causatum***. *[T104 — **Caput XII § 7 OPENS: *Causatum Per Se / Per Accidens Ex Parte Causae***. Hitherto treated causa-per-se/per-accidens; now causatum-per-se/per-accidens. Causatum-per-se/per-accidens ex-parte-causati already defined c. VIII § 17 p. 561. **Definitions**: ***Causatum per se ex parte causae = causatum quod ab alio qua tali essentiam accipit aut habet*** (cujus causa est alterum qua tale) — e.gr. aedificium = causatum-per-se-ex-parte-causae respectu-architecti (architectus qua talis = vera causa aedificii). ***Causatum per accidens ex parte causae = causatum quod ab alio essentiam accipit aut habet sed non ut tali*** (cujus causa est alterum sed non ut tale) — e.gr. aedificium = causatum-per-accidens-ex-parte-causae respectu-Musici (if Musicus simul = Architectus — vera-causa-aedificii but aedificium ab-eo non-ut-tali).]*

— ❦ —

*[T103 — **Caput XII § 6 Note VI**: the massive anti-polemic refuting ***causa-per-accidens = principium influens in effectum non intentum*** as proposed definition. **Veltheim's Metaphysica-positive-non-polemica disclaimer**: contest-by-number-not-weight imposes on imperitiores. **Core refutation**: if that formula were definition of causa-per-accidens *in communi*, ALL causes (efficient/material/formal/final — except causae-agentes-ex-intentione) would be causae-per-accidens — absurd. Worked examples: ignis-comburit-stipulas, materia+forma-lapidis, sanitas — all *principia influentia in effectus non intentos*. **Exception + refutation**: perhaps only in-genere-causae-efficientis? But even then — by what natural judgment to argue from efficient-per-accidens to in-communi? **Key demonstratum**: ***causa-efficiens-per-accidens EX-PARTE-CAUSAE = vera-causa*** but ***causa-efficiens-per-accidens EX-PARTE-EFFECTUS NON-vera-causa***. So the chain *efficient-per-accidens-is-cause → every-per-accidens-is-cause → in-genere-cause → distinctio-est-divisio* is invalid. **The MASSIVE homo-vivus/mortuus parallel**: absurd to ***dividere*** causam-in-genere in per-se/per-accidens — just like ***homo-in-genere*** cannot be divided into *homo-vivus / homo-mortuus* (mortuus = alienans-determinatio tollens-significationem-hominis). **Objection**: *ubi-nullus-influxus-est, quomodo-causa-esse-potest? qui-concipit-causam-per-accidens, concipit-aliquam-causalitatem*. **Response**: parallel — *qui-concipit-hominem-mortuum, concipit-aliquam-humanam-naturam*; but *mortuus* tollit-significationem-hominis. Does *per accidens* tollere-significationem-causae? **Answer**: more-accurate Philosophers never-denied aliquid-posse-esse-simul-causam-per-accidens-et-veram-causam — but denied (a) ***omnis-causa-per-accidens respectu-eius-cuius-causa-per-accidens-dicitur = vera-causa***; (b) ***causa-per-accidens-qua-talis = vera-causa***. **Final nomen-causae argument**: *Quicquid-habet-nomen-causae merito-habetur-pro-vera-causa nisi-praegnans-ratio deferendo-rationem*; Veltheim: argument-stat-tamdiu-quam ratio-praegnans-non-ostenditur; sed-talis-ostensa-fuit by all-more-accurate Philosophers. In-sensu-composito-ac-formali: ***nulla causa per accidens est vera causa***. Those who said *per accidens = alienans-determinatio* spoke of causa-efficiens-per-accidens ex-parte-effectus-simpliciter — ulterius-in-doctrina-causae-efficientis.]*

— ❦ —

*[T102 — **Caput XII § 6 Notes IV + V**. **Note IV** (ex-parte-causati parallel): causa-per-accidens-ex-parte-causati is ***nunc-plane-non-vera-causa***, ***nunc-vera-causa***, but ***nunquam qua-talem*** vera causa. Reason: in-esse-suo causatum either *nullatenus-procedit-ab-ea* OR *procedit-sed-non-ut-tale*. Full argument. **Note V — SINGULARIS CAUTIO: simpliciter vs secundum quid**: ***ne confundamus causam-per-accidens ex-parte-causati SIMPLICITER-talem cum causa-per-accidens ex-parte-causati SECUNDUM-QUID***. **Ligna-finder worked example**: fiffor-lignorum qui a-tergo-stantem ex-ignorantia-invincibili et contra-omnem-intentionem laedit = vera-causa-efficiens-laesionis + *tamen in-suo-modo adhuc causa-per-accidens*. **Key reasoning**: ***causa libera*** = certa quasi-species of causa-efficiens; causa-libera + causa-efficiens-naturalis are *ejusdem generis sed non ejusdem ordinis*. Three-question levels: (1) crude: *fiffor-lignorum ex-parte-causati vera-causa-per-se fissionis-et-laesionis?* Yes-both; (2) genus-of-efficient-cause: *fiffor efficient-cause-per-se of laesio?* Yes still; (3) FREE-cause-modus: *fiffor causa-libera-laesionis?* NO — causa-libera of fissio, NOT of laesio. Hence sano-sensu *fiffor = causa-per-accidens-libera laesionis-ex-parte-causati*. Objection on contradiction defeated: ***diversitas respectus tollit omnem contradictionem*** — just as vera-causa-efficiens non-tamen-libera is no contradiction, so vera-causa-per-se simul causa-per-accidens-libera no contradiction. **Moral/forensic conclusion**: in-moral-ac-civili-foro usus-dudum-obtinuit ut agens-non-liberum habeatur-pro-non-agente; ***voluntas distinguit morales, civiles, forenses actiones***. Deferred to doctrina-causae-efficientis.]*

*[T101 — **Caput XII § 6 Note III**: the great *sensu-materiali/diviso vs sensu-formali/composito* distinction. **In prior sense (materiali/diviso)**: affirmative most-true — ***omne quod est causa per accidens ex parte causae, si non spectetur ut causa per accidens, est vera causa*** (formale causae = causalitas in ordine ad illud causatum). Argument: ***quicquid veram dicit rationem causandi aliud veramque causalitatem in ordine ad id ipsum, hoc & potest esse & est ipsius vera causa***. Musician-syllogism: Musicus-aedificans-vera-causa-aedificii + Musicus-aedificans-causa-efficiens-per-accidens → aliquid quod est causa per accidens est vera causa. **In posterior sense (formali/composito)**: affirmative most-false — ***causa per accidens ex parte causae qua talis NON est vera causa***. Reason: quatenus-causa-per-accidens non-dicit-causalitatem-imo-nec-potentiam-causandi. Argument: Musicus-aedificans-qua-Musicus NON-vera-causa + Musicus-aedificans-qua-Musicus causa-per-accidens → causa-per-accidens-qua-talis NON vera causa.]*

— ❦ —

*[T100 — **Caput XII § 6 Note II**: ex-parte-causae test via TWO criteria. **(1)** can ***potentia causativa / ratio causandi*** be attributed? If NO → cannot be causa-per-se nor causa-per-accidens ex-parte-causae. If YES → fit to undergo one denomination or other. **(2)** can ***true causalitas*** be attributed through which it becomes/is true cause? Two axioms of perpetual truth: ***Quicquid non dicit rationem causandi, nec causa per se nec per accidens ex parte causae esse potest***; ***Quicquid non arguit causalitatem, nec causa per se nec per accidens ex parte causae est***. Once both apply, the ***final test***: ***was this (which is true cause) true cause ut tale, or not ut tale?*** YES → per se; NO → per accidens. **Massive worked example**: man who is BOTH Architect AND Musician erecting a building; ***idem simul esse et non esse impossibile*** — so both propositions true: *Architectus est vera causa aedificii* + *Musicus est vera causa aedificii*; but *ut Musicus* no sane-mind affirms (Musical-art no-respect-to-building); *ut Architectus* self-evident. So **Architectus-aedificat = causa per se ex parte causae; Musicus-aedificat = causa per accidens ex parte causae**.]*

*[T83 — **Caput X Note X CLOSES + § 8 opens Possibile Phyicum vs Morale**. **Note X close**: Veltheim's final argumentative resolution of the physica-vs-moralis distinction via the common Philosophical-Theological consequence: *to-lie fights-with-perfectio-moralis-Dei → man-sins; to-eat fights-with-perfectio-naturalis-Dei → man-does-not-sin*. **Deus's actions ad extra** also come under perfections — natural (create, conserve) + moral (keep-pacts, punish-crimes) though not essential-sensu-essentialitatis. Veltheim's ***ψευδὲς*** charge against adversary's narrow *perfectio moralis = habitus-acquisita*; **sapientia parallel refutation** — adversary would distinguish *sapientia creata vs increata* if we denied Deo-sapientia-habitus, so adversary must distinguish *perfectio moralis increata vs creata*. The ***mendacium repugnat Deo not physice but in genere morum*** final clarification — if remove fallendi-intentio and substitute boni-finis (teach-another-falsum-esse-quod-dicitur), falsum-proferre is not malum. **The MASSIVE linking conclusion**: *Cur Deus non potest mentiri?* decisio linked to *Cur Deus legem naturae in homine aliter formare nequiverit?* via ***Deus naturam-rationalem-humanam aliter-condere-non-potuit quam ea ratione ut quicquid Dei-veritati-justitiae-perfectionibus-aliis-in-genere-morum-repugnat dedeceat etiam creaturam-intelligentem***. **CAPUT X § 7 NOTE X CLOSES**. **§ 8 Possibile Phyicum vs Morale** — δύναμις (potentia-Phyicae-considerationis) vs ἐξουσία (potestas); latro-vs-innocent-viator worked example. **Note I usage**: Latin potentia-vs-potestas following Graecorum δύναμις-vs-ἐξουσία. **Note II opens Scripture examples**: ***Gen. XLIII:32 non possunt Aegyptii = non licet*** (Vatablus Interpres + Luther's "sie dürfen nicht"); ***1 Cor. X:21 οὐ δύνασθε = non juste*** (Flacius — not de-facto-impossibilitas but iuris). T84 picks up Acts 10:47 and further examples.]*

*[T82 — **Caput X § 7 Note X: adversary's physica-vs-moralis conflation refuted via Slevogt + perfectio-moralis-essentialis-in-Deo defense**. **Slevogt citation ingeminated from *de esse possibili***: ***repugnat aliquid fieri a Deo quod tamen fieri potest a creatura*** — 2 Tim. 2:13 + Hebr. 6:18 — if Deus could mentiri, He simul-esset-prima-veritas-et-non-esset-prima-veritas (contradictionem implicat); Slevogt refutes adversary's conflation ***NON POTEST SE NEGARE ≠ NON VULT SE NEGARE***. **Adversary's *calumnia-Velthemii* complaint**: Veltheim allegedly makes *impossibile-est-Deum-mentiri = Deus-non-vult-mentiri*; adversary's clarification: mentiri *repugnat voluntati-divinae* which *conspirat* with divine perfection, *sine impedimento extrinseco* so omnimoda-libertas-constat. **Veltheim's rebuttals**: **(1)** Adversary's own words quoted at length show he treats actions-impossible-to-Deo as *those-repugnant-to-Dei-perfectionibus-moralis-practicae-considerationis*; adversary ***contra proprium cordis et conscientiae testimonium*** — standard pattern of this trifler; question-what-has-this-to-do-with-me rhetorical reset; adversary's own ***quod Deus quaedam non posse agere dicitur, provenit ex proprio placito*** suffices to repel. **(2)** The *attemperatus-ad-magnitudinem-et-praestantiam-Dei* leads via *perfectionem-Dei* to the crucial question — ***perfectio physica or moralis?*** Veltheim: ***MORALIS***, since question is *de actionibus in genere morum = mentiri, promisso-cadere, perjurium*. **Adversary's objection**: Veltheim mis-labels any Dei-perfection moral since (a) all perfections in Deo are essential;
